title: Brunswick is king in final Varsity Maine boys soccer poll of 2026
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
Once Brunswick survived the Class A North tournament, all that was left was the Class A final, which the Dragons won 2-0 against Thornton Academy to claim their second state championship of the decade. Brunswick finishes the season at the unanimous No. 1 team in the Varsity Maine boys soccer poll.
The Dragons spent four weeks at the top of the rankings, which tied with Lewiston for the most this fall. Scarborough was the other No. 1, holding that spot in the season’s first poll.
Yarmouth moved up a spot from last week to No. 2 after winning the Class B title, the Clippers’ third in a row. Hall-Dale, which earned its third straight Class C title, is seventh, and Class D champ Monmouth is ninth.
This is the final Varsity Maine boys soccer poll of the 2026 season. The top 10 teams are voted on by the Varsity Maine staff, with first-place votes in parentheses, followed by total points.
1. Brunswick (9) 90
2. Yarmouth 79
3. Thornton Academy 66
4. Camden Hills 44
5. Lewiston 41
6. John Bapst 32
7. Hall-Dale 29
8. Scarborough 25
9. Monmouth Academy 24
10. South Portland 14
Others receiving votes: Falmouth 13, Cape Elizabeth 10, Fort Kent 9, Gorham 7, Edward Little 6, Telstar 6.

title: Trump’s ego is disastrous for the US
text:
The adverse influence of President Trump’s ego on virtually every foreign policy decision and action is not always recognized. Examples abound.
- Trump’s tariffs invite foreign leaders to appeal and fawn to him personally.
- Advice of military experts regarding Iran was ignored. The president knew better.
- Sixty judges who ruled against him regarding the 2020 election were personally insulted, hurting the judiciary’s reputation and the rule of law.
- His threat of military action against Greenland and Denmark, a NATO ally, violated foreign policy principles, friendship and common sense.
- His acceptance of Putin’s word on Ukraine aggression over his own staff’s and allies is traitorous.
Actions determined by Trump’s ego greatly harm the U.S., hurting our diplomatic, military and economic relationships with the world.
Raymond Tillman
Westbrook

title: ProInfoNet named finalist for 2026 Maine Family Business Awards as company marks 30 years
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine-based consulting firm was selected among 26 finalists from 505 nominations following its 30th anniversary celebration.
ProInfoNet, a Maine-based independent IT consulting and strategic advisory firm, has been named a finalist for the 2026 Maine Family Business Awards, presented by the Institute for Family-Owned Business.
ProInfoNet is one of 26 businesses selected as finalists from an original field of 505 nominations. Seven award recipients will be announced at the Maine Family Business Awards gala on Thursday, Nov. 19, at Brick South at Thompson’s Point in Portland.
The recognition follows an important milestone for the family-owned company, which celebrated its 30th anniversary in December 2025.
Founded by Jim Rogers in 1995 as a one-person consulting operation from his home office in Bangor, ProInfoNet has grown to over 30 full-time employees with offices in Bangor and Portland. Today, the company serves more than 320 organizations across Maine, New England, and nationwide.
“When I started ProInfoNet, I wasn’t thinking about building a family business. I was focused on doing good work, treating people well and helping our clients succeed,” Jim Rogers, founder and CEO of ProInfoNet, said. “To see what that has grown into, and to have our family and our team carrying those values forward, makes this recognition especially meaningful.”
Over the past three decades, ProInfoNet has expanded from traditional IT consulting into healthcare technology, broadband infrastructure and strategic advisory services. Its work has helped bring more than $130 million in funding to over 2,800 healthcare sites and supported broadband initiatives reaching more than 2 million residents.
“What I’m most proud of is that we’re continuing to grow without losing the values that got us here,” Jeff Rogers, vice president of ProInfoNet, said. “The company looks very different than it did 30 years ago, but our commitment to our clients, our people, and the communities we serve hasn’t changed. As we look ahead, our responsibility is to carry that foundation forward while continuing to evolve.”
The Maine Family Business Awards recognize family-owned companies for business success, family participation, community and industry contributions, work environment, communication and innovation.
ProInfoNet plans to attend the Nov. 19 gala, where the 2026 award recipients will be announced.

title: Alleged spy plot targeting CEO Jensen Huang raises questions about Nvidia's future
text:
SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — Investigations into whether Nvidia’s CEO was the target of a “foreign intelligence effort” are raising questions about the future of the chipmaker, which became one of the world’s most valuable companies by providing technology that powered the artificial intelligence boom.
Jensen Huang has been synonymous with Nvidia since he co-founded it more than 30 years ago. The company now faces potential damage to its reputation and stock price, uncertainty over a possible successor and new scrutiny from shareholders and elected officials.
President Donald Trump said Monday that the FBI is investigating Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese government agent. But Trump said he spoke with the executive and believes Huang “had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.”
With a valuation of more than $4 trillion, the company has outsized importance as a Wall Street behemoth and provider of chips relied upon by AI developers. Law enforcement and members of Congress, as well as Nvidia’s board and shareholders, are all asking questions about the affair. The company’s shares dropped more than 4% Monday and continued sinking Tuesday morning.
Nvidia’s identity has been tied to Huang himself
Huang has said he has more than 60 direct reports in a corporate structure that keeps him at the center of decision-making. As various investigations ramp up, the succession plan to replace Huang is unclear.
“The Nvidia board is between a rock and a hard spot. They have almost no good options. Jensen is Nvidia,” said David Yoffie, a professor at Harvard Business School. “And if he has done something wrong and he needs to be removed and they have no successors, that’s a terrible outcome.”
Replacing Huang would be challenging in part because his public profile is so closely associated with Nvidia.
Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, a professor of leadership at the Yale School of Management, compared Huang’s relationship with Nvidia to Steve Jobs’ role at Apple. Down to Huang’s signature leather jacket, like Jobs’ turtleneck, Nvidia is “symbolically and substantively, inextricably intertwined around his personal aura.”
Other tech executives, such as Oracle’s Larry Ellison and Microsoft’s Bill Gates, have also been deeply intertwined with the success of their companies, making it hard to separate them. But in those cases, the companies “can still be successful long after the original founders have taken on a lesser role,” said Dan Morgan, vice president and senior portfolio manager at investment firm Synovus Trust.
If Huang resigns or is removed by the board, speculation on possible replacements has turned to figures including Nvidia co-founder Chris Malachowsky, who is a senior technology executive at the company, and Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress.
Nvidia employs more than 40,000 people worldwide, and there are “lots of other great leaders” within the company, said Bob O’Donnell, president, founder and chief analyst at TECHnalysis Research.
“I think it’s important that the company starts to let some of these other folks come out as spokespeople so people feel trust, they feel good about Nvidia and their future, even without Jensen,” O’Donnell said, although he said he does not think Huang will leave his post.
Huang had the ‘Midas touch,’ but his reputation is at risk
During his 33-year tenure at the helm of Nvidia, Huang built a reputation as a trusted business leader and an established voice within the technology world. He cultivated close relationships with other tech executives, as well as with Trump, helping to persuade him to take a lighter touch on regulating AI.
“Everybody wanted to have that Midas touch of his when it comes to technology,” O’Donnell said.
But the scandal is a growing liability for Huang and Nvidia at a delicate time for the AI industry after the midterm elections in the U.S. ushered in a wave of Democrats promising tougher regulation. Top Democrats Sen. Mark Warner and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries said Monday they are interested in investigating further.
A shareholder on Monday sued Nvidia and Huang, accusing them of deceiving investors in their responses to media reports about Huang’s affair with the purported Chinese spy. The complaint filed in a California court says the company misled investors about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, who news reports said is suspected of working for Chinese intelligence, and the national security implications.
The New York Times identified her as a business executive and Chinese citizen.
Sonnenfeld said he places the odds that Huang stays on as CEO at roughly 50-50, but those odds are “slipping by the moment.”
“He has lost the confidence and trust of his key constituents, his board, his employees,” said Sonnenfeld, who is also founder and president of the Chief Executive Leadership Institute. “And every employee knows that if anybody else had done this, they would have been fired long ago.”
Some experts are more confident in the company’s stability going forward. Morgan, of Synovus Trust, said that if Huang is required to step down to a lesser role at Nvidia following the company’s investigation, he is “still confident that the company will continue to maintain its lead in the GPU AI chip market.”
But at the same time, the affair “sounds more like a made-for-TV melodrama than a real story,” he said.
___
Huamani reported from Los Angeles. Associated Press Technology Writer Barbara Ortutay in Oakland, California, contributed to this report.

title: Cheverus’ Skip Capone retires after decades of coaching football in Maine
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
For 50 years, Skip Capone has viewed coaching football as one of the greatest ways of building relationships and helping young people develop.
“My entire professional career has been trying to point kids in the right direction,” Capone said.
On Monday, news broke that Capone, 71, had retired as Cheverus High’s head football coach after three seasons. Capone said Tuesday that he does plan to hang up his coaching whistle, though he anticipates staying connected to the game through his involvement with the Maine chapter of the National Football Foundation and as a committee member for the James J. Fitzpatrick Trophy Award.
“I was blessed with some great coaches at the high school level and the college level and they inspired me to get into coaching,” Capone said. “It’s always been way more than Xs and Os. It’s about relationships and just trying to help kids develop.”
Capone added, “I think I’ve finally repaid my debt to the greatest game ever invented.”
A 1973 graduate of Portsmouth High in New Hampshire (Capone said he talks with his high school coach Tom Daubney on a monthly basis), Capone played football at Plymouth State College. His first assistant gig was in 1977 at Dover, New Hampshire, followed by college stops at Plymouth State and Southwest Missouri State, before returning to New England and coaching at Winnacunnet High in Hampton, New Hampshire.
“Then I had the opportunity to come to Lewiston in 1983 as the head football coach. I was there for 14 years,” as the football coach, Capone said. He led the Blue Devils to the 1987 Class A title and taught physical education at Lewiston for 35 years.
Capone said he was looking to step away from coaching for a year when he was offered a stipend position at Bates College as the offensive line coach. That began a 22-year stint with the Bobcats.
Capone returned to the high school sidelines as an assistant for Jason McLeod at Portland High and also spent a season as a part-time coach/confidant for Sam Weiss at Oceanside before taking the Cheverus positon in 2024.
This season Cheverus was 3-5 in the regular season, before losing to Biddeford in the B South quarterfinal. Capone’s three-season record at Cheverus was 9-18.
“Cheverus is a great place to coach. I coached some great kids. The parents were awesome,” Capone said. “It’s just time. I’ll be 72 in January.”
Capone said he considers himself lucky to have coached against and with “a litany” of great coaches in what he termed “a golden age of high school athletics,” from the late 1970s to the early 2000s. Capone rattled off many names across multiple sports, noting they were coaches “who dedicated their lives to helping kids and had a lot of success along the way.”
Capone’s legacy will be the hundreds, if not thousands, of connections he’s made across multiple states. It seems almost every coach in Maine knows Skip Capone.
Take Brandon Dorsett at Falmouth High for instance. Dorsett grew up in Portland, playing for the Bulldogs and Colorado State when Capone was coaching at Bates. Dorsett first met Capone when the two were player and coach with the semi-professional Maine Sabers.
“Having him as one of my coaches was great,” Dorsett said. “He just is a caring person. He cares about the kids.”
This season Dorsett and Falmouth squared off against Cheverus and Capone.
“He gave me a great big hug and we talked,” Dorsett said. “Everyone who has ever played for him just admires him.”

title: Drivers keep hitting Waymos and taking off, police records show
text:
PHOENIX(InvestigateTV) — Waymo’s own roadside assistance crews have been telling police about a surprising pattern: drivers who crash into the company’s robotaxis frequently take off.
“It’s quite shocking how many people just take off,” a Waymo roadside assistance specialist told a Phoenix police officer.
An investigative analysis of more than four years of police records backs that up.
Nearly half of the Waymo crashes reported to police in metro Phoenix were hit-and-runs. Accounting for miles driven, Waymos were involved in police-reported hit-and-runs at 2.4 times the rate of drivers in Maricopa County.
Waymo reviewed the methodology and said its researchers “appreciated the rigor and thought” behind it. But the company argues it is impossible to determine whether its vehicles are actually involved in more hit-and-runs, or whether Waymo simply reports the incidents to police more consistently than the general public.
‘They just leave’
Body camera footage from March 2024 shows Chandler Officer Seth Chavez responding to a crash near Ray and Price roads where someone hit the back of a driverless Waymo and drove away. Chavez told the roadside specialist waiting at the scene that he’d never handled a call quite like it.
“People rear-end these things all the time,” the specialist responded. “Most of the time, they just leave.”
Months later, in October 2024, a truck damaged a Waymo near Buckeye Road and 2nd Street in Phoenix and drove off. Another Waymo roadside specialist let the responding Phoenix officer in on the same secret.
“I don’t know how many of these reports you do, but I’m surprised at how many hit-and-runs we honestly get, and where it’s a good amount of damage,” the Waymo specialist said. “Like, do you not realize there’s cameras on these?”
43 of 88 crashes
Arizona’s Family Investigates spent 10 months collecting police crash reports and body camera footage from the five cities in Waymo’s Valley service area: Phoenix, Scottsdale, Chandler, Mesa and Tempe.
There were 88 police-reported crashes involving Waymo vehicles from Sept. 1, 2020, through Dec. 31, 2024. Of those collisions, 43, or 49%, were classified as hit-and-runs in which the Waymo stayed and the other driver left. In most cases, the damage was minor.
To compare the rate of those crashes with human drivers, Arizona’s Family worked with a traffic safety researcher to calculate hit-and-run rates per million miles driven for Waymo and for the general public in Maricopa County.
Waymo: ‘The standard today is not perfection’
Camille Dredge, Waymo’s senior director for ride-hail operations, spoke with Arizona’s Family in 2025.
“The standard today is not perfection,” Dredge said. “Collisions will and can occur. We are absolutely prepared to respond to them.”
Waymo declined a request for a new interview about the findings, providing written responses instead.
In a statement, Waymo said the safety of riders and communities is its “absolute priority.” The company said that across more than 90 million fully autonomous miles in Phoenix, its vehicles cut crashes involving serious injuries or worse by 90% compared with human drivers.
Waymo said hit-and-runs are uncommon relative to the more than 4 million autonomous miles its vehicles drive each week across more than 15 U.S. cities. The company did not say whether it tracks hit-and-runs internally or how many it has recorded.
Dredge did not offer a theory for the hit-and-runs. In a few cases, the reason seems apparent. In a 2020 Mesa crash, among the earliest in the records, officers suspected the driver who hit a Waymo was impaired.
“You’re real loopy,” an officer told him on body camera video. “Your speech is slurred.”
Most police reports, however, offer no clue about why drivers leave.
Experts point to confusion, sudden braking
Missy Cummings, a George Mason University professor, and Phil Koopman, a professor emeritus at Carnegie Mellon University, are two leading researchers on autonomous vehicles.
“We researchers and the government need to do more to try to figure out what is going on with this and how to mitigate it,” Cummings said.
They offered two possible explanations for why drivers leave. The first is that drivers are confused about how to exchange information with an autonomous vehicle.
“I’ve noticed that police have trouble interacting with these vehicles. Emergency responders have trouble interacting with these vehicles. They’re not sure what to do,” Koopman said. “Ordinary drivers don’t go through how-to-talk-to-a-robotaxi training.”
“If there’s no one there to trade insurance cards with, then what do you do?” Cummings said.
A 2022 Chandler police report illustrates the problem. After a minor crash in a 7-Eleven parking lot near Warner and Dobson roads, the at-fault driver walked up to the Waymo with her “driver’s license and vehicle registration in hand,” according to the report. But the vehicle was driverless, and with no one to give her information to, the woman left.
Waymo said it invests heavily in educating drivers on how to exchange insurance information. Once drivers submit their information through one of its digital options, the company said, they don’t need to wait at the scene.
The second theory Cummings and Koopman offered is that Waymos may be prone to a type of crash that gives human drivers an incentive to flee.
“I’ve done an analysis on the publicly available data, and Waymos get hit from behind two times more than your average human driver does,” Cummings said.
She pointed to what researchers call phantom braking, when an autonomous vehicle stops suddenly for something that isn’t there.
“Everyone hears about hallucinations with generative AI. These are real hallucinations,” Cummings said. “The cars see something that isn’t there. And the car’s response is to do an emergency braking because, to them, it appears that something is there.”
“If they’re not sure, the safe thing, tactically, is to stop,” Koopman said. “But what you have to take into account is that following drivers, if there’s no reason to brake, they’re not expecting it.”
Waymo disputes that sudden braking is a significant factor. The company said rear-end crashes are the most common type of crash for both human and autonomous drivers. It said that over 270 million autonomous miles, Waymos were involved in 41% fewer rear-end crashes causing airbag deployment than human drivers in its cities.
A peer-reviewed analysis by Waymo found its vehicles were fully stopped in 72% of rear-end crashes that deployed airbags and 20% of those causing injuries. The company said the analysis found its vehicles were not hard braking in any of the airbag crashes or in 75% of the injury crashes.
‘It should be on the robotaxi companies’
Some drivers do wait for Waymo’s roadside team and exchange information. Arizona law requires drivers who hit an unattended vehicle to locate the owner or leave their contact information.
Both Cummings and Koopman said Waymo should make the information exchange easier.
“If robotaxi companies are putting vehicles on public roads that interact with other people, it should be on the robotaxi companies to figure out how to make that interaction happen,” Koopman said.
Waymo said drivers do not need to wait for a company representative to arrive at the scene.
People involved in a crash with a Waymo can:
- scan the QR code on the driver’s side door
- contact Waymo through its app
- fill out a form at Waymo.com/notify
- call 844-263-9885
- email insurance@waymo.com
- speak with a roadside assistance representative, if one is at the scene

title: Close call at LAX airport as plane turns in front of another aircraft taking off
text:
Close call at LAX airport as plane turns in front of another aircraft taking off
An Air France plane taking off from Los Angeles International Airport made a wrong turn early Saturday morning, putting it in the path of an American Airlines jet, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.
The close call happened when Air France Flight 28, an Airbus A350 headed for Tahiti, took off and made an “unauthorized turn” to the south, the FAA said.
Moments later, American Airlines 1660, an Airbus A321 headed for Dallas, was cleared to take off from a parallel runway heading straight toward the other plane.
“Air traffic control immediately issued corrective instructions to the Air France flight,” the FAA said in a statement.
“Air France 028 heavy, fly heading 270 immediately,” the controller warned the pilots in audio captured by ATC.com. “You were instructed to climb… not turn to a heading.”
At the closest point, the two aircraft were about 4,000 feet apart and within 1,000 feet of the same altitude, according to the tracking site Flightradar24. After they separated, both aircraft safely continued to their destinations.
“Sorry about that,” the air traffic controller told the American pilots. “That aircraft just turned in front of you. They were instructed they were on the right departure, but you know, pilot deviation.”
A pilot deviation is a term for an action taken contrary to air traffic control instructions that can result in future penalties.
The close call in Los Angeles comes months after a summer marked in part by high-profile aviation incidents, including plane crashes, emergency landings and multiple separate close calls. Close calls in the sky can happen for a variety of reasons and with varying degrees of severity.
In June, Delta Air Lines pilots aborted their approach for landing at Boston Logan International Airport as an American Airlines flight was accelerating for takeoff on an intersecting runway.
The same month, a flight school-owned Beechcraft 76 Duchess plane came within 500 feet of a JetBlue Airways passenger jet landing at Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport.
In April, a Republic Airways plane landing at New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport strayed into the flight path of a Jazz regional jet landing on a parallel runway.
Last year, most notably, 67 people died when an Army Black Hawk helicopter and an American Airlines regional jet collided over the Potomac River.

title: State to hear comments on owner of Lewiston hospital this month
text:
The state will hold a public hearing Nov. 20 to determine whether Prime Healthcare Foundation, the California-based owner of Central Maine Medical Center in Lewiston, is complying with commitments to provide safe care.
The hearing will be at Kirk Hall Auditorium at Central Maine Community College at 1250 Turner St. in Auburn from 2-3:30 p.m. Attendance is in-person or remote by registering online.
The Maine Department of Health and Human Services is inviting the public to share information about whether Prime is meeting multiple conditions from the state that allowed it to acquire Central Maine Healthcare, which includes hospitals in Lewiston, Bridgton and Rumford, and several physician practices.
The new owner promised to maintain essential health services and safe staff-to-patient ratios across Central Maine Healthcare, in addition to reestablishing trauma center status in Lewiston by 2028. The system must also continue operations at long-term care facilities in Auburn and Rumford, according to the state’s conditions of approval.
The state is calling Prime’s word into question. Last month, officials released a report detailing issues with sterilization equipment at Central Maine Medical Center that went unaddressed until the state’s investigation. Along with workforce changes, from provider turnover to nurse terminations to a canceled emergency department staffing contract, patients and community members have spoken out in concern for their hospitals.
Public comments must specifically relate to the conditions of approval.
Through Nov. 30, the health department will accept written, signed comments by mail, email or hand delivery to the office at 41 Anthony Ave. in Augusta.

title: Meghan Markle’s father cut off his ankle monitor, DOJ says
text:
TAMPA, Fla. (AP) — The 82-year-old estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, was ordered to jail Tuesday because he removed an electronic monitoring device from his ankle, just days after he was charged with possession of child sexual abuse material.
Thomas Markle was arrested and appeared in federal court in Tampa, Florida, after authorities learned he had cut off the device at 1:45 a.m., First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said.
“Release conditions are court orders, not suggestions,” Essayli said.
Markle’s arrest on Friday in Lakeland, Florida, followed the seizure of approximately 78 items from storage units in the Los Angeles area, including slides, film negatives and books that contained suspected child sexual abuse images, said Essayli, a federal prosecutor in California.
Markle was living in a senior care center at the time. But U.S. Magistrate Judge Lindsay Griffin agreed Tuesday that Markle now must be kept in custody. Authorities have not said where he will be held while his case remains in court ahead of a likely transfer to California.
In her written order, Griffin noted Markle’s “housing situation” had become “untenable,” but did not elaborate. Defense attorney Mary Claire Wolf wanted to keep him out of custody but has not found a suitable place for Markle to stay, according to a hearing summary.
Essayli told The Associated Press he didn’t know why the ankle device was removed. It also wasn’t clear where it occurred. An email and phone message seeking comment from Wolf were not immediately returned.
Still pending, besides the charges: a mental competency exam for Markle.
He had a stroke earlier this year while living in the Philippines and had to have his left leg amputated. That forced him to return to the U.S.
The Sun, a British tabloid newspaper, reported that Meghan’s half brother found a collection of child sexual abuse images while clearing out their father’s home in the Philippines. That discovery led to information about the two U.S. storage units in California, which Markle had rented since 2008.
Markle’s daughter, Meghan, married Prince Harry at Windsor Castle in 2018. They have two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet. She is an American citizen and an actor who starred in the U.S. television drama “Suits.”
She recently said she was “deeply distressed” by allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images had been found at her father’s former home. She also revealed that a letter containing “troubling allegations” about him had been sent to police in London in 2019.
“It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated,” Meghan said of the letter. “I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children was for one reason: to protect them.”

title: UMF, Maine DOE work to bring more students into regular classrooms
text:
FARMINGTON — Three Maine elementary schools are helping develop a statewide approach to educating students with disabilities alongside their peers, part of a five-year initiative that recently brought more than 150 educators and school administrators to the University of Maine at Farmington.
The fourth annual Inclusive Education Leadership Symposium on Oct. 8, organized by UMF and the Maine Department of Education, drew participants from communities stretching from Millinocket to Sanford to discuss ways to make general education classrooms more accessible to students with different learning needs.
The gathering is part of the Maine Inclusive Education Project, a federally supported initiative running from 2025-30 that seeks to reduce the separation of students receiving special education services from their peers and increase opportunities for students to learn together.
Leeds Central School, Downeast School in Bangor and Turner Elementary School are serving as model sites for the project. The schools are developing classroom practices, schedules and support systems designed to accommodate a wider range of student needs.
The three schools also serve as training and observation sites for other educators, hosting scheduled visits from school leaders, working with UMF student teachers and sharing their experiences at conferences. Their work will contribute to ongoing research intended to inform broader changes in Maine schools.
Kate MacLeod, UMF associate professor of special education, and Jessica Apgar, assistant professor of special education, lead the university’s involvement in the initiative.
“It is a wonderful opportunity to gather a group of school leaders from across the great state of Maine, celebrate their vision, honor their work, and support them to build more inclusive schools,” MacLeod said in a university news release.
At the symposium, participants worked with state and national education specialists to develop plans for improving inclusion in their own districts.
Jennifer Greer, Lindsey Hayes and Cat Merkle of the Collaboration for Effective Educator Development, Accountability, and Reform Center led a keynote workshop. The center receives funding from the U.S. Department of Education’s Office of Special Education Programs.
Additional sessions were led by UMF faculty, center representatives and Tracy Whitlock of the Maine Department of Education’s Office of Special Services and Inclusive Education.
Whitlock said the symposium gives school administrators an opportunity to work together on plans that can be carried back to their districts.
“School leaders are busy and the Inclusive Education Leadership Symposium provides time and space for them to come together as teams to learn, collaborate and plan for meaningful inclusion for all of their students,” Whitlock said.
The initiative focuses on more than classroom placement. Participating schools are examining how staffing, scheduling, instructional practices and school culture can support students with disabilities while maintaining access to challenging academic instruction.
The goal is to develop approaches that other Maine schools can adapt, allowing students with disabilities to participate more fully in general education and school activities.
The Maine Inclusive Education Project is supported by federal funding and a partnership between the Maine Department of Education and UMF.

title: Bangor man pleads guilty to distributing, possessing child sexual abuse material
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A Bangor man plead guilty in federal court Tuesday to distributing and possessing child pornography.
According to court records, in February of 2026, Tyler Jewett, 30, distributed 17 videos containing child sexual abuse material to another user online.
Investigators say they found multiple images and videos of child sexual abuse material on several of Jewett’s devices.
Officials say he admitted that he used the internet to access child sexual abuse material and that he had distributed it online in February.
Jewett will be sentenced at a later date.

title: Six Maine fire departments cited by state in connection with Searsmont explosion
text:
Six Maine fire departments cited by state following investigation into Searsmont lumber mill explosion
The Maine Department of Labor (MDOL) announced Tuesday that six local fire departments have been cited in connection with the May 15 fire and explosion at the Robbins Lumber mill in Searsmont.
The MDOL said the Maine Occupational Safety and Health (MEOSH) program, which investigates workplace safety and health incidents involving public employers, conducted investigations of the Searsmont, Morrill, Montville, Belmont, Appleton and Lincolnville fire departments, along with the Searsmont Rescue Department, in regard to compliance with state and federal workplace safety and health standards.
MEOSH issued citations to all six fire departments related to the lack of an effective accountability system for tracking the locations of firefighters who were at the scene of the May 15 fire and explosion, which resulted in the deaths of three people and left 10 others injured.
In addition, MEOSH issued citations to five departments related to the use of personal protective equipment (PPE), including firefighter gear and breathing apparatus, to keep personnel safe from the hazards of a fire scene.
"We are responsible for ensuring that people working for state, county, and municipal governments and other public employers have safe workplaces," said Kate Burkhart, director of the MDOL's Bureau of Labor Standards Workplace Safety and Health Division, which manages MEOSH. "We do that best when we balance enforcement with supporting public employers as they address violations to improve safety, mitigate hazards and reduce the risk of future harm to employees."
The MDOL said that all six fire departments have augmented their accountability systems and that most of those departments, along with others in Knox County, are in the process of implementing a single accountability system that will improve safety for all firefighters, especially when responding to a fire in mutual aid communities.
All five departments cited over PPE use have resolved the immediate deficiencies and have committed to attending Respiratory Protection Program Training in January in Waldo County, according to the MDOL.
Burkhart said the state has suspended nearly all of the $108,000 in civil penalties in consideration of the remediation efforts, as all of the departments and local governments made significant efforts to resolve the citations and to further improve workplace safety for firefighters and emergency responders.
The MDOL has discretion to suspend or reduce civil penalties in some situations when a public employer corrects the workplace safety and health citations.
Burkhart also said that suspending the civil penalties will allow the towns to prioritize their limited resources to support safety improvements for their emergency responders moving forward.
"These efforts require time, energy and resources from local elected officials, fire and rescue department leadership, and the paid and volunteer firefighters and EMTs," Burkhart said.
The Bureau of Labor Standards (BLS) is coordinating with the Maine Fire Chiefs' Association and Maine Fire Service Institute to provide training in February for the chiefs and officers of the cited departments in an effort to support the departments' efforts to improve internal operations, as well as the coordination and incident command of major mutual aid emergencies.
The BLS said it is also partnering with the Searsmont Rescue Department to develop and deliver training on PPE standards and compliance for rescue department managers.

title: Native American women made history in tribal, state and federal elections
text:
Native American women made history in tribal, state and federal elections
A third-grade field trip to the Navajo Nation Council sparked Crystalyne Curley’s political ambition when she witnessed a fiery debate erupt between two tribal lawmakers.
“I thought to myself at a very young age, that’s where I want to be,” Curley said.
On Election Day, Curley surpassed that childhood dream and broke a barrier she says she never imagined as a nine-year-old: She was elected the first woman president of the Navajo Nation.
Election Day brought a wave of milestone victories, from the nation’s first Black female governor to the first openly gay man and the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate. It also marked a turning point for Native American women, whose leadership in their families and communities has rarely translated to formal political power.
Related video above: Keisha Lance Bottoms on working with the Trump administration
Peggy Flanagan became the first Native American woman elected to the Senate, Deb Haaland the first to win a state governorship, and Curley the first to lead one of the largest tribes.
“This is a win for all Navajo women,” Curley told The Associated Press.
Jordan James Harvill, a Cherokee Nation citizen and strategist with the advocacy group Advance Native Political Leadership, said decades of political organizing are bearing fruit as more Native women run for and win office.
“This is a seismic shift that is happening in our communities,” he said.
The Navajo Nation elects its first woman president
Lene Bitsui supported Curley in the Navajo Nation election because she felt she was best positioned to restore order to the tribal government after what she sees as a period of dysfunction. But when Bitsui cast her ballot, she felt pessimistic.
“I thought our people weren't ready for a female president,” Bitsui said. “I was wrong, and I feel so happy to have been wrong.”
The modern, centralized Navajo government has been led by men since its establishment under federal pressure over a century ago. Navajo has the largest land base of any federally recognized tribe, spanning 27,000 square miles (70,000 square kilometers) in Arizona, New Mexico and Utah, and is second in population to the Cherokee Nation in Oklahoma.
Some Navajo people believe traditional teachings prohibit women from holding top government positions. Others say women's absence from the presidency stands in contrast to the matrilineal structure of Diné society.
“You see the language of tradition used to both deride the possibility of a woman being president and to say that women’s leadership is needed now,” said Jennifer Nez Denetdale, a professor of Diné studies at the University of New Mexico.
Curley, who narrowly defeated attorney Justin Jones, according to unofficial results, told the AP she faced sexist rhetoric while campaigning and expects to be held to a higher standard as the first woman president.
“As women, we have to work twice or triple as hard, especially within Navajo politics,” said Curley, who also was the first female to lead the tribe's legislative branch as speaker of the tribal council.
After Curley and her running mate Chris Deschene take office in January, they plan to transition the Navajo Nation away from coal development, historically a major economic engine for the tribe, and reassert its leading role in national discussions around federal Indian policy.
The Seneca Nation of Indians in western New York also elected its first woman president, longtime council member Tina Abrams, on Tuesday.
Native women make gains in U.S. Congress
At her Senate victory celebration in St. Paul, Minnesota, Democrat Flanagan, a citizen of the White Earth Nation and the state’s outgoing lieutenant governor, credited supporters from her community.
“I could not run for the U. S. Senate without Native women. I could not exist in the way that I do without Native women,” Flanagan said.
More than 230 years after the U.S. Senate was established, only four Native people have served in the chamber, all men.
“This is a win that shows we can break every single glass ceiling,” Harvill said.
A victory for Democrat Mary Peltola, a Yup’ik woman, in Alaska's still unsettled Senate race, would put two Native women in the chamber.
In the House, Kansas Democrat Sharice Davids, Ho-Chunk, and Oklahoma Republicans Josh Brecheen, Choctaw, and Tom Cole, Chickasaw, won reelection. New York Democrat Claire Valdez, a citizen of Ysleta del Sur Pueblo, and Michigan Democrat Sean McCann, a citizen of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation, became the first Native Americans elected to represent their states in Congress.
Deb Haaland notches another first in New Mexico
Haaland’s political career has been defined by historic milestones. She was one of the first two Native women elected to Congress in 2018 before becoming the first Native American to lead a U.S. Cabinet agency, the Interior Department.
Now, in her home state of New Mexico, the Laguna Pueblo citizen will break ground as the first female Native governor of a U.S. state.
“I think it's a long time coming,” said Haaland, who traces her ancestry in what is now New Mexico back 800 years.
She is tasked with making good on campaign promises to make life more affordable for struggling New Mexicans and address persistently poor education outcomes in the state.
Haaland, who is affectionately known as “Auntie Deb” in parts of Indian Country, was tearful while reflecting on the support she has received from Native voters and other Native women in politics, including Davids and Flanagan.
“It makes me very happy that we're able to have a presence,” Haaland said. “It’s not just a slogan. It matters that people feel represented.”

title: ‘Marriage is a gift’: Officer shot 6 times in line of duty celebrates the wedding he almost missed
text:
BUFFALO, N.Y. (WKBW) - Months after a New York police officer was shot six times in the line of duty, he celebrated a moment that once seemed far from certain: marrying his fiancée.
Buffalo Police Officer Marc Hurst, a nine-year veteran officer, was shot six times May 26 while responding to a domestic violence call – once in each calf, once in the upper thigh, once in the upper arm and twice in his bulletproof vest. He remembers realizing that despite being shot multiple times, he was still breathing and able to think.
“I was still thinking, so I couldn’t have been that bad, as good as you can be for being shot multiple times. I just remember, and I believe it’s just from the Lord, this overwhelming peace,” Marc said.
As he focused on getting out of the house where the shooting took place, another thought crossed his mind: his upcoming wedding to his then-fiancée, Haley Hurst.
“I remember being down on the ground and focusing on getting out of the house that we were in but also being like, ‘You know what? She’s gonna be really ticked off if I miss this wedding,’” Marc said.
Marc was rushed to the hospital, and one of his friends in the police department called Haley with the terrifying news.
“I was like, ‘You need to tell me what’s going on,’” Haley recalled. “And he said that Marc had been shot. I was obviously freaking out, like, ‘He’s been shot everywhere.’”
Marc suffered serious injuries but survived. After six days in the hospital, he wowed his fellow officers as he walked out on his own two feet. Last month, he received the City of Buffalo’s Medal of Honor.
Through it all, Haley has been by his side.
“It’s been humbling and emotional,” she said. “Even when I would go back and forth from the hospital to get him more clothes and everything that week, like thinking about, ‘Oh my God, we still get married in a couple of months, and we almost didn’t.’”
The couple got married Friday.
Marc said surviving the shooting has changed the way he looks at moments that might otherwise seem ordinary from watching his nieces walk down the aisle to seeing family and friends gathered together.
“When you go through something traumatic like this, you appreciate even the littlest things a little bit more,” he said. “I’m just so thankful that we are celebrating our marriage… and my family and my fiancée is not mourning the loss of me.”
But for Marc, the wedding was about much more than celebrating. It was also a reminder of what he nearly lost.
“To see Haley coming down the aisle, I can’t even put it into words right now, compared to what could have been. I’m just so grateful,” he said. “Marriage is a gift. Haley’s a gift… and I’m just so, so blessed.”
Police identified the man accused of shooting Marc as 33-year-old Minhaz Siddiqui. He was charged with multiple felonies, including first-degree attempted murder.

title: DoorDash driver mysteriously disappeared after making his last delivery, reports say
text:
BEAVER COUNTY, Pa. (Gray News) - Authorities are searching for a DoorDash driver who disappeared after making deliveries last month in Pennsylvania.
Zachariah Schuck, 32, was last seen on the evening of Oct. 22 while working in the Monaca area, according to North Sewickley police.
Investigators said Schuck completed his last known DoorDash delivery at about 6:30 p.m. His cellphone signal was lost around 8 p.m., and he has not been heard from since, WTAE reported.
Schuck was last seen between 7:30 and 8 p.m. near Route 51 in Monaca. Authorities later found his vehicle abandoned. Police have not released details about any evidence recovered from the car.
Police describe Schuck as 6 feet tall and approximately 160 pounds, with brown hair and green eyes. He was last seen wearing a blue and red flannel shirt, blue jeans and brown boots.
The circumstances of Schuck’s disappearance remain unclear. Investigators have not said whether foul play is suspected.

title: Helping people in Maine recover at home or manage a chronic or terminal condition
text:
Helping people in Maine recover at home or manage a chronic or terminal condition
November is Hospice, Home Care, and Caregiver Awareness Month. Rachael Pillar, FNP-C, family nurse practitioner with Northern Light Home Care & Hospice spoke with Maine's Total Coverage about what hospice and home care are, how to take advantage, and the supports available in Maine.
What is Home Care?
Home Care is a short-term clinical treatment provided by nurses, physical therapists, occupational therapists in a patient's home to help them recover from an illness, injury, surgery, or manage a chronic condition. This is intermittent help which typically happens a few times per week, rather than 24/7 care.
How does someone qualify for Home Care?
To qualify, you must meet the following criteria:
- You need an order from your doctor.
- You must have a skilled need such as needing nursing care, physical therapy, and/or occupational therapy.
- You must be considered homebound. This means that leaving your home takes a considerable and taxing effort and generally you need help to do so, such as assistance from a person, wheelchair, walker or special transportation. (You may still leave home for infrequent or short trips out such as for a doctor appointment or church.)
- You need to have had a face-to-face meeting with your primary care provider or specialty care provider related to your main reason for home care within the last 90 days prior to your referral or within 30 days of starting services.
What are some benefits to receiving in-home care?
Receiving in-home nursing and therapy allows you to have one-on-one medical care in your own familiar living environment, helping you to recover faster and stay safe. Nurses can help to prevent hospital readmission by catching potential complications early and treating them on-site to avoid emergency room visits.
Physical therapists and occupational therapist can assess your living spaces to remove hazards like a loose rug or electrical cords while teaching you proper balance techniques.
In-home support eliminates stressful commutes and waiting rooms. Nurses and therapists come to you so that you can save your strength/energy for hobbies and things that matter to you.
What is Hospice and why should someone choose it?
Home Hospice Care is in-home support for both the patient and the family. This service can keep the patient in the comfort of their own home rather than having to go to the emergency room for care. Hospice philosophy focuses on managing pain, providing comfort, and increasing the patient's quality of life.
How do you qualify for hospice and get the service?
To qualify for Hospice, you must have a terminal diagnosis with a life expectancy of six months or less and you should choose palliative or comfort care instead of curative treatment. You will need a formal certification from both your primary care physician/attending physician and a hospice medical director. You would start by discussing this with your primary care provider or specialist and have them send in a referral, if appropriate.
What are the benefits of Hospice Care?
There are several benefits to choosing hospice care.
- Prioritizes comfort, dignity, and quality of life when a terminal illness no longer responds to curative treatments. Rather than "giving up", the focus shifts to comprehensive pain management and comfort and maximizing quality of life.
- Avoids invasive procedures and unwanted ER visits, maximizing meaningful time with family.
- Care is managed by an entire team of professionals, including skilled nurses, home health aides (CNAs), medical social workers, spiritual care coordinators, and grief support coordinators.
- 24/7 clinical support hotline with availability through the night and/or nurse visits to handle sudden changes in condition.
- Grief support to help with ongoing grief and emotional needs provided to the families for 13 months.
- All prescriptions used to manage pain and symptoms of the terminal diagnosis are fully covered.
- Necessary medical equipment such as hospital beds, oxygen tanks, certain medical supplies are delivered straight to the home at no cost to the family.
Many families delay hospice until the very final days of life, but starting a hospice program early (when receiving a six-month prognosis) maximizes the benefits of these services. This allows both the patient and the family to build trust with the care team, control pain before it becomes severe, gives families the emotional support needed to find closure, and have grief support after their loved one passes.
What kind of support is available for caregivers?
We provide a variety of caregiver support from respite support to advocating for resources to 13 months of grief support after their loved one passes. Respite means a temporary break.
Finding respite for caregivers to have time to take care of themselves is necessary for sustaining their role as a caregiver. Finding that break may involve connecting with other caregivers and/or hospice volunteers and arranging temporary relief services like home health aides, daytime adult health centers, area agencies on aging, and support groups. Resources may include education on the importance of self-care for caregivers and developing customized care plans.
Medical social workers, spiritual care coordinators, and grief support coordinators may also provide support to caregivers.
We have a Becoming a Caregiver website at www.northernlighthealth.org/Caregiving which has information and resources available.
For more information
Patients can talk to their provider about a referral for home care or hospice. Anyone who has questions about Northern Light Home Care & Hospice services can go online or call 1.800.757.3326.

title: Wildfire in White Mountain National Forest more than 50% contained
text:
The Wild River Fire just over the Maine border in New Hampshire now encompasses 821 acres and is 53% contained, the U.S. Forest Service said on Tuesday.
The Forest Service first responded to the fire in an area of the White Mountain National Forest about 7 miles southeast of Gorham, New Hampshire, on Nov. 1. It’s on the northwest side of the Wild River, just west of Mount Hastings in Maine’s Oxford County.
Early last week, the Forest Service estimated that the fire had grown from a few hundred acres to nearly 1,000 acres. At that point, it was just 11% contained.
As firefighters shifted to the offensive late last week, they narrowed their estimate of the Wild River Fire to about 856 acres. Over the weekend, they pegged it at about 821 acres, where it still stood Tuesday.
While the fire’s footprint has been slow to shrink, firefighters’ containment of the blaze has grown exponentially over the weekend and into early this week.
The Forest Service estimated the fire was roughly 20% contained by Friday, 29% by Sunday and, on Tuesday, they said the Wild River Fire was approximately 53% contained.
The portion of the perimeter contained in the first full week of fighting was largely limited to the banks of the Wild River and a stretch of the blaze’s northeast border, which is roughly a half-mile from the state line.
However, Tuesday’s update showed progress in other areas, including along a brook on the west side of the fire, and segments of the fire’s jagged northern edge.
The size of the response — which peaked at 140 assigned personnel on Friday — dwindled over the weekend and was down to 88 assigned personnel as of Tuesday.
“As fire behavior has moderated, and the potential for the fire to spread continues to be reduced, incident managers have begun adjusting resources to better align with operational needs,” the Forest Service said in its update Monday.
As they did last week, officials detailed the large-scale response at a public meeting in Shelburne, New Hampshire, on Tuesday night.
Ben Wagner, an operations section chief assigned to the wildfire, said they have divided the fire into three sectors: One encompasses nearly the entire south side of the blaze, along the Wild River, while the northeast and northwest edges make up the other two. A division of firefighters is assigned to each of the three sectors.
Wagner said much of the area that has yet to be contained is in mountainous terrain, which can be especially hazardous for firefighters to navigate.
“If you can imagine hiking 2,500 vertical feet carrying chainsaws and leaf blowers and everything you need, and then breaking your leg on that mountain,” Wagner said, “the arduous work would then be to take that person and hike them down the mountain and cross over a river — and trying to do that within daylight.”
No firefighters have been injured during the response, due in large part to only attacking the fire where and when it’s safe to do so, officials said Tuesday.
But some conditions have gone the Forest Service’s way. For instance, Wagner explained that the spread of the fire, which has been thriving off felled hardwood, has naturally slowed or halted in areas with conifer fuels. Water sources, like brooks and creeks, have also served as natural means of controlling the spread.
And the icing on the cake has come in the form of sorely needed precipitation.
“The rain, the snow, the increase in moisture that’s permeating down into the ground, has really helped us a great deal in holding this fire where it’s at,” Wagner said.
He later added: “For as difficult a ground it is to work, we do have some things that are working in our favor.”

title: Obituary: Emily Rachel Kopans
text:
PORTLAND – Emily Rachel Kopans passed away peacefully on Nov. 4, 2026, in Portland. Emily was born in Chicago, Ill., on Jan. 24, 1944, to David E. Kopans, M.D. and Edith G. Kopans.
She grew up in and attended public schools in Newton, Mass., graduated from the University of Wisconsin, Madison, Wis., with a Bachelor of Arts and a Master’s in Education from the University of Maine, Orono.
Her professional career was as a guidance counselor, where she positively influenced the lives of many young students at Deering High School, Messalonskee High School, and Waterville Junior and Senior High Schools, all in Maine and where she lived her entire adult life.
For all who knew her, her love of her beloved dogs Maggie, Chelsea, Samantha and Bubba knew no bounds. She was a passionate lover of dogs and all animals. Her friendships were deep and long and will be positively remembered by many. She loved gardening, writing and reading. She abhorred prejudice of all kinds.
She was predeceased by her parents and two brothers. She is survived by her special friend Keith Hamilton of Florida, and brother Daniel B. Kopans, M.D. and his spouse Barbara of Waban, Mass., and sister Elizabeth K. Frantz, attorney, and her spouse Jon Steffensen, attorney, also of Waban, Mass.
Services will be private.

title: A familiar face and a helping hand: Grocery store employee marks 30 years
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
CHESTERFIELD, Va. (Aging Untold) — Kenny Minor has spent 30 years working at the Food Lion, his first job out of high school. Customers and management say he remains one of the store’s most dependable employees.
A fixture in the community
Janice Judkins, a customer who has shopped at the store for roughly 25 years, said Minor has been a constant presence throughout that time.
“Kenny has been here the entire time since I’ve been over on this side of town,” Judkins said.
Minor’s duties include keeping aisles clean, stocking restrooms and assisting customers.
Store manager Jack Glass said Minor regularly helps shoppers locate items and carries groceries to their cars.
“He’s taking groceries to the car. Whenever they need to find something on the shelf, Kenny will take them to the item,” Glass said.
Walking to work through the years
Customers say they have seen Minor walking to work for decades, regardless of weather conditions.
“Every time I’m driving, whether it’s on the weekends or to work, I’m always seeing Kenny, walking to work. Even all the way back to COVID, he was determined to get here,” Judkins said.
Brenda Lewis, a customer, said Minor’s presence at the store stands out.
“When I saw him today I was so glad to see him,” Lewis said. “Well, he’s very accommodating, he’s very polite and people just love his personality.”
When asked what keeps him coming back after 30 years, Minor said, “I want to help people.”

title: Democrats plan to use new power to rein in Trump’s education agenda, but their tools are limited
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Democrats in Congress are preparing to flex their soon-to-be majorities in opposition to some of President Donald Trump’s marquee education policies, starting with the dismantling of the U.S. Education Department. But with Trump threatening to use his veto power, they may be limited to opening investigations and using federal funding as leverage.
The White House has given no sign of backing away from its campaigns to close the department and to end diversity, equity and inclusion policies. But Democrats are preparing to use their oversight and appropriations powers to push back against Trump administration decisions that have reverberated through schools and universities.
Rep. Bobby Scott of Virginia, the top Democrat on the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, said he plans to “leave no rock unturned” as he takes the helm of the panel’s investigative powers, which include authority to issue subpoenas and hold hearings.
The committee is preparing to explore the Trump administration’s dismantling of the Education Department, its oversight of federal student loans and its anti-discrimination policies, Scott said. Under Trump, the Education Department has prioritized investigations into transgender issues while backing away from addressing systemic racism in schools.
A day after the midterm elections, Scott sent a letter to 10 federal agencies reminding them to preserve records that might become part of a congressional review.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, called on Democrats to “hold the Trump administration accountable for dismantling the Department of Education and turning its back on students.”
Trump officials denounced Democrats’ plans, with Education Department spokesperson Savannah Newhouse saying they’re plotting to “prematurely sabotage” Education Secretary Linda McMahon. White House spokesperson Liz Huston accused Democrats of failing American students with “disastrous leadership” before Trump returned to office.
Investigations aren’t likely to stop Trump agenda
Congressional investigations can be used to apply political pressure and uncover how decisions were made, but they are unlikely to present a substantial brake on Trump’s education policies that have outraged Democrats over the last two years. And with Trump pledging to veto Democratic bills he sees as harmful, there’s little optimism for legislative countermeasures.
“We’re very happy that this Congress is unlikely to pass legislation like the legislation that was passed last year,” said Diana Autin, executive director of the SPAN Parent Advocacy Network, a nonprofit based in Newark, New Jersey.
Still, she said, “it’s not very likely that they will be able to undo the harm that’s already been done.”
Democrats on the Senate Appropriations Committee are exploring harder checks through the budgeting process. Some are planning to add conditions to spending bills aimed at reining in the Trump administration’s education agenda.
“I think there will be an interest in using the power of the purse to establish guardrails and prevent these abusive practices,” Sen. Chris Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat on the Appropriations Committee, told The Associated Press.
Last year, Democrats failed to secure broad language in a funding bill to block further dismantling of the Education Department. Now, with majorities in both chambers, they’re preparing to try again. Van Hollen described it as one avenue to “stop the bleeding” but not necessarily to reverse the dismantling that has been done.
“It’s a little harder to try to rebuild an entity just through an appropriations bill,” he said. “But we can certainly try to prevent further damage and then seek to reverse the harm that’s been done.”
There’s also interest in conditioning federal funding to rein in Trump’s battle to reshape higher education, Van Hollen said, including the White House’s repeated efforts to cut funding at Harvard and other prestigious universities. “That said,” he added, “we’re dealing with an administration that has demonstrated no respect for the law.”
Education advocates are pushing Democrats to go a step further. Some hope to see appropriations language ordering the administration to reverse decisions moving Education Department functions to other agencies, including one that put special education programs under the Department of Health and Human Services, and another that put the investigation of school discrimination claims under the Justice Department.
“I think it’s going to become more and more apparent that they don’t have the authority just to keep dismantling some of these offices,” said Aaron Ament, president of the advocacy group Student Defense, which is representing plaintiffs in a lawsuit challenging the dismantling of the Education Department.
Some want Democrats to pass bills, despite veto threat
Some advocates are hoping the next Congress will be in place in time to approve the nomination of a replacement for Harmeet Dhillon, an assistant attorney general who spearheaded the Justice Department’s sweeping investigations into elite universities. She announced her resignation last Thursday in the wake of the midterms. Alarming to some education advocates, however, is Trump’s decision promoting Stephen Miller, the architect of some of Trump’s most hard-line policies, to chief of staff.
Todd Wolfson, president of the American Association of University Professors, said that the higher education environment was so tough that the organization endorsed candidates for the first time during the midterms. Those candidates included Abdul El-Sayed, a former professor, who won a bitter campaign for Michigan’s open Senate seat. Now, Wolfson is looking not just at reversing some of what has happened during the Trump administration, but building a campaign for a free public higher education system.
“Most other countries have figured this out, and we can too,” Wolfson said.
But with Trump’s veto power, such a change is unlikely in the next two years.
Trump’s second term in office has been marked by seismic change in education policy. Trump officials cut the Education Department’s staff by nearly half and signed intergovernmental agreements parceling its top duties to other agencies. In higher education, the administration has mounted a battle to eliminate DEI practices and curb international enrollment, using federal funding as leverage to advance policies favored by the White House.
Yet education issues receded to the background in midterm elections that became a referendum on Trump’s deeply unpopular economic policies and the Iran war. As Democrats sort out a vast oversight agenda, education is expected to fall farther down the list of priorities, behind big topics like Trump’s self-enrichment and federal immigration raids.
Despite their new power, there’s little optimism that Democrats will be able to override Trump’s veto on big education bills. Some advocates want lawmakers to try anyway.
“Even if he vetoes them, let’s put the pressure on to get it to his desk, and then you see what the contrast is,” said Randi Weingarten, president of the American Federation of Teachers union.
Some on the right are pushing for last-minute legislation to advance Trump’s agenda. A day after the midterms, the Heritage Foundation asked Republican lawmakers to propose a bill to close the Education Department and strip any mention of it from federal law. In what amounts to a political Hail Mary, the group argued the agency has failed to prove its value since it opened in 1980.
The letter asked Republicans to collaborate with McMahon “to sunset this failed bureaucracy.”
___
Hollingsworth reported from Mission, Kansas.

title: Tracking a late week storm possibility for Maine
text:
Tracking a late week storm possibility for Maine
Uncertainty remains in the forecast track and its impacts on northern New England
Tracking a late week storm possibility for Maine
Uncertainty remains in the forecast track and its impacts on northern New England
Looking ahead to late week, forecast models continue to disagree on the track of a potential coastal storm. More support is building for a coastal track, but how close it gets will determine our impacts. The best chance for accumulating snow will be in the White Mountains and higher elevations, with some wet snow possibly reaching the foothills. Along the coast, precipitation would most likely fall as rain. Strongest winds will likely be near the coast, though confidence in wind impacts remains low for now.
There is still plenty of uncertainty with this system, particularly regarding snowfall amounts and wind. Behind the storm, temperatures should gradually return to more seasonable levels, with drier weather developing heading into next week.

title: Hannah Pingree announces 22-person transition committee
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - Governor-elect Hannah Pingree announced her transition committee Tuesday morning in Augusta.
The 22-person committee brings together volunteers from across Maine to help find the people who will lead state agencies and serve in her cabinet.
“It’s why I am selecting people who are capable, who are collaborative, and who are ready to roll up their sleeves to help me make these decisions,” Pingree said.
Co-chairs describe approach
Co-chair Roger Katz is a former Augusta mayor and Republican state senator. He said the search will reach beyond party lines.
“And this is important, no matter how someone voted. Because good people and good ideas don’t belong to one party,” Katz said.
Fellow co-chair Maulian Bryant serves on the Penobscot Nation Tribal Council and leads the Wabanaki Alliance. She said she and Pingree share a perspective on Maine’s future.
“Hannah and I are both mothers. And that really shapes how you do this work. We’re thinking about the long run because we’re raising kids in this state. What kind of Maine are they going to inherit?” Bryant said.
Committee members
The committee includes former L.L.Bean CEO Steve Smith and former Maine Senate Majority Leader Eloise Vitelli.

title: Proposed landfill leachate facility raises a lot of questions about PFAS contamination
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
John Krueger of Northport is a former division director of licensing and enforcement at the Maine Department of Environmental Protection and former director of the State of Maine Health and Environmental Testing Laboratory.
Our society’s decisions about the wastes associated with the Juniper Ridge Landfill (JRL) reveal something larger about how we manage the byproducts of modern life. Waste does not simply disappear; it accumulates, moves, and eventually settles somewhere.
Recently, in a Bangor courtroom, the discussion centered on environmental justice — on who benefits from our disposal choices and who bears the harm. As we begin to confront the toxicity of PFAS‑contaminated leachate (the leakage of pollutants from a landfill), we find ourselves facing a new set of difficult questions about responsibility, risk, and the fate of these persistent chemicals.
Understanding and deciding how to handle leachate from landfills that contain PFAS is no simple task. PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances) is not one chemical but a family of more than two dozen compounds, each with its own behavior, mobility, and resistance to treatment. Maine’s “sum of six” health standard of 20 ng/L was created to simplify analysis by focusing on six PFAS compounds relevant to drinking water. No one is planning to drink landfill leachate, but the standard provides a reference point.
In reality, the Juniper Ridge Landfill leachate contains many more PFAS compounds with a combined concentration roughly 150 times higher in total PFAS compounds than the drinking‑water limit. The highest concentrations of PFAS compounds in JRL leachate are short‑chain PFAS that are not included in the “sum of six,” and these short‑chain compounds are also the hardest to remove consistently.
A pilot study conducted on JRL leachate demonstrates this clearly: while treatment can reduce some PFAS, short‑chain compounds remain stubbornly persistent. The study highlights the gap between regulators metrics and the full chemical reality.
Another layer of complexity involves where treatment or disposal might occur, and where treated or untreated leachate ultimately returns to the Penobscot River. Juniper Ridge Landfill produces roughly 17 million gallons of leachate per year. Transporting that volume requires approximately nine 5,000‑gallon tanker truckloads daily. Pine Tree Landfill (PTL) in Hampden adds its own leachate. The chemistry of the two landfills is strikingly similar: both contain high concentrations of short‑chain PFAS in their leachate that are not included in the “sum of six,” and both pose the same treatment challenges.
This brings us to the proposed expansion of leachate storage at the landfill in Hampden. PTL is the successor facility to the Sawyer landfill/Sawyer Environmental Recovery Facility, located on the same Hampden site.
The Pine Tree Landfill already has a direct pipeline to the Bangor wastewater treatment plant, which does not remove PFAS. Increasing storage capacity at PTL could permit both the Pine Tree and Juniper Ridge landfill leachate to be held, mixed, and potentially pumped directly to the Bangor wastewater treatment plant and discharged to the river without PFAS removal. While treatment options are being studied, the infrastructure being proposed could make bypassing treatment easier than performing it. That is the structural risk at the heart of this permit.
A public hearing before the Hampden Planning Board on Tuesday offers an important opportunity for residents to participate and to understand this application. Citizens can ask about spill prevention, control, and countermeasure plans for storage of U.S. Environmental Protection Agency PFAS designated hazardous substances, about contingency planning, about treatment reliability, and about what safeguards will prevent untreated PFAS‑laden leachate from being disposed of improperly. They can ask whether treatment will be required, not merely planned.
In the end, any decision about Juniper Ridge leachate must confront a simple truth: Without clear, enforceable commitments to PFAS treatment, expanded storage at Hampden could become a pathway for untreated waste to reach the Penobscot River. The choices we make now will determine who bears the burden of these chemicals for generations to come.

title: Maine parent advocate defends special education rule challenged by private schools
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - A Maine parent advocate is pushing back against a lawsuit brought by private schools over a state special education regulation, saying the rule protects students with disabilities from being denied an education or removed from school without enough notice.
The Maine Association of Independent Schools and seven private schools, including Foxcroft Academy and Washington Academy, sued the Maine Department of Education over the regulation. The plaintiffs say the changes will have a “significant effect” on the safety of students and staff.
What the lawsuit says
Tara Walker, a Portland-based attorney from Fisher Phillips who is representing the plaintiffs, said the schools are concerned about what the rule says, what it leaves out and how it was enacted.
Walker said a judge or hearing officer would have to sign off on a change in placement for a student with special needs. She said that could prevent schools from taking immediate action when a student’s behavior puts them or others at risk.
Walker said private schools sometimes have more resources than public schools to care for children with disabilities—leading some districts to choose to place students in a private institution to have their needs met.
“The incentives for this rule run backwards. So, the school district may have risk by changing the students’ school or enrolling them in a different school — but no risk or very limited risk if the student does something unsafe on the premises. Whereas a private school has a lot of the risk,” Walker said.
The complaint says the policy was enacted as part of an emergency rule—something Walker said prevented those most affected by the change from making their voices heard.
Criticism from advocates
Carrie Woodcock, executive director of the Maine Parent Federation, said her organization has worked with families whose children were rejected by an academy because of a disability. She said that practice violates the federal Individuals with Disabilities Education Act and puts Maine at risk of losing federal funding.
The Maine Parent Federation is a federally funded nonprofit that advocates for children with disabilities and provides parent training.
Woodcock said the rule requires schools that accept public tuition dollars to participate in the process for deciding where a student with a disability should be educated. Many Maine academies receive tuition paid by the municipalities where students live, sometimes because the academy is the only school in town.
Special purpose private schools, one of which is named as a plaintiff in the lawsuit, provide specialized education to children with disabilities. Woodcock said those specialized schools also receive tuition from municipalities when an IEP determines it is the best placement for a child.
She said placement decisions should involve a student’s individualized education program, or IEP, team rather than being made unilaterally by a school, and that the new rule prevents that.
“You have to come back to the IEP team. You have to have a meeting. You can’t just put that kid out the next day,” Woodcock said. “You can’t say, I’m sorry, we can’t meet this kid’s needs. He can’t come back tomorrow, which is what was occurring in our state.”
Woodcock said families can face yearslong waits for another placement when a child is told not to return to a school, forcing some guardians to take an extended leave from work.
Schools respond
Jeff Burroughs, president of the Maine Association of Independent Schools, issued a statement in response to the federation’s criticism.
“Private schools in Maine are rightly proud of their strong special education programs that they offer in support of the families they serve, some of which are the only programs available for students to remain in their community,” Burroughs said. “While, like all schools, general education schools may not be the most appropriate setting for all children, we are very proud to serve as many as we can, and our member schools do so inclusively, fairly and equitably.”
Dan Walker, counsel to the association, also issued a statement.
“Private schools have always been subject to the Maine Human Rights Act, which prohibits discrimination against students based on their disability status,” Walker said. “The emergency rule establishes a parallel process, to one which already existed, for families and schools to address issues that arise in those settings. The legal challenge, however, is based on the Department’s abandonment of a framework to ensure student safety.”
