title: Ole Miss student apologizes after video showing women making racist gestures sparks backlash
text:
Ole Miss student apologizes for video that shows her and another woman making racist gestures outside student's apartment
One of two women in a viral video seen making monkey noises and gestures outside of a Black Ole Miss student's apartment said in a statement that her "actions were insensitive, inappropriate, and deeply harmful."
The video, recorded outside an off-campus apartment complex where Ole Miss students live, shows three women walking past a student's door. Two appear to make monkey noises and gestures.
In a letter from her attorney, Alaina Kunes, a freshman at the University of Mississippi, apologized to those she offended.
"Before the incident on Nov. 6, I never met the women involved and was unaware of their race; however, I recognize my actions were insensitive, inappropriate, and deeply harmful. I would have never intentionally made those noises or gestures toward a person of color. I have apologized to the women, and I pray they will forgive me. I can never truly understand the pain I have caused them, and it was never my intention. These girls deserve to feel seen and understood, and what I did is not a reflection of who I am trying to become," Kunes said. "Over the past several days, my family and I have received death threats and harassment. I am grateful for the authorities working to ensure our safety. As I intend to cooperate fully with the University’s investigation, I ask for privacy for my family. I understand the seriousness of this situation and remain committed to taking responsibility and learning from this embarrassing ordeal." 
The Black Student Union issued a statement condemning the incident and calling for a full investigation, appropriate disciplinary action and support for the student targeted.
The university said it condemns the behavior shown in the video, calling it offensive, hurtful and unacceptable. Ole Miss said it has offered support and resources to the students and is investigating through its Office of Conflict Resolution and Student Conduct and its Office of Equal Opportunity and Regulatory Compliance.
The university has said federal privacy laws limit what it can share about individual students or potential disciplinary action.

title: California voters reject measure to tax the wealth of billionaires
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
California voters reject measure to tax the wealth of billionaires
California voters have rejected a first-in-the-nation tax on the net worth of billionaires following a contentious ballot fight that generated huge spending by some prominent tech leaders eager to stop their taxes from going up.
The measure's failure is a win for Democratic leaders who opposed it, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, who's deciding whether to run for president in 2028. Critics of the tax, known as Proposition 40, said it would have prompted ultrawealthy taxpayers to leave the state.
The "no" side raised roughly 10 times as much as the "yes" side. Google co-founder Sergey Brin alone dumped more than $100 million into a political action committee working to defeat the measure.
The measure would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of Californians whose net worth exceeds $1 billion. Most of the money would have been used to backfill federal funding cuts to healthcare, and 10% would have gone toward education and food-assistance programs. SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, which backed the tax, said it was necessary to replace an estimated $100 billion the state will lose in federal healthcare funding over five years.
Proposition 40 was the nation's biggest test yet on an idea progressives have long championed: raising taxes on the ultra-rich by targeting the main way they make their money — through their investments as opposed to the paychecks they receive from work.
The measure attracted support from liberal leaders beyond the state, including Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, who rallied in cities across California in the race's closing weeks to urge voters to pass it.
Billionaires donated millions of dollars to a political action committee, Building a Better California, working to defeat the measure. The committee, which backed other measures on the ballot designed to nullify the tax, raised more than $333 million, nearly a third of which came from Brin.
Brin, along with his fellow Google co-founder Larry Page, was among the billionaires who started cutting ties with the state in anticipation of the possible tax. Another tech mogul, Mark Zuckerberg, said he would remain in the state for eight years and made a deal with Meta to help him pay the tax without losing his ownership stake in the company.
Some traditional Democratic allies, including Planned Parenthood and the California Medical Association, were part of a coalition opposing it. They were concerned about how the tax revenue would be divvied up and about the potential impact on the state's budget if there was a mass exodus of wealthy taxpayers. California's budget relies heavily on the income tax of the state's richest residents.
"Proposition 40 was a reckless experiment conducted on our state's economy with little regard for the harms it would cause," the coalition said in a statement.
Robert Swonger, an auto glass technician living near Sacramento who's politically independent, said before voting concluded Nov. 3 that he planned to vote against it.
"Obviously, I would like billionaires not to have as much money as they do," he said. "But I don't believe taxing them out of existence is going to work."
Progressive politicians, including Sanders and Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, have long supported a federal wealth tax. Newsom says a California wealth tax would disadvantage the state, but he supports a national minimum tax on anyone with a net worth above $100 million.
Days before Sanders held rallies in California cities last month, Newsom told reporters that the senator's focus on wealth inequality was "spot-on." But he said that "on this issue, we fundamentally disagree."
Supporters of the California tax started running ads recently in New Hampshire, New Mexico and Virginia, states that will vote early in the Democratic presidential primary in 2028, that criticize Newsom for his opposition to the measure.

title: Is an Aldi in Windham’s future?
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Aldi is eyeing Windham for the site of its second grocery store in Maine.
The Windham Planning Board discussed plans to build an Aldi in North Windham at its Nov. 9 meeting.
The Germany-based supermarket chain opened a Portland location earlier this year.
The proposed 19,432-square-foot structure and about 100 parking spaces would be built on Roosevelt Trail between the Walmart and McDonald’s. A vacant building would be demolished to make room for the Aldi.
The site plan, submitted on Sept. 22, also includes a truck delivery entrance from Roosevelt Trail, a reconfigured entrance at the McDonald’s driveway, as well as stormwater, grading and utility work.
Representing Aldi at the hearing were Andrew Kurmin, of LJB Engineering, the civil engineers working on the project, and Richard Derbes, director of development for Aldi.
Board member Melissa Young asked if the idea of reconfiguring the McDonald’s entrance had been evaluated based on traffic safety, noting the frequency of bad driving in the area, and asked if the required traffic movement permit would just look at inbound and outbound traffic, or if it would also include other traffic flows. Town Planner Natalie Thomsen said Aldi would look at every intersection and entrance.
The next steps for the project include a site walk, after Aldi submits its final plan, as well as a public hearing. No date was set at the meeting for either of these steps.

title: 3 men charged with plotting terror attacks, including one involving UK airbase used by US Air Force
text:
US charges 3 over alleged terror plots targeting Jewish communities and a UK airbase used by US Air Force
Three men, including one already jailed in the United States, were accused by U.S. authorities Tuesday of being Iran-supported operatives who plotted nearly 20 attacks on Jewish communities in Europe and the U.S. as well as a planned assault on a British airbase used by the U.S. Air Force.
Charges against Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, were outlined in a superseding indictment unsealed in Manhattan federal court. Only al-Saadi is in custody.
U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald in New York said in a news release that al-Saadi, who was arrested in the spring, continued to coordinate with his co-defendants in the days leading up to the attempted September terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, United Kingdom, where U.S. bombers and troops had been stationed.
“These defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran that targeted Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, and the British military base, RAF Fairford, housing American service members,” McDonald said. "The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical — it is very real.”
Attorney General Todd Blanche said: “Anyone who plans a terrorist plot on a military base housing American servicemembers will be prosecuted by the United States government.”
The new indictment offers fresh insight into an episode that has been shrouded in mystery for more than a month after five men were detained after midnight on Sept. 27 on suspected explosives and terrorism offenses after three suspicious vans were spotted traveling toward the base in western England.
A sixth suspect, a British-Iranian dual national, was arrested several days later. All the men were released on bail.
British authorities linked the incident to Tehran, and though Iran denied involvement, the arrests prompted the U.S. to withdraw its bombers that had been stationed there. The bombers were redeployed to their home bases in the United States.
RAF Fairford, located 100 miles west of London, has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East.
According to the indictment, al-Saadi used coded language in communications with relatives from jail to direct that money be passed along to others who could carry out attacks.
The indictment alleged that the three men conspired together to use a network of contacts in the United Kingdom to commit terrorist attacks on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, which included the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Kata’ib Hizballah.
In June, al-Saadi pleaded not guilty to charges that he plotted at least 18 attacks in Europe in retaliation for the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran. He called himself a “prisoner of war.” He has been held without bail since. His lawyers did not immediately respond to requests for comment Tuesday on the latest development.
Both Kata’ib Hizballah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps have been designated by the U.S. government as foreign terrorist organizations. U.S. prosecutors say Al-Saadi was a Kata’ib Hizballah commander.

title: ‘A lot of people knew her’: 18-year-old college freshman found dead in her dorm room
text:
WICHITA, Kan. (KWCH/Gray News) - A first-year student-athlete has been found dead in her dorm room over the weekend at Newman University.
According to the university, a resident found 18-year-old McKenzie Rohr, a member of Newman’s new track and field team, in her room on Sunday.
First responders were called to the scene where she was pronounced dead.
The Sedgwick County Medical Examiner’s Office said it was working to determine the 18-year-old’s cause of death.
Newman University President Kathleen Jagger noted there was no indication of suicide and that an investigation is underway.
Jagger said the university did not have all the details surrounding Rohr’s death.
“It’s just a tragedy. And whenever you lose a young person, no matter the age, you know it seems premature, and no one’s ready for it,” Jagger added.
First-year student Vincent Cuhlman said Rohr was dedicated to athletics and her studies.
“A lot of people knew her as a good friend to be around,” he said.
A candle was burning in the university chapel in Rohr’s memory. Newman staff said they were also providing additional therapists and religious resources for students who needed support.
“It’s a big change, and it’s a lot to unpack,” Ba Nguyen, a second-year Newman student, said. “That’s why it’s really necessary to talk to people about it.”
The university confirmed a memorial service for Rohr has also been planned for Wednesday night.
Jagger asked for prayers for Rohr’s family, friends and the university community.

title: Quarry Tap Room keeps liquor license after Hallowell City Council vote
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
HALLOWELL, Maine (WABI) -The Quarry Tap Room will keep its liquor license after a vote by the Hallowell City Council on Monday night.
The council approved the license with one member recusing themselves.
Police chief reverses recommendation
Police Chief Zachary Kindelan said officers have responded to 15 incidents at the Tap Room. Eleven of them ended in an arrest or summons.
Kindelan had originally recommended against renewing the license. He reversed course after meeting with bar staff Monday.
Supporters fill meeting
Supporters filled the Community Theatre, where the council meeting was held. Employees and residents spoke about what the establishment means to them and its impact on the community.
“We feel great. You know, all along we felt we didn’t really do anything wrong. It was unfortunate. Social media kind of took over the firestorm and created a whole lot of buzz,” said Steven Lachance, co-owner of the Quarry Tap Room.
No one spoke against the license renewal during the public comment period.

title: Hannah Pingree says there’s ‘no easy solution’ to Maine’s $1B budget gap
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
AUGUSTA, Maine — Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree said Tuesday there will be “no easy solution” to the $1 billion gap in her first two-year budget, but she would not say whether new taxes or the state’s rainy day fund are on the table.
The Democrat spoke as she introduced the 22-member committee of volunteers that will help pick her Cabinet. It is led by Roger Katz, a former Republican state senator and Augusta mayor, and Maulian Bryant, the executive director of the Wabanaki Alliance.
The budget is their most urgent problem. Pingree must send lawmakers a balanced proposal by early February, weeks after her Jan. 6 inauguration. Democrats expanded their legislative majorities in last week’s wave election following outgoing Gov. Janet Mills’ passage of a millionaire tax and use of $155 million from the reserve fund for $300 relief checks.
Asked about income taxes, sales taxes or the rainy day fund, Pingree instead pointed to property taxes and federal cuts to Medicaid and SNAP.
“Mainers are hurting right now,” she said. “I’ve made a commitment to middle- and low-income Mainers that they are already paying too much.”
Pingree said she will meet soon with Elaine Clark, Mills’ outgoing budget commissioner. She wants her own pick to lead the Department of Administrative and Financial Services to be “ready on day one to help us advance a budget.”
Committee members include state Sen. Peggy Rotundo, D-Lewiston, the outgoing chair of the Legislature’s budget committee, and former Senate Majority Leader Eloise Vitelli, D-Arrowsic. Katz, himself a former legislative leader and appropriator, said the committee would recruit talent “no matter how someone voted.”
Republicans have not responded to Pingree’s comments. After last week’s losses, the new House minority leader, Rep. Ken Fredette, R-Newport, said his party has to govern alongside Pingree and Democrats and can’t “just be the party of no.”
On Tuesday, Pingree said her Cabinet “could include independents and Republicans.” She aims to name every commissioner before she takes office, and she said transition committee members were picked with the understanding that they were not interested in a Cabinet job.

title: State to hear comments on owner of Lewiston hospital this month
text:
The state will hold a public hearing Nov. 20 to determine whether Prime Healthcare Foundation, the California-based owner of Central Maine Medical Center in Lewiston, is complying with commitments to provide safe care.
The hearing will be at Kirk Hall Auditorium at Central Maine Community College at 1250 Turner St. in Auburn from 2-3:30 p.m. Attendance is in-person or remote by registering online.
The Maine Department of Health and Human Services is inviting the public to share information about whether Prime is meeting multiple conditions from the state that allowed it to acquire Central Maine Healthcare, which includes hospitals in Lewiston, Bridgton and Rumford, and several physician practices.
The new owner promised to maintain essential health services and safe staff-to-patient ratios across Central Maine Healthcare, in addition to reestablishing trauma center status in Lewiston by 2028. The system must also continue operations at long-term care facilities in Auburn and Rumford, according to the state’s conditions of approval.
The state is calling Prime’s word into question. Last month, officials released a report detailing issues with sterilization equipment at Central Maine Medical Center that went unaddressed until the state’s investigation. Along with workforce changes, from provider turnover to nurse terminations to a canceled emergency department staffing contract, patients and community members have spoken out in concern for their hospitals.
Public comments must specifically relate to the conditions of approval.
Through Nov. 30, the health department will accept written, signed comments by mail, email or hand delivery to the office at 41 Anthony Ave. in Augusta.

title: Thomas Markle, father of Meghan, cut off his ankle monitor, DOJ says
text:
TAMPA, Fla. (AP) — The 82-year-old estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, cut an electronic monitoring device off his ankle, just days after his arrest for keeping child sexual abuse material in storage units in California, authorities said Tuesday.
Thomas Markle was in custody awaiting a hearing in federal court in Tampa, Florida, First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said.
He was arrested shortly after he cut off the ankle bracelet at 1:45 a.m., Essayli said.
Markle’s arrest on Friday followed the seizure of approximately 78 items, including slides, film negatives, and books that contained suspected child sexual abuse images in storage in the Los Angeles area, Essayli said.
During his arrest last week, he was taken from a senior care center in Lakeland by ambulance. Hours later, a judge allowed Markle to be released on the condition that he be electronically monitored, which typically means wearing an ankle tether.
The judge also ordered a mental competency exam and a report by Nov. 20.
His daughter, Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex married Prince Harry at Windsor Castle in 2018. They have two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet. She is an American citizen and actor who starred in the U.S. television drama “Suits.”
Meghan recently said she was “deeply distressed” by allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images had been found at her father’s former home. She also revealed that a letter containing “troubling allegations” about him had been sent to police in London in 2019.
“It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated,” Meghan said of the letter. “I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children was for one reason: to protect them.”
Thomas Markle was living in the Philippines this year when he suffered a stroke and had his left leg amputated. That forced him to return to the U.S.
His arrest followed reports by The Sun, a British tabloid newspaper, that Meghan’s half brother found a collection of child sexual abuse images while clearing out their father’s home in the Philippines. That discovery led to information about two U.S. storage units in California, which Markle had rented since 2008.

title: Ranked choice voting counting process underway in Augusta
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - Work is underway in Augusta to verify votes cast across Maine’s 2nd Congressional District.
Unofficial first-round results show Republican Paul LePage leading Democrat Matt Dunlap. LePage received 49.894% of the vote, just short of a majority, so the state is preparing for a ranked-choice tabulation.
Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said the law requires that the Secretary of State’s office “produce a result for certification that is 50% plus one of the vote at a minimum.”
Dunlap concedes, count still must be certified
LePage leads by about 5,400 votes, and Dunlap has conceded the race. The state still has to complete the count and certify the winner.
Bellows says a change in the outcome is unlikely, but not impossible.
“If the vote verification process uncovered something surprising, for example, if a municipality had misreported the results and it had a statistical impact on the race, flipping the race to Matt Dunlap, and that was confirmed here in the presence of all of the observers and the media, then we would certify the race for Matt Dunlap,” Bellows said.
How the verification works
Workers are checking vote totals against those reported by towns, scanning ballots, and uploading vote records. If neither candidate has a majority after verification, the state will tabulate the next available choices on eliminated candidates’ ballots.
There were more than 6,000 blank ballots and more than 100 votes for an official write-in candidate.
As of Monday evening, ballots have been counted in these counties: Androscoggin, Aroostook, Franklin, Hancock, Kennebec, Oxford, Penobscot, Waldo and Washington.
Campaign representative observes
Lauren LePage, the former governor’s daughter and a campaign representative, is watching the process.
“Yes, everything seems to be going very smoothly. The Secretary of State’s office has been very communicative with everyone in the room. And so, so far everything has been as it’s expected to be,” said Lauren Lepage.
She said her father is already in Washington, taking part in new member orientation for Congress.
Representatives for Dunlap’s campaign did not attend the tabulation proceeding Monday morning. Dunlap’s campaign has been contacted for comment and has not yet responded.
Bellows says the process could take four to five days. The public can watch it live on the Maine Secretary of State’s YouTube page.

title: Temps near normal, showers for some
text:

An active weather pattern and a cooling trend
Tuesday is a seasonable day with highs in the low to mid 50s, partly sunny skies, and the chance for a stray shower. Winds are light from the west. Scattered showers are likely in the mountains in the late afternoon. Those showers will move south and east after sunset, clearing the Midcoast late in the evening.
Veterans Day is a nice fall day, dry for most, but a few flurries or isolated showers are possible across northern Maine. Farther south, it will be partly cloudy and cool with highs in the 40s and low 50s.
Thursday through Saturday will be a gloomy stretch for Maine as a storm system passes to the south and east. Ahead of the storm, scattered showers are possible on Thursday, falling as rain along and near the coast, snow in the mountains, and a mix of both in between.
Friday into Saturday, expect more of the same. Rounds of showers with cold rain or wet snow, or a mix of both. Temperatures will be running below average, with highs in the 30s and 40s.
Clouds may linger Sunday, but a dry day is likely, with temperatures returning to average (highs around 50 degrees). Next week starts cool and quiet.

title: Death Notice: Walter E. “Wally” Arsenault
Planning for Jay data center moves forward, but deal not yet final
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
JAY — A proposed $550 million data center at the former Androscoggin Mill is showing signs of life again, with its original development partner back in discussions and a public meeting tentatively planned for December.
Town Manager Shiloh LaFreniere told the Select Board on Monday, Nov. 9, that JGT2 Redevelopment LLC, owner of the former mill property on Riley Road, has resumed efforts to move forward with Sentinel Data Centers, which withdrew from the project in June.
“They’re moving forward again with Sentinel,” LaFreniere said. “But they have not reached a final agreement yet.”
The renewed discussions could revive one of Jay’s most significant redevelopment proposals since the paper mill closed in 2023, potentially restoring a major source of investment and employment to the community. State environmental permitting is moving ahead, although updated construction schedules, investment figures and job projections have not been announced.
LaFreniere said JGT2 partner Tony McDonald contacted the town to provide the update but was hesitant to announce another development milestone before an agreement was finalized.
“He’s a little afraid of crying wolf multiple times and not having what he says actually commence,” she told the board, referring to previous setbacks.
Despite that caution, McDonald wanted town officials and residents to know the project was progressing, she said.
A public information meeting is tentatively being considered for Dec. 10 at the former mill property. LaFreniere said the event could run from about 4-8 p.m. in an open-house format, with representatives available to discuss electrical infrastructure, water consumption and other aspects of the proposal.
The date and arrangements have not been finalized.
Meanwhile, Main-Land Development Consultants Inc. delivered a copy of the project’s Site Location of Development Act amendment application to the town office shortly before Monday’s meeting. A separate air emissions license application was expected to arrive by mail within the next day or two.
“The town will have copies of the applications at the office,” LaFreniere said, adding that the documents would also be accessible through the Maine Department of Environmental Protection.
The applications concern redevelopment of part of the former mill at 300 Riley Road. According to the public notice, buildings would be reused to house computing equipment, while former parking and rail yard areas would accommodate heating, ventilation and air conditioning equipment.
Maine Public reported Monday that pre-application documents also describe a new subsurface wastewater disposal system and two diesel-powered emergency generators rated at 3.25 megawatts each.
The original development, announced earlier this year, called for about 1 million square feet of data center space, an investment of $550 million, roughly 800 construction jobs and more than 100 permanent positions.
During a March presentation to the Select Board, McDonald described the facility as a co-location data center serving multiple customers. He estimated an initial electrical demand of about 82 megawatts and said its closed-loop cooling system would require about 300,000 gallons of replacement water daily.
Those figures were tied to the earlier proposal and have not been confirmed for the latest plans.
The project’s electricity requirements attracted statewide attention as lawmakers considered legislation temporarily restricting permits for large data centers. McDonald sought an exemption for the Jay development, citing its reuse of existing industrial infrastructure and potential economic benefits.
Gov. Janet Mills vetoed the proposed moratorium in April, citing concerns about its potential impact on redevelopment projects such as the one in Jay.
Less than two months later, Sentinel informed JGT2 it would not proceed with the project at that time, putting the development on hold while the property owner explored other possibilities.
JGT2 purchased the former Androscoggin Mill property in December 2023, following the end of papermaking operations earlier that year. The company has since undertaken demolition and site preparation work aimed at attracting new businesses to the industrial property.
The latest permitting effort signals renewed activity at the site, though the future of the development still depends on a final agreement and the necessary regulatory approvals.
Residents will be able to review application materials through the town office and DEP, with further details about the proposed December public meeting expected to be announced.

title: Death Notice: Robert H. Easter
Letter: Federal permitting reform bill would reverse environmental protections
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
This is in response to the recent column by Peter Dugas and Jeff Marks supporting the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA). This bill, as currently drafted, would be the most significant reversal in environmental and community protections in decades by favoring fossil fuel projects.
David Watkins of the Union of Concerned Scientists writes: “BAAJA undermines bedrock environmental laws while granting the fossil fuel industry more power, more access to public lands, and less accountability. In return, it includes tenuous renewable energy and transmission provisions, many of which could be achieved under current law. Without significant improvements, which seem unlikely, enactment of BAAJA could be worse than the status quo, which is already terrible.”
Fossil fuels are more expensive, more polluting, and more hazardous to our health than wind and solar. We need common sense legislation that will enable the transition to clean energy sources and cease subsidizing the fossil fuel industry with our tax dollars. Without subsidies, this industry will likely rapidly become a small player in the energy market.
The Senate bill was seemingly crafted without meaningful input from broad categories of stakeholders, including environmental groups and scientific experts. The Senate plans to vote on it soon after the November elections. Please reach out, now, to Sens. Susan Collins and Angus King, to ask them to vote “no” on this latest version of BAAJA.
Bob Lodato
Charleston

title: Appeals court limits order for LinkedIn to disclose journalists' communications in leak probe
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A judge must narrow an order requiring LinkedIn to divulge journalists’ communications on the social media platform to the Trump administration as part of a leak investigation, a federal appeals court ruled Tuesday in a case with profound free-speech implications.
A three-judge panel from the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals said the government isn’t entitled to a “blanket” order for LinkedIn to disclose a broad array of user records belonging to the journalists, whose employer isn’t identified in court records.
“A request by the government to scoop up reporters’ records wholesale and ascertain the identity of their sources would tip the balance against informed discourse in a manner inimical to democratic health,” Judge J. Harvie Wilkinson III wrote in the court’s unanimous opinion.
But the panel also rejected LinkedIn’s request to entirely quash the district court’s “substantially overbroad” disclosure order. The panel recognized that the journalists’ First Amendment rights must be balanced against the administration’s duty to protect national security information.
“Serious security and speech claims are in tension in this case. There is space under law for both,” wrote Wilkinson, who was nominated to the court by Ronald Reagan, a Republican.
The panel also included Judge James Andrew Wynn, who was nominated by Democratic President Barack Obama, and Judge Nicole G. Berner, who was nominated by Democratic President Joe Biden.
U.S. District Judge Elizabeth Hanes, a Biden nominee based in Newport News, Virginia, issued the order that LinkedIn challenged in the case.
Republican President Donald Trump’s administration opened its leak investigation when an unidentified news organization published an article about a top-secret U.S. military operation in a foreign country, revealing classified information.
The journalists targeted by the leak investigation had reported on nearly 1,000 stories on many topics over the 18-month period covered by the judge’s order. The order would unmask every confidential source that the targeted journalists communicated with on LinkedIn over that span.
“While that order may catch sources relevant to the government’s investigation, it will also inevitably sweep in every other confidential source with whom the targeted journalists spoke,” Wilkinson wrote.
The panel returned the case to Hanes with an instruction to narrow the disclosure order.
“That court was right to accord the government considerable latitude in pursuing and maintaining the integrity of its investigation,” Wilkinson wrote. “Even so, that latitude is not infinite. It is not appropriate for district courts to approve requests purely because the records requested are logistically feasible to compile.”

title: Hegseth impeachment vote on to-do list as lame duck session gets underway
text:
Hegseth impeachment vote on to-do list as lame duck session gets underway
Congress was back in session on Monday for the first time since Democrats won back control of the House and Senate, but Republicans still have a few more weeks in charge before power changes hands.
Hegseth impeachment vote on to-do list as lame duck session gets underway
Congress was back in session on Monday for the first time since Democrats won back control of the House and Senate, but Republicans still have a few more weeks in charge before power changes hands.
The lame duck session got off to a dramatic start on Monday as a Republican lawmaker revived an effort to impeach one of President Donald Trump's most controversial cabinet members. 
Rep. Thomas Massie, an outgoing GOP congressman from Kentucky, introduced a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday.
It was the first day that Congress was back in session following sweeping Democratic victories in the midterm elections. Democrats won back control of the House and Senate, but Republicans have a few more weeks in charge before power changes hands in January.
Massie's resolution outlines a range of charges against Hegseth, in part alleging that he acted unlawfully while carrying out military action in Iran without authorization from Congress. It also claims that Hegseth suppressed free speech and ignored laws designed to minimize civilian casualties.
"There are a lot of politically motivated people who may have substantial policy disagreements, but their disagreements are with success," Hegseth told reporters on Monday, adding that he is not worried about the impeachment push.
"There's no argument in these impeachment articles that he's ineffective," Massie said during a press conference on Monday. "The argument here is that he has broken laws and he has violated the Constitution. So, that's the question put in front of my colleagues."
The House could vote on the articles of impeachment as soon as this week. Massie said that he is unsure whether it will get sufficient support in the House or in the Senate, where a two-thirds majority would be needed to convict Hegseth.
Democratic leadership in both chambers, including Rep. Hakeem Jeffries and Sen. Chuck Schumer, has endorsed the effort.
Meanwhile, President Trump continued to defend Hegseth on Monday. The secretary is expected to hold a press conference on Tuesday morning with a more detailed rebuttal. It will be his first formal briefing since May.
What else is on the lame duck to-do list?
Republicans are under pressure to approve as many GOP priorities and judicial nominees as possible before Democrats take power in the new year.
Much of the focus in the final stretch will likely go towards governing funding negotiations. Congress faces a Dec. 11th deadline to reach a spending deal, or risk another possible government shutdown. Lawmakers are also expected to consider an annual defense bill, which sets policy for the Pentagon.
Those talks could get complicated as some Democrats have called for withholding federal funding as leverage to end the war with Iran.
At least some legislation up for debate in the lame-duck session has bipartisan support, including bills to overhaul college sports rules and expedite permitting reviews for energy projects. Still, the future of those proposals is uncertain.
Leadership elections are also on the agenda. The race for House Republican leadership will be in the headlines on Tuesday, as Rep. Steve Scalise and Rep. Jim Jordan are vying for the top spot. House Speaker Mike Johnson has said that he will step down from his leadership role.

title: Gay sex ban overturned in Trinidad and Tobago, ending British colonial-era law
text:
Gay sex ban overturned in Trinidad and Tobago: What the ruling says about LGBTQ+ rights and post-colonial identity
A British court has overturned a law prohibiting gay sex in Trinidad and Tobago, marking a milestone for LGBTQ+ rights in the twin-island Caribbean nation and nullifying a colonial-era law dating back over a century.
In its ruling, London-based Judicial Committee of the Privy Council — the highest appeals court for several former British colonies — said that it agreed with a lower court ruling that had previously struck down the islands’ government law, which had criminalized “buggery” and “indecency” between gay partners.
The law had allowed for prison terms of up to five years for “buggery” and two years for “gross indecency.” In contemporary legal systems, the term “buggery” is largely obsolete and considered offensive.
Ruling that Trinidad and Tobago’s law was unconstitutional, Privy Council Judge Philip Sales said: “Those laws cannot be regarded as reasonably justifiable in a society that has a proper respect for the rights and freedoms of the individual.”
“Laws which seek to criminalize such activities cannot be justified,” Sales said.
Trinidad and Tobago, an independent country, remains a republic in the British Commonwealth.
While a number of other former colonies have overturned or repealed colonial-era sodomy laws — with England and Wales decriminalizing gay male sex in the 1960s — similar restrictions remain in dozens of others.
The Privy Council had been asked to rule on Trinidad and Tobago’s law after it was challenged by Jason Jones, an LGBTQ+ rights activist who was born in Trinidad and lives in the U.K. Jones first challenged the law in the High Court of Trinidad and Tobago, winning a victory in 2018, but the islands’ Court of Appeal overturned that ruling in 2025. Jones and his attorneys then took the case to the Privy Council for a final appeal.
Activists and legal experts say the judgment could pave the way for similar challenges from campaigners in other former colonies that still criminalize gay sex. At least four other former British colonies in the Caribbean — Jamaica, Guyana, Grenada and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines — criminalize sexual activity between men, according to the UK charity Human Dignity Trust, though not all are in the Privy Council’s appellate jurisdiction.
Ahead of the ruling, Jones said he had filed his lawsuit to kick off a movement toward equality, though he acknowledged there was a long road ahead.
“My case is not just about decriminalizing (gay sexual acts in) countries in the Commonwealth that carry these British colonial-era laws. It’s about making people aware (of) how homophobia is being weaponized to take away our democratic rights,” he said.
Beyond LGBTQ+ rights, the case highlights how Britain’s imperialist legacy continues to influence the legal systems of some of its former colonies and has led many to question why some now-independent countries still cling to policies dropped by their former ruler decades ago.
“We have to still think about the fact that these laws were inherited from our colonial masters,” said Ria Mohammed, an attorney and director of the Caribbean Centre for Human Rights. “They (the British) have long since abandoned them. So why are we holding on to them?”
An ancient law
The origin of the law goes back centuries, with England passing a “Buggery Act” during Henry VIII’s rule in the 1500s. The British Empire later enacted a version of it in Trinidad and Tobago with a 1925 act.
After Trinidad became independent, it kept the ban in place due to a savings law clause that shields pre-independence laws from being challenged, Mohammed said. The clause was originally created by the British as a temporary measure to prevent legal vacuums as ex-colonies transitioned to independence, but some ex-colonies including Trinidad and Tobago continue to implement them. Critics say that has allowed outdated policies that no longer meet modern societal standards to remain in force in some countries.
In 1986, Trinidad and Tobago repealed the sexual offenses laws of the 1925 act and introduced new, tougher measures which increased prison sentences for offenders and punished women for indecency, too. It was this move that paved the way for Jones’ challenge to the law.
Jones’ lawyers argued that the new 1986 measures were distinct from those in the colonial-era act of 1925, so they weren’t protected by the savings law clause and could indeed be challenged.
“This is no longer blaming Henry VIII and the British. This is our own homegrown homophobia,” Jones told CNN.
The Privy Council agreed, ruling on Tuesday that the criminalization of private sexual acts between consenting adults is not immune to challenge.
It ruled that clauses that immunize old laws from challenge based on fundamental constitutional rights “should be interpreted narrowly” so they don’t protect large areas of old law from scrutiny.
“Whatever might have been the position in 1986, the current understanding of the fundamental individual right to respect for private and family life is that it protects such a core part of human identity as one’s sexual orientation and the sexual activities carried out in private between consenting adults to give expression to that identity,” Sales said.
The ‘ultimate irony’
The judgment applies to Trinidad and Tobago only. However, activists hope it could pave the way to challenges against gay sex bans in some of the other former colonies that still use the London-based court as their highest appeals court.
“The decision is going to be binding in Trinidad and Tobago. But as a matter of logic, if you are a part of the appellate structure of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council … it is unlikely that a case from a different jurisdiction would be decided in a different way,” Mohammed said.
As a result, the outcome of the case is likely to be closely watched across the English-speaking Caribbean, where several former colonies have kept the Privy Council as their final court of appeal while also continuing to maintain laws against gay sex.
In some of these countries, Jones’ case has renewed debate about whether they should replace the Privy Council with the Caribbean Court of Justice as their final court of appeal.
Five countries (Belize, Guyana, Barbados, Saint Lucia and Dominica) have already done so.
Mohammed said it was ironic that to settle a challenge on a colonial-era policy, Trinidad and Tobago had to use the judicial system of its former colonial ruler.
“That is the ultimate irony, and it also is a moment for us to sit and reflect about what are we really doing?” she said. “It really is about us having a mature conversation about what kind of society do we want to build.”

title: Housekeeper finds woman dead in cruise ship cabin, man standing at door with bloody hands, FBI says
text:
(AP) - A cruise ship passenger accused of killing his wife after the vessel set off from Texas told authorities that he struck her in their cabin and strangled her after an argument caused him to “snap,” according to an FBI affidavit made public Tuesday.
Jason Watford, 48, appeared in federal court on a murder charge in Galveston, where the MSC Seascape had departed over the weekend but returned to port after security aboard the ship discovered a body in his room.
The victim was identified as Susan Watford, the suspect’s wife, FBI spokesman Connor Hagan said. He added that a child was found unharmed when law enforcement responded. Court records show that Jason Watford had previously pleaded guilty to a charge of assaulting his wife in 2024.
Javier Martinez, a public defender assigned to represent Jason Watford, did not respond to a phone message Tuesday. A man who said he is Watford’s son declined to comment when reached by phone.
Couple had boarded the ship together, authorities say
The MSC Seascape is a towering white vessel that has 2,270 cabins and can host nearly 5,900 guests on five- and seven-night trips to the Caribbean, according to the company’s website.
In an interview with FBI agents Monday, Watford said he and Susan boarded the vessel together Sunday and started to argue while having dinner at one of the ship’s restaurants, according to the affidavit. The argument continued in their room, it said. Watford told agents he struck the woman several times and “applied pressure” to her neck, the affidavit said.
“Subject stated that Victim 1 and he continued to engage in an escalating verbal dispute that caused him to ‘snap,’” the agent wrote in the affidavit, referring to the couple.
Jason Watford opened their room’s door for a ship housekeeper with blood on his hands and clothes, according to court records. The housekeeper spotted a woman on the floor with facial injuries, and an investigator on the cruise ship contacted authorities.
Surveillance video showed that Watford entered the room at 7:46 p.m. and Susan went in about 25 minutes later, authorities said. At 9:15 p.m., he was seen on the video leaving the room wearing a different shirt and pants from when he answered the door for the housekeeper, according to the complaint, and sat on the hallway floor looking at his phone.
Husband was taken into custody after ship returned
Watford was taken into custody the next morning after the vessel returned to Galveston, where a passenger on the ship posted a video of Watford being escorted off the ship in handcuffs.
Court records show Watford, of Tyler, Texas, was arrested in September 2024 after Susan Watford told an officer that her husband grabbed her wrist during an argument over money in Smith County, about 100 miles (161 kilometers) east of Dallas.
The officer wrote that Susan Watford had recorded audio of the incident in which her husband could be heard becoming aggravated as she yelled at him to back away, court records show. She ran and used a stun gun, according to court records.
Jason Watford pleaded guilty to assault causing bodily injury to a family member and was placed on community supervision for 15 months, court records show.
The cruise resumed its voyage Monday. MSC Cruises said in a statement that it was cooperating with authorities and providing support to those impacted.
Watford’s next court appearance in Galveston was set for Monday.
Homicide investigations on cruise ships are uncommon. Earlier this year, a teenager was charged with murder and aggravated sexual abuse in the death of his 18-year-old stepsister on a Carnival Cruise ship out of Florida.
___
Associated Press writer Claudia Lauer in Philadelphia contributed.

title: University of Maine at Fort Kent opens Student Veteran Center
text:
FORT KENT, Maine (WAGM) - The University of Maine at Fort Kent has opened its first Student Veteran Center in Cyr Hall, giving student veterans a place to spend time between classes.
The center opened as the school held its annual veterans ceremony honoring those who served.
Ceremony at Veterans Square
The national anthem played, flags were raised, and a wreath was laid before James Moulton, a combat veteran of 11 years, spoke at the podium. Moulton is retired from the service and is a full-time student at UMFK.
“When you’re full-time, active duty, let’s say, or any kind of sergeant military, you’re used to a set structure routine. And coming out of that can be super difficult,” Moulton said.
He said he and his family moved to Fort Kent without knowing anyone.
“And going into a whole new setting where, quite literally, my family and I, we moved up here and we didn’t know anybody,” Moulton said.
The Student Veteran Center
Moulton searched across the country for a place to start that next chapter of his life. Fort Kent’s peaceful setting and small classes stood out to him. And now the university has a space for students like him.
“The center opening up is a great thing for veterans. Since a lot of us, we like a quiet space, we can get kind of a way to unwind. It definitely helps out with that, especially for commuting students, for some of us that live pretty far away. There’s some big gaps between classes,” Moulton said.
Stacy Martin, student life coordinator at UMFK, helped create the center. She said it gives veterans two spaces: one for quiet and one for connection.
“It’s a really cozy space on campus that there’s like an office space so they could just sit and do some more quiet time, and then in the other space it’s more like a comfortable cozy hangout where there’s games, old-fashioned games, cards, also an air fryer, a fridge, and a place for them to have snacks,” Martin said.
UMFK President Deb Hedeen said the campus is small and the student veteran population is smaller. She said having any student veterans was reason enough to open the center.
“But even if we only have a few, they still deserve to have a space to be able to spend time,” Hedeen said.
School leaders hope the center draws more military and veteran students, like Moulton, to campus.

title: Video shows small plane clipping pickup truck while landing on busy Florida road
text:
Video shows small plane clipping pickup truck while landing on busy Florida road
New video captures the tense moment a small plane made an emergency landing on Bayshore Road in North Fort Myers, Florida, surprising drivers and leaving everyone involved safe.
Brian Adams, a Lee County resident, was driving his blue Nissan when he saw the plane descending toward the road.
"My first thought is, 'boy, that's flying really low,'" Adams said. "Then almost immediately you go, 'oh no, it's about to land right in front of me.'"
The Lee County Sheriff's Office said the two people aboard the plane, Eric Santana and Armando Gomez, were safe. Juan Torres, whose truck was struck by the plane, was also not hurt.
Adams said he spoke with Torres immediately after the landing.
"I talked to the guy in the truck real quick," said Adams. "He asked me how I was doing. I go, 'I'm not the one that was hit by a plane.'"
Video Below: Driver captures plane making emergency landing
The plane's owner was not aboard and said his flight instructor was at the controls, according to the information provided.
The sheriff's office also noted that the same plane previously made an emergency landing on U.S. 98 in August. Santana and Gomez were returning to Fort Myers following that landing in Sebring.
Adams said he was relieved everyone involved was safe.
"I am definitely going to stick with commercial aircraft myself if I'm traveling," Adams said.
On Sunday, another plane crashed in Southwest Florida, leading to the rescue of the pilot from mangrove in Estero Bay.
The pilot was identified as Curt Hosterman. He was flying from Page Field when the plane's engine shut off over Fort Myers Beach. He said restarted it and turned back toward Page Field, but the engine shut off again before he could reach the airport. The Lee County Sheriff's Office Aviation Unit rescued him from the aircraft.
Video Below: Pilot ID'd after emergency landing in Estero Bay mangroves

title: Pingree, Golden vote with fellow Democrats as House Republicans stifle Hegseth impeachment
text:
House Republicans effectively halted the effort by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Kentucky, and Democrats to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday.
Massie filed the resolution in the House on Monday as lawmakers returned to Washington. Tuesday’s vote was a procedural attempt by Republicans to stop the impeachment push by sending the matter back to committee, the Associated Press reported.
The motion passed 211-204, with multiple Democrats and Republicans missing the vote. Massie was the lone Republican to cross party lines.
Maine’s U.S. Reps. Chellie Pingree and Jared Golden joined fellow Democrats in voting against sending it back to committee.
Massie’s resolution included eight counts of impeachment. It largely focused on the war in Iran but also included references to Hegseth’s role in carrying out military actions in Yemen and Venezuela, AP reported.
However, Tuesday’s vote may only delay the matter, with Democrats set to take control of both the House and Senate in January.

title: Novel by Maine author was shortlisted for literary prize
text:
A book by Maine novelist Elizabeth Strout was shortlisted for the Booker Prize.
The novel, “The Things We Never Say,” is about a friendly high school history teacher who secretly struggles with suicidal feelings, until a near-death experience renews his desire to live. He then discovers a worldview-altering secret about his wife, which he must grapple with alongside his horror at the results of the 2024 presidential election.
When writing the novel, Strout took inspiration from an obituary photo of a kind-looking upstate New York man, and from an acquaintance’s story about rescuing a drowning man.
“The Things We Never Say” was among six books shortlisted for the prize, which was ultimately awarded to M John Harrison’s post-apocalyptic novel “The End of Everything,” the first science fiction novel to win the Booker award, the leading prize for English language literature.
The other shortlisted books were “The Disappearers” by Marlon James, “Black Bag” by Luke Kennard, “May We Feed the King” by Rebecca Perry and “John of John” by Douglas Stuart.

title: ICE increases security at Scarborough facility amid vandalism, armed protests
text:
ICE increases security at Scarborough facility amid vandalism, armed protests
Vandalism and the presence of near-daily protesters, some of them armed, has led to increased security at the Scarborough ICE facility, according to a spokesperson for the agency
ICE increases security at Scarborough facility amid vandalism, armed protests
Vandalism and the presence of near-daily protesters, some of them armed, has led to increased security at the Scarborough ICE facility, according to a spokesperson for the agency
Vandalism and the presence of near-daily protesters, some of them armed, have led to increased security at the Scarborough ICE facility, according to a spokesperson for the agency.
There has been a small group of protesters outside the Scarborough facility ever since ICE agent David Brouillette shot and killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a Colombian father, when he was leaving for work in Biddeford last July.
According to the lawyer for Guerrero's widow and members of Maine's congressional delegation, Guerrero was not the intended target of the ICE operation and was in the U.S. under a valid federal work authorization.
Nearly four months after his death, ICE observers still have a presence outside the agency's facility on Manson Libby Road in Scarborough. Some are monitoring the movements of agents in and out of the facility and sharing that information on social media. Others are calling for the prosecution of Brouillette and "abolishing" ICE entirely, arguing that the Trump administration's immigration crackdown is unlawful and is spreading fear within immigrant communities in Maine.
Those fears were cited by the Maine Immigrant Rights Coalition on Monday, when the organization notified community members that recent sightings of "several new vehicles" arriving at the Scarborough facility were assigned to building security, not immigration enforcement.
"We understand that any increase in immigration enforcement presence can cause fear and uncertainty," wrote Ruben Torres, the director of advocacy and policy at the Maine Immigrant Rights Coalition. "We are sharing this update to provide context and help community members distinguish this change in Scarborough ICE building security from broader enforcement activity."
Democratic congresswoman Chellie Pingree took to Facebook to share a similar message, writing that security had increased specifically because of armed protesters.
"Mainers deserve to know what’s happening in their communities and I’m continuing to monitor the situation closely," wrote Rep. Pingree. "Maine has endured too much chaos and violence at the hands of this rogue, unaccountable agency already."
On Tuesday, at least one protester could be seen outside the Scarborough facility with a firearm. Open carry is legal in Maine, assuming the firearm holder is legally allowed to possess one.
A spokesperson for ICE told Maine's Total Coverage Tuesday that the agency's officers are "under constant threat from violent agitators." The spokesperson claimed that there have been six different occasions of vandalism at the Scarborough facility in the past three months.
ICE would not disclose whether the agency had plans for increased enforcement operations in Maine, citing "operational security purposes."

title: Brewer considers changes to data center rules
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Brewer Planning Board voted Monday to recommend that the City Council approve changes to the city’s rules governing data center projects.
A public information session on the proposed changes is scheduled for 6 p.m. Tuesday, Nov. 24, at the Brewer Auditorium. The Brewer City Council is scheduled to consider the amendments Dec. 8 and again Jan. 12, 2027.
In its meeting notice, the city said it isn’t currently negotiating with any data center developers. The amendments would establish rules for evaluating future proposals and would not approve a particular development.
The amendments would strengthen requirements governing data center development and operations while increasing the allowable size from 20 to 50 megawatts in the Industrial 2 zoning district, which is primarily located behind the Brewer landfill.
The proposed amendments “are intended to balance economic opportunity with strong local oversight,” according to the notice. “They are designed to encourage investment that could strengthen Brewer’s tax base while ensuring that any future development remains subject to rigorous review, clear performance standards, and ongoing accountability to the community.”
The city said it worked with a noise engineer to develop stronger noise standards and ongoing monitoring requirements.
The amendments would require closed-loop cooling for server racks and IT equipment, with all process wastewater treated by Brewer’s wastewater system.
They would also require supporting studies addressing noise, water supply, wastewater and public safety, along with monitoring and reporting before construction and during operation.
A developer would be required to enter into a binding community benefit agreement with the city, subject to City Council review and approval.

title: Lynda Yarborough Giard (1942-2026)
Trump says FBI is looking at Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged Chinese agent
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Monday that the FBI is investigating Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese government agent, but said he doesn’t think the executive who has helped to develop artificial intelligence has a reason to worry.
“I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he’ll be in good shape,” Trump said at a White House briefing.
The sudden emergence of Huang’s infidelity has rocked the political class and America’s tech sector, creating new concerns about whether China has been able to access the cutting-edge chips designed by Nvidia that are powering the development of artificial intelligence.
Trump suggested the extraordinary step of directly involving himself in a counterintelligence investigation, a sign of his friendly relationship with Huang and the possible geopolitical stakes.
“I did speak to him today just to see if he’s feeling all right, how you’re doing,” Trump said. ”He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.”
Huang — a singular figure in the technology landscape and one of the world’s wealthiest people — has acknowledged he had an affair, issuing an apology to his wife and to the company in an open letter posted on Nvidia’s website. The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence determined that the woman was gathering information for Beijing.
“I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security,” Huang said in his letter.
Nvidia announced Sunday it was conducting an independent investigation into reports that Huang was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.”
The episode also is attracting congressional scrutiny, with top Democrats Sen. Mark Warner and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries saying Monday they are interested in investigating it further. Jeffries said the Nvidia issue came up during a closed-door session with the CIA director and the Director of National Intelligence that was primarily about Iran.
“We’re going to need a full briefing, specifically as it relates to the Nvidia issue, so we can all get to the bottom of what has happened,” he said, “and what the implications are in terms of America’s national security.”
China has denied a plot to ensnare Nvidia’s chief
Trump is slated to meet next week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, but he was noncommittal about bringing up the situation with Xi.
“No, I don’t think so,” Trump said. “I mean, maybe. I’m sure President Xi will ask me about it. I just know Jensen very well. I just think he’s a very honorable man.”
FBI counterintelligence investigations often examine efforts by foreign powers to spy on the United States, whether by surreptitiously stealing technology designed by American companies, covertly waging foreign influence campaigns aimed at shaping public opinion or cultivating relationships with powerful political and industry figures. Such investigations can take years and do not necessarily culminate in criminal charges. China has been regarded across presidential administrations of both political parties as a persistent counterintelligence threat.
China denied Monday that it engaged in an attempt to ensnare Huang. “The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China,” Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.
Beijing earlier had dismissed The New York Times report saying Huang had developed a close relationship with a Chinese citizen named Alice Huang, who ran a company that last year faced claims it was illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China.
Huang has had Trump’s ear on AI regulation
Huang and Nvidia play a critical role in the artificial intelligence industry as many of the world’s leading AI developers rely on the company’s specialized chips to power their systems. Huang has also helped persuade Trump to take a lighter touch on regulating AI, arguing that existing laws could cover any security issues stemming from the technology and that individual companies should behave responsibly with the products they develop and release.
Huang also has lobbied Washington to loosen limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China in recent years, winning Trump’s approval for selling its H200 chips this year. It’s unclear if Beijing would allow Chinese companies to buy those chips in large quantities. Nvidia said in a regulatory filing in August that it has sold only a small amount to China as such sales are restricted by the Chinese government.
The H200 chips are not Nvidia’s most cutting-edge models, but they are still advanced. Previously, Huang also lobbied Trump to be allowed to sell Nvidia’s less-advanced H20 chips, which were designed to comply with U.S. export restrictions on China.
In an exclusive interview with The Associated Press in June, Huang said: “National security should always be the top concern of all technologies. But having said that, you know, you have to be very specific about the risk that you’re concerned about, before setting up policies for export controls.”
Nvidia shares dropped more than 4% in trading Monday. Nvidia stock has shed roughly 11% of its value since last Wednesday.
Attention turns to a data center company in Singapore
The New York Times said Alice Huang was a former executive of a Singapore-based data center company called Megaspeed International, whose website prominently touts its partnership with Nvidia.
Many offices in Singapore were closed Monday for a holiday. Megaspeed and the Singapore Ministry of Home Affairs did not immediately reply to requests for comment.
Nvidia is one of the world’s most valuable publicly traded companies, alongside Apple and Microsoft. Its sales of computer chips to China have at times been targeted by U.S. regulators seeking to limit Beijing’s access to such technology.
“The key questions are whether he was aware of any espionage activities and whether any confidential or strategically sensitive information was compromised,” said George Chen, a partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, a Washington-based consultancy.
“Those questions require evidence rather than speculation,” he added in a text message to reporters.
Chinese media have largely focused on Huang admitting to the affair and state media outlets have mainly echoed the official government line. Some have said the New York Times report was aimed at destabilizing U.S.-China relations.
“Whenever China-US relations begin to improve, there are often those firing shots from the shadows,” the state-owned Global Times said.
___
Associated Press writers Chan Ho-him in Hong Kong, Huizhong Wu in Bangkok, Barbara Ortutay in San Francisco and Eric Tucker and Lisa Mascaro in Washington contributed to this report. Huamani reported from Los Angeles.

title: Flagg scores season-high 43 points in Mavs' win over Paces
text:
Cooper Flagg scores season-high 43 points in Mavericks' win over Paces
Maine native also finished with 10 rebounds, marking his fourth straight double-double
Cooper Flagg scores season-high 43 points in Mavericks' win over Paces
Maine native also finished with 10 rebounds, marking his fourth straight double-double
Maine native Cooper Flagg scored a season-high 43 points and grabbed 10 rebounds in the Dallas Mavericks' 125-122 win over the Indiana Pacers.
Flagg, 19, of Newport, also finished Monday's game in Dallas with a team-high six assists and three steals while also blocking a shot.
According to the Mavericks' basketball communications department, Flagg became the second teenager in NBA history to record at least 40 points, 10 rebounds and five assists in a game. The first player to achieve that feat was Kevin Durant, who finished with 42 points, 13 rebounds and six assists for the Seattle SuperSonics in a over the Golden State Warriors on April 16, 2008.
This also marked the fourth straight game in which Flagg has finished with a double-double. Flagg recorded 19 points and 10 rebounds in a 112-111 loss to the San Antonio Spurs on Nov. 4; 21 points and 10 rebounds in a 112-100 win against the Utah Jazz in an NBA Cup game on Nov. 6; and 25 points and a career-high 12 assists in a 130-93 victory against the Brooklyn Nets on Sunday.
"Whenever I get out there on the court, it just goes back to being a competitor and trying to make as many winning plays as I can and trying to make the easy, right basketball play out there," Flagg said after Monday's game.
The 2025-26 NBA Rookie of the Year is off to a strong start in his second NBA season. Entering Tuesday, Flagg is tied for 11th in the league in scoring with an average of 25.9 points per game. He is shooting 50% from the field and is averaging 6.9 rebounds, 6.9 assists, 2.2 steals and 0.8 blocks per game.
Flagg and the Mavericks will be back in action on Thursday, when Dallas faces the Minnesota Timberwolves on the road.

title: Gorham holds community meeting about gas safety at Narragansett Elementary
text:
Gorham holds community meeting about gas safety at Narragansett Elementary School
Officials in the town of Gorham held a meeting with members of the community Monday night to discuss safety at Narragansett Elementary School following recent natural gas issues.
Classes at Narragansett Elementary were canceled on Nov. 4 after a gas odor was reported that morning. The school reopened on Nov. 5 after no gas leaks were detected during an inspection conducted by the Gorham Fire Department, Johnson & Jordan and Unitil.
Officials believed that the gas odor was caused by an air handler that was drawing in gas that had been vented outside from the building's regulators. Additional testing was conducted before students arrived at the school on the morning of Nov. 5.
During the community meeting, officials said daily air quality checks at the school will continue.
"The risk with gas is when it goes 'boom.' For it to go 'boom,' there has to be a certain level of gas within the environment, and we call the minimum level of that the lower explosive limit. So when I get to the lower explosive limit, I can possibly go 'boom,'" said Gorham Assistant EMS Chief Phil MacCallum.
In December 2025, Narragansett Elementary was evacuated in the middle of a school day and then closed for two straight days following a gas leak.

title: Obituary: Bradley D. Krehel
text:
HARPSWELL – Bradley D. Krehel 67, of Harpswell, died on Nov. 6, 2026 at 12:09 a.m., at home with family by his side. He was a five time U.S. Martial Arts Hall of Fame Inductee. In 1994 he travelled with karate team to China, Hong Kong and Korea.
He enjoyed the outdoors hiking, bird hunting and fly fishing. He was a missionary in the ’80s to help build hospitals and shelters in Nicaragua, Guatamala and Costa Rica. Brad loved playing the drums with the Christian Worship band “Word for Word”. Brad loved to make his sisters laugh.
His greatest love was his wife Michelle and their cats.
He retired from General Dynamics – Bath Iron Works where he worked for 17 years as a senior planner working in OP Cycle Mgmt Department. He graduated from Southern Connecticut State University, New Haven, Conn., in 1981, with a Bachelor of Science in Economics.
Predeceased by his mother Maureen J. Dunphy Pavelko, stepdad Robert Pavelko and father John J.
