title: Maine Soccer Coaches Name 2026 Regional All-star Teams Across All Classes
Why Susan Collins lost
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Gordon L. Weil formerly wrote for the Washington Post and other newspapers, served on the U.S. Senate and EU staffs, headed Maine state agencies and was a Harpswell selectman.
In 1987, I testified for Susan Collins to be confirmed as Maine Commissioner of Professional and Financial Regulation, a position both my wife and I had previously held. My support proved justified as she did well in the post. She deserves great credit for her efforts reforming workers compensation.
Collins was smart, competent and a member of a prominent Republican family that placed public service above political partisanship. She once told me that she prized that tradition and sought to honor it. But political moderation became impossible. Adjusting to the GOP’s rightward shift became both a challenge and the ultimate source of the loss of her U.S. Senate seat.
When she went to Washington in 1997, she embodied that moderate tradition and promised to serve no more than two terms, evidence of her Senate tenure being public service not the beginning of a career stretching until 2027. The changing political atmosphere and her own political ambition had their effect on her moderate stance.
In Maine, the Republican Party abandoned its good-government legacy for more conservative partisanship. To avert challenges from the right, Collins accommodated the new GOP. She maintained the image of civil moderation, allowing the GOP to hold onto the Senate seat by tolerating her lack of complete loyalty.
In Washington, she also adjusted to conservative reality. To gain Senate influence, she had to serve her party’s needs, accepting its national policies while her demeanor allowed her to continue to project moderation at home. But she needed to manage her political balance as Maine moved toward the Democrats. By 2020, her election margin had narrowed.
She served with fellow Republican Sen. Olympia Snowe, a moderate dedicated to compromise. The contrast showed in the office space and committee assignments each was given by GOP leadership. Collins could see the rewards of party loyalty, while Snowe stuck to her independence. Ultimately Snowe chose to leave the Senate, while Collins climbed.
In Congress, members vote themselves “earmarks,” payments enabling each to take credit for bringing home federal money. Earmarks were temporarily abandoned, but returned when incumbents could not resist their value in convincing voters to send them back for more. To help her keep her seat, the party made Collins a prime harvester of federal cash.
With a bit of good luck, Collins rose to leadership of the Appropriations Committee, supposedly having a key role in deciding federal spending. That helped in doling out earmarks, but the GOP’s unquestioning acceptance of President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill meant her legislative power was limited. She never exercised the influence she might have expected, but she hung on.
She could not use her almost demure image as protection in every situation. She continues to be attacked for her vote to confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court. To many, he seemed sure to vote to overturn Roe v. Wade, but Collins interpreted her interview with him as assurance that he would not reverse its precedent.
The undercurrent of his failure to perform as she expected was that either she had been easily duped or that she was not telling voters the truth when she went along with Trump’s nominee. She could never overcome such negative vibes.
Though the Maine media may have cast her as a titan based on her five terms, she isn’t in the same league as Margaret Chase Smith, Ed Muskie, Bill Cohen or George Mitchell. All of them became nationally known figures and took political risks, bringing reflected credit to Maine. That aura may still matter to Maine voters, and it was missing.
Her claim to moderation became hollow as time passed. She occasionally expressed opposition to Trump, though it usually made no difference in critical votes. She was not a leader who boldly took him on, ready to take political risks. Her statements lacked force and became temporizing — speaking just enough to suit the needs of the moment.
Any person who holds public office long enough loses support, because some constituents will always be disappointed by their actions. To some degree, political campaigning is meant to remind voters of the best and gloss over problems. Campaigns depend on attacking the opponent. Collins did all that, and some ads run by her backers conflicted with her image.
She lost because of Trump, though not only because she had followed the loyalist GOP leadership. She failed to recognize that her earmarks for firehouses meant little compared with the cost of gas, heating oil and food, increased by his tariffs and, above all, the Iran war.
On Feb. 28, the day the war with Iran began, Trump began to lose the midterms, ultimately toppling the Republican Congress. I believe Collins might have saved herself if she had taken the risk of becoming the outspoken leader Maine wanted and needed. The winner by default was Troy Jackson.

title: Your guide to holiday fun across western Maine and beyond
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
FARMINGTON — From high school gym craft fairs to the 50th anniversary of Chester Greenwood Day, western Maine’s holiday season is packed with events this year.
At least a dozen craft fairs are scheduled across Franklin and Oxford counties in November, giving shoppers plenty of chances to buy handmade gifts close to home. December brings tree lightings, festivals of trees, library storytimes, holiday concerts and fireworks at Sugarloaf.
The busiest stretch comes Dec. 4-6. Farmington marks the 50th annual Chester Greenwood Day, Livermore hosts Olde Fashioned Christmas at the Norlands, and holiday events are planned in Rangeley, Stratton, Kingfield and other communities.
Organizers sometimes change times, locations or snow dates, so visitors should check with event hosts before heading out.
CRAFT FAIRS
Holiday shoppers can find handmade gifts nearly every weekend in November and into December.
Temple: The Temple Craft Fair will be held Nov. 14 from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m. at Temple Town Hall.
Rangeley: The RLRS Class of 2027 Craft Fair will be held Nov. 14 from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. at Rangeley Lakes Regional School, 43 Mendolia Road. Juniors will raise money for class activities, with concessions and a 50/50 raffle also planned.
Farmington: The Mt. Blue High School Fall Craft Fair will be held Nov. 21 from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m. at Mt. Blue High School. Vendors from across Maine will sell handmade items, and the fair will also include concessions and basket raffles.
Fayette: Friends of Starling Hall will hold its Holiday Craft Fair on Nov. 21 from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m. at Fayette Central School. Area craftspeople will sell handmade gifts. A Sunday snow date is planned.
New Vineyard: The New Vineyard Public Library will sponsor its annual Craft and Bake Sale on Nov. 21 from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. at Smith Hall. Wreaths, hand-painted items and baked goods will be available.
Rangeley: The 31st annual Holly Fair will be held Nov. 21 from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. at the Congo Barn, 2 High St. Handmade items, gift baskets, jams, baked goods and specialty canned goods will be available.
Jay: The Spruce Mountain High School Holiday Craft Fair will be held Nov. 28 from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. at the school, 33 Community Drive. The annual fair moves to Thanksgiving weekend this year, making it a Small Business Saturday stop.
Waterford: The Waterford Inne Winter Market will be held Nov. 29 from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m.
Oxford: The Oxbow Beer Garden Holiday Pottery Sale will be held Nov. 29 from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m.
Rangeley: The Good Shepherd Holiday Fair will be held Dec. 4-5 at the Church of the Good Shepherd. Times are still to be announced.
Farmington: The UMF Chester Greenwood Day Craft Fair will be held Dec. 5 at the Olsen Student Center. Craftspeople and student entrepreneurs will sell gifts during Chester Greenwood Day festivities.
Bethel: A Christmas Fair and Tea is scheduled for Dec. 5 and is listed on the Bethel Area Chamber of Commerce calendar. Additional details are still to be announced.
Mercer: The Hometown Holiday Market will be held Dec. 5 from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m. at the Mercer Community Center, 1015 Beech Hill Road. Local makers and vendors will gather for holiday shopping.
Carrabassett Valley: The Holiday Artisans Market will be held Dec. 12-13 on the second floor of the Sugarloaf Mountain Hotel. UpCountry Artists will present more than 15 artists selling jewelry, paintings, textiles and ceramics during Sugarloaf’s Tree Lighting Festival.
Jay: The St. Rose of Lima Christmas Craft Fair is returning Nov. 21 from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m.
Phillips: The Phillips Area Community Center Holiday Craft Fair is expected to return at 21 Depot St. Date and time are still to be announced.
Wilton: A holiday craft fair is expected in Wilton. Date, time and location are still to be announced.
Festivals, parades and tree lightings
Kingfield: First Friday Artwalks will be held Nov. 6 and Dec. 4 beginning at 5 p.m. in downtown Kingfield. Local galleries and shops will open their doors, with the December walk doubling as a holiday shopping night.
Farmington: Ladies Night Out will be held Nov. 12 in downtown Farmington. Downtown merchants will host an evening of holiday shopping. Hours are still to be announced.
Rangeley: The Lighting of the Giving Tree will be held Nov. 28 at Lakeside Park. Gifts collected at the tree go to neighbors in need. Rangeley Adventure Company will also host Flannel Friday on Nov. 27.
Farmington: The Chester Greenwood Day Tree Lighting will be held Dec. 4 at 5 p.m. at the Franklin County Superior Courthouse, 140 Main St. The lighting will kick off the anniversary weekend.
Farmington: The 50th annual Chester Greenwood Day will be held Dec. 5 in downtown Farmington. The celebration honors Farmington native Chester Greenwood, who patented an improved earmuff design in 1877. This year’s parade theme is “Inventions Through Time,” and the Franklin County Chamber of Commerce is accepting float registrations. Parade time and the full schedule are still to be announced. The Rotary Club of Farmington traditionally holds its Festival of Trees the same day. The festival is scheduled for Dec. 5. We will be back at the Farmington community center this year. The trees will be open to the public for viewing at 11 a.m. and the auction will start at 6 p.m.
Livermore: Olde Fashioned Christmas at the Norlands and the Festival of Trees will run Dec. 4 from 4-7 p.m., Dec. 5 from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., and Dec. 6 from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. at the Washburn-Norlands Living History Center, 290 Norlands Road. The Jay-Livermore-Livermore Falls Chamber of Commerce and the Norlands will host the ninth annual celebration, with decorated trees and family activities. Saturday will also include crafts and a cookie walk. Admission is free.
Stratton: The Christmas Market and Festival of Trees will begin at 4 p.m. Dec. 4 at 8 Rangeley Road.

title: Who will lead Democrats, Republicans in the next session of Congress?
text:
Who will lead Democrats and Republicans in the next session of Congress?
House Republicans are bracing for a leadership battle after Speaker Mike Johnson announced he will not seek the minority leader position, setting up a contest between Steve Scalise and Jim Jordan.
Who will lead Democrats and Republicans in the next session of Congress?
House Republicans are bracing for a leadership battle after Speaker Mike Johnson announced he will not seek the minority leader position, setting up a contest between Steve Scalise and Jim Jordan.
House Republicans are preparing for a leadership battle today after Speaker Mike Johnson announced he will not run for minority leader, following Democrats flipping more than 40 seats in the chamber.
"I decided not to run for a minority leader," Johnson said. "I just didn't feel, after a lot of prayer and reflection, I didn't feel like that was the best thing for me to do."
On Monday, Johnson was asked if he would commit to serving out his two-year term in the 120th Congress.
"I'm still in charge here until early January, and we're going to do our duty," Johnson said. "After that, my commitment and my objective is to help my team ensure that the Republican Party has a very successful 120th Congress, and we'll see how all that develops, and that's my commitment."
Who is trying to lead the Republican Party?
This decision sets up a contest between Rep. Steve Scalise of Louisiana and Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio for the position of House minority leader. The two lawmakers previously faced off three years ago in a bid to become House Speaker.
Who will lead the Democratic Party?
Democrats are expected to hold their leadership elections later this month. In the Senate, Chuck Schumer is seeking to become the next Senate majority leader, while House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is vying for speaker of the House. Both leaders are facing resistance from some progressive members within their party.
"I'm gonna work hard to talk to every single member about what we've been able to do together over the last two years," Jeffries said.
So far, no one has officially stepped up to challenge Jeffries or Schumer for their respective leadership positions. However, Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said overnight that he is not closing the door on challenging Schumer next week.

title: House Republicans quash effort to impeach Defense Secretary Hegseth
text:
House Republicans quash effort to impeach Defense Secretary Hegseth
The House on Tuesday turned aside a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, halting an effort to remove the Pentagon chief for his conduct in office and his handling of the war in Iran.
The vote came as Republicans grapple with the fallout from sweeping midterm losses that some in the party have blamed on the war in Iran and the resulting surge in gas prices. But after President Donald Trump signaled strong support for Hegseth, GOP lawmakers largely stood by the secretary Tuesday. They rejected the impeachment effort led by Kentucky Republican Thomas Massie and backed by Democrats.
The vote may only delay an impeachment push against Hegseth, with Democrats set to take control of the House and Senate in January.
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become the next speaker when Democrats take charge in January, stood firmly behind the push, saying Hegseth has “abused his power” and “undermined America’s national security.”
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer endorsed Hegseth’s impeachment as well.
Hegseth rebuked the effort Tuesday in his first news conference in months, portraying Massie as a rogue lawmaker and arguing he had committed none of the high crimes required in the Constitution for his removal. He framed the effort as an indictment against the nation’s service members and their successes and said it was undermining American forces “in real time.”
“This is not patriotism,” Hegseth said. “This is sabotage.”
Massie's resolution included eight counts of impeachment. It largely focused on the war in Iran but also included references to Hegseth's role in carrying out military actions in Yemen and Venezuela.
Massie, a Kentucky Republican leaving Congress in January after losing his primary to a Trump-backed opponent, says Hegseth has “knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders."
Hegseth holds rare press conference
Tuesday morning, Hegseth gave a defiant and politicized defense of his stewardship of the U.S. military in his first news conference at the Pentagon in six months. He chose to hit back at the rising bipartisan anger over battlefield strategy while offering few details about intermittent operations against Iran or fatal strikes on alleged drug-smuggling boats in Latin America.
Trump praised Hegseth’s performance at the briefing in a social media post, while Vice President JD Vance said in his own post that the impeachment effort is “a ridiculous show that stands in for actual policymaking.”
Hegseth said the impeachment resolution “tells our enemies — Iran, the cartels, every adversary watching — the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership for successfully executing lawful military operations.”
An impeachment vote is looming in the House
Massie filed the resolution in the House on Monday, giving Republican leaders two days to bring it to a vote. Tuesday's vote was a procedural attempt to stop the impeachment push outright by sending the matter back to committee.
If the impeachment resolution had advanced, it would have set the stage for a dramatic vote Wednesday on whether to impeach a key Trump Cabinet member following sweeping losses for Republicans in last week's midterm elections, which many at least partly blamed on the Iran conflict and its economic impact. If the resolution had passed the House, it would ultimately be sent to the Senate, where a two-thirds vote would be needed for Hegseth's removal.
“The law requires our military to withdraw from hostilities within 60 days if Congress does not authorize the activity,” Massie wrote on social media Tuesday. The Iran war "has been underway for 256 days. Congress has not authorized it. Hegseth is breaking the law."
Massie’s resolution had eight counts of impeachment that focused on U.S. military actions or changes on Hegseth’s watch. They include reported reductions in staff and resources at a Pentagon office focused on mitigating civilian harm, which preceded a U.S. missile striking an Iranian primary school during the war, killing up to 168 people.
Another article of impeachment focused on Hegseth’s attempt to punish Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly, a retired Navy pilot, for participating in a video that called on troops to resist unlawful orders. Massie also called out U.S. military strikes on alleged drug-smuggling boats in Latin America and the failure to rescue survivors, which Massie argued will encourage adversaries to treat American forces the same way.
What constitutes “high crimes and misdemeanors” is not spelled out in the Constitution, leaving it to lawmakers to decide what are impeachable acts.
Hegseth said Massie’s concerns are not impeachable, calling them “policy disagreements, not high crimes, not misdemeanors, not treason, not bribery, not the kinds of offenses the founders intended when they wrote the impeachment clause.”
House Speaker Mike Johnson called it a “political gambit for attention” and predicted Republicans would defeat it “one way or the other.”
Jeffries said Monday that he was a “hard yes” on the resolution. He called Hegseth the “architect” of the war in Iran.
This isn't the first impeachment attempt in recent years
Hegseth cast Massie's resolution in historic terms, arguing that no defense secretary has been impeached in the nation's 250-year history “for carrying out lawful military operations.”
But more recently, a Cabinet official in President Joe Biden's administration, Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas, was impeached by House Republicans over his handling of the U.S.-Mexico border. The Senate dismissed all impeachment charges, shutting down his trial before arguments even began.
Mayorkas, who did not appear to testify before the impeachment proceedings, put the border crisis squarely on Congress for failing to update immigration laws during a time of global migration. Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer had said then, in April 2024, that House Republicans’ charges failed to meet “the high standard of high crimes and misdemeanors” and could set a dangerous precedent.
Republican Rep. Nick LaLota, who voted to impeach Mayorkas, said he didn't believe Hegseth had committed any impeachable offense.
“Impeachment has been watered down,” LaLota said.
Before Mayorkas, no sitting Cabinet secretary had ever been impeached. It was nearly 150 years ago that the House voted to impeach President Ulysses S. Grant’s war secretary, William Belknap, over a kickback scheme in government contracts. He resigned before the vote.
Trump offers support for Hegseth
Trump backed Hegseth in the wake of Massie's impeachment resolution, pointing to the U.S. military raid to capture then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January as well as operations against Iran that he asserts have “obliterated” its navy and air force.
“Pete Hegseth gets an “A” PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!” Trump wrote Tuesday on Truth Social.
Iran, however, has been able to keep striking U.S. military bases in the Middle East and has disrupted shipping in the Strait of Hormuz during the more than 8-month-old conflict, driving up global oil prices.

title: Meghan Markle’s father cut off his ankle monitor, DOJ says
text:
TAMPA, Fla. (AP) — The 82-year-old estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, was ordered to jail Tuesday because he removed an electronic monitoring device from his ankle, just days after he was charged with possession of child sexual abuse material.
Thomas Markle was arrested and appeared in federal court in Tampa, Florida, after authorities learned he had cut off the device at 1:45 a.m., First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said.
“Release conditions are court orders, not suggestions,” Essayli said.
Markle’s arrest on Friday in Lakeland, Florida, followed the seizure of approximately 78 items from storage units in the Los Angeles area, including slides, film negatives and books that contained suspected child sexual abuse images, said Essayli, a federal prosecutor in California.
Markle was living in a senior care center at the time. But U.S. Magistrate Judge Lindsay Griffin agreed Tuesday that Markle now must be kept in custody. Authorities have not said where he will be held while his case remains in court ahead of a likely transfer to California.
In her written order, Griffin noted Markle’s “housing situation” had become “untenable,” but did not elaborate. Defense attorney Mary Claire Wolf wanted to keep him out of custody but has not found a suitable place for Markle to stay, according to a hearing summary.
Essayli told The Associated Press he didn’t know why the ankle device was removed. It also wasn’t clear where it occurred. An email and phone message seeking comment from Wolf were not immediately returned.
Still pending, besides the charges: a mental competency exam for Markle.
He had a stroke earlier this year while living in the Philippines and had to have his left leg amputated. That forced him to return to the U.S.
The Sun, a British tabloid newspaper, reported that Meghan’s half brother found a collection of child sexual abuse images while clearing out their father’s home in the Philippines. That discovery led to information about the two U.S. storage units in California, which Markle had rented since 2008.
Markle’s daughter, Meghan, married Prince Harry at Windsor Castle in 2018. They have two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet. She is an American citizen and an actor who starred in the U.S. television drama “Suits.”
She recently said she was “deeply distressed” by allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images had been found at her father’s former home. She also revealed that a letter containing “troubling allegations” about him had been sent to police in London in 2019.

title: Ellsworth City Council recount delayed by Maine’s 2nd District race ranked-choice runoff
text:
Ellsworth is pausing its City Council election recount after state officials took custody of the city’s state ballots for the ranked-choice runoff between Republican Paul LePage and Democrat Matt Dunlap, who are vying to represent Maine’s 2nd Congressional District.
Ellsworth officials will complete its recount — requested by Tiffany Dilda Gaspar, who was seven votes short of second-place winner Robert Grant Sr. — once the state ballots are returned, according to Amy Kenney, the city’s communications director.
The state ballots are needed for the recount to ensure no municipal ballots were misplaced among them.
The Ellsworth recount marks the second year in a row in which the city council race is under scrutiny. Last year, a city recount confirmed initial results that area businessman and conservative activist John Linnehan lost by just two votes. Linnehan was elected to the city’s School Board this year after decades of failed runs for state and local public offices.
Though the ranked-choice runoff is currently underway, LePage has already declared victory and Dunlap has conceded. LePage joined incoming congressional members in Washington D.C. this week for orientation. The Bangor Daily News and its election results partner Decision Desk HQ have not yet called the race.
It was not immediately clear when the state ballots would be returned to Ellsworth.
In the interim, outgoing city councilors Patrick Lyons, who serves as the governing body’s chair and did not seek reelection, and Nancy Smith, who lost her November reelection bid, will continue to serve on the council. Lyons and Smith will both be at the council’s Monday meeting, according to city officials.
The winners in the races for the city’s school board and library board of trustees will be sworn in during the November council meeting, Kenney said.
Ellsworth officials have not yet announced a timeline for when the council recount will take place, but it is dependent on the state ballots being returned to the city.
All ballots will be reviewed during the recount, but only votes for Grant and Gaspar will be counted, according to city officials.
Ellsworth’s official City Council election results slightly varied from the unofficial results released on election night because the city had not initially tallied auxiliary ballots, which are paper ballots that couldn’t be processed by voting machines, Kenney said.
Auxiliary ballots can’t be counted by voting equipment for various reasons, like the voter using a pencil, incorrectly filling in the oval or making extra marks on the ballot, Kenney said.
Once the auxiliary ballots were counted after election night, the tallies marginally changed, though they had no effect on the election outcome.
Following the recount, former councilor Casey Hanson, who won first place in the November election, and the other winning candidate — either Grant or Gaspar — will be sworn into office.

title: Trump says FBI is looking at Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged Chinese agent
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Monday that the FBI is investigating Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese government agent, but said he doesn’t think the executive who has helped to develop artificial intelligence has a reason to worry.
“I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he’ll be in good shape,” Trump said at a White House briefing.
The sudden emergence of Huang’s infidelity has rocked the political class and America’s tech sector, creating new concerns about whether China has been able to access the cutting-edge chips designed by Nvidia that are powering the development of artificial intelligence.
Trump suggested the extraordinary step of directly involving himself in a counterintelligence investigation, a sign of his friendly relationship with Huang and the possible geopolitical stakes.
“I did speak to him today just to see if he’s feeling all right, how you’re doing,” Trump said. ”He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.”
Huang — a singular figure in the technology landscape and one of the world’s wealthiest people — has acknowledged he had an affair, issuing an apology to his wife and to the company in an open letter posted on Nvidia’s website. The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence determined that the woman was gathering information for Beijing.
“I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security,” Huang said in his letter.
Nvidia announced Sunday it was conducting an independent investigation into reports that Huang was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.”
The episode also is attracting congressional scrutiny, with top Democrats Sen. Mark Warner and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries saying Monday they are interested in investigating it further. Jeffries said the Nvidia issue came up during a closed-door session with the CIA director and the Director of National Intelligence that was primarily about Iran.
“We’re going to need a full briefing, specifically as it relates to the Nvidia issue, so we can all get to the bottom of what has happened,” he said, “and what the implications are in terms of America’s national security.”
China has denied a plot to ensnare Nvidia’s chief
Trump is slated to meet next week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, but he was noncommittal about bringing up the situation with Xi.
“No, I don’t think so,” Trump said. “I mean, maybe. I’m sure President Xi will ask me about it. I just know Jensen very well. I just think he’s a very honorable man.”
FBI counterintelligence investigations often examine efforts by foreign powers to spy on the United States, whether by surreptitiously stealing technology designed by American companies, covertly waging foreign influence campaigns aimed at shaping public opinion or cultivating relationships with powerful political and industry figures. Such investigations can take years and do not necessarily culminate in criminal charges. China has been regarded across presidential administrations of both political parties as a persistent counterintelligence threat.
China denied Monday that it engaged in an attempt to ensnare Huang. “The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China,” Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.
Beijing earlier had dismissed The New York Times report saying Huang had developed a close relationship with a Chinese citizen named Alice Huang, who ran a company that last year faced claims it was illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China.
Huang has had Trump’s ear on AI regulation
Huang and Nvidia play a critical role in the artificial intelligence industry as many of the world’s leading AI developers rely on the company’s specialized chips to power their systems. Huang has also helped persuade Trump to take a lighter touch on regulating AI, arguing that existing laws could cover any security issues stemming from the technology and that individual companies should behave responsibly with the products they develop and release.
Huang also has lobbied Washington to loosen limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China in recent years, winning Trump’s approval for selling its H200 chips this year. It’s unclear if Beijing would allow Chinese companies to buy those chips in large quantities. Nvidia said in a regulatory filing in August that it has sold only a small amount to China as such sales are restricted by the Chinese government.
The H200 chips are not Nvidia’s most cutting-edge models, but they are still advanced. Previously, Huang also lobbied Trump to be allowed to sell Nvidia’s less-advanced H20 chips, which were designed to comply with U.S. export restrictions on China.
In an exclusive interview with The Associated Press in June, Huang said: “National security should always be the top concern of all technologies. But having said that, you know, you have to be very specific about the risk that you’re concerned about, before setting up policies for export controls.”
Nvidia shares dropped more than 4% in trading Monday. Nvidia stock has shed roughly 11% of its value since last Wednesday.
Attention turns to a data center company in Singapore
The New York Times said Alice Huang was a former executive of a Singapore-based data center company called Megaspeed International, whose website prominently touts its partnership with Nvidia.
Many offices in Singapore were closed Monday for a holiday. Megaspeed and the Singapore Ministry of Home Affairs did not immediately reply to requests for comment.
Nvidia is one of the world’s most valuable publicly traded companies, alongside Apple and Microsoft. Its sales of computer chips to China have at times been targeted by U.S. regulators seeking to limit Beijing’s access to such technology.
“The key questions are whether he was aware of any espionage activities and whether any confidential or strategically sensitive information was compromised,” said George Chen, a partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, a Washington-based consultancy.
“Those questions require evidence rather than speculation,” he added in a text message to reporters.
Chinese media have largely focused on Huang admitting to the affair and state media outlets have mainly echoed the official government line. Some have said the New York Times report was aimed at destabilizing U.S.-China relations.
“Whenever China-US relations begin to improve, there are often those firing shots from the shadows,” the state-owned Global Times said.
___
Associated Press writers Chan Ho-him in Hong Kong, Huizhong Wu in Bangkok, Barbara Ortutay in San Francisco and Eric Tucker and Lisa Mascaro in Washington contributed to this report. Huamani reported from Los Angeles.

title: Rain & Snow Showers Possible This Afternoon & Evening
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A disturbance approaching from the Great Lakes Region will bring us a chance for some scattered rain and snow showers this afternoon mainly from Bangor northward. Otherwise expect partly to mostly cloudy skies today with highs in the 40s to near 50°. The disturbance will cross through the state this evening bringing more widespread rain showers through the state during the evening and first half of tonight. Northern locales will see a mix of rain and snow showers while the remainder of the state sees a chance of just plain rain showers. The shower activity will move out by midnight or shortly after... followed by mostly cloudy skies for the remainder of the night. Low temperatures tonight will drop to the 30s.
Veterans Day on Wednesday looks good with morning clouds giving way to some breaks of sunshine by late morning into the afternoon. High temperatures will climb to the 40s to near 50°. High pressure will nose in for Thursday giving us another decent day under partly to mostly cloudy skies and highs in the 40s.
We continue to keep our eyes on a potential storm for Friday into the weekend. There is still some uncertainty with regard to the track of the system which will determine what types of precipitation we see and how much precipitation we see. However... there is more agreement in the data this morning showing an inland track as being less likely and the data leaning towards more of an offshore track. The question now is... how far offshore will the storm be? Either way... an offshore track means lesser impact for Maine with just light precipitation expected. It’ll be cold enough so that rain and snow will be possible from Friday afternoon through the day Saturday. The exact track will be the key so stay tuned for updates as we get closer.

Thursday: Partly to mostly cloudy. Highs in the 40s to near 50°.

title: Death Notice: Beverley Jane Andrews
Democrats will now control more states. Could that mean an effective end to the Electoral College?
text:
Democrats have gained control in more states. Could that mean an effective end to the Electoral College?
The midterm elections already upended national politics. And with the number of state governments that have flipped to Democratic control, they also could change the way the U.S. elects a president.
The sudden blue tint to so many more statehouses opens the door to enough states joining 18 other Democratic-run states in a deal that would effectively neuter the Electoral College. It would remake the battle for the presidency into one for the most votes nationwide, rather than candidates concentrating on a half dozen or so swing states.
The states that have joined what is known as the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact account for 222 Electoral College votes. Once the number of states involved is high enough for the 270 electoral votes needed to win the presidency, the arrangement would effectively require a candidate to win the national popular vote to get an Electoral College majority.
It's not clear that the strategy has support from all the newly elected lawmakers and governors in the key states, and it's almost certain to draw legal challenges from conservative groups. If it does go forward, it could land before the conservative-majority Supreme Court.
Yet the sweep of the Democratic wins for governor and in state legislatures has the plan's supporters optimistic. In Tuesday's elections, Democrats won full control in six states representing 71 Electoral College votes: Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Minnesota, with its 10 electoral votes, had joined the compact when it was previously under full Democratic control in 2023.
Some governors express support while others are noncommittal
“We can do away with it,” Wisconsin's new Democratic Gov. David Crowley said of the Electoral College, now that he has a legislature in his party's hands for the first time in 16 years. “I am interested in having those conversations with the state Legislature.”
Over the weekend, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a likely 2028 contender for the Democratic presidential nomination, said he would like his newly Democratic legislature to take steps toward making the Electoral College obsolete.
"I think that the national popular vote makes sense. My views on that have not changed," Shapiro said on a liberal podcast. "I’ll work with lawmakers to figure out what the right mechanism is for moving forward on that."
If Pennsylvania and Wisconsin supported the compact, reaching the 270 threshold would require Michigan and either Arizona or Nevada to join. Michigan's new Democratic governor, Jocelyn Benson, did not respond to a request for comment.
Not every Democratic governor is embracing the push yet. In a television interview on Monday, Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs declined to say whether she favored her state joining the compact. She said she's focused on other things, like the cost of living.
Nevada’s previous experience with the issue also is a cautionary tale for supporters.
In 2019, then-Democratic Gov. Steve Sisolak vetoed a measure that would have committed Nevada to joining the compact after it was passed by Democratic majorities in both houses of the Legislature. Sisolak said at the time that the popular vote idea would diminish the influence of smaller-population states like Nevada in national elections.
Democrats passed another measure to join the compact in 2023, but couldn't figure out a way around the state's then-Republican governor. The incoming administration of its new Democratic governor, Aaron Ford, did not respond to requests for comment.
Republicans will use their diminished power to push back.
“Our Constitution gives states a voice in choosing the president for a reason,” Tyler August, the Republican leader in the Wisconsin Assembly, said in a statement Tuesday. “This would undermine that balance and disenfranchise Wisconsin voters by letting results in other states override their choice."
Two presidents 16 years apart lost the popular vote
The idea of shifting to a national popular vote gained traction among Democrats after Republican George W. Bush won the 2000 presidential election by inching ahead of Democrat Al Gore in the Electoral College even while losing the popular vote. It became turbocharged after Republicans again won the White House that way in 2016 with Donald Trump's victory over Democrat Hillary Clinton.
Under the National Popular Vote plan, the candidate who wins the popular vote nationwide would receive the Electoral College votes from the states that have joined the compact.
There's nothing inherently partisan about the idea, said Patrick Rosenstiel, a Republican strategist in Minnesota who is a senior consultant to the popular vote movement. Occasionally GOP-majority legislative chambers, including the Oklahoma Senate, have passed proposals to join the compact, but the bills haven’t gone further.
He said his own presidential vote is essentially meaningless because Minnesota has reliably voted Democratic in presidential elections for decades, leaving him with no say in the outcome and steering the vast majority of the candidates' attention elsewhere.
“I don't believe I've ever been relevant in the outcome of a presidential election,” he said. “National popular vote forces campaigns to focus on every persuadable voter in every precinct across the nation.”
Rosenstiel said the national popular vote campaign has been revving up to push the issue when the newly Democratic state legislatures convene at the start of the year. He said the organization has already lined up legislative sponsors.
The compact could create constitutional concerns
Republicans no longer have the power to stop the change in the Democratic-controlled states, but some conservative groups are prepared for a fight. The change “disenfranchises voters in member states if enacted, violates the United States Constitution, and undermines America’s Founders’ intent,” wrote analysts for the America First Policy Institute, a pro-Trump think tank, in September.
There also is no guarantee the proposals will pass. Derek Muller, a Notre Dame law professor who is skeptical of the idea, said some might have second thoughts now that it's gone from a symbolic protest vote to a real possibility. He said there will be constitutional concerns, as well, that will likely lead to legal challenges.
The Constitution lets states run elections, and the Supreme Court in a case stemming from electors who sought to find a substitute for Trump in 2016 has ruled that states can require electors to vote for the presidential candidate they're pledged to.
Muller flagged potential legal hurdles to the popular vote plan. States have the power to run their elections but not set rules that will determine the outcome in other states' contests. Additionally, each state ballot is different, and some would potentially have third-party candidates who wouldn't appear elsewhere, leading to the dilution of a vote for a Democrat or Republican in one state compared to another.
That could violate the 14th Amendment's requirement that everyone have “equal protection of the laws.” The U.S. Supreme Court also might decide that states can't join a compact to change one of their core constitutional duties, unless they get congressional approval.
“I think the Supreme Court will be interested,” Muller said.
Bauer reported from Madison, Wis. Associated Press writers Marc Levy in Harrisburg, Pa., Jacqueline GaNun in Lansing, Mich., Jessica Hill in Las Vegas and Mikella Schuettler in Phoenix contributed to this report.

title: Pingree, Golden vote with fellow Democrats as House Republicans stifle Hegseth impeachment
text:
House Republicans effectively halted the effort by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Kentucky, and Democrats to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday.
Massie filed the resolution in the House on Monday as lawmakers returned to Washington. Tuesday’s vote was a procedural attempt by Republicans to stop the impeachment push by sending the matter back to committee, the Associated Press reported.
The motion passed 211-204, with multiple Democrats and Republicans missing the vote. Massie was the lone Republican to cross party lines.
Maine’s U.S. Reps. Chellie Pingree and Jared Golden joined fellow Democrats in voting against sending it back to committee.
Massie’s resolution included eight counts of impeachment. It largely focused on the war in Iran but also included references to Hegseth’s role in carrying out military actions in Yemen and Venezuela, AP reported.
However, Tuesday’s vote may only delay the matter, with Democrats set to take control of both the House and Senate in January.

title: Hall-Dale boys, Maranacook girls set standard in Class C soccer
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone—because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s Go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
LEWISTON — Minutes after his team won the Class C boys soccer championship on Saturday afternoon, Hall-Dale coach Jesse Rowe left no doubt as to when the preparation for each season begins.
“We set out for this the day after the (state championship) finishes,” said Rowe, who just wrapped up his eighth season as the team’s head coach. “Tomorrow, we’ll start thinking about the future, but we’ll enjoy the next 24 hours, for sure.”
That familiar formula has worked for Hall-Dale, which won its third straight Class C crown with a 1-0 win over Fort Kent.
Hall-Dale has been a contender in Class C South for years and reached its first Class C final in 2012 (a 2-0 loss to Houlton). The Bulldogs were expected to reach the playoffs each season, but were unable to punch through for a state crown.
The Bulldogs finally broke through in 2024, going 16-2 and winning their first Gold Ball with a 1-0 victory over Washington Academy on a cold, windy afternoon at Cameron Stadium in Bangor.
The mindset of the program changed on that day, according to Rowe.
“As soon as you get a taste of it (it changes),” Rowe said. “Someone said, ‘Winning is like a drug.’ We’ll celebrate this and it’ll be fun, but literally, right after it, the expectation is, ‘Can we be back in this game again?’ That’s our focus. We used to be the lovable loser, but now it’s three in a row and it feels good.”
In three state title game wins, the Bulldogs have outscored their opponents 4-0.
“Once we won (the first title), we felt a lot of teams would doubt us after losing almost our entire starting lineup,” said Hall-Dale senior forward Collin McArthur, who had the assist on Greyson Cary’s goal against Fort Kent. “We knew, from there, (the title game) was the standard. And if we could (win) last year’s (title game), we were going to win (the next one).”
Like Hall-Dale, the Maranacook girls soccer team has established itself as the top program in Class C, winning its second consecutive state crown and third in the past five years with a 2-0 victory over Fort Kent.
Unlike the Bulldogs, however, the Black Bears were no sure thing this season. Maranacook graduated a large senior class from last year’s title winner.
“I think it’s different every year,” said Maranacook coach Travis Magnusson. “We always have high expectations, but I don’t think we came into the year with, ‘We’re going to win the state championship.’ We had a goal of trying to get to the semifinals or regionals. … This one feels really special, because no one expected us to do it.”
The Black Bears have played in every C South final since 2021, and in that stretch has 103 wins and just six losses.
Still, for the players, the idea of a state championship came during the season. The Black Bears had a challenging schedule, but finished 17-1, including two wins over Mountain Valley Conference rival, and Class C South’s top seed, Mt. Abram.
“It motivates us,” said Maranacook senior Cooper Davis. “I think it pushes us to play our best game, because we know everybody is going to give us their best game. It just makes us have to play better every time.”
Maranacook rose to the occasion, outscoring opponents 8-0 in the playoffs.

title: Global carbon pollution dips slightly as Iran war oil shock jolts emissions, scientists say
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Global carbon pollution dips slightly as Iran war oil shock jolts emissions, scientists say
Global carbon pollution dropped this year ever so slightly, but it's more because of oil shocks reverberating from the Iran war than anything the world has done to fight climate change, scientists said in a new study.
In 2026, the world emitted 42.2 billion tons of heat-trapping carbon dioxide from the burning of fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas. It’s a 0.4% decrease from last year, according to the scientists of the Global Carbon Project.
“It’s downwards which sounds good, but this is largely driven by the war in Iran, what’s happened in the Strait of Hormuz,” said study co-author Glen Peters, a scientist at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research in Norway. “So in a way, a little bit of good news, but for the wrong reasons.”
Related video above: As oil heating costs soar, expensive Mass Save plan falls short
The war in Iran has effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping artery for petroleum products, pushing up global prices of gasoline and oil.
They found oil emissions dropped nearly 2% and natural gas fell 0.3%, while coal was up 0.6%.
The international team of more than 140 scientists uses data from around the world to calculate the yearly emissions figure with estimates for the last few months of the year, and then present them at the U.N. climate negotiations in Antalya, Turkey. Their findings were also published in the journals Earth System Science Data Discussions and Nature Climate Change. Peters said they are certain that this was related to the war-triggered energy shocks because of both the timing and type of fuel emission drops.
If the overall carbon dioxide emission drop were due solely to a rise in renewables and a systemic drop in fossil fuel use, oil emissions “would slowly come up to a peak and then slowly decline afterward, whereas what we see this year is oil emissions are going up and then suddenly BANG, down 2%,” Peters said.
Previous carbon pollution drops
This is the third time global carbon pollution dropped in the 21st century. The other two times were because of the global recession in 2009 and the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.
In those past two crises, people hoped the recovery from the shocks would emphasize clean energy, Peters said, "but at the end of the day, we seem to go back to where we were before.”
Outside experts greeted the figures with a mix of hope and skepticism that it will last.
Niklas Höhne, co-founder of Germany’s NewClimate Institute, said “permanent shifts are happening” especially with skyrocketing switches to electric cars and trucks, especially in Asia. So he thinks the global peak of carbon emissions is near or here.
But Malte Meinshausen, a climate science and policy expert at the University of Melbourne in Australia, said oil-producing nations and companies not affected by the blockage of the Strait of Hormuz reaped “tremendous windfall gains,” and it boosts their efforts to look for oil outside the Middle East. That, he said, will dampen any short-term effects of reduced carbon emissions from the war.
More than 1,000 tons per second of pollution
The 42 billion tons of carbon dioxide emitted this year comes to about 1,335 tons (1,211 metric tons) of the transparent, heat-trapping gas going into the air every second.
“We shouldn’t lose sight of the bigger picture. The world is still pumping more than a thousand metric tons of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere every second," Mohamed Adow, director of the environmental group Power Shift Africa, said in an email.
“It’s very abstract to think about the magnitude of stuff we throw in the atmosphere every year, but it’s a ginormous number,”said Peters. “If it was black and not transparent, the sky would be dark.”
And even though the amount of heat-trapping gases from fossil fuels dropped slightly, overall global carbon dioxide emissions went up 1%. That's because of land use changes, such as deforestation and human-caused peat fires, that increased faster than fossil fuel burning decreased, the study said.
China's emissions drop raises eyebrows and hope
Most of the world's biggest carbon-polluting nations — China, the United States, Europe, Japan — showed about a 1% drop in emissions this year, but Peters attributed it to the oil shock. India's fossil fuel pollution went up 4.4% this year, the study found.
China's emission drop raised eyebrows and hope for some experts. Experts have been waiting for China's ever-growing emissions to start dropping.
“China is giving us real reasons to be optimistic that its emissions may have peaked," Adow said. “It’s building the world’s first major electrostate, investing at extraordinary speed and scale in solar power, wind energy, electric vehicles and the infrastructure to support them. This isn’t a temporary response to an oil crisis. It’s a fundamental transformation of China’s economy that is steadily reducing its dependence on fossil fuels.”
University of Michigan environment dean Jonathan Overpeck said, “We're not phasing out fossil fuels fast enough, but some progress is better than no progress.”

title: Woman speaks out after being seen making racist gestures outside Ole Miss students’ apartment
text:
OXFORD, Miss. (WMC/Gray News) — A woman who apologized after she was seen making racist gestures in a viral doorbell camera video outside an apartment where three Black Ole Miss students live has now been identified as Alaina Kunes.
Kunes said in a statement sent to WMC that her actions were “insensitive, inappropriate, and deeply harmful.” She said she had apologized to the women who live at the apartment and plans to cooperate with the university’s investigation.
Kunes is the first of three white women seen walking past the apartment’s front door in the Ring doorbell camera video. Two appear to mimic monkey behavior and noises as they pass. The second woman seen making the gestures has not been identified.
In her statement, Kunes said she had not met the apartment’s residents and did not know their race before the Nov. 6 incident.
“I would have never intentionally made those noises or gestures toward a person of color,” she said. “I have apologized to the women and I pray they will forgive me.”
She continued, “I can never truly understand the pain I have caused them and it was never my intention. These girls deserve to feel seen and understood and what I did is not a reflection of who I am trying to become.”
Kunes also said she and her family have received death threats and experienced harassment. She thanked authorities for working to ensure their safety and asked for privacy for her family.
“As I intend to cooperate fully with the University’s investigation, I ask for privacy for my family,” she said. “I understand the seriousness of this situation and remain committed to taking responsibility and learning from this embarrassing ordeal.”
Tasha Bolton contacted WMC about the incident. The video belongs to her daughter. Bolton’s daughter is a Black freshman at Ole Miss and shares the off-campus apartment with two other Black roommates. The university said it leases student housing at the apartment complex.
In a statement released Sunday, Ole Miss condemned the behavior and said it had reached out to those targeted to offer information, resources and support. The university said the incident is under investigation and noted that student conduct records and any potential disciplinary action are protected by the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act.
Bolton previously told WMC that the family has an attorney and plans to make a statement. She said she did not want to speak with the station until she had an opportunity to speak with the university.

title: A note to ‘46’: Donald Trump’s private message to Joe Biden revealed in new memoir
text:
(AP) - President Donald Trump, who for years disputed his loss in the 2020 election and publicly decried the result having been stolen from him by Democratic forces, privately lauded incoming President Joe Biden as someone he believed “will be true to yourself and the American people.”
That sentiment, along with others, was part of the letter Trump left for Biden upon leaving office in January 2021. Biden showed the note to some members of his staff after his inauguration in 2021 but didn’t let anyone read it, describing it later that day as “very generous” but otherwise saying he considered it to be private.
Inclusion of the letter in Biden’s “Promise Me, America,” his White House memoir slated for release Nov. 17, was first reported Tuesday by The New York Times. The Associated Press has reviewed a photocopy of the two-page letter, handwritten in Trump’s trademark black Sharpie on White House stationery and addressed “To ‘46,’” denoting Biden’s place as the 46th U.S. president.
“Many presidents have come and gone who simply governed as Republicans or Democrats,” Trump wrote. “Largely, they did not change history, they were just swept along in its relentless tide. This will not happen to you because I know how much you love the American people.”
At the time of transition, Biden was said to have been surprised by how gracious he thought the letter was, given the animosity between the political rivals. Trump had opted out of other presidential traditions, like attending Biden’s inauguration, or hosting the incoming president and first lady for tea at the White House.
Trump has said he thought it was up to Biden to share the letter, calling it “a nice note” during a September 2023 interview with NBC’s “Meet the Press,” adding, “I took a lot of time in thinking about it.”
Elsewhere in the memoir, the first excerpt of which was published Monday by the Atlantic, Biden wrote of the deep damage Trump has inflicted, with an administration determined to “tear down institutions and inflame hatreds.”
Lamenting Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency and his aggressive reversal of many of his policies, Biden wrote of Trump’s “dismissive and destructive nature,” describing his predecessor and successor as someone “who seemed unable to tolerate the idea that someone else’s accomplishments might be worth building on rather than tearing down.”
But Biden’s harshest characterization so far was focused on Trump’s role in the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol, as Congress met to certify the 2020 election, which Biden had won. Writing that Trump “led an insurrection,” Biden said Trump’s ”goal was to remain in power after the American people had voted him out of office."
“What Trump did on January 6, 2021, should never be forgotten,” Biden wrote. “It should follow him to his grave.”
Asked for comment on both the letter and Biden’s memoir, White House communications director Steven Cheung called the former president “a disgrace” who “should have heeded the President’s wise words, but instead he tried to destroy this country and weaponize the justice system against his political enemies.”
___
Meg Kinnard can be reached at http://x.com/MegKinnardAP

title: There was no ‘Margaret Chase Smith moment’
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Andrew Shuttleworth Fowler lives in Westbrook. He was 11 when Susan Collins was first elected to the Senate.
“I have now had my Margaret Chase Smith moment,” Sen. Susan Collins told the New York Times last Wednesday, a day after Troy Jackson ended her Senate career.
Constituents had urged her to find one, she said. She had. “The best comparison is we each lost our last race for the Senate.”
If losing her seat was as close as she could come to following in Smith’s footsteps, I’ll take it. But those of us who did the urging had something more in mind.
We had in mind June 1, 1950, when Smith, in her second year in the Senate, stood on the floor with Joe McCarthy two rows behind her and condemned the politics of “fear, ignorance, bigotry and smear.” “I do not want to see the Republican Party win that way,” she said.
McCarthy retaliated. He had her removed from the Senate’s investigations subcommittee and gave the seat to a California freshman named Richard Nixon. He backed a primary challenger against her. She kept opposing him, and in 1954 she voted to censure him. He was finished within a year.
She lost in 1972, three full terms after that speech. The speech is why we remember her.
Collins wants credit for voting to convict Donald Trump in 2021. She was right to do it. “It is never enough,” she complains.
But a year earlier, she had voted to acquit him. She told CBS News that being impeached was “a pretty big lesson.” He had learned something, she said. He had: his party would protect him.
Two years before that, she vouched for Brett Kavanaugh’s respect for precedent when she voted to put him on the Supreme Court. She reminded us that abortion-rights groups had been wrong about nominees before. They were right about this one. “I feel misled,” she said in 2022, and yet she does not regret the vote.
“I want results and they want angry rhetoric,” Collins told the Times.
Women lost the federal constitutional right to abortion. That was a result.
Heating oil averaged $6.05 a gallon in Maine last week, up 82% from a year earlier because of a war she voted five times not to stop. That was a result.
Mainers on marketplace health plans saw premiums rise 77% on average after she voted to end the shutdown without their subsidies. Enrollment fell by more than 6,000. That was a result.
She voted to advance the largest Medicaid cut in the program’s history, then voted against it once it would pass without her. The state estimates more than 31,000 Mainers will lose MaineCare in January because of it. That was a result.
In June, she voted for $70 billion more for ICE and the Border Patrol, telling Mainers the money would pay for training and body cameras. Five weeks later, a federal agent without a body camera shot a young father dead on a Biddeford street. He was not the man they were looking for. That, too, was a result.
The senator reminds us she brought home $1.5 billion for 672 projects. Her campaign manager calls it an opportunity Maine “has walked away from.”
Nobody in Maine would turn down a new fire station. But a fire station does not heat a house or insure a family. What she brought home, we’ll keep. We could not afford what came with it.
Collins has said for years that her Senate desk once belonged to Margaret Chase Smith. It is a good desk. Smith stood behind it in 1950, and in a soft and trembling voice said what her party did not want to hear.
Collins inherited the furniture. She did not inherit the nerve. Last Tuesday, Maine took the desk back.

title: Top Runway model, '227' actress, dies at 74 after 'long, courageous battle' with MS
text:
Top Runway model, '227' actress Toukie Smith dies at 74
A top model and actress who appeared on the NBC sitcom "227" has died at the age of 74.
Toukie Smith died following a "long, courageous battle" with multiple sclerosis, her twins Airyn and Julian, who she shared with former partner Robert De Niro, announced.
Smith and De Niro — who began dating in 1988 — welcomed Airyn and Julian in 1995 through a surrogate. The former couple split about a year later, but while they often stepped out together, they rarely shared more insight into their romance.
Her children confirmed to E! News and The Hollywood Reporter that Smith died on Nov. 4.
Smith attended the Fashion Institute of Technology and began her modeling career in 1972, eventually appearing in a photo campaign for Yves St. Laurent and on the pages of such magazines as Vogue, Cosmopolitan, and Seventeen.
In 1978, Bloomingdale's named her its model of the year.
She later appeared as Eva Rawley on the Marla Gibbs-starring NBC sitcom "227."
In the 1989 show, Smith's character was an artist who moved into the Lexington Place building — whose landlord is Gibbs' Mary Jenkins — and recurred on the comedy during its final two seasons through May 1990.
Smith's children said in a statement that their mom "shared in a remarkable family legacy that helped shape American fashion and culture" and that "her beauty, grace and unmistakable presence helped pave the way for generations of Black models and designers in fashion."
The model and actress also appeared on three episodes of NBC's "Miami Vice" as Angie, the assistant to the pop singer Caitlin Davies (Sheena Easton) — and wife of Don Johnson's Sonny Crockett — on the show's fourth season.

title: Passing showers tonight, dry again on Wednesday
text:
Passing showers tonight, dry again on Wednesday
Passing showers tonight, dry again on Wednesday
Rain and snow showers will continue tonight, especially across the mountains and foothills, as a cold front moves through. A few showers could spread into other areas, but activity should remain fairly limited.
Tomorrow looks to be another day with a mix of sunshine and clouds; afternoon temperatures climb to near 50.
Looking ahead, a developing late-week coastal storm remains uncertain, with forecast models still disagreeing on its track. However, recent trends suggest this will likely be a lower-impact system. Significant accumulating snow is becoming less likely outside the mountains, but many areas could still see their first snowflakes of the season! They may not stick around long, though. Higher elevations could pick up a couple of inches if the storm track cooperates.
Below-average temperatures arrive late this week and stick around through the weekend. Upslope rain and snow showers may linger through Sunday before high pressure brings drier conditions early next week. Overall, first flakes are possible for many, but significant snowfall is looking increasingly unlikely outside the mountains.

title: UFC's Dana White appears with Trump at a White House briefing — but won't be his press secretary
text:
UFC's Dana White appears with Trump at a White House briefing — but won't be his press secretary
After bringing UFC to the White House lawn this summer, President Donald Trump has now brought it to the briefing room, too.
Trump made a surprise appearance before reporters Monday with UFC chief Dana White and briefly stood aside as his longtime friend took questions — milking a joke that began over the weekend, when Trump said he had offered White the job of White House press secretary.
"I've always wanted to do this," White said, before bellowing, "Who has the first question?" He then clarified, "I have zero political aspirations."
The joke — and the briefing — were the latest in a series of unexpected choices by the president since Republicans' sweeping losses during last week's midterm elections. Trump's briefing room stop was so hastily organized that officials didn't have time to affix the presidential seal to the lectern from which he spoke.
The president had announced on social media Saturday that he wanted "the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior" as his next chief spokesman — catching White off-guard at a boxing match in London. "He called me and told me that he had done this," White said Monday. "The last 24 hours of my life has been insane."
Trump said he had been having a "very bad press day" and thought suggesting White as the 38th White House press secretary in the nation's history might be good for a laugh.
"We thought we'd have a little fun and we brought Dana here," Trump said. "He would be fantastic."
White tells Trump, 'I do not want to be in politics, no'
Some reporters in the press room played along. White was asked if he had any advice for Trump on the possibility of issuing a posthumous pardon for Pete Rose, baseball's all-time hits leader.
"I don't advise the president on anything ever," White responded. "But yeah, I think it's fair." Trump then interjected to say, "I'd give Pete Rose a pardon."
At one point, White marveled, "I can't believe you actually have questions for me."
Trump eventually took over. But after answering about half an hour of questions on the midterms, the war in Iran and a variety of serious topics, the president turned to White and asked, "Would you like to be press secretary of the United States of America" or "just want to stay with this ridiculous UFC?"
"Thank you for the offer," White said, before allowing, "I do not want to be in politics, no."
Trump post-midterm moves have been peculiar
In the hours after Trump's Saturday post landed, neither the White House nor UFC would provide clarity on whether it was serious. Then, on Sunday night, Trump finally said, "I was kidding, but I think Dana likes the idea, and he is a very capable guy."
Trump has long relished doing the norm-busting unexpected as president, but he's leaned even more into that tendency around the election.
The day before balloting began, Trump used what was billed as a speech outlining his closing argument for why his party deserved to continue to control Congress to instead talk up his costly and problem-plagued effort to overhaul the Lincoln Memorial's Reflecting Pool.
On Wednesday, after Democrats won all over the country, including notching Senate seats in deep red states like Texas, South Carolina and Kansas, he took reporters on a tour of the White House ballroom's construction site and even signed a steel beam.
The following day, Trump declared the Oval Office would become a national monument — even though that won't prevent future presidents from undoing the gilded flourishes he's packed it with.
On Friday, the White House promoted a glitzy new website celebrating plans for a towering memorial arch in Trump's honor, despite a court order blocking work on it.
The White House press secretary position is open due to the brief, tumultuous week when Trump tried out Katie Zacharia as press secretary. She struggled in her sole appearance before reporters and left the job after five days.
The post had been vacant since Karoline Leavitt left at the end of August.
Trump and White go way back
Trump has frequently attended UFC events with White. The pair have been friends for decades, and White spoke at the last three Republican National Conventions.
Trump even allowed White's sport to take over the White House's South Lawn in June for the celebration of America's 250th year of independence and the president's own 80th birthday. A wire-mesh Octagon was constructed under " The Claw," a spaceship-like metal arch fitted with lights, sound equipment and large screens.
"He's really very unique," Trump said, describing his friend, in the White House briefing room. "The only problem is he'll talk for a little while and then he's going to beat the hell out of you."

title: Fort Fairfield Water Exceeds Standard Copper Level
text:
FORT FAIRFIELD, Maine (WAGM) -Copper levels in Fort Fairfield’s drinking water are above the allowed standard.
The Fort Fairfield Utilities District mailed a notice to customers and posted the notice on the town website. The notice states that testing done by the utilities district in late August found 1.75 milligrams of copper per liter in the town’s drinking water. This exceeds the allowed standard of 1.3 milligrams per liter. District officials say while copper is an essential nutrient, drinking water above the standard for short periods may cause gastrointestinal discomfort. Exposure over several years can lead to liver or kidney complications. Officials say Fort Fairfield residents using town water that have Wilson’s disease, or other specific personal health concerns, should consult their doctor.
The Utilities District General Manager Noah Bernard says the high level of copper is not an emergency and says it isn’t necessary for residents to use alternative water sources, such as bottled water. The Fort Fairfield Utilities District is currently working to correct the problem by reviewing its corrosion control treatment plan, increasing lead and copper testing, and continuing water quality parameter testing. Officials expect the problem to be solved by March of 2027. Anyone with questions or looking for more information on the issue should contact the Fort Fairfield Utilities District at 472-0622.

title: Understanding the impeachment process for government officials
text:
Understanding the impeachment process for government officials
House lawmakers are pushing to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over his role in U.S. military actions in Iran, Yemen, and Venezuela, alleging "high crimes and misdemeanors."
Understanding the impeachment process for government officials
House lawmakers are pushing to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over his role in U.S. military actions in Iran, Yemen, and Venezuela, alleging "high crimes and misdemeanors."
Note: The House voted Tuesday night against advancing the impeachment against Hegseth, likely ending the process this congressional session.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is facing a push for impeachment from some House lawmakers over his role in U.S. military actions in Iran, Yemen, and Venezuela, which they claim amount to "high crimes and misdemeanors."
"In the 250 years of our American republic, no Secretary of War or Secretary of Defense has ever been impeached for carrying out lawful military operations," Hegseth said.
Impeachment is a formal charge of misconduct or wrongdoing by a government official. The process begins with House lawmakers determining if there is enough evidence to justify impeachment. If a majority in the House votes in favor, the matter moves to the Senate.
While no defense secretary has been impeached for military operations, a secretary of war has been impeached for other reasons. According to the Get the Facts data team, William W. Belknap, who served as secretary of war in 1876, was impeached for "disregard for his office and accepting payments in exchange for making official appointments."
A House vote on Hegseth's impeachment could happen in the coming days. If approved, he would join a list of federal judges, one U.S. senator, two cabinet secretaries, and three presidents—including President Donald Trump, who was impeached twice by the House, according to the Get the Facts team.
If the impeachment reaches the Senate, the official would face a trial that could result in acquittal or removal from office.

title: Inflation numbers are in. Try our calculator to estimate the cost difference of various groceries
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Inflation ran hotter than expected last month. Use our calculator to check grocery prices
U.S. inflation was higher than expected last month, a sign that the rising prices that powered sweeping Democratic victories in last week's midterm elections will continue to pose challenges for the White House and the Federal Reserve.
Video above: Inflation has driven up family expenses by hundreds per month since January 2025
The consumer price index rose 0.4% from September to October, the Labor Department said Tuesday, down from 0.6% the previous month. The government did not report a yearly inflation rate because last year's government shutdown meant no data was released for October 2025.
Excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core prices rose 0.3%, the same as the preceding month. Both figures were a tenth of a point higher than forecast.
Calculate how inflation has changed your grocery costs
The Get the Facts Data Team built a calculator that estimates the average cost of select grocery items and compares it with the price from the previous month. These costs are based on the national average, and items are calculated per pound, gallon, ounce, liter or dozen.
This calculator provides an estimate based on BLS inflation data and is not the actual total you paid for groceries.
U.S. markets dipped immediately after the inflation report and Treasury yields ticked higher.
The data shows that inflation remains noticeably above the Federal Reserve's target of 2%, and Americans' struggles with high prices were evident as they ousted Republican majorities from the House and Senate last week. Yet with solid gains in both chambers, Democrats in Congress will soon face the challenge of how to address voters' affordability concerns. President Donald Trump has acknowledged voter anger over the Iran war and gas prices but has shown no sign yet of changing course.
The AP Voter Poll, a survey of 100,000 voters, found about two-thirds blamed Trump's policies for higher costs. About 9 in 10 said the cost of living was a "crucial" or "major" factor in their vote.
