title: How to find the best Black Friday, Cyber Monday and Travel Tuesday travel deals for 2026
text:
(Expedia via Stacker) - Black Friday is one of the biggest days of the year for travel deals, covering everything from flights and hotels to vacation packages and activities. It falls on Friday, Nov. 27 this year, but many travel deals start early and extend through Cyber Monday and Travel Tuesday.
The best way to snag great Black Friday travel deals is to prepare in advance: Pick where you want to go, check sale dates and set price alerts. That way you can book fast when deals go live.
You should also join free travel loyalty programs, so your Black Friday getaway can help you earn points towards your next trip.
Here’s everything you need to know to find the best travel deals in 2026, according to Expedia and Hotels.com:
When do Black Friday travel deals start?
That’s one of the best parts: they often start well before Black Friday itself. Many companies from airlines and hotel chains to booking platforms, release their Black Friday deals about a week ahead of Black Friday.
Don’t wait until Nov. 27 to start planning, and check back for new special offer drops throughout Thanksgiving weekend.
Where can I find the best Black Friday, Cyber Monday and Travel Tuesday travel deals?
Hotels and Lodging
Don’t be afraid to shop around. Keep an eye out for company announcements and emails about Black Friday promotions and be sure to compare prices to get the best deal. Hotel companies and airlines may offer discounted rates or fares at select properties or on select flights. Booking through an online travel platform can make it easier to browse for discounts across brands and boutique hotels.
Flights
Travel Tuesday emerged as a big day for flight discounts a few years ago, but many travel sites will run deals on flights all weekend long. This is another time to shop around. If you can’t find a deal on the airline site, try online booking platforms, which offer savings when you book your flights, hotel and other trip necessities all in one place.
Vacation Packages, Activities and Car Rental
Many sites offer everyday discounts on vacation packages, and Black Friday is a good time to look for special offers.
You can also use online travel aggregators to quickly compare Black Friday deals on activities and car rentals, without having to visit a bunch of different sites.
Cruises
Cruise lines frequently run Black Friday, Cyber Monday and Travel Tuesday offers, and not just on their own websites. Promotions can run the gamut from discounts on specific routes, free on-board perks, or other perks like a free plus-one. Be sure to shop around to find the best deals.
How can I prepare in advance for Black Friday travel deals?
- Sign up for loyalty programs (they’re free): Some companies will offer special discounts or promotions to members, so it pays to sign up ahead of time to make sure you don’t miss the chance at special member pricing. Plus, you’ll collect reward points you can redeem on future trips.
- Stay flexible on destination and travel dates. Being open to travel on off-peak days or to less-popular destinations can help you score the best deals.
- Save hotels in advance. Make sure you know where you want to stay. Many travel apps have trip boards where you can “favorite” hotels in the weeks before sales starts so you can book your preferred properties more easily when the discounts open up.
- Consider a travel rewards credit card if you’re a frequent booker. There are tons out there to choose from, and most come with benefits beyond just earning more rewards. Airline credit cards often include other perks like free checked bags or priority boarding, and hotel cards may include access to complimentary room upgrades or other benefits. Almost all co-branded credit cards let you earn towards future travel with every purchase.
How can I tell if I’m getting a good deal during Black Friday, Cyber Monday and Travel Tuesday?
- Turn on Price Tracking for the hotels and flights you’re watching. Price tracking is a common feature on many booking platforms that helps you view price history and spot genuinely good deals.
- Choose refundable rates. Filter for hotels that offer free cancellation so you can easily snap up a good deal and worry about the logistics later. Avoid offers that are restrictive or won’t let you make changes.
- Read the fine print. Sometimes it’s only a “deal” because there are inconvenient flight layovers or the dates are a destination’s bad weather season. Do a little due diligence to make sure what you’re getting is as great a deal as it seems.

title: South Portland’s tank farm has been linked to chronic health risks. Now what?
text:
Carolyn Hurwitz feels stuck in South Portland.
When she bought her house — her first — less than half a mile from the Citgo terminal a couple of years ago, she said she didn’t know her new neighborhood would smell like a crew was doing constant road work right outside the house.
She notices it first thing in the morning. An avid runner, she said she sometimes pulls her shirt up over her face when she jogs on the Greenbelt.
A report recently released by the Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention found that South Portland residents living near the more than 100 petroleum tanks in the city owned by six companies could be at a higher risk of cancer and other chronic health issues as a result of long-term exposure to carcinogenic emissions detected there.
It found that monitors along the fence line of some of the tank farms regularly logged long-term average benzene concentrations in ambient air that exceeded state guidelines, according to one and half years of data collected by the Department of Environmental Protection.
Benzene is a known carcinogen, and acute exposure can cause fatigue, dizziness, irregular heartbeat and headaches. High long-term exposure can cause cancers, including leukemia. There is no safe level of exposure to benzene, according to the World Health Organization.
A day after the CDC and DEP presented their findings to the City Council, Citgo announced that it will cover its share of additional fenceline testing and invest in technology to reduce emissions. A spokesperson for Global Partners did not say whether the company has specific plans in light of the report findings.
The four other oil companies with holdings in the city did not respond to requests for comments about whether they have plans to reduce emissions.
The South Portland City Council will host a workshop on Dec. 1 to discuss avenues to reduce toxic air emissions from the petroleum tanks, such as licensing fees for oil companies, mandating better emissions control technology and collaborating with state legislators on statewide policy.
“There’s no magic answer for how to protect these people in the short term while they’re waiting for action and waiting for something that would reduce these levels in their communities,” said Gail Carlson, an environmental science professor at Colby College. “I don’t want to sugarcoat it.”
What can the Maine DEP do?
The Maine DEP, the regulating body over these petroleum tank farms, issues air quality emissions licenses and is responsible for evaluating compliance with state and federal regulations. It’s also in charge of enforcing federal regulations.
Beyond requesting additional testing, it’s not intervening at this point. And it legally doesn’t have to.
“Health guidelines are just that,” Carlson said. “They’re just a recommendation.”
The Clean Air Act, through national ambient air quality standards, sets legally binding limits for a handful of dangerous chemicals like carbon monoxide and lead, but not benzene, acrolein and about 100 other chemicals that are monitored by state guidelines. It’s ultimately up to the DEP to decide whether to take further action.
The DEP recommended another year of data collection along the fence lines of the South Portland Terminal and Citgo and nearby homes to understand how quickly the benzene concentrations dissipate.
The DEP is planning to use optical gas imaging to see if it can figure out which activities in the storage facilities contribute to emissions, said Eric Kennedy, bureau director of the air quality division of the DEP. After that, there might be a more concrete plan, he said.
“We can’t solve the problem when we don’t know exactly what the problem is,” he said.
Carlson is not surprised that the DEP isn’t taking more proactive steps. It’s a government agency with limited capacity and resources to take on a large pollution control project, she said.
Some residents aren’t surprised, either, noting that the agency was unwilling to take enforcement action when petroleum companies violated emissions limits nearly 10 years ago.
“The agency hasn’t taken this as seriously as the residents who have to live next to these tank farms do,” said Chelsea Byun, a nearby resident and former Portland Press Herald editor.
Three petroleum companies operating in South Portland — Sprague, Global and Gulf Oil — were sued by the EPA in the past 10 years for violating emissions caps for volatile organic compounds dating back decades. The companies had to pay damages and were ordered to reduce emissions.
What could the Legislature do?
In 2021, the Maine Legislature mandated that petroleum companies take steps to reduce evaporation and emissions, such as installing floating roofs in tanks. It required fence line monitoring (including of volatile organic compounds like benzene), monthly inspections and twice-a-year testing of heated tanks.
Rep. Victoria Morales, who used to represent part of South Portland, sponsored a sweeping bill in 2021 that would have instituted a robust licensing program for air emissions, require a public hearing in the municipality in question, set steep civil penalties for violators that would be transferred to the affected municipality and require companies seeking air emissions licenses to directly outline steps to protect community health.
The bill faced opposition from leaders of oil companies, like Chris Gillies, the president of the Portland Pipe Line Corporation. He said that the proposed procedural changes, especially the daily penalties, would add undue costs that would threaten the companies’ ability to do business in the state. Kennedy, who works for the DEP, said that it would place an administrative burden on the regulators.
The bill was carried over and ultimately killed in 2022.
Rep. Matt Beck, who currently represents South Portland, sponsored a bill last spring at the request of the City Council that would have required operators of oil terminal facilities to give advance notice to the public each time they planned to load or offload oil.
There was strong opposition from oil companies and the Mills administration, which voiced concern about bad actors getting access to fuel logistics information, and Beck said it became clear it wasn’t going to pass.
The bill was watered down to just require warning signs posted along the fence line to let people know about the risk from the volatile organic compounds. The bill failed this spring.
Beck said he’s interested in working with South Portland municipal leaders to try to craft targeted legislation in the next session.
What can the city do?
Mayor Elyse Tipton has lived in Cash Corner for more than 15 years. Her husband, a cardiac patient, walks around the neighborhood at least once a day. Tipton has been contacted by residents who just moved to the area and are looking to start a family.
“It feels very personal,” she said. “We are talking about people’s health.”
The City Council plans to discuss any tools that are available to them, including licensing fees for oil facilities in which companies would need to meet a certain emissions threshold to do business, an ordinance that would require oil companies to adopt best available emissions control technology and a setback for residential development a certain distance from the tanks, City Manager Scott Morelli said.
The council will also discuss whether to pursue additional testing, funded by the petroleum companies in question.
What is the petroleum companies’ responsibility?
Petroleum companies are responsible for regular maintenance and upgrades to keep their facilities up to code.
Carlson is skeptical that the companies will invest more money in costly technology when it isn’t legally required.
“That’s never going to happen,” she said.
Next year, Citgo plans to upgrade two floating roofs, or technology within a tank that creates a seal between the liquid product and the atmosphere. The company plans to upgrade two more tanks in 2028.
It also launched continuous emissions monitoring of benzene along the fence line about a month ago.
Karl Schmidt, the vice president of supply and marketing at Citgo, said the data has been enlightening, particularly because it’s so variable. He said he doesn’t yet know when it will be available to the public.
“We hear the community’s concerns about the study findings and we take those concerns seriously,” Schmidt said.
Reid Lamberty, a spokesperson for Global, said that the company will continue working with the DEP to meet the state’s monitoring and reporting requirements. He said he does not think that his company’s terminal emits high concentrations of benzene.
Hurwitz hopes something changes soon.
She tends to native plants in her yard, and has planted grapes, blueberries and hazelnuts, though she’s hesitant to eat what grows in her garden.
“I like my life here,” she said. “I would like to want to live here.”

title: China's trade surplus surpasses $1 trillion for a 2nd straight year, as exports surge 35%
text:
China's trade surplus surpasses $1 trillion for a 2nd straight year, as exports surge 35%
China’s trade surplus exceeded $1 trillion for a second straight year, according to official data released Tuesday, as pressure mounts for greater balance in trade with Beijing.
Exports in October surged 35.2% from a year earlier, the customs agency said. Exports have grown rapidly this year, supported by high-tech goods like semiconductors and autos.
Imports rose 41.6% year-on-year.
Between January and October, China logged a $1.04 trillion trade surplus, even as the trade surplus narrowed last month to $105.3 billion from $133.5bn in September as imports picked up pace.
Related video: President Trump '100%' backs bill to make data centers pay more, potentially lower electricity costs
That puts China on track for surpassing last year’s record $1.2 trillion trade surplus in 2026.
“We expect Chinese exports to stay strong for the rest of this year, led by electronics and autos,” said Dave Chia, an economist at Moody’s Analytics.
China's imports soared in October, partly because of a recovery in shipments of crude oil from the Persian Gulf.
Overcapacity in many industries, excess domestic savings and weakened domestic demand are still leading China to ship its goods abroad as some countries move to protect their own industries, said Alicia García-Herrero, chief economist for Asia Pacific at French bank Natixis.
The situation is not sustainable, she said.
Businesses are feeling the pressure of ferocious competition as China’s economy has slowed, said Cinders Zhou, who sells eyewear for a manufacturer in Linhai city in eastern China’s Zhejiang province.
“It comes down to product quality, or rather the increasing lack of it across the industry, since there’s significant homogenization,” said Zhou, whose company makes frames and lenses sold both in and outside China. “That has forced everyone to compete on price,” she said.
Trade curbs by the European Union pose an important risk at a time of heightened U.S. trade barriers and tariffs, Chia said.
Still, the EU's trade measures apply to only a small part of China’s exports, said Nguyen Hoang Nam with Capital Economics.
China has insisted it is not seeking to expand its surplus but wants more balanced global trade.
However, strong exports have helped offset sluggish domestic demand. The economy is forecast to meet Beijing’s official target of a 4.5% to 5% annual growth this year, slightly slower than last year’s 5% expansion.
China’s exports to the U.S. grew 32.9% in October year-on-year, building on a low base after China-U.S. trade was hit last year by Trump’s elevated tariffs. China's exports to the EU in October rose 24.3% year-on-year. They rose 17.2% in January-October.
For the first ten months, the trade surplus with the U.S. was around $266.5 billion, while for the EU, the 10-month difference was more than $310 billion. In 2025, the EU recorded a roughly $410 billion trade deficit with China, or more than $1.1 billion each day.
Figures reported by China often differ from those reported by its trading partner.
Also in October, China's semiconductor exports soared 137.1% in terms of value from the year before. Exports of autos rose 37.6%.
China’s exports could be vulnerable to setbacks for the artificial intelligence industry, a concern that deepened with the Democratic victories in the U.S. midterm elections given the public backlash against expansion of data centers.
“If the AI boom slows or turns into a correction, lower chip and electronics prices and smaller shipping volumes would hit China’s exports hard,” Chia said.
Trade is likely to be among top issues on the agenda in planned meetings between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping next week on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders summit in China’s technology hub Shenzhen.
A two-month extension of a trade truce until January has provided some relief to exporters, though it’s unclear how long that may last.
U.S. and European trade policies have added “a lot of difficulties” for Chinese businesses to expand in the markets, said Wang Xin, head of the Shenzhen Cross-Border E-Commerce Association, an industry group.

title: Robert “Bob” McKechnie (1945-2026)
Better late than never for a true celebration of America
text:
How dispiriting it was that July 4 came and went this year with so few positive and inspiring celebrations of America’s 250th birthday. With a crook and a narcissist in the White House, we got wrestling matches, car races and the destruction and defacement of the people’s property all across our nation’s capital. With so many of our nation’s hard-fought values being trampled by the White House and Republican Congress, state and local communities struggled to rouse pride in our country.
Little did we know that the most meaningful celebration of our nation’s founding would take place late in this anniversary year — on Nov. 3.
We reaffirmed, resoundingly, the core of our democracy, with citizens turning out in record numbers to exercise their right to vote. Not only did our democracy hold, the power of the people prevailed over mountains of money. And we elected dozens of excellent candidates who care about our country and our communities, and whose diversity on so many fronts reflects the strength of America.
Happy 250th, America. Thank you for reminding us what’s truly worth celebrating about our democracy.
Kathy Mills
Yarmouth

title: US Air Force relocates aircraft from a base in England because of a threat, US official says
text:
LONDON (AP) — The U.S. Air Force has relocated aircraft from a base in eastern England because of a threat, U.S. officials told The Associated Press.
The Military Air Tracking Alliance, a team of about 30 open-source analysts that routinely analyzes military and government flight activity, said that it spotted 13 U.S. aircraft stationed at RAF Mildenhall departing for bases in Scotland, Spain and Germany.
The Wall Street Journal, which first reported the evacuation, said that the threat related to Iran. The report cited “people familiar with the matter.”
The relocation of the aircraft came less than two months after the U.S. Air Force withdrew its bombers from another U.S.-run base in Britain, RAF Fairford, as police investigated a suspected terror plot linked to Iran. Bombers flying out of RAF Fairford had been used to strike Iran during the Middle East conflict.
Some of the aircraft that were relocated were permanently based at RAF Mildenhall, while others were there on rotation and included a combination of Osprey aircraft and midair refueling tankers, the Military Air Tracking Alliance said.
The base also raised its alert level to FPCON Charlie — the second highest level — the organization said. That applies when an incident occurs or intelligence is received indicating that some form of terrorist action targeting personnel or facilities is likely.
The decision to move the aircraft was proactive rather than reactive, a U.S. official said, adding that the U.S. military is agile to potential threats. Some of the planes that left were in transit while others were permanently stationed at RAF Mildenhall and they may return, the official said. The official didn’t elaborate on the nature and source of the threat.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that the United States is “constantly repositioning forces around the world for a variety of reasons,” and referred questions to the Pentagon, which didn’t provide immediate confirmation.
An official from the U.S. Air Force in Europe told the AP that the U.S. is “taking coordinated and appropriate actions” to ensure the safety and security of U.S. and U.K. personnel and their families. The official said that aircraft are rotated between bases for various reasons, including training and “real world requirements.”
The official said that the U.S. military constantly assesses a variety of factors that determine what security measures are implemented. The official wouldn’t provide further information on movement of assets or specific force protection for reasons of operational security.
Both officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak publicly about sensitive military matters.
The U.K. prime minister’s office said that British air bases are safe and their security is a top priority. The office said that the U.K. is in constant communication with the U.S., sharing intelligence and assessing threats together.
RAF Mildenhall, a U.K. base operated by the U.S. Air Force, hosts the 100th refueling wing, the only permanent refueling wing in the European region. It operates the KC-135 Stratotanker, a four-engine jet aircraft with a wingspan of 131 feet (40 meters) that can carry up to 83,000 pounds (nearly 38,000 kilograms) of cargo.
Five men were detained on Sept. 27 after three suspicious vans were spotted traveling toward RAF Fairford. The U.K.-owned base has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East, including the Iran war.
Other arrests followed and two men have been charged under the National Security Act.
The U.K. Defense Ministry said in a statement that it doesn’t comment on the activity of other nations and said aircraft and other assets move regularly according to operational requirements.
___
Konstantin Toropin reported from Washington.

title: This Maine couple traveled 991 miles to complete an ambitious hunting goal
text:
Outdoors
The BDN outdoors section brings readers into the woods, waters and wild places of Maine. It features stories on hunting, fishing, wildlife, conservation and recreation, told by people who live these experiences. This section emphasizes hands-on knowledge, field reports, issues, trends and the traditions that define life outside in Maine. Read more Outdoors stories here. 
A Maine couple spent much of the fall traveling dirt roads, scouting hunting grounds and pursuing four different game animals. By the first week of rifle deer season, Lauren Waycott and Melvin Waycott IV had each harvested a turkey, bear, moose and deer, completing Maine’s hunting Grand Slam.
The couple’s hunting app recorded 991 miles on dirt roads between the start of their cow moose hunt and the end of the first week of rifle deer season.
Those miles included scouting for deer in the North Maine Woods, traveling between hunting camps and even taking time to hunt partridge after their cow moose hunt.
The Waycotts decided to pursue the goal after Melvin and Lauren’s father were both drawn for moose permits. Lauren’s father listed her as his subpermittee, allowing her to hunt and tag a moose on his permit.
They knew other hunters who had completed a Grand Slam, but hadn’t heard of another married couple accomplishing it together in the same year.
Lauren got the first of her four animals during the spring turkey season, when she harvested a 19-pound tom while hunting with her father.
The couple’s next successes came during bear season.
On Sept. 15, Lauren went on a guided hunt with Good Ole Boys Guide Service and harvested a 265-pound sow, her second bear. A few days earlier, on the opening day of bear trapping season, Melvin had trapped a 276-pound boar.
Later in September, Lauren returned to some of her favorite turkey hunting spots to help Melvin fill his tag. He harvested a 17.5-pound tom, giving each of them two of the four animals needed for the Grand Slam.
In October, the couple turned their attention to moose.
Melvin hunted with Tobey Brooke Guide Service and, on Oct. 13, harvested a bull with a 42-inch antler spread that weighed 652 pounds.
Just 10 days later, the three hunters headed north again, this time to Wildlife Management District 5 for Lauren’s father’s moose hunt. They were guided by Blackwater Guide Service.
Shortly after first light on Oct. 27, Lauren harvested a 352-pound cow moose.
Rather than heading home, Lauren and her father continued north to Wildlife Management District 1, where they had already rented a camp for a week of deer hunting. They had booked the cabin before receiving their moose permits, so the timing allowed them to spend two consecutive weeks hunting in the North Maine Woods.
Melvin stayed home that week to pursue a buck he had been watching on trail cameras.
On the evening of Nov. 3, Lauren and her father decided to try some unfamiliar hunting ground. At 4:10 p.m., she harvested an eight-point buck weighing 188 pounds.
With that deer, Lauren completed her Grand Slam.
The following morning, her father harvested his first-ever patch buck, a seven-point deer weighing 208 pounds.
Then, on Nov. 7, as Lauren and her father were packing up their camp to head home, she received the call they had been waiting for.
Melvin had harvested the eight-point buck he had been pursuing. It weighed 220.6 pounds and was his second patch buck.
The couple’s season also benefited others. All three deer harvested by the family were donated to the Hunters for the Hungry program.

title: Franklin County Sheriff’s Report, October 31st – November 8th
Woman credits free BRCA gene study with catching her cancer risk early
text:
OMAHA, Neb. (Aging Untold) — A Nebraska nurse practitioner says a free genetic research study likely saved her life after she learned she carries a BRCA2 gene mutation, despite having little family history of cancer.
Erin Thoman, a 34-year-old mother of four, said cancer was not something she had considered a personal risk. That changed after her sister, also a nurse, participated in the Genetic Insights Project at Nebraska Medicine.
“She didn’t really think much of it and so offered to do it to kind of help out with the study,” Thoman said. “Then she found out that she had the BRCA2 gene mutation.”
Thoman and her mother were then tested through the same study and both learned they also carry the mutation.
“We definitely were all surprised,” Thoman said.
Preventive surgeries ahead
Everyone carries two types of BRCA genes. When functioning properly, they repair DNA, keep other genes healthy and prevent cancerous changes in cells, according to Johns Hopkins Medicine.
When a mutation damages either gene, a person’s risk of developing cancer increases.
Inheriting damaged copies of the BRCA genes can increase the risk for breast and ovarian cancer in women, and breast and prostate cancer in men.
For Thoman, the path forward was clear.
“I wanted to not have that stress of wondering, is today the day I find out I have cancer?” Thoman said.
She has met with a breast surgeon at Nebraska Medicine and has additional appointments scheduled with a surgeon who would remove her ovaries and fallopian tubes.
The double mastectomy is expected to drop her breast cancer risk from around 60% to less than 10%.
“I’m very fortunate that I have four healthy kids, I no longer need those parts, so let’s just get rid of them,” Thoman said. “Honestly, I feel like this is a blessing. I have the opportunity to prevent it and be around a long time to watch my kids grow up.”
About the Genetic Insights Project
Thoman is one of 15,000 people in the Omaha metro area to receive genetic results through the free study. Researchers want to enroll up to 100,000 people in Nebraska and 3 million nationwide.
Participants provide a blood sample or complete an at-home saliva kit, which is sent to Helix, a genetic testing company. The screening looks for three gene mutations known to increase risk for several diseases, including multiple types of cancer.
Dr. Doug Stoller, a cardiologist involved in the study, said the goal is early detection.
“The goal here is to detect as early as possible and prevent even the possibility that cancer could ever start,” Stoller said.
About one in 75 people screened learn they carry a genetic mutation.
“Many participants that find that they carry one of these variants actually are found to have very early-stage disease already by the time that they actually get their screening done,” Stoller said.
More than half of those who test positive did not know they were at risk.
Thoman said she is now encouraging others to sign up.
“It’s free, it’s super easy and it’s just nice to know if you have that risk,” she said.
Learn more about the Genetic Insights Project, including eligibility requirements.

title: Trump nominates Justice Department official to a EEOC seat that was left open by Democrat's firing
text:
Trump nominates Justice Department official to a EEOC seat that was left open by Democrat's firing
President Donald Trump has nominated a Justice Department official to an open seat on a key civil rights agency, signaling his administration's determination to forge ahead with efforts to dismantle diversity policies it claims discriminate against white workers and others.
The White House announced late Monday that it has tapped Matt Zandi to fill a seat previously held by Jocelyn Samuels, one of two Democratic commissioners fired by Trump before the end of their terms in an unprecedented move to seize control of the EEOC, a bipartisan agency created by Congress through the 1964 Civil Rights Act.
Zandi currently serves as chief of staff for the Justice Department's civil rights division, which saw the mass departure of career lawyers as it shifted to investigating employers and schools for what it considers unlawful diversity and transgender policies.
He would serve a five-year term ending July 1, 2031.
Zandi's confirmation would further shift the balance of power at the EEOC to the right. Currently, there are two Republican commissioners — Andrea Lucas, who is the chair, and Brittany Panuccio — and one Democrat — Kalpana Kotagal, whose term expires next year.
Under Lucas, the EEOC has steadfastly enforced Trump's civil rights priorities, often in tight cooperation with the Department of Justice.
Zandi's nomination comes as the EEOC prepares for several major regulatory changes, including ending a 60-year-old requirement to collect demographic workforce data from many employers and revising rules for enforcing the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act, which Lucas has said improperly extended protections for workers seeking abortions, birth control or fertility treatments.
The Trump administration has yet to nominate anyone to fill a fifth seat, left open by the firing of Democrat Charlotte Burrows.
The impending Democratic takeover of the Senate majority in January raises the possibility that the EEOC won't have five commissioners for the remainder of Trump's term. Leading Democratic senators have vowed not to confirm any of Trump's nominees to the EEOC in protest of his firing of the Democratic commissioners, which they say stripped the agency of its historic independence and bipartisanship.
Sen. Tammy Baldwin, a Wisconsin Democrat, criticized Zandi's nomination as further politicizing the EEOC, which enforces the country's employment anti-discrimination laws.
"For a bipartisan commission, the custom is to pair nominees from the two parties. This would be the third Republican commissioner in a row without a pairing, an overtly partisan decision of the administration," Baldwin said Tuesday, speaking during a Senate committee hearing on the confirmation of Catherine Eschbach to be EEOC general counsel.
However, Trump's approach to the EEOC received a major vindication after the Supreme Court upheld his decision to fire the heads of several independent agencies, significantly expanding presidential power. The ruling prompted Samuels to drop a lawsuit challenging her dismissal from the EEOC.
Zandi and Eschbach are likely to be confirmed while Republicans control the Senate.
Senate Republicans have mostly praised Trump's approach to civil rights enforcement, and Lucas and Panuccio sailed through their confirmations despite unanimous opposition from Democrats.
"Under this administration, EEOC has sharpened its focus on even-handed enforcement of employment discrimination laws," Sen. Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana Republican, said during the hearing on Eschbach, whom he praised.
The EEOC had no comment. The Department of Justice didn't reply to a request for comment from Zandi.

title: Trump moves to cut SNAP benefits for 6.3 million people
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Gray News) - The Trump administration proposed a rule that could cut food stamp benefits for 6.3 million people.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture proposal, released Monday, would limit automatic eligibility for SNAP to low-income households that receive cash assistance through the TANF program.
Households receiving noncash or nominal TANF services would no longer automatically qualify for SNAP under the proposal.
According to the proposal, the change would save $44.6 billion between 2027 and 2031. It is the Trump administration’s latest effort to curb SNAP spending, citing concerns about waste and fraud.
The proposal targets a policy known as “broad-based categorical eligibility,” which allows states to use TANF benefits such as child care or workforce training to qualify households for SNAP without applying the program’s standard income eligibility limit.
The changes would make SNAP eligibility more standardized and “preserve benefits for the truly needy,” the rule said.
The USDA also estimates that 1.8 million children would also lose eligibility for free school lunches under the proposed rule.
Nearly 18% of SNAP recipients, or about 6.3 million people, would lose benefits under the change.
The public will have 30 days to comment on the proposed rule.

title: 3 charged following deadly shooting at youth football championship game
text:
MADISON, Mo. (KMOV/Gray News) - Three people have been charged in connection with a shooting at a Missouri youth football championship game that killed one and injured three others earlier this month.
Carl Tucker, 18, faces one count of first-degree murder and three counts of aggravated battery with a firearm following the shooting. He faces an additional count of first-degree murder as an alternative theory charge.
Jeffery Mosby, 42, faces charges of aggravated discharge of a firearm, reckless discharge of a firearm, aggravated unlawful use of weapons and possession of a controlled substance.
Brianna Simms, 31, also faces a charge of obstruction of justice after police said she provided false information to investigators.
The shooting occurred during a youth football championship game at Madison Senior High School on Nov. 1.
A fight then broke out on the field, and adults ran onto the field to break it up. According to law enforcement, a second altercation then arose at the entrance before gunfire erupted.
Four people were shot, including Steve Smith, 64, a grandfather who died from his injuries.
“Mr. Smith was at a youth football game — a place where families should be able to gather, enjoy watching their children and grandchildren and share in the excitement of the game,” Madison County State’s Attorney Tom Haine said. “Instead, his family is now mourning his death. It is difficult to comprehend how an event like this could end in such tragedy.”
The other shooting victims were a 36-year-old man who was shot in the face, a 33-year-old man who suffered a gunshot wound to the hip and a 22-year-old woman shot in the thigh.
Additional people were also injured in the ensuing crowd surge.
“This was a 9-and-under and a 12-and-under football game, and these kids heard gunshots ringing out,” Haine said. “If anyone knows anything about this case, we encourage you, for the sake of these children and for the sake of justice in our community, to bring it to our attention.”
The investigation into the shooting remains ongoing.
Authorities have additionally noted a person of interest in the case, but that person has not been immediately charged with a criminal offense.

title: Good Samaritan breaks window to free 3-year-old girl from car sinking in pond
text:
ST. PETERS, Mo. (KMOV/Gray News) - A Missouri mother is extremely grateful to a good Samaritan who rescued her 3-year-old daughter after the family’s SUV rolled into a pond.
Austin Collins was dropping his kids off at a school bus stop Thursday morning in St. Peters when he saw an SUV roll from a parking lot, down a hill and into a pond. A 3-year-old girl named Melody was inside at the time.
“I just saw a big ol’ splash, and immediately, everyone just ran over and took action,” Collins said.
He called 911 then jumped into the pond to help the toddler.
“I was honestly holding onto the vehicle to stay afloat,” Collins said. “I didn’t know how deep it was at the time.”
Collins said someone handed him a hammer, and he used it to break a window to free Melody. He cut his hand on the broken glass in the process.
“I knew that as soon as I grabbed the little girl, she would potentially get cut,” he said. “So, I ended up just taking my hand and clearing as much glass as I could before I grabbed her.”
Mom thankful her little girl is still alive
Melody’s mother, Megan Kohlhaas, was helping her other kids get on the bus when the incident happened.
“So, I’m just waving bye to them, making sure he gets on the bus, and next thing, I know, the kids are all screaming, ‘The car! The car!’ And it just rolls backwards,” Kohlhaas said.
She said the quick response from others helped save her daughter’s life.
“Even just finding the hammer and how fast someone was able to pass it on to someone in the water and break in and that we had that time is just a miracle,” she said.
Kohlhaas said she is thankful Melody is still alive.
“I’m just thankful she’s alive, and I can’t stop thinking about the man and all the people that helped,” Kohlhaas said. “Without him, we would’ve lost her.”
Collins credited Kohlhaas for how the group responded.
“Kudos to the mom. She definitely created that urgency early on so that we all could pull together,” he said. “It really outlines what we can do as a community when somebody is in need: we just all pull together.”
Melody is doing just fine after the incident. A GoFundMe has been created to help Kohlhaas replace her car.
Information from investigators on why the SUV was able to roll away is pending.

title: Portland councilors discuss proposed Amtrak Downeaster station relocation
text:
Portland councilors discuss proposed Amtrak Downeaster station relocation
Councilors raised questions about the proposed location and the city's role in the planning process Monday night during a workshop
Portland councilors discuss proposed Amtrak Downeaster station relocation
Councilors raised questions about the proposed location and the city's role in the planning process Monday night during a workshop
Portland city councilors raised questions Monday night about plans to relocate the Amtrak Downeaster station and the city's role in determining its future location.
During a workshop, representatives from Northern New England Passenger Rail Authority, NNEPRA, discussed potential locations for the station, identifying site 3 as the only viable option.
The proposed location would move the Downeaster station from Thompson's Point to the southern end of St. John Street and Fore River Parkway, a site along the main rail line. Relocating the station here would eliminate the need for trains to travel 15 minutes off the main line to reach the station.
NNEPRA representatives said the other location faces significant obstacles.
Several councilors questioned the planning process and the extent of the city's involvement in selecting the preferred location.
Mayor Mark Dion said the City Council does not have the authority to make the final decision or veto NNEPRA's plans. However, he suggested the city could work toward making site 3 the best possible outcome.
NNEPRA said the $48 million in federal funding is tied to the proposed project at site 3. Officials maintained that relocating the station to the main rail line would improve rail operations and help support expanded passenger rail service.
The City Council ended the meeting expecting to revisit the issue in December, when members can vote on three recommendations: keeping the existing station at Thompson's Point, exploring ways to make site 2 viable, or support site 3 with conditions.
The council's recommendation would serve as an advisory statement rather than a binding decision on the station's location.
Meanwhile, NNEPRA representatives said the authority plans to continue working towards the lengthy process of formally obligating its federal grant funding.

title: Can a Maine registered sex offender vote at a school?
text:
NORRIDGEWOCK — Town officials say they were faced with a predicament last week on Election Day.
What should poll workers do when a known registered sex offender shows up at an elementary school to vote, during school hours?
The answer, state elections officials say, is that election staff should let the person vote — but keep a watchful eye.
The Maine Department of the Secretary of State recommends that people who may be under restrictions, due to past convictions or bail or probation conditions, vote absentee to avoid any problems, spokesperson Jana Spaulding said in an emailed statement.
But if someone who has restrictions on contact with children shows up to vote in-person at a school polling place, the office recommends the election warden or a law enforcement officer monitor the voter, Spaulding said.
“The town cannot prohibit the individual from voting but can minimize their time in and out of the voting place,” she said.
Being a registered sex offender does not necessarily make it illegal to be at a school while it’s in session.
The secretary of state’s office pointed to a section of Maine law that makes it a misdemeanor criminal offense for people convicted of certain sex offenses against minors under the age of 14 to have direct or indirect contact with minors in certain locations, like schools, childcare facilities or recreational facilities. The office also noted bail or probation conditions ordered by a judge could include such a restriction if there is a connection to the offense.
For Norridgewock Town Manager Richard LaBelle, who also is town clerk and oversees elections, the answer of what to do was not so clear during voting on Tuesday, Nov. 3.
LaBelle said in a phone call that the situation began to unfold mid-morning when he and other staff recognized a voter at the town’s polling place, the Mill Stream Elementary School gymnasium, as being a registered sex offender.
The state registry shows eight registered sex offenders live in Norridgewock. LaBelle said he can recognize most of them because of his role leading municipal government.
Unsure of what exactly to do, poll workers let the man vote, LaBelle said. Meanwhile, LaBelle went outside to get the Somerset County sheriff’s deputy detailed to the voting location. After the person voted, the deputy escorted him away from the school, LaBelle said.
Voters, unless they need accessible doors, are directed to enter and exit the gymnasium through its outside doors, instead of entering the school through the main entrance.
LaBelle said, in addition to law enforcement, he consulted with administrators for Skowhegan-based Maine School Administrative District 54, as well as staff the secretary of state’s office.
The secretary of state’s office indicated initially the situation was a non-issue, according to LaBelle. However, LaBelle said he was frustrated that as of Friday the state office had not provided the town with any formal, written guidance. LaBelle said he was also considering requesting an opinion from the Office of the Maine Attorney General if that is what it would take to get clarity.
LaBelle received that written guidance Monday afternoon from Chief Deputy Secretary of State Kate McBrien, a few hours before Spaulding provided a nearly identical response to the Morning Sentinel. McBrien’s email to LaBelle noted she consulted with the attorney general’s office.
“While I can’t speak for all municipalities,” LaBelle said in an email Tuesday, “I know the Town of Norridgewock will continue to promote absentee voting as a way of participation, but we will also be diligent in identifying registered sex offenders in our community and cross-referencing publicly available records to determine whether a registered sex offender has restrictions from being at a school.”
MSAD 54 Superintendent of Schools Jonathan Moody said he fielded a concern from one parent and sent a letter to families Friday to address anyone else who may have had questions.
In the letter, Moody largely responded to the question of whether school should be canceled on election days.
He said in the email that Mill Stream Elementary School was designed to be a resource for the community, not just a school.
And although modeling civic engagement is a benefit of hosting the polling place, it is not the main reason the district continues to hold classes, Moody said.
Instead, he wrote, it comes down to safety: Many students rely on school for food and a safe place to go during the day. It is the same kind of consideration district officials take into account when calling a snow day, Moody wrote.
For the last six years, the district has worked with the Somerset County Sheriff’s Office and the town to ensure law enforcement is present during elections, Moody wrote. He acknowledged, however, the district’s communication and coordination with law enforcement during elections is an area that could still use improvement.
“We have already begun discussing these concerns with our partners and will use what we have learned to strengthen our planning and procedures for future elections,” the superintendent wrote.
Moody invited families with concerns to attend the next parent advisory meeting, scheduled for Wednesday, Nov. 18, at 6 p.m. The meeting is set to be held virtually.

“Every time I walk into the building, it has this weird juxtaposition of being totally strange and foreign and yet oddly familiar,” said
Frank renovated the 1765 building’s plumbing, electrical and refrigeration systems, while adding new lighting, artwork and tableware, though they still have the tables and chairs from Arrows.

title: Investigators recover voice recorder from jet crash in Florida that killed 9
text:
(AP) - Investigators said Monday they have recovered the cockpit voice recorder from a business jet that plummeted from the sky amid severe weather in Florida last week, killing all nine people on board.
The recorder was found at the site where the Bahamas-bound Learjet slammed into the ground and erupted in a fireball Nov. 1, the National Transportation Safety Board said in a statement posted to social media.
If data from the device can be recovered, it could provide crucial details about what the pilots said to each other as they encountered turbulence, ice formed on the wings and they lost control of the aircraft.
It was not immediately known if the recorder had been damaged or if it was working in the first place. The NTSB said the device was being evaluated at a lab in Washington.
From photos the agency posted online, showing the recorder’s orange-painted metal shell, it appeared to be in decent shape, aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti told The Associated Press.
“It’s very plausible that any info on the recorder survived,” Guzzetti said. “If they can recover it, and it’s from the accident flight, that will be a huge help to investigators.”
He noted that when the NTSB recovered the cockpit voice recorder from a medical transport plane that crashed in Philadelphia in January 2025, killing seven people, it turned out the device likely had not been functioning for several years.
Witnesses captured dramatic video as the business jet plunged nose-first into the ground, and air traffic control transmissions recorded the disturbing moments as the pilots realized their fate. But the cockpit voice recorder could shed light on other aspects of the crash, including why the Learjet appeared to steer around a large storm cell only to head directly into a rapidly developing smaller one.
Investigators have said pieces of a key part of the tail called the elevator, which controls the plane’s pitch, were found more than a mile away from the main crater, confirming the plane started to break apart before impact.
The co-pilot told air traffic controllers that the plane was being thrown up and down more than 700 feet (213 meters), and she asked them for a better route through the area.
Generally, it takes 12 to 18 months for the NTSB to complete a crash investigation, but complicated cases can take longer. The NTSB’s roughly 400 workers are pursuing more than 1,200 active investigations.
Investigators will review maintenance records and any history of problems with the plane. They will also interview officials at Upper Jets, the company that operated the flight, as well as air traffic controllers and people who work at the airport in Austin, Texas, from where the plane departed.

title: Tennessee judge dismisses case from Dolly Parton's manager alleging her nephew threatened her estate
text:
Tennessee judge dismisses case from Dolly Parton's manager alleging her nephew threatened her estate
A Tennessee judge on Monday dismissed a case brought by Dolly Parton’s longtime manager who was seeking an injunction against her nephew and head of security, alleging he had threatened her estate and its employees.
The manager, Danny Nozell, asked for the dismissal on Thursday after the two sides came to an agreement. The order from Chancellor I’Ashea L. Myles finalizes that request without prejudice, meaning it can be filed again.
Nozell, who runs She’s Alive, an entity founded to manage and protect Parton’s estate, had secured a temporary restraining order against Bryan Seaver and his security company, Squadron Augmented Protection Services, in September.
The complaint seeking the temporary restraining order said Seaver had threatened violence and the destruction of Parton’s legacy and business empire. Nozell wanted to turn the order into a permanent injunction against Seaver. The two sides were to have publicly argued the claims on Tuesday.
Seaver's lawyers said in a statement that he “cares deeply about his Aunt Dolly, her music, her family, and the legacy she left behind.”
“He has made a career out of protecting his aunt while she was alive and remains committed to Dolly and his family” the statement, released Monday, said. “Mr. Seaver is grateful to put this misunderstanding behind him so that the entire family can continue to grieve peacefully and ensure that the bright light of Dolly's legacy remains completely untouched.”
Related previous coverage in the player at the top: Hear what Seaver had to say in announcing Parton's death on Aug. 25
The dismissal brings a sudden and quiet end to a serious rift in the beloved country superstar's inner circle that began while she was sick with cancer and spilled into public view in the weeks after her Aug. 25 death.
Neither side nor court documents have revealed anything about why the complaint was withdrawn, though one court filing said the sides had reached an agreement.
Emails requesting details and comment were sent to lawyers for Nozell and She's Alive.
Seaver, who Parton had handpicked to announce her death, said in court filings that he considered Nozell a close friend and ally before the restraining order, and said the text messages Nozell cited as evidence of his threats were a “private conversation between two friends who were both frustrated, grieving and discussing strategy.”
Parton was a widely adored singer, songwriter, philanthropist and country music icon who rose from a log cabin in the Tennessee mountains to a stardom that spanned generations with songs including “Jolene,” “Coat of Many Colors,” “9 to 5” and “I Will Always Love You.” She also left behind a business empire, much of it based in her hometown, that employed many of her close friends and family.

title: Planning for Jay data center moves forward, but deal not yet final
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
JAY — A proposed $550 million data center at the former Androscoggin Mill is showing signs of life again, with its original development partner back in discussions and a public meeting tentatively planned for December.
Town Manager Shiloh LaFreniere told the Select Board on Monday, Nov. 9, that JGT2 Redevelopment LLC, owner of the former mill property on Riley Road, has resumed efforts to move forward with Sentinel Data Centers, which withdrew from the project in June.
“They’re moving forward again with Sentinel,” LaFreniere said. “But they have not reached a final agreement yet.”
The renewed discussions could revive one of Jay’s most significant redevelopment proposals since the paper mill closed in 2023, potentially restoring a major source of investment and employment to the community. State environmental permitting is moving ahead, although updated construction schedules, investment figures and job projections have not been announced.
LaFreniere said JGT2 partner Tony McDonald contacted the town to provide the update but was hesitant to announce another development milestone before an agreement was finalized.
“He’s a little afraid of crying wolf multiple times and not having what he says actually commence,” she told the board, referring to previous setbacks.
Despite that caution, McDonald wanted town officials and residents to know the project was progressing, she said.
A public information meeting is tentatively being considered for Dec. 10 at the former mill property. LaFreniere said the event could run from about 4-8 p.m. in an open-house format, with representatives available to discuss electrical infrastructure, water consumption and other aspects of the proposal.
The date and arrangements have not been finalized.
Meanwhile, Main-Land Development Consultants Inc. delivered a copy of the project’s Site Location of Development Act amendment application to the town office shortly before Monday’s meeting. A separate air emissions license application was expected to arrive by mail within the next day or two.
“The town will have copies of the applications at the office,” LaFreniere said, adding that the documents would also be accessible through the Maine Department of Environmental Protection.
The applications concern redevelopment of part of the former mill at 300 Riley Road. According to the public notice, buildings would be reused to house computing equipment, while former parking and rail yard areas would accommodate heating, ventilation and air conditioning equipment.
Maine Public reported Monday that pre-application documents also describe a new subsurface wastewater disposal system and two diesel-powered emergency generators rated at 3.25 megawatts each.
The original development, announced earlier this year, called for about 1 million square feet of data center space, an investment of $550 million, roughly 800 construction jobs and more than 100 permanent positions.
During a March presentation to the Select Board, McDonald described the facility as a co-location data center serving multiple customers. He estimated an initial electrical demand of about 82 megawatts and said its closed-loop cooling system would require about 300,000 gallons of replacement water daily.
Those figures were tied to the earlier proposal and have not been confirmed for the latest plans.
The project’s electricity requirements attracted statewide attention as lawmakers considered legislation temporarily restricting permits for large data centers. McDonald sought an exemption for the Jay development, citing its reuse of existing industrial infrastructure and potential economic benefits.
Gov. Janet Mills vetoed the proposed moratorium in April, citing concerns about its potential impact on redevelopment projects such as the one in Jay.
Less than two months later, Sentinel informed JGT2 it would not proceed with the project at that time, putting the development on hold while the property owner explored other possibilities.
JGT2 purchased the former Androscoggin Mill property in December 2023, following the end of papermaking operations earlier that year. The company has since undertaken demolition and site preparation work aimed at attracting new businesses to the industrial property.
The latest permitting effort signals renewed activity at the site, though the future of the development still depends on a final agreement and the necessary regulatory approvals.
Residents will be able to review application materials through the town office and DEP, with further details about the proposed December public meeting expected to be announced.

title: Police investigate whether burned Ohio State University students were victims of hazing
text:
COLUMBUS, Ohio (AP) — Police are investigating whether two Ohio State University students who were treated for deep burns after being engulfed in flames at an outdoor fraternity party were victims of hazing.
The university placed the Sigma Alpha Epsilon fraternity on interim suspension after a video circulated on social media showing a large group surrounding two young men on fire Saturday. A student who watched the video called police the next day to report a possible hazing incident, according to an audio recording of the call.
“They stood around watching while this kid just burned,” said the student, who was sent the video in a group chat with her sorority members.
The video shows a ring of people standing outside, many wearing the school’s red and white colors, laughing and shouting at two men on the ground with their pants on fire. One lunges at the other, and they both roll on the ground. The shouting takes on a more panicked tone as they struggle to remove their clothing. One onlooker holds a small fire extinguisher but doesn’t successfully deploy it.
According to the Columbus Police report, the victims were both students who were treated for “moderate” second- and third-degree burns. The university has not said how the fraternity is linked to the event, but the report lists the president of the fraternity as part of the investigation.
The report also lists hazing as the charge being investigated and notes that university authorities also are looking into whether hazing occurred.
Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine signed “Collin’s Law” in 2021 toughening penalties for hazing in the wake of a student’s death at a fraternity house at Ohio University. The law’s definition of hazing includes participating in or coercing anyone into behavior that creates a substantial risk of mental or physical harm and is tied to initiation into an organization or continued membership.
Under that law and the federal Stop Campus Hazing Act, signed by President Joe Biden in 2024, Ohio State maintains a public list of hazing violations and penalties. It shows that so far this year, four fraternities, one sorority and one co-ed group have been sanctioned for hazing. Sigma Alpha Epsilon does not appear on the list for the last five years, though the student newspaper The Lantern said it has been sanctioned at least seven times since 2001.
According to the newspaper’s archives, the chapter over the years has been found to have violated policies related to alcohol, hazing and endangering behavior, and at one point had its disciplinary probation extended for failing to comply with sanctions.
Sigma Alpha Epsilon eliminated its “pledging” process for all its chapters nationwide in 2014 in part due to injuries and deaths.
In 2022, 46 members of the SAE chapter at the University of New Hampshire were charged with hazing. Most agreed to perform community service and avoided conviction; the three who went to trial were acquitted because the judge said the state didn’t prove the acts were a “condition of initiation into, continued membership in or association with” the fraternity.
___
Ramer reported from Concord, New Hampshire. Julie Carr-Smyth also contributed from Columbus.

title: Maine's Jordon Hudson sues Airbnb hosts for leaking video of her shirtless ex-boyfriend
text:
Jordon Hudson, Bill Belichick’s ex-romantic partner, is suing the owners of an Airbnb in Winthrop, Massachusetts, over viral Ring camera footage showing the former New England Patriots head coach shirtless.
In the civil complaint, filed Friday, Hudson claims the hosts leaked the video to the public, outing Hudson and Belichick as a couple and violating their privacy. The pageant contestant and former cheerleader also argues the leaked footage subjected her to “ridicule and denigration.”
Hudson filed the complaint against the Airbnb hosts — Elise McDevitt and Craig Nolan — in Suffolk County Superior Court. She asks the court to bar the Winthrop couple from disclosing or distributing any personal or private information about her to third parties. The lawsuit states that Hudson believes McDevitt and Nolan may possess additional private videos or information about her that they could exploit financially.
Hudson also asks the court to find the couple liable for “egregious” privacy, consumer protection and contract violations, seeking unspecified financial damages.
As of Monday afternoon, court records did not show any filings from McDevitt and Nolan in response to the lawsuit or list an attorney representing them.
According to the complaint, Hudson and Belichick stayed at the Airbnb for four nights in June 2023, when their relationship was not yet public. During that time, a doorbell camera captured Belichick walking shirtless outside the property.
Nolan and McDevitt saved the video “without the knowledge or authorization of Mr. Belichick or Ms. Hudson,” according to the lawsuit. After McDevitt shared the video with Hudson during the stay, Hudson repeatedly asked McDevitt to delete the footage.
“When McDevitt finally responded, she ominously stated: ‘We will delete it from ring, but as you know, unfortunately, videos are never totally deleted,’” the lawsuit reads.
The suit claims that McDevitt told Hudson she would not release the video, but also “not-so-subtly urged Ms. Hudson to leave a good review on Airbnb by stating: ‘We would appreciate a good review (heart emoji).’” Hudson complied, hoping a five-star rating would prevent McDevitt from sharing the footage with the media.
Despite this, in November 2023, the video showing Belichick shirtless was released publicly online. The footage quickly “went viral” and “became infamous,” the lawsuit states.
When confronted by Hudson about the leak, McDevitt initially denied sharing the video, saying she would contact Ring to find out what happened. McDevitt later made a “thinly veiled” threat over text, intending to discourage Hudson and Belichick from suing, the suit claims.
“If you decide to take any legal action, we will respond and the discovery process would presumably not be welcomed by the person in the video,” the text message reads.
In May 2025, McDevitt admitted to Hudson over text that she and Nolan sent the footage “to a few people” to figure out whether the shirtless man was Belichick, according to the lawsuit.
“I don’t know what happened from there, but we did delete it from the camera, as I assured you,” the text reads, according to the lawsuit. “We were never happy that it was released and never commented that it was our home on any social media channels. You guys should come back lol!”
The complaint argues that McDevitt and Nolan “relished” the media coverage of the leaked footage, including by speaking anonymously to sports journalist Pablo Torre for his podcast.
During the interview, the Winthrop couple gave Torre a second video of Belichick outside the Airbnb, according to the lawsuit. McDevitt and Nolan also shared private information about Hudson’s stay with Belichick at the short-term rental property.
“This unwanted scrutiny and the ensuing media stories, which contain false information, have caused significant damage to Ms. Hudson,” the lawsuit reads.
Hudson reported what happened to Airbnb, and the short-term rental booking company barred McDevitt and Nolan from offering stays on its website, according to the suit. McDevitt reacted with a deluge of “hostile” texts to Hudson, according to the lawsuit.
“Now that you destroyed our livelihood, we are weighing our options about whom we will talk to and what we will discuss with them,” one alleged text reads.
Story by Susannah Sudborough, MassLive.com.

title: Janet Mills calls for $3B increase in federal heating assistance
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Gov. Janet Mills is calling on Congress to give a $3 billion boost to federal heating assistance.
That comes as Maine grapples with skyrocketing heating oil prices, which hit a record high of $6.05 a gallon two weeks ago. The most recent statewide average is 79% higher than this time last year.
Approximately half of all Maine homes use oil as their primary heating source, making the state particularly vulnerable to such price shocks.
“No one should be cold in their homes because Trump decided to wage an unnecessary, unwanted war with Iran,” Mills said in a statement. “That’s why I’m joining my fellow New England governors to call on Congress to release billions in federal funding for LIHEAP to provide immediate relief for vulnerable families as winter approaches.”
In a Monday letter to Congress, Mills joined New England’s other governors to call for the supplemental heating assistance, either through an annual appropriation increase or one-time emergency funding. She sent a similar letter to Maine’s congressional delegation in October.
The Trump administration released about $37 million in low-income heating assistance for Maine in October, one of the earliest releases in the program’s history. An additional $1.4 million was awarded to the state’s four federally recognized tribes. 
But the National Energy Assistance Directors Association projects that heating oil prices will increase by 50% this winter. The governors warned that would erode the purchasing power of existing federal aid.
“While our states are working to mitigate the immediate impact of rising energy costs on vulnerable households and continue to invest heavily in energy efficiency, weatherization, and other long-term solutions, these efforts cannot fully offset the immediate financial pressures facing families this winter,” the New England governors wrote.
The Mills administration has taken steps to ease the financial strain of higher energy costs, including enrolling Mainers who receive public health insurance and food or heating assistance in an electric bill discount program and sending $300 checks to 500,000 Mainers.
Oil prices have increased globally since February, when the Iran war effectively halted fuel shipments out of the Strait of Hormuz, a site of passage for a fifth of the world’s natural gas and oil. Russia and Ukraine have carried out attacks on each other’s energy infrastructure, and Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen have attacked Saudi energy sites, further straining global fuel supplies.
Rising energy costs were one factor in turning many voters against Republicans in the midterm elections, including U.S. Sen. Susan Collins’ defeat.
Eligibility for federal heating assistance is based on income, household size and resource availability. Applications are available online or through local community action agencies.

title: House to vote on impeachment effort against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
text:
House halts impeachment effort against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth faces impeachment articles introduced by Rep. Thomas Massie, with President Trump and Republican leaders defending him ahead of a critical House vote.
House halts impeachment effort against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth faces impeachment articles introduced by Rep. Thomas Massie, with President Trump and Republican leaders defending him ahead of a critical House vote.
Note: The House voted Tuesday night against advancing the impeachment against Hegseth, likely ending the process this congressional session.
The House is set to vote tonight on whether to advance impeachment articles against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, as President Donald Trump and Republican leaders defend him against allegations of abuse of power and unlawful military actions.
President Trump praised Hegseth’s performance during his first Pentagon press conference in six months, saying, “He won two wars. He was in charge. We all won.”
Hegseth strongly rejected the impeachment effort, calling it “a farce, and it’s a stunt, and everybody knows it.”
Kentucky Republican Rep. Thomas Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment, accusing Hegseth of abusing his power, waging war without congressional approval, and mishandling military operations, including actions that led to civilian casualties.
“I mean, in some aspects he has been effective, and that’s what we’re impeaching him for — his effectiveness in breaking the law and violating the Constitution,” Massie said.
Hegseth and the administration have denied the allegations, insisting all military operations were lawful.
“It’s a political spectacle. A personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment,” Hegseth said.
House Republican leaders are also defending Hegseth and working to block the impeachment articles from reaching the House floor. House Speaker Mike Johnson said, “The idea that you would impeach the Secretary of War at a time of international conflict sends a terrible message to our enemies and our allies, and we’re not going to play that game.”
Even if the impeachment effort fails, the defense secretary could face further scrutiny when Democrats take control of Congress in January.
If the House votes to impeach Hegseth, it would not immediately remove him from office. Impeachment is a formal charge requiring a simple majority vote in the House, but removal would require a conviction by a two-thirds majority in the Senate. If the House moves forward, Hegseth would become only the third Cabinet official in U.S. history to be impeached. The most recent was President Biden’s Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas, who faced impeachment over his handling of the border but retained his position after the Senate dismissed the charges.
Tonight’s vote is not directly on impeachment but could determine whether the effort advances. If Republican leaders succeed, the resolution could be sent to committee, effectively sidelining it. If they fail, the House could move directly to a debate and vote on impeachment. Under House rules, lawmakers have until tomorrow to take up Massie’s resolution.

title: There was no ‘Margaret Chase Smith moment’
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Andrew Shuttleworth Fowler lives in Westbrook. He was 11 when Susan Collins was first elected to the Senate.
“I have now had my Margaret Chase Smith moment,” Sen. Susan Collins told the New York Times last Wednesday, a day after Troy Jackson ended her Senate career.
Constituents had urged her to find one, she said. She had. “The best comparison is we each lost our last race for the Senate.”
If losing her seat was as close as she could come to following in Smith’s footsteps, I’ll take it. But those of us who did the urging had something more in mind.
We had in mind June 1, 1950, when Smith, in her second year in the Senate, stood on the floor with Joe McCarthy two rows behind her and condemned the politics of “fear, ignorance, bigotry and smear.” “I do not want to see the Republican Party win that way,” she said.
McCarthy retaliated. He had her removed from the Senate’s investigations subcommittee and gave the seat to a California freshman named Richard Nixon. He backed a primary challenger against her. She kept opposing him, and in 1954 she voted to censure him. He was finished within a year.
She lost in 1972, three full terms after that speech. The speech is why we remember her.
Collins wants credit for voting to convict Donald Trump in 2021. She was right to do it. “It is never enough,” she complains.
But a year earlier, she had voted to acquit him. She told CBS News that being impeached was “a pretty big lesson.” He had learned something, she said. He had: his party would protect him.
Two years before that, she vouched for Brett Kavanaugh’s respect for precedent when she voted to put him on the Supreme Court. She reminded us that abortion-rights groups had been wrong about nominees before. They were right about this one. “I feel misled,” she said in 2022, and yet she does not regret the vote.
“I want results and they want angry rhetoric,” Collins told the Times.
Women lost the federal constitutional right to abortion. That was a result.
Heating oil averaged $6.05 a gallon in Maine last week, up 82% from a year earlier because of a war she voted five times not to stop. That was a result.
Mainers on marketplace health plans saw premiums rise 77% on average after she voted to end the shutdown without their subsidies. Enrollment fell by more than 6,000. That was a result.
She voted to advance the largest Medicaid cut in the program’s history, then voted against it once it would pass without her. The state estimates more than 31,000 Mainers will lose MaineCare in January because of it. That was a result.
In June, she voted for $70 billion more for ICE and the Border Patrol, telling Mainers the money would pay for training and body cameras. Five weeks later, a federal agent without a body camera shot a young father dead on a Biddeford street. He was not the man they were looking for. That, too, was a result.
The senator reminds us she brought home $1.5 billion for 672 projects. Her campaign manager calls it an opportunity Maine “has walked away from.”
Nobody in Maine would turn down a new fire station. But a fire station does not heat a house or insure a family. What she brought home, we’ll keep. We could not afford what came with it.
Collins has said for years that her Senate desk once belonged to Margaret Chase Smith. It is a good desk. Smith stood behind it in 1950, and in a soft and trembling voice said what her party did not want to hear.
Collins inherited the furniture. She did not inherit the nerve. Last Tuesday, Maine took the desk back.

title: Women veterans call for greater representation in battle for services
text:
More than 2.1 million women veterans live in the U.S. today. By 2040, they are projected to make up 18% of all veterans, making them the fastest-growing group of veterans, according to the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs. (Adobe Stock) Listen to this story here. By Kathryn Carley Nov 11, 2026 To mark Veterans Day, women veterans are calling for […]
More than 2.1 million women veterans live in the U.S. today. By 2040, they are projected to make up 18% of all veterans, making them the fastest-growing group of veterans, according to the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs. (Adobe Stock)
Listen to this story here.
By Kathryn Carley
Nov 11, 2026
To mark Veterans Day, women veterans are calling for greater female representation within the military to address the high rate of sexual assaults and lack of adequate mental health care.
Under the Trump administration, the Pentagon has removed several high-ranking female military officers and blocked the promotions of dozens more.
Rebecca Cornell du Houx, executive director of the Sisters in Arms Center in Augusta, which provides emergency shelter to women veterans and their children, said women leaders are more likely to champion policies demanding safety and respect.
“It is really necessary that we create a culture where sexual assault, harassment isn’t permitted, and it goes back to ensuring that we have women in leadership positions,” Cornell du Houx asserted.
One in three active-duty service members reported incidents of unwanted sexual contact or sexual assault to the Department of War last year, up from one in four in 2023, but Cornell du Houx noted many assaults still go unreported. Military sexual trauma significantly increases the risk of suicide and homelessness for women veterans, who now make up 10% of the overall homeless veteran population.
The Sisters in Arms Center offers them a temporary safe haven, counseling, access to services and help finding an affordable home. Cornell du Houx has been working with state lawmakers to ensure the center receives adequate funding but noted another sexual trauma counselor is needed. She added based on what women veterans have given to their country, they deserve greater support.
“Women have incredible determination and because they’ve had to climb the ladder and do everything to prove themselves over and over again that they have incredible endurance and strength,” Cornell du Houx emphasized.
She noted during her most recent deployment overseas, women service members were often overseeing active military operations and arranging for childcare back home. She stressed women veterans at the Sisters in Arms Center are grateful for all financial donations as well as the people who drop off essential living or cleaning supplies — small gestures to make a difference on their path to recovery.
