title: Hegseth says impeachment push is about 'policy disagreements,' not high crimes
text:
Hegseth says impeachment push is about 'policy disagreements,' not high crimes
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth dug in for a fight Tuesday against his potential impeachment in Congress, telling reporters that a rogue lawmaker is targeting him over “policy disagreements” and not the high crimes or offenses the nation’s founders intended.
The embattled Pentagon chief spoke at his first press briefing from the five-sided building in six months, launching a counteroffensive against outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie’s effort to impeach him over his handling of the unpopular war against Iran and other actions.
“In the 250 years of our American republic, no Secretary of War or Secretary of Defense has ever been impeached for carrying out lawful military operations,” Hegseth told reporters.
The briefing was Hegseth’s first since May even as the U.S. military has kept up intermittent operations against Iran as well as fatal strikes on alleged drug-smuggling boats in Latin America.
Rep. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican who lost his primary to a Trump-backed opponent, filed the impeachment resolution in the House on Monday. It sets the stage for a dramatic vote on whether to remove a prominent Trump administration figure following sweeping losses for Republicans in last week's midterm elections that many at least partly blamed on the Iran conflict and its economic impact.
The resolution largely focuses on the war in Iran but also includes references to Hegseth’s role in military actions in Yemen against Iranian-backed Houthi rebels and Venezuela. Massie said Hegseth’s actions amount to “high crimes and misdemeanors” and his leadership at the Pentagon “warrants impeachment.”
A vote in the House could come by midweek, putting pressure on Republicans — many of whom blamed their election wipeout on the Iran war — but next steps are highly uncertain.
Trump has backed Hegseth, pointing to the raid to capture then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January as well as military operations against Iran that he asserts have “obliterated” its navy and air force.
Iran, however, has been able to keep striking U.S. military bases in the Middle East and has disrupted shipping in the Strait of Hormuz during the course of the more than 8-month-old conflict, driving up global oil prices. Trump told reporters Monday that the Iran war “militarily is effectively over" and repeated his often-made claim that Iran “would love to make a deal.”
Hegseth also has been defending his stewardship of the U.S. military.
“There’s a lot of politically motivated people who may have substantial policy disagreements, but their disagreements are with success,” he told reporters Monday after a speech at the Naval War College in Rhode Island. He added that “if we want to litigate” the military actions that the Trump administration has taken, “I’m happy to do it all day long.”
He also released a video on social media last week that argued impeachment would be “all about the politics of personal destruction” and that “won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”
Afterward, scores of Pentagon political appointees posted images of Hegseth emblazoned with the words, “Stand. Fight. Defend the Republic.”
Sean Parnell, the Pentagon’s top spokesman, released a statement saying that “despite threats of sham witch hunts from Democrats,” Hegseth is “100% committed to leading the Department until the end of President Trump’s term in office.”

title: Woman speaks out after being seen making racist gestures outside Ole Miss students’ apartment
text:
OXFORD, Miss. (WMC/Gray News) — A woman who apologized after she was seen making racist gestures in a viral doorbell camera video outside an apartment where three Black Ole Miss students live has now been identified as Alaina Kunes.
Kunes said in a statement sent to WMC that her actions were “insensitive, inappropriate, and deeply harmful.” She said she had apologized to the women who live at the apartment and plans to cooperate with the university’s investigation.
Kunes is the first of three white women seen walking past the apartment’s front door in the Ring doorbell camera video. Two appear to mimic monkey behavior and noises as they pass. The second woman seen making the gestures has not been identified.
In her statement, Kunes said she had not met the apartment’s residents and did not know their race before the Nov. 6 incident.
“I would have never intentionally made those noises or gestures toward a person of color,” she said. “I have apologized to the women and I pray they will forgive me.”
She continued, “I can never truly understand the pain I have caused them and it was never my intention. These girls deserve to feel seen and understood and what I did is not a reflection of who I am trying to become.”
Kunes also said she and her family have received death threats and experienced harassment. She thanked authorities for working to ensure their safety and asked for privacy for her family.
“As I intend to cooperate fully with the University’s investigation, I ask for privacy for my family,” she said. “I understand the seriousness of this situation and remain committed to taking responsibility and learning from this embarrassing ordeal.”
Tasha Bolton contacted WMC about the incident. The video belongs to her daughter. Bolton’s daughter is a Black freshman at Ole Miss and shares the off-campus apartment with two other Black roommates. The university said it leases student housing at the apartment complex.
In a statement released Sunday, Ole Miss condemned the behavior and said it had reached out to those targeted to offer information, resources and support. The university said the incident is under investigation and noted that student conduct records and any potential disciplinary action are protected by the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act.
Bolton previously told WMC that the family has an attorney and plans to make a statement. She said she did not want to speak with the station until she had an opportunity to speak with the university.

title: California voters reject measure to tax wealth of billionaires
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — California voters have rejected a first-in-the-nation tax on the net worth of billionaires following a contentious ballot fight that generated huge spending by some prominent tech leaders eager to stop their taxes from going up.
The measure’s failure is a win for Democratic leaders who opposed it, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, who may run for president in 2028. Critics of the tax, known as Proposition 40, said it would have prompted ultrawealthy taxpayers to leave the state.
Most Californians vote by mail, and any ballot postmarked by Election Day that arrives within a week is counted, meaning it often takes days or even weeks for close races to be settled. The Associated Press determined Monday that ‘no’ had received enough votes to win.
The “no” side raised roughly 10 times as much as the “yes” side. Google co-founder Sergey Brin alone dumped more than $100 million into a political action committee working to defeat the measure.
The measure would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of Californians whose net worth exceeds $1 billion. Most of the money would have been used to backfill federal funding cuts to healthcare, and 10% would have gone toward education and food-assistance programs. SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, which backed the tax, said it was necessary to replace an estimated $100 billion the state will lose in federal healthcare funding over five years.
Proposition 40 was the nation’s biggest test yet on an idea progressives have long championed: raising taxes on the ultra-rich by targeting the main way they make their money — through their investments as opposed to the paychecks they receive from work.
Proponents say they could put the measure back on the ballot in 2028
The measure attracted support from liberal leaders beyond the state, including Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, who rallied in cities across California in the race’s closing weeks to urge voters to pass it.
The “Yes on 40” campaign said the measure sought to protect healthcare for Californians and that they will put a tax back on the ballot in 2028 if patients are not protected.
“Buying an election is not the same as winning the debate,” the measure’s proponents said in a statement on Monday. “The billionaires may have bought themselves a temporary victory at the ballot box, but they have not bought themselves an end to this debate, and this is only round one.”
Billionaires donated millions of dollars to a political action committee, Building a Better California, working to defeat the measure. The committee, which backed other measures on the ballot designed to nullify the tax, raised more than $333 million, nearly a third of which came from Brin.
The AP Voter Poll indicates that the majority of young voters in California — those younger than 30 — voted “yes” on Proposition 40. Older voters were far less supportive, with roughly 7 in 10 voters who were 65 and older saying they voted “no” on the ballot measure.
About half of voters with a household income under $100,000 annually said they were in support of the initiative. Closer to 6 in 10 California voters with an income of $100,000 or higher said they were opposed.
Brin, along with his fellow Google co-founder Larry Page, was among the billionaires who started cutting ties with the state in anticipation of the possible tax. Another tech mogul, Mark Zuckerberg, said he would remain in the state for eight years and made a deal with Meta to help him pay the tax without losing his ownership stake in the company.
Some feared the measure could drive wealthy taxpayers out of state
Some traditional Democratic allies, including Planned Parenthood and the California Medical Association, were part of a coalition opposing it. They were concerned about how the tax revenue would be divvied up and about the potential impact on the state’s budget if there was a mass exodus of wealthy taxpayers. California’s budget relies heavily on the income tax of the state’s richest residents.
“Proposition 40 was a reckless experiment conducted on our state’s economy with little regard for the harms it would cause,” the coalition said in a statement.
Robert Swonger, an auto glass technician living near Sacramento who’s politically independent, said before voting concluded Nov. 3 that he planned to vote against it.
“Obviously, I would like billionaires not to have as much money as they do,” he said. “But I don’t believe taxing them out of existence is going to work.”
Progressive politicians, including Sanders and Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, have long supported a federal wealth tax. Newsom says a California wealth tax would disadvantage the state, but he supports a national minimum tax on anyone with a net worth above $100 million.
Days before Sanders held rallies in California cities last month, Newsom told reporters that the senator’s focus on wealth inequality was “spot-on.” But he said that “on this issue, we fundamentally disagree.”
Supporters of the California tax started running ads recently in New Hampshire, New Mexico and Virginia, states that will vote early in the Democratic presidential primary in 2028, that criticize Newsom for his opposition to the measure.

title: Millinocket Marathon Takes Place Saturday December 5th With A 10 AM Start Time, Now In Its 11th Year
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Countdown Is On For Maine’s Most Fun, One-Of-A-Kind Winter ‘Marathon’
They're prepping the lines and counting down the days till one of Maine's most fun, one-of-a-kind winter marathons kicks off.
It's a marathon that's not just a huge local hit, but is internationally known for its awesomeness, too. (Check this video out and tell me that's not cool!)
The Millinocket Marathon will take place this year on Saturday, December 5th with a start time of 10 AM. Typically, folks start to show up the day before (Friday) for opening festivities and bib pickup.
Read More: Look Up, Maine! November's Night Sky Is Going to Be Incredible
The race started 11 years ago as a fun way to inject some excitement and some revenue into the sleepy little former mill town.
It went from a flash mob of just a few dozen people to an event that brings thousands of people into the Katahdin area each year.
Funded entirely by donations and run entirely by a small army of volunteers, this race brings folks of all walks of life, ability levels, and ages (the youngest last year was 8, the oldest 85) together for what participants have called one of their favorite "races" of all time.
Lynn Marie Casey is from Millinocket and has run the half marathon once before. She says the event is something you have to be a part of to understand.
"The Millinocket Marathon has grown so much in the last 11 years; I love how people from all around have come and participated and have grown to love our quaint little town. One would have to come and experience it; having it in December in northern Maine is definitely not what a mid-summer race would feel like."
"There have been years when it was -20°; the racers and walkers still come, some in athletic wear and some in Paul Bunyan attire and also carrying a chainsaw....The best thing is how our town comes together to welcome all the racers and their loved ones to the area and the camaraderie we all share at each mile marker during the race on the Golden Road, from tasting Oysters, Fireball Shots, BBQ's, baked goods, etc. It's like no other race."
Casey says that for those interested in preparing ahead of time for the race, she would suggest getting your body ready for running in the cold.
"...train well, get out there in the early mornings and get at least a good five to ten miles on a day, pack for temps from 0° to 30° wind, snow and rain."
The race is an official United States Track & Field qualifier for the NYC, Boston, and Chicago Marathons, with one 13.1-mile loop for the half marathon and two 13.1-mile loops for the full marathon.
According to organizers, the terrain encompasses everything from gravel to paved to logging roads.
"The first mile exiting town on Poplar Road is a paved climb. The next six miles are run on the Golden Road, which is a gravel, privately owned logging road. The race secures permission to run on the Golden Road via multiple permit applications, both of which require additional insurance."
"The final six miles are on pavement starting on the Millinocket Lake Road and working back into town. Runners MUST keep to the LEFT side of the road, facing oncoming traffic."
The race course is often lined with "pop-up" watering stations (never guaranteed, but many show up, year after year, to help runners along the way)
Denise Deshane has been participating in one of those stations called "Top of the Hill Bar & Grill" for the past couple of years.
They hand out everything from water, Gatorade, and even shots of Fireball, to goodies and treats for runners to grab along their way.
"I think seeing the smiles and hearing the appreciation from the runners and walkers for us being there to support them in every bit of weather that has been thrown at us all."
It's not the course, necessarily, that's the draw for this race, although the views are incredible.
What people always come back to is the amazing sense of camaraderie they feel when running it, and the atmosphere in town during the event.
Aside from the actual running of the marathon, there are so many other things to do, too.
There's a running list of places to stay, events, and special celebrations at the Millinocket Marathon & Half Marathon Runners Facebook Page.
Festivities usually begin a night or two before the race, as people travel into the area.
You can expect concerts and breakfasts, spaghetti suppers and artisan fairs, Christmas portraits and fundraisers. There's a ton of activity in the area that spans the weekend.
Last year, former Boston World Series-winning Red Sox pitcher (from 2003 to 2005), Bronson Arroyo, brought his band to town and kicked things off with a show at one of the local spots in town.
If you are planning to visit the area that weekend, don't forget to check out the antler wings while you're there.
Read More: How Moose Wings Transformed Millinocket's Eyesore Into Art
To find out more information on the Millinocket Marathon, you can check out their Facebook Page or the Crow Athletics website for a schedule and links to register for the race.

title: Carey Price, Patrice Bergeron among 6 inducted into Hockey Hall of Fame
text:
Carey Price, Patrice Bergeron among 6 inducted into Hockey Hall of Fame
Carey Price first visited the Hockey Hall of Fame as a teenager.
The longtime Montreal Canadiens goaltender joked over the weekend he wouldn’t mind trying one of the interactive games — specifically featuring a netminder sporting very familiar equipment — that sits among the many tributes to the sport’s history.
“It’s pretty special to be able to look around,” Price said before adding with a smile: “I was hoping to get the chance to shoot on myself downstairs.”
The 39-year-old was once at the pinnacle of his craft. Now he’s taken his place alongside the game’s greats.
Price was inducted into the hall as part of the 2026 class alongside Patrice Bergeron, Pekka Rinne, Keith Tkachuk and Cindy Curley in the player category Monday. Brian Burke was enshrined as a builder.
“When I was a kid, I had a dream that I can vividly remember,” Price, who played all 15 of his NHL seasons for the Canadiens, said during his speech in downtown Toronto. “I was walking down a red carpet, just like in the Bell Centre. As I was walking, I approached a mountain of a figure.
“It was Patrick Roy, the very image of what I wanted to be.”
The No. 5 pick of the 2005 draft, Price won the Hart Trophy as league MVP and the Vezina Trophy as its top goaltender in 2015.
He finished with a 361-261-79 record, .917 save percentage, 2.51 goals-against average and 49 shutouts across 712 games in a career cut short by injury.
Price had even better numbers in high-pressure moments before a knee issue ended his playing days beyond the 2021-22 campaign. He owned a .919 save percentage, 2.39 GAA and eight shutouts in 92 playoff games. He was at his best during his final postseason, carrying the underdog Canadiens to the 2021 Stanley Cup final.
“All I can ever really remember wanting to be was a hockey player,” said an emotional Price, who was in his second year of eligibility. “Growing up in a remote community, there was a very slim chance of this happening without a relentless desire and an opportunity.
“That opportunity was provided with sacrifice. As a parent of a young family, I now understand what the biggest of many was — it was time.”
Bergeron urges young hockey players to chase their dreams
The 41-year-old Bergeron, a record-setting six-time Selke Trophy winner as the NHL’s top defensive forward after being selected 45th overall in 2003, helped the Boston Bruins to a Cup victory in 2011.
The center had 1,040 points (427 goals 613 assists) in 1,294 regular-season games. He added 128 points in 170 playoff games before retiring in 2023.
“I hope my journey inspires future generations to dream big (and) believe in themselves,” said Bergeron, who spent all 19 of his NHL seasons with Boston, including the final three as captain. “And never stop chasing those dreams.”
Price, who also won the Ted Lindsay Award as the league’s most outstanding player voted on by the NHL Players' Association in 2015, and Bergeron enjoyed success representing Canada together.
The duo was on the 2014 Olympic team that topped the field before capturing the World Cup of Hockey two years later. Bergeron also claimed gold at the 2010 Games on home soil to go along with victories at the 2005 world junior hockey championship and the 2004 men’s worlds.
“To the boys, I have enough memories to last three lifetimes,” Price said of his teammates. “I wish I could do it all over again. Thank you for clearing the front of the net, blocking shots and backchecking.
“As a forward now, I do none of these things.”
Rinne says he wasn't a top prospect
Rinne, 43, finished with a 369-213-75 record in 15 seasons with the Nashville Predators. The 2018 Vezina winner from Finland — selected 258th overall in 2004 — had a .917 save percentage, 2.43 GAA and 60 shutouts in 683 regular-season games.
“If there’s something that I want to pass on to any young athlete who’s watching tonight, it’s this: You don’t have to be the most highly touted prospect,” he said. “You don’t have to have everything figured out when you’re young. Your path doesn’t have to look like anyone else’s.
“Mine certainly didn’t.”
Curley captained the U.S. to three silver medals at the women’s worlds in the 1990s.
“I’m often called the pioneer, but I’d like to think I just grew up with women’s hockey,” said the 62-year-old. “Hockey is a very special game that gave so much more to me than I could ever give back.”
Burke had a management career that included stops with the Hartford Whalers, Vancouver Canucks, Anaheim Mighty Ducks, Toronto Maple Leafs, Calgary Flames and Pittsburgh Penguins following a stint at the league office.
“When I first got the call from the selection committee, I paused,” said the 71-year-old, who won the Cup with Anaheim in 2007. “Nobody starts playing hockey at 13 years old in Minnesota and says, ‘Someday I’m going to be in the Hockey Hall of Fame.’
“Unless you’re an idiot.”
Tkachuk registered 1,065 points (538 goals, 527 assists) in 1,201 games in 18 seasons.
“This game has welcomed me at every level,” said the 54-year-old. “I accept this honor with gratitude to everyone who has been part of my journey.
“I am honored to be here tonight — and now forever.”

title: Bangor man pleads guilty to distributing child sexual abuse material
text:
A Bangor man pleaded guilty Tuesday to distributing and possessing child sexual abuse material.
Tyler Jewett, 30, entered his plea in U.S. District Court in Bangor, according to the U.S. attorney’s office.
Jewett sent 17 videos of child sexual abuse on Telegram in February to an account that had previously been run by an Ohio man. By the time Jewett sent the messages, the intended recipient had been arrested for attempting to sexually abuse multiple children, and an FBI agent had taken over the Telegram account.
Investigators searched Jewett’s Essex Street home and seized multiple devices in May. They found multiple images and videos of child sexual abuse on several devices.
For the distribution charge, Jewett faces up to 20 years in prison and up to a lifetime of supervised release. For the possession charge, he faces up to 20 years in prison, a $250,000 fine and up to a lifetime of supervised release.
He will be sentenced at a later date.

title: Daycare provider sentenced to up to 50 years in prison in toddler’s death
text:
EMMETSBURG, Iowa (KTIV/Gray News) - An Iowa judge has sentenced a daycare provider to prison after nearly a four-year infant death investigation.
On Monday, 31-year-old Hannah Priest was sentenced to up to 50 years in prison for one count of child endangerment resulting in the death of Sebastian Jespersen, a 23-month-old who died in 2023.
Priest was the child’s daycare provider at the time.
In September 2023, Priest initially pleaded not guilty, then changed her plea to guilty in October 2026.
On Jan. 19, 2023, Priest reportedly found the infant unresponsive on his sleeping cot.
EMTs responded to the daycare and the child was taken to a hospital in Des Moines.
A few days later, on January 24, 2023, the child died at the hospital.
An autopsy by the Iowa State Medical Examiner determined that the infant had died from brain trauma consistent with inflicted injuries.
After an investigation carried out by the Iowa Department of Criminal Investigation, Priest was arrested on Sept. 1, 2023.
During a May 2023 interview, court documents showed Priest admitted to being frustrated with the infant around naptime because he hadn’t gone to the bathroom yet that day.
She also admitted to putting the infant in the cot by the shoulders and may not have known her own strength while doing so.
During the interview, Priest reportedly admitted to setting him into the cot out of frustration.
Court documents stated that over the course of three interviews between Priest and investigators, she maintained that the infant was acting normally before she put him down for a nap that afternoon.
She had also denied that the infant suffered any accidental head injuries that day. Also denying that any other kids at the daycare struck the 23-month-old child.
Authorities said Priest would be eligible for parole.

title: Texas man accused of cruise ship murder had argued with woman in their cabin, FBI says
text:
A cruise ship passenger accused of killing a woman shortly after the vessel departed from Texas told FBI agents he beat and choked her in their cabin after an argument caused him to “snap,” according to court documents.
Jason Watford, 48, of Tyler, Texas, was set to make an initial federal court appearance on a murder charge Tuesday in Galveston. He was being held at a county jail. It was not immediately clear if he had a lawyer who could respond to the allegations.
A man who said he is Watford’s son declined to comment Tuesday when reached at a phone listing in public records for relatives.
The alleged killing happened aboard the MSC Seascape, a towering white vessel that has 2,270 cabins and can host nearly 5,900 guests on five- and seven-night trips to the Caribbean, according to the company’s website.
The woman, who was not immediately identified, was killed Sunday after the vessel left Galveston, according to an FBI affidavit filed in federal court. A ship investigator contacted authorities to report that the woman was found dead in her room with multiple facial injuries.
A housekeeper who knocked to deliver towels saw the woman lying motionless on the floor and what looked like blood on Watford’s hands and pants when he opened the door, the affidavit said.
In an interview with FBI agents after the ship returned to Galveston on Monday morning, Watford said he and the woman had boarded the vessel together Sunday and began arguing while having dinner at one of the ship’s restaurants, according to the affidavit. The argument continued in their room, it said.
Watford told agents he struck the woman several times and “applied pressure” to her neck “for approximately four to five minutes” until he became exhausted, the affidavit said. He said she lay motionless for about 10 minutes until the housekeeper arrived.
Surveillance video showed that Watford entered the room at 7:46 p.m. and the victim went in about 25 minutes later, authorities said. At 9:15 p.m., he was seen on the video leaving the room wearing a different shirt and pants, according to the complaint, and sat on the hallway floor looking at his phone.
MSC Cruises said authorities told the ship to return to Galveston after the crew reported the passenger’s death, and that the vessel resumed its voyage Monday. The company said it was cooperating with authorities and providing support to those impacted.
Homicide investigations on cruise ships are uncommon. Earlier this year, a teenager was charged with murder and aggravated sexual abuse in the death of his 18-year-old stepsister on a Carnival Cruise ship out of Florida.
___
Associated Press writer Claudia Lauer in Philadelphia contributed.

title: Get ready for the holiday season at the Friends of Rockland Public Library Festival of Lights Silent Auction
text:
ROCKLAND — Mark your calendars for the annual Festival of Lights Silent Auction of holiday Trees, Wreaths and Stockings, from 1 to p.m. Saturday, Nov. 28 at the Rockland Public Library. The yearly event features a dazzling array of creatively decorated small trees, wreaths and colorful stockings (handmade made by talented volunteers) just in time for holiday decorating and gifting.
“Our annual Festival of Lights Silent Auction delights everyone who attends and has grown into one of Rockland’s most beloved holiday traditions,” Joni Hall, auction co-chair. said. “We’re so grateful for the tremendous generosity and creativity of our local businesses and of course to our community for supporting the event. Wait till you see this year’s gorgeous auction and raffle items.”
Each item is decorated with a specific theme by a local business and contains gift certificates and other offerings from that business. This year’s contributors include 250 Main Hotel, Primo restaurant, Jess’s Market and other popular local businesses. There will be free apple cider and cookies available to all during the auction.
The event also includes raffles for an individual tree, wreath and stocking as prizes for those feeling particularly lucky! Raffle tickets are $3 each or 2 for $5, with tickets available at the library checkout desk and the Book Stop downstairs. Raffle ticket sales start Nov. 14 and continue through the Silent Auction. The winning tickets will be drawn at 4 p.m. on Nov. 28. Need not be present to win.
All proceeds from this popular holiday event go directly to support the Rockland Public Library.
The Friends of Rockland Public Library is a volunteer organization whose mission is to support the work of the library. The Friends raise funds to help pay for library computers, children’s books, the interlibrary loan program and programs for children and adults so that the library remains a valuable resource for the community. Visit https://friendsofrocklandpubliclibrary.org/ for more information or to join the Friends.

title: Portland firefighters respond to gas leak in Back Cove
text:
Portland firefighters respond to gas leak on Mayland Street in Back Cove
The Portland Fire Department said crews responded to the scene of a gas leak in the city's Back Cove neighborhood Tuesday morning.
The department said a 4-inch gas line ruptured in the area of 7 Mayland St., which is near the intersection of Ocean Avenue.
Maine's Total Coverage learned that people within 300 feet of the gas leak were evacuated, and that an excavator hit the gas line.
A resident told Maine's Total Coverage that they heard a loud hiss for about 30 minutes.
Ocean Avenue Elementary School, which is more than 400 feet away from the scene according to Google Maps, went into a shelter-in-place after the Portland Fire Department directed school officials to do so at about 10 a.m. Tuesday.
"Students remained in their classes and continued their work as usual," Interim Principal Emily Parr said in a message sent to the families of Ocean Avenue School students. "After about twenty minutes, the fire department informed us that the leak was located, was being fixed, and there were no ongoing safety concerns for our community. Out of an abundance of caution, we decided to hold indoor recess for all grade levels. Students and staff did a great job following our protocols and carrying on with their learning!"
Maine's Total Coverage also learned that Tuesday marked the first day of construction for two homes that are being built on Mayland Street.

title: One Injured, Two Displaced in Sheridan Fire
text:
SHERIDAN, Maine (WAGM) - One man was taken to the hospital after a garage fire spread to a Sheridan home yesterday.
According to the Ashland Fire Department, a call came in at 3 p.m. on Monday reporting a structure fire at 27 Dupree Street in Sheridan. Ashland Fire Chief Donald Bouley says the fire started in the garage and quickly spread to the house. According to Chief Bouley, a man who was not a resident of the home was working in the garage when the fire started and was taken to the hospital for smoke inhalation. Bouley says the injured man was released from the hospital Monday night. The home is a total loss, and two residents have been displaced.
Ashland firefighters received mutual aid from the Portage, Masardis and Mapleton fire departments. Firefighters used three fire trucks to shuttle water to the scene. Approximately 20 firefighters spent five hours at the scene extinguishing the fire, leaving around 8 p.m. Bouley says the home was on a dead-end street, so no roads were closed during the incident. Chief Bouley says they have determined the cause of the fire to be accidental, and the fire is no longer under investigation.

title: Poetry reading explores caregiving, grief and being human
text:
BASS HARBOR — On Wednesday, Nov. 18 at 5:30 p.m., poet Kristie Billings will read from and sign her new book, “Everything at Once” at the Bass Harbor Memorial Library. Her recent collection of poetry explores dementia, loss, caregiving, love and being human.
“Kristie’s big-hearted poems take us on an unflinching journey through grief. Billings is a daughter, a caregiver, a mourner, and a woman confronting her own aging. She lives each of these roles deeply. She’s talking to herself and to us at the same time, with language that is direct, full of raw emotions, and grounded in the details of her struggles” a press release quotes Stuart Kestenbaum, Maine Poet Laureate from 2016 to 2020.

title: Video: Drone delivers food to ape stranded during Florida flooding
text:
Video: Drone delivers food to ape stranded during Florida flooding
A Florida sanctuary had to deliver food to one of its chimpanzees by drone after historic flooding made it difficult for staff to access the property.
Save the Chimps, a sanctuary in Fort Pierce, shared a video on social media showing the damage floodwaters left behind.
The flooding followed heavy downpours that swamped eastern Florida and brought more than 20 inches of rain to some areas. Gov. Ron DeSantis issued an emergency declaration for multiple counties.
The sanctuary's canals overflowed, submerging roads typically used to deliver food. One chimpanzee, a 38-year-old named Kaleb, was left without access to food, according to The Associated Press.
Staff members used a drone purchased earlier for emergencies to deliver food and blankets to Kaleb.
Video showed Kaleb grabbing a brown bag from the drone and eating a banana.
Staff said the sanctuary's residents are safe but need help recovering from the damage.
The sanctuary reported road damage that will require significant resurfacing. Roof repairs and mold remediation are also needed, while vehicles and equipment were damaged.

title: House schedules procedural vote on GOP lawmaker's effort to impeach Pete Hegseth
text:
House schedules procedural vote on GOP lawmaker's effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
The House is expected to take up an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday, as Kentucky Congressman Thomas Massie calls for lawmakers to hold him accountable for the Trump administration's military actions.
Video in player above: Defense secretary calls impeachment effort "a political spectacle"
According to House Majority Leader Steve Scalise's schedule, lawmakers will consider a procedural motion related to Massie's resolution at 5:30 p.m.
Massie said in a social media post that the first vote will determine whether the resolution is sent to committee or otherwise blocked from moving forward.
"If we can overcome that effort, we will proceed to a real debate and vote on the Articles of Impeachment," Massie wrote.
The vote will come just hours after Hegseth held a rare press conference Tuesday morning, his first in more than 180 days, to address the impeachment effort.
Hegseth called the proposal a political stunt and defended the administration's military operations in Iran and Yemen and against suspected drug traffickers.
"It's a farce, and it's a stunt, and everybody knows it," Hegseth said.
The press conference came after Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Monday.
The 34-page resolution accuses the defense secretary of violating the Constitution and federal law. Tap here to read the full resolution.
Hegseth rejected the accusations, arguing military action under the Trump administration has been carried out lawfully.
"In the 250 years of our American republic, no Secretary of War or Secretary of Defense has ever been impeached for carrying out lawful military operations, and in our case, successful ones at that," he said.
President Donald Trump also weighed in on Truth Social after Hegseth’s remarks.
"Hegseth gets an "A" PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER," he said.
While speaking with reporters Monday night, Massie argued that Hegseth's actions warrant impeachment regardless of political disagreements over the administration’s military policies.
"A lot of people are saying, 'Well, I think Peter Hegseth is effective. He's good at his job, and so I don't want to vote for these articles of impeachment.' Well, the reality is we're not indicting him for being bad at his job. In fact, he was very effective at killing schoolchildren in Iran. He was very effective at extrajudicial killings. There's no argument in these impeachment articles that he's ineffective. The argument here is that he's broken laws and violated the Constitution."
The House's procedural vote will determine whether lawmakers move forward with consideration of the impeachment articles or stop the effort at this stage.

title: Massachusetts company buys two Waldo County campgrounds
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Two Waldo County recreational vehicle campgrounds were sold to Moorings RV on Oct. 26.
One, located at 191 Searsport Ave. in Belfast, sold for $1.5 million, according to a real estate transfer tax document filed with the state. The other, located at 246 West Main St. in Searsport, sold for $1 million.
Moorings RV, based in Quincy, Massachusetts, is part of the Modern America Campgrounds portfolio, which encompasses 19 Maine properties and 18 others across the Northeast.
The Belfast property has 53 RV sites and nine lodges. The Searsport property has 45 RV sites.
Both sites have a kayak launch, private ocean access, and games of horseshoes and cornhole. The Belfast property additionally features a playground and laundry facility.
Both campgrounds were previously owned by New Hampshire-based company Nester Family Properties.
Moorings RV did not respond to a request for comment.

title: Several pounds of cocaine found after chase reaches 120 mph on Maine highway
text:
Several pounds of cocaine found after chase reaches 120 mph on Maine highway
An Auburn man is facing multiple charges after police say he led them on a high-speed chase and had several pounds of what investigators believe is cocaine.
Just after midnight on Tuesday morning, a deputy from the Sagadahoc County Sheriff's Office stopped a vehicle on the northbound side of Interstate 295 near Exit 37 in Bowdoinham after clocking the vehicle at 90 miles per hour.
The deputy identified the driver as Lawz Lepenn, 44, and learned he was on probation for aggravated drug trafficking. The deputy called for backup, but when a Topsham Police Department K-9 team arrived and Lepenn was asked to get out of his vehicle, police say he drove off.
Police say the ensuing chase north on I-295 reached 120 mph as Maine State Police deployed spike strips near Exit 109 on Interstate 95 in Augusta. Police say Lepenn drove over the spike strips but continued going for about a mile before his vehicle was disabled.
The deputy chasing Lepenn had to stop his chase after also hitting the spike strip.
Police say Lepenn ran into the woods after his vehicle stopped. Police used a drone and were able to find him running away near the Augusta State Airport and police took him into custody.
Police say Lepenn had tossed a sports bag onto the highway when he ran from his vehicle. When police searched the bag, they found over three pounds of what preliminary testing showed to be cocaine HCl.
Lepenn was charged with aggravated trafficking of scheduled drugs and eluding a police officer. He was taken to Two Bridges Regional Jail in Wiscasset, where he was being held without bail on a probation violation. He was scheduled to be arraigned on Thursday.

title: Cooper Flagg joins Kevin Durant in achieving rare stat
text:
In the Mavericks’ game against the Indiana Pacers on Monday, Cooper Flagg achieved a feat that hasn’t been seen in the past 18 years of NBA history.
Flagg scored 43 points, 10 rebounds and six assists, the most points he’s scored so far this season. That places him in the company of Hall of Famer Kevin Durant, the only other teenager in NBA history to score at least 40 points, 10 rebounds and five assists in a single game.
Durant scored 42 points, 13 rebounds and six assists in the final game of his rookie season in 2007-08.
The Mavericks narrowly beat the Pacers 125 to 122.
With that accomplishment, Flagg continues an impressive career. In the Maverick’s season opener, he scored 32 points. That’s the most any teen has ever scored during an NBA season opener.
Last season, he averaged 21 points per game, a new record for rookies. He is also the youngest player to score 50 points in a single game and the second-youngest to score 1,000 points total. Those accomplishments helped earn him the Rookie of the Year title in 2025.

title: Senate Republicans vote to keep Thune as leader after steep election losses
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Senate Republicans reelected South Dakota Sen. John Thune as their leader Tuesday after a tense day of private discussions about steep losses in the midterm elections that cost them their majority.
Thune was always expected to prevail, as he is popular with his GOP colleagues and was running unopposed in the secret-ballot election. But Senate Republicans vented their frustrations in three separate meetings Tuesday after an election wipeout that cost them at least seven Senate seats.
Some Republicans had tried to delay the leadership decision, but the conference voted 31-15 to proceed with a vote after Thune made his case to his colleagues, laying out his vision for the minority and also promising that they will try and do as much as they can in their final two months in the majority.
“We’re going to make the most of the time we’ve got,” Thune said after he was elected by acclamation, without a roll call vote.
As for next year, Thune said that told his colleagues that they will “come out swinging, and realize we’ve got a lot of work to be done to get back in the majority.”
The day’s meetings were a combination of venting and thoughtful conversation, with some senators who won and lost elections this year sharing their thoughts and others questioning if they should be quickly endorsing their leadership slate after a significant defeat.
West Virginia Sen. Jim Justice said that there was a “legitimate argument that, good gracious, if we lost as badly as we lost, why would we continue on with the same leadership?”
Republicans’ angst and indecision come as frustrated Republicans are just beginning to reckon with what the election results mean for their future — and for their relationship with President Donald Trump, as voters resoundingly rejected their two years of single-party rule in Congress and the White House. Two additional Senate races remain uncalled in Alaska and Mississippi that could further deplete their numbers.
“If you don’t think after losing seven Senate seats minimum that we need to change course, I don’t know what planet you’re on,” said Missouri Sen. Josh Hawley, who voted to delay the elections. He said he wasn’t aware of anyone else running for leader, but “maybe there would be” if they waited.
No alternative to Thune emerged
Thune, who replaced Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky as leader in early 2025, pushed back on the idea of a delay, questioning what it would achieve. Several senators backed him up, including his South Dakota colleague Mike Rounds, who countered the calls for postponement with the successful motion to vote immediately.
Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia, who was reelected to her leadership position as GOP policy chair, said that Thune wasn’t the reason they suffered losses. “I don’t think it was the fault of our leadership, quite frankly,” she said.
Sen. Roger Wicker, R-Miss., said he had confidence in the newly re-elected slate. The discussion was mainly “about policy,” he said.
Republicans in the meeting were also pushing Thune to stay in session around the clock in the coming weeks to push through war spending and other party priorities before they lose power in January. Republicans are trying to wrap up the year’s work — funding the government, confirming Trump’s nominees and seeing if there are some issues where they can work with Democrats, including an energy permitting bill that moved forward on a bipartisan vote Monday evening.
Before the vote on Thune, the conference adopted a resolution to maximize the time they have left and to “confirm every judicial nominee and every executive nominee that the conference approves of.”
“We need a plan to get the Republican agenda done,” said Florida Sen. Rick Scott.
Wisconsin Sen. Ron Johnson circulated a letter before the meeting asking for the delay. He said the conference needs to do some “real soul-searching” but also conceded that there was no one else on the ballot.
“That’s part of our problem, who would want the job?” he said on Monday, turning to a reporter and joking, “Do you want it?”
Oklahoma Sen. Jim Lankford said that there was “widespread support” among Republican senators for Thune, who has made it a point to hear out different viewpoints before he makes major decisions and has maintained close relationships with the rank and file — a different approach from his predecessor, McConnell.
Lankford said he supported having the elections on Tuesday because many of the new GOP senators were already in town for freshman orientation.
Thune has navigated Trump in his first two years as leader
Thune has spent much of the last two years navigating Trump, who has often been at odds with the Senate.
While backing Trump on most policies, Thune has refused to change Senate rules and scrap the filibuster to pass voting legislation that would require proof of citizenship for all voters — a position that frustrated Trump and enraged some in the president’s political base.
Still, Trump hosted Thune and his family at the White House in October. He said Monday that the GOP leader is “a very fine man.” The election is “up to the Senate,” Trump said.
Thune has emphasized his collaborative approach to his colleagues and pointed out what they did get done in the last two years — including Trump’s sweeping tax and spending cuts legislation and an attempt at reining in the chaotic annual spending process.
“We’re not going to be running this place next year, the Democrats are,” Thune said afterward. “But you can be assured that we will be very, very active in asserting conservative priorities.”

title: Hegseth defends record amid impeachment effort
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth defended his military record Tuesday amid a potential impeachment in Congress, arguing the effort was over mere “policy disagreements” and high crimes and misdemeanors.
Hegseth held his first Pentagon news conference in six months, a day after Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky reintroduced eight articles of impeachment. Hegseth called the effort “a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment.”
Massie’s resolution cites U.S. military action in Yemen and Venezuela, but the case centers on the war with Iran, which Massie says the Trump administration waged without congressional approval.
“There’s no argument in these impeachment articles that he’s ineffective,” Massie said. “The argument here is that he’s broken laws and he’s violated the Constitution.”
Hegseth said the military operations at issue were lawful.
“I stand behind every one of these operations,” he said. “I was proud to execute them, and I would do it again tomorrow.”
President Donald Trump said Monday he stands by Hegseth. On Tuesday, he further backed Hegseth on social media, giving the secretary’s press conference an “A plus, plus, plus.”
Several House Democrats have said they’ll support impeachment, including Rep. Steny Hoyer of Maryland. Massie says he’s confident other House Republicans will join him, but it remains unclear how many will vote with him.
Rep. Darrell Issa (R-Calif.) said he expects the effort to fail if it reaches the Republican-controlled Senate.
“Look, this is a reaction by a member who was defeated in the primary,” Issa said. “It’s popular with Democrats. It’s going to die in the Senate.”
The House could first vote on whether to set the resolution aside or send it to committee. If neither happens, lawmakers could vote on whether to impeach Hegseth later this week.

title: States like Maine need the Electoral College
text:
I’m writing in response to the letter of Nov. 5 regarding the abolition of the Electoral College.
A constitutional amendment is required to get rid of the Electoral College. Three-fourths (38) of the states would have to ratify the amendment. What’s in it for them? With the Electoral College, smaller states, such as Maine, have a more equal voice in the election of our nation’s president. Without it, larger states such as California and Texas would overshadow smaller states and, effectively, would dictate who would be our president.
Why would small states ratify an amendment that would effectively silence their votes? That’s why the Founding Fathers set up the Electoral College.
Mary Caliandro
Long Island

title: Maine suspends $107K in fines related to deadly Searsmont explosion
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Maine Department of Labor has cited seven emergency departments for safety violations after a fatal sawmill fire and explosion but is suspending almost all of the penalties so the towns can pay for new equipment and training to address the problems.
The May 15 explosion at Robbins Lumber in Searsmont killed three people and injured more than a dozen others. Sparks from machinery at the base of a silo ignited wood dust, triggering a massive blast.
The settlement details, published Tuesday by the Maine Department of Labor, require these fire and rescue departments to overhaul safety protocols, buy new equipment and send members to mandatory state training.
The most significant equipment purchase — a personnel tracking system that uses tags that firefighters attach to a board at an emergency scene so incident commanders can maintain a live headcount — is being funded by Knox County and donations.
Almost 300 emergency personnel from 46 fire departments responded, but the state inspected only those whose personnel suffered serious injuries or died. Mill safety conditions are regulated by the U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration.
The Maine Department of Labor fined the fire and rescue departments, which rely almost entirely on volunteers, $108,000 for citations as small as deficient record keeping to as serious as a failure to keep a live headcount of responding firefighters and staging the firefighter treatment and rest area within a possible blast zone.
All but a $1,000 fine against the Montville Fire Department was suspended. The department had been cited for the same problem — not testing that respirators fit properly — by OSHA in August 2025, according to the settlement agreement, and it was the only repeat violation.
While it’s unclear if much of the conduct that was cited could’ve prevented the serious injuries in Searsmont, the placement of the rescue and treatment area did put the EMS personnel in danger, said Kate Burkhart, the director of the Bureau of Labor Standards’ workplace safety division.
Inspectors cited Searsmont Rescue for setting up a firefighter rest area within 50 feet of the initial fire. Rescue Chief Sarah Tompkins and Lily Robbins, a volunteer EMT, were both injured in the explosion.
“When the explosion occurred, they were right there,” Burkhart said.
But Burkhart said suspending the fines will allow the mostly small cash-strapped towns to invest in safety improvements rather than paying state penalties. She said that will result in the kind of systemic change that will protect people more than any single corrective action.
“We did not waive them, we suspended them,” Burkhart said of the fines. “If any department does not meet their obligations, we can collect those penalties. It’s like a carrot and a stick wrapped in one.”
She emphasized that all the departments have worked hard over the last six months to improve safety in the wake of the catastrophic losses they experienced, including two fire trucks that burned. Tuesday’s release offers new details on how the departments involved in the explosion are adapting and learning from it.
Local leaders like Morill First Selectman Randy Place welcomed the state’s supportive approach.
“Town staff and the fire department immediately started correcting all issues that the DOL identified,” Place said. “Morrill greatly appreciated how the DOL handled our case, providing help and understanding while the town struggled with the loss of our young firefighter.”
Andrew Cross, a 27-year-old volunteer firefighter from Morrill, died at the scene. Searsmont Assistant Fire Chief Wayne Woodbury and mill co-owner Alden Robbins were severely burned and died weeks later. Eleven firefighters, two EMTs and several mill workers were injured.
State inspectors cited six departments — Appleton, Belmont, Lincolnville, Montville, Morrill and Searsmont — for not using a formal personnel tracking system during the disaster. The new system they’re implementing in response will help track firefighters and EMS personnel especially in a situation where multiple departments are on scene, said Belmont Fire Chief Ron Harford. That kind of a fire response is increasingly common as the number of volunteers at fire departments across the state has declined. Harford said his firefighters are already using the new tag-in and tag-out system at the fire station to prepare for future calls.
In Searsmont, the explosion has motivated more people to volunteer for its fire and EMS services, Selectman Chris Staples said. The town doesn’t dispute the labor department’s findings, said Selectman Pete Milinazzo.
“The town will move ahead and be better in the future than we were in the past — not that we’ve been terrible in the past,” Milinazzo said. “As a town and rescue department, every day we’re striving to do better than the day before.”
Five departments faced protective gear and mask citations for allowing their firefighters to wear heavy breathing gear without ensuring they had required medical evaluations and annual mask fit-tests, and not maintaining written plans.
Under the settlement terms, department leaders must complete safety workshops put on by the state and the Maine Fire Chiefs Association and Maine Fire Service Institute in February 2027 to keep the fines fully suspended.
Harford in Belmont said as a volunteer fire chief, every call is a learning experience. “It’s horrible how it’s all happened, but we live and learn from it,” he said.

title: Suspect in custody as FBI investigates a possible killing aboard a cruise ship out of Texas
text:
Texas man charged in cruise ship murder had argued with woman in their cabin, FBI says
A cruise ship passenger was charged Tuesday with killing a woman after the vessel departed from Texas this weekend, telling FBI agents that he beat and choked her in their cabin after an argument caused him to “snap,” court documents showed.
The woman, who was not immediately identified, was found dead Sunday after 48-year-old Jason Watford opened their room’s door for a ship housekeeper with blood on his hands and clothes, according to an FBI affidavit filed in federal court. The housekeeper spotted the victim lying on the floor with facial injuries, and an investigator on the cruise ship contacted authorities.
Watford was taken into custody the next morning after the vessel returned to Galveston, Texas. A video posted on social media shows him being escorted off the ship in handcuffs.
Watford, of Tyler, Texas, made an initial federal court appearance on a murder charge Tuesday in Galveston, and was being held in a county jail. His public defender, Javier Martinez, did not respond to requests for comment by The Associated Press. His next hearing is scheduled for Nov. 16.
A man who said he is Watford’s son declined to comment Tuesday when reached at a phone listing in public records for relatives.
The death happened aboard the MSC Seascape, a towering white vessel that has 2,270 cabins and can host nearly 5,900 guests on five- and seven-night trips to the Caribbean, according to the company’s website.
In an interview with FBI agents Monday, Watford said he and the woman boarded the vessel together Sunday and started to argue while having dinner at one of the ship’s restaurants, according to the affidavit. The argument continued in their room, it said.
Watford told agents he struck the woman several times and “applied pressure” to her neck “for approximately four to five minutes” until he became exhausted, the affidavit said. He said she lay motionless for about 10 minutes until the housekeeper arrived.
Surveillance video showed that Watford entered the room at 7:46 p.m. and the victim went in about 25 minutes later, authorities said. At 9:15 p.m., he was seen on the video leaving the room wearing a different shirt and pants from when he answered the door for the housekeeper, according to the complaint, and sat on the hallway floor looking at his phone.
Investigators did not provide details on Watson’s relationship to the woman.
MSC Cruises said authorities told the ship to return to Galveston after the crew reported the passenger's death, and that the vessel resumed its voyage Monday. The company said it was cooperating with authorities and providing support to those impacted.

title: Documentary on Bangor Humane Society to premiere Thursday in Orono
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The first documentary about the Bangor Humane Society will premiere Thursday evening, November 12th, at Black Bear Cinemas in Orono.
It’s produced by Five Road Films. Director and producer Keith Travers donated his time and resources to make the 45-minute documentary. He and his wife, Danielle Travers spent about a year filming the animals, 22 staff members and more than 100 volunteers at the shelter.
Woof LLC, Danforth’s Downhome Grocery and Mason’s Brewing donated to the project. Travers says he used that funding to purchase memory cards to store footage on.
“I was overwhelmed by the amount of people that volunteer their time and the passion that they have for that work,” said Travers. “I’ve done other documentaries but this one just kind of called out to me.”
Why the film was made
About a year earlier, Travers had heard about an email sent to the Bangor Humane Society. The tone of the email stuck with him.
“I deemed it pretty negative,” he says. “And I thought there was some misunderstandings about how the Humane Society works.”
Travers approached BHS about a documentary to show what really goes on behind the scenes.
“And we jumped in with all of our feet,” says Kathryn Ravenscraft, Director of Development & Communications for the Bangor Humane Society. “Yes, even our furry bosses were up for it too.”
Travers says he lost count of how many hours were put into filming and editing the 45-minute production. But he says, he was truly humbled by the amount of volunteers that donate their time to the amimal shelter.
“A lot of animals come in here under traumatic circumstances. They might be wandering the streets or people just can’t take care of them anymore. The people here, really, they go through a lot emotionally,” says Travers. “I wouldn’t says it’s shocking but I was overwhelmed by the amount of people that volunteer their time and the passion that they have for that work.”
What viewers may take away
Travers hopes those who watch the documentary will take understand the emotional rollercoaster that comes with working at an animal shelter.
“Maybe a little more compassion for the animals, but also for the people that are here,” says Travers. “I know sometimes people come in and they are upset because they didn’t get the service they think they deserve. And there’s usually a reason for that. So just to take a step back and understand what’s going on behind the scenes.”
“95 to 97% of our animals, the end is just walking out into their new lives. And that’s what we’re doing here. So it’s nice to be able to tell that,” says Ravenscraft.
Paws and take a bow
Humane: Inside Bangor Humane Society premieres on Thursday, November 12th at Black Bear Cinemas in Orono. The film starts at 6:30 p.m. but they’ll be rolling out the red carpet beforehand for some VIPs (that’s very important pets).

title: Woman runs onto high school football field during game and strangles player, police say
text:
WAYNE COUNTY, Ky. (WKYT/WYMT/Gray News) - A Kentucky woman is facing a felony charge after police say she strangled a high school football player during a game.
Kayla Barrett, 36, was charged with second-degree strangulation after Monticello Police say she assaulted a Wayne County High School football player during an Oct. 30 game against North Laurel High School.
Police say a Wayne County player was running with the ball when a tackle that ended out-of-bounds erupted into a melee between players. Barrett, of Laurel County, was standing near the sideline and chose to get involved, according to police.
“From what I understand, she ran toward the action, and somewhere in that scuffle, she grabbed one of the Wayne County athletes by the back of the neck and began choking him and shaking him,” Monticello Assistant Chief Joshua Smith said.
Police say the player who was strangled said he had trouble breathing because of the attack. He was taken to the hospital, where he was treated and released. Police believe he will be OK.
Barrett left the game after the attack, according to police.
“When it all happened, she left. She quickly left the area and drove off,” Smith said. “Our officer was able to get her identified.”
Barrett was arrested last Tuesday by the Kentucky State Police. She has since been released on bond.
“Hopefully, she’s not allowed back at a sporting event,” Smith said. “As far as the police department is concerned, our student-athletes and their protection is one of our biggest areas that we want to make sure they’re always safe.”

title: House Republicans quash effort to impeach Defense Secretary Hegseth
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The House on Tuesday turned aside a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, halting an effort to remove the Pentagon chief for his conduct in office and his handling of the war in Iran.
The vote came as Republicans grapple with the fallout from sweeping midterm losses that some in the party have blamed on the war in Iran and the resulting surge in gas prices. But after President Donald Trump signaled strong support for Hegseth, GOP lawmakers largely stood by the secretary Tuesday, blocking the effort in a near party-line vote.
The effort was led by Kentucky Republican Rep. Thomas Massie and backed by Democrats. The vote Tuesday may only delay an impeachment push against Hegseth, with Democrats set to take control of the House and Senate in January.
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become the next speaker when Democrats take charge in January, stood firmly behind the push, saying Hegseth has “abused his power” and “undermined America’s national security.”
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer endorsed Hegseth’s impeachment as well.
Hegseth rebuked the effort Tuesday in his first news conference in months, portraying Massie as a rogue lawmaker and arguing he had committed none of the high crimes required in the Constitution for his removal. He framed the effort as an indictment against the nation’s service members and their successes and said it was undermining American forces “in real time.”
“This is not patriotism,” Hegseth said. “This is sabotage.”
Massie’s resolution included eight counts of impeachment. It largely focused on the war in Iran but also included references to Hegseth’s role in carrying out military actions in Yemen and Venezuela.
Massie, a Kentucky Republican leaving Congress in January after losing his primary to a Trump-backed opponent, says Hegseth has “knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders.”
Hegseth holds rare press conference
Tuesday morning, Hegseth gave a defiant and politicized defense of his stewardship of the U.S. military in his first news conference at the Pentagon in six months. He chose to hit back at the rising bipartisan anger over battlefield strategy while offering few details about intermittent operations against Iran or fatal strikes on alleged drug-smuggling boats in Latin America.
Hegseth said the impeachment resolution “tells our enemies — Iran, the cartels, every adversary watching — the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership for successfully executing lawful military operations.”
Trump praised Hegseth’s performance at the briefing in a social media post, while Vice President JD Vance said in his own post that the impeachment effort is “a ridiculous show that stands in for actual policymaking.”
Trump celebrated the House vote later Tuesday, saying on social media that it was the exoneration of “a Great American Patriot.”
Impeachment effort falls short
Massie filed the resolution in the House on Monday as lawmakers returned to Washington. Tuesday’s vote was a procedural attempt to stop the impeachment push outright by sending the matter back to committee. The motion succeeded 211-204, with a number of Democrats missing the vote.
Massie’s resolution had eight counts of impeachment that focused on U.S. military actions or changes on Hegseth’s watch. They include reported reductions in staff and resources at a Pentagon office focused on mitigating civilian harm, which preceded a U.S. missile striking an Iranian primary school during the war, killing up to 168 people.
“The law requires our military to withdraw from hostilities within 60 days if Congress does not authorize the activity,” Massie wrote on social media Tuesday. The Iran war “has been underway for 256 days. Congress has not authorized it. Hegseth is breaking the law.”
Another article of impeachment focused on Hegseth’s attempt to punish Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly, a retired Navy pilot, for participating in a video that called on troops to resist unlawful orders. Massie also called out U.S. military strikes on alleged drug-smuggling boats in Latin America and the failure to rescue survivors, which Massie argued will encourage adversaries to treat American forces the same way.
What constitutes “high crimes and misdemeanors” is not spelled out in the Constitution, leaving it to lawmakers to decide what are impeachable acts.
Hegseth said Massie’s concerns are not impeachable, calling them “policy disagreements, not high crimes, not misdemeanors, not treason, not bribery, not the kinds of offenses the founders intended when they wrote the impeachment clause.”
House Speaker Mike Johnson called it a “political gambit for attention” and predicted Republicans would defeat it “one way or the other.”
Some Republicans were critical of Hegseth in the run-up to the vote, but said they didn’t believe he had committed impeachable offenses. Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon, a Republican who is retiring after this year, said he didn’t agree with the “merit” of the impeachment although he is “critical of the secretary.”
“I have a lot of other things I thought were failures by the secretary,” Bacon said. “We control the agenda. We should be doing hearings.”
This isn’t the first impeachment attempt in recent years
Hegseth cast Massie’s resolution in historic terms, arguing that no defense secretary has been impeached in the nation’s 250-year history “for carrying out lawful military operations.”
But more recently, a Cabinet official in President Joe Biden’s administration, Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas, was impeached by House Republicans over his handling of the U.S.-Mexico border. The Senate dismissed all impeachment charges, shutting down his trial before arguments even began.
Mayorkas, who did not appear to testify before the impeachment proceedings, put the border crisis squarely on Congress for failing to update immigration laws during a time of global migration. Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer had said then, in April 2024, that House Republicans’ charges failed to meet “the high standard of high crimes and misdemeanors” and could set a dangerous precedent.
Before Mayorkas, no sitting Cabinet secretary had ever been impeached. It was nearly 150 years ago that the House voted to impeach President Ulysses S. Grant’s war secretary, William Belknap, over a kickback scheme in government contracts. He resigned before the vote.
Trump offers support for Hegseth
Trump backed Hegseth in the wake of Massie’s impeachment resolution, pointing to the U.S. military raid to capture then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January as well as operations against Iran that he asserts have “obliterated” its navy and air force.
“Pete Hegseth gets an “A” PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!” Trump wrote Tuesday on Truth Social.
Iran, however, has been able to keep striking U.S. military bases in the Middle East and has disrupted shipping in the Strait of Hormuz during the more than 8-month-old conflict, driving up global oil prices.
___
Associated Press writer Steve Peoples in New York and Lisa Mascaro in Washington contributed to this report.

title: Senate Republicans vote to keep Thune as leader after steep election losses
text:
John Thune reelected as Senate Republican leader after tense day of discussions about midterm defeats
Senate Republicans reelected South Dakota Sen. John Thune as leader of the GOP conference after a tense day of discussions about steep losses in the midterm elections that cost them their majority.
Thune was always expected to prevail, as he is popular with his GOP colleagues and was running unopposed in the secret ballot election. But Senate Republicans vented their frustrations in three separate meetings on Tuesday after an election wipeout that cost them at least seven Senate seats.
Some Republicans had tried to delay the leadership decision, but the conference voted to proceed, said Wisconsin Sen. Ron Johnson, who had pushed to postpone. He walked out of the room as the voting began.
West Virginia Sen. Jim Justice said after the first meeting that "we want to be thoughtful and do the right thing."
Justice said there was a "legitimate argument that, good gracious, if we lost as badly as we lost, why would we continue on with the same leadership?"
At the same time, the current GOP leadership "didn't cause this problem to happen," Justice said. "They do a good job."
The angst — and the indecision — comes as frustrated Republicans are just beginning to reckon with what the election results mean for their future. Two additional Senate races remain uncalled in Alaska and Mississippi that could further deplete their numbers.
Several senators had already called on Republican leadership to delay the elections, which include contests for other party leaders as well and are held in the small Old Senate Chamber.
Missouri Sen. Josh Hawley said he isn't aware of anyone else running for leader, but "maybe there would be" if they waited.
"I just think that we've got a lot of things that we've got to think through, and I think that to just rush into this and just ratify all of the same leadership, what message does that send?" Hawley told reporters after walking out.
"If you don't think after losing seven Senate seats minimum that we need to change course, I don't know what planet you're on," he said.
Thune, who replaced Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky as leader in early 2025, said before the meeting that they would have a "very fulsome, robust conversation about where we go from here and then we'll see what the consensus of the conference is."
No alternative to Thune has emerged
Hawley said the discussion was a "frank" and "honest" open microphone meeting and some senators discussed their own races this year — some who won, and some who lost.
Republicans in the meeting were also pushing Thune to stay in session around the clock in the coming weeks to push through war spending and other party priorities before they lose power.
"We need a plan to get the Republican agenda done," said Florida Sen. Rick Scott.
Before the meeting, Johnson, the Wisconsin senator, had circulated a letter asking for the delay. He said the conference needs to do some "real soul-searching" but conceded that there's no one else on the ballot.
"That's part of our problem, who would want the job?" he said, turning to a reporter and joking, "Do you want it?"
Oklahoma Sen. Jim Lankford said that there is "widespread support" among Republican senators for Thune, who has made it a point to hear out different viewpoints before he makes major decisions and has maintained close relationships with the rank and file — a different approach from his predecessor, McConnell.
Lankford said he supported having the elections on Tuesday because many of the new GOP senators are already in town for freshman orientation.
"It's a pretty complicated role to be able to manage," Lankford said of Thune's leadership post. "No one wants that job."
Walking into the meeting, South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds said most senators are ready to move forward. It is time to have "leadership in place," he said.
Thune has navigated Trump in his first two years as leader
Thune has spent much of the last two years navigating President Donald Trump, who has often been at odds with the Senate.
While backing Trump on most policies, Thune has refused to change Senate rules and scrap the filibuster to pass voting legislation that would require proof of citizenship for all voters — a position that frustrated Trump and enraged some in the president's political base.
But Trump hosted Thune and his family at the White House in October. He said Monday that the GOP leader is "a very fine man." The election is "up to the Senate," Trump said.
The soul-searching comes as lawmakers are trying to wrap up the year's work — funding the government and seeing if there are some issues where they can work together, including an energy permitting bill that moved forward on a bipartisan vote Monday evening.
When he gets the chance to speak at the meeting, Thune is expected to emphasize his collaborative approach to his colleagues and point out what they did get done in the last year — including the tax and spending cuts legislation and an attempt at reining in the chaotic annual spending process.
In a Senate floor speech Monday, his first extended remarks since the election, Thune said the midterm election was a "tough night" and previewed his pitch to his colleagues who may be looking for answers on how they will navigate the minority.
Republicans will be willing to work with Democrats, Thune said, but "the American people are not looking for socialist government and leftist fantasies."
___
Associated Press reporter Seung Min Kim contributed to this report.

title: Jared Golden hasn’t decided how he’ll vote on Pete Hegseth impeachment
text:
U.S. Rep. Jared Golden is keeping his options open on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, saying he will judge each of the eight charges on its own merits as the House takes a procedural vote Tuesday evening.
“The decision to impeach is a serious one,” Golden’s office said in a statement. “As he did on previous impeachment proceedings, he will vote on each article independently and on the merits.”
That is how the centrist Democrat and Marine veteran from Maine’s 2nd District handled President Donald Trump’s first impeachment in 2019, when he voted for the abuse of power charge and against the obstruction of Congress charge. Golden, who is leaving Congress in January, has also pressured Hegseth on security and budget matters.
Maine’s other House member has made up her mind. U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, a progressive from the 1st District, who won a 10th term last week, called for Hegseth’s removal in an election night speech and said Tuesday she will vote to impeach.
If Tuesday’s vote advances, the charges brought by outgoing Republican U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, a former Trump ally turned bitter rival, will be weighed by the full House on Wednesday or Thursday. Most Democrats are expected to vote in favor.
The impeachment push, which Hegseth on Tuesday blasted as a “farce” from “one disgruntled and defeated congressman,” comes as Democrats who routed Republicans in last week’s midterm elections have pledged to launch investigations into the Trump administration.
Massie charges that Hegseth violated the Constitution by failing to get congressional approval before launching the Iran war and defying several votes to end it. He also accuses Hegseth of sidestepping laws to prevent civilian deaths, including more than 100 children at an elementary school in Iran on the first day of bombing in February.
Further charges allege Hegseth oversaw extrajudicial killings of suspected drug traffickers on boats, the kidnapping of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro “under the guise of narcotics law enforcement,” and retaliation against Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Arizona, one of several veteran Democrats who reminded troops in a video last year that they can refuse illegal orders.
“It’s a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment,” Hegseth said in a rare news conference Tuesday.
Pingree said the administration kept the war going past the War Powers Act’s 60-day limit without congressional authority. She called the civilian deaths charge particularly damning.
“He has defunded offices in the Pentagon that track and respond to where civilians are … a critically basic function,” she said. “It’s a war crime and morally wrong.”
Republican House leaders may try to block the vote. Pingree said the outcome could hinge on House absences, which she expected to favor Democrats this week with more Republicans away from Washington.
If the House impeaches Hegseth, Senate GOP leaders could try to dismiss the charges or refer them to a committee. The Senate has never convicted an impeached Cabinet member, which would require a two-thirds vote.
A trial could give Democratic Sen.-elect Troy Jackson an early chance to act on his critiques of the Iran war, depending on whether it comes before or after he is sworn in.
“Congress has to do oversight, has to watch what’s going on and be part of the process,” Jackson told MSNOW on Tuesday. “Unfortunately, Republicans let that go over the last two years, and we have to take it back.”
Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican whom Jackson ousted in last week’s election, voted against Hegseth’s confirmation and has joined Democrats in several votes to end the Iran war, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Independent Sen. Angus King’s office said it was too early to discuss charges still pending in the House.
