title: How to find the best Black Friday, Cyber Monday and Travel Tuesday travel deals for 2026
text:
(Expedia via Stacker) - Black Friday is one of the biggest days of the year for travel deals, covering everything from flights and hotels to vacation packages and activities. It falls on Friday, Nov. 27 this year, but many travel deals start early and extend through Cyber Monday and Travel Tuesday.
The best way to snag great Black Friday travel deals is to prepare in advance: Pick where you want to go, check sale dates and set price alerts. That way you can book fast when deals go live.
You should also join free travel loyalty programs, so your Black Friday getaway can help you earn points towards your next trip.
Here’s everything you need to know to find the best travel deals in 2026, according to Expedia and Hotels.com:
When do Black Friday travel deals start?
That’s one of the best parts: they often start well before Black Friday itself. Many companies from airlines and hotel chains to booking platforms, release their Black Friday deals about a week ahead of Black Friday.
Don’t wait until Nov. 27 to start planning, and check back for new special offer drops throughout Thanksgiving weekend.
Where can I find the best Black Friday, Cyber Monday and Travel Tuesday travel deals?
Hotels and Lodging
Don’t be afraid to shop around. Keep an eye out for company announcements and emails about Black Friday promotions and be sure to compare prices to get the best deal. Hotel companies and airlines may offer discounted rates or fares at select properties or on select flights. Booking through an online travel platform can make it easier to browse for discounts across brands and boutique hotels.
Flights
Travel Tuesday emerged as a big day for flight discounts a few years ago, but many travel sites will run deals on flights all weekend long. This is another time to shop around. If you can’t find a deal on the airline site, try online booking platforms, which offer savings when you book your flights, hotel and other trip necessities all in one place.
Vacation Packages, Activities and Car Rental
Many sites offer everyday discounts on vacation packages, and Black Friday is a good time to look for special offers.
You can also use online travel aggregators to quickly compare Black Friday deals on activities and car rentals, without having to visit a bunch of different sites.
Cruises
Cruise lines frequently run Black Friday, Cyber Monday and Travel Tuesday offers, and not just on their own websites. Promotions can run the gamut from discounts on specific routes, free on-board perks, or other perks like a free plus-one. Be sure to shop around to find the best deals.
How can I prepare in advance for Black Friday travel deals?
- Sign up for loyalty programs (they’re free): Some companies will offer special discounts or promotions to members, so it pays to sign up ahead of time to make sure you don’t miss the chance at special member pricing. Plus, you’ll collect reward points you can redeem on future trips.
- Stay flexible on destination and travel dates. Being open to travel on off-peak days or to less-popular destinations can help you score the best deals.
- Save hotels in advance. Make sure you know where you want to stay. Many travel apps have trip boards where you can “favorite” hotels in the weeks before sales starts so you can book your preferred properties more easily when the discounts open up.
- Consider a travel rewards credit card if you’re a frequent booker. There are tons out there to choose from, and most come with benefits beyond just earning more rewards. Airline credit cards often include other perks like free checked bags or priority boarding, and hotel cards may include access to complimentary room upgrades or other benefits. Almost all co-branded credit cards let you earn towards future travel with every purchase.
How can I tell if I’m getting a good deal during Black Friday, Cyber Monday and Travel Tuesday?
- Turn on Price Tracking for the hotels and flights you’re watching. Price tracking is a common feature on many booking platforms that helps you view price history and spot genuinely good deals.
- Choose refundable rates. Filter for hotels that offer free cancellation so you can easily snap up a good deal and worry about the logistics later. Avoid offers that are restrictive or won’t let you make changes.
- Read the fine print. Sometimes it’s only a “deal” because there are inconvenient flight layovers or the dates are a destination’s bad weather season. Do a little due diligence to make sure what you’re getting is as great a deal as it seems.

title: Hogtied by rising costs, Maine meat farmers rely on loyal clients
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Deedee Caldwell makes weekly beef deliveries to markets and restaurants. Between stops one recent Thursday, she recounted the growing challenges her cattle farm in Turner faces.
Nearly every input, from her electric bill to the cost of wood shavings for cattle bedding, has shot up dramatically in price. Caldwell Family Farm used to be able to get a load of chicken manure fertilizer from Hillandale egg farm in Turner for as little as $275. But Hillandale went out of business in 2024, and a truckload of pelletized chicken manure from Connecticut now costs Caldwell $9,000.
Because of the drought, her land couldn’t produce as much hay and silage as Caldwell needed in 2025 to feed the cattle, so the farm had to buy $45,000 of corn silage last winter.
At the end of summer, it cost Caldwell $350 for diesel to fill her delivery truck. A week later, it was $450, and that was before diesel jumped to more than $6 a gallon. The petroleum-based plastic bags her farm uses to package its meat cost 45 percent more this year.
Last year she bought 75 fewer head of cattle than she needed because the cost had more than doubled in two years. “There will be some businesses that, for the first time in two decades, I won’t be able to deliver to this winter, because I don’t have the beef,” she said.
Caldwell has raised prices on her animal welfare-certified, pasture-raised beef as little as possible, but still lost a few lucrative restaurant accounts in Portland this year, as restaurateurs face their own financial struggles.
“We’ve been going drastically behind in terms of making a living for a couple of years,” Caldwell said. “My grandpa told me when I was a little girl, ‘Deedee, if you get up a little earlier, work a little harder, go to bed a little later, you’ll always be able to pay your bills.’ And it doesn’t work that way anymore.”
Wholesale and retail prices of local meat are creeping upward as Maine meat farms grapple with these unprecedented burdens. As some grocers and restaurateurs balk at the price hikes and switch to cheaper commodity meats, local meat farmers are now more reliant on — and grateful for — the chefs, shop owners and residents who remain loyal customers.
“There’s a really wonderful network in Maine of restaurants, small stores and butcher shops that are really committed to supporting these products,” said Mark Law, CEO of Rosemont Market & Bakery. “They believe it’s the right thing to do, but they also recognize that the quality of the product is superior, and it makes a difference for their customers.”
‘DEATH BY A MILLION CUTS’
“We want to make sure our farmers are getting the volume they need to sustain their business,” said Jack Barber, co-owner of Barber Brothers Meat & Provisions in South Portland. “And if they need to make another price increase, we’ll absorb as much as we can into our costs and try not to pass it on to the customers, because not having local meat would be a travesty.”
Law said Rosemont has absorbed some farm price increases as well, like with their holiday turkeys. “This year, we’ve made a conscious effort to lower our margin a little bit so we can keep our prices the same and commit to volume for (the farmers),” he said. “They’ve been under such duress economically, we want to really support them by selling as much as possible.”
Gabe Clark, co-owner of Cold Spring Ranch in New Portland, has seen costs at his cattle and pig farm jump 30 percent since 2024.
“This seems like a unique, tough situation this year,” Clark said. “I don’t think there’s a single part of our production costs that has gone down in price, and usually we see some give and take. It’s death by a million cuts.”
Clark usually raises his meat prices just once a year. Last year, for the first time, he had to increase prices three times. “The only way to address these increases in costs is to pass it on to consumers,” he said. “And it’s hard because consumers are facing higher costs across the board themselves.”
Pork chops go for around $2 a pound at the supermarket. Chris Wilcox, owner of Sawyer’s Butcher & Delicatessen in Portland, pays twice that much per pound for whole local pigs. After Wilcox and his team of skilled whole-animal butchers break down the carcasses, chops sell for about $14-$15 a pound.
Sawyer’s can offer specialty cuts you won’t find at supermarkets, like coppa pork roasts and beef steak cuts like Denver, merlot, hanger and flat-iron. Sawyer’s sells other parts wholesale to local restaurants — pig heads, jowls, marrow bones — putting the entire animal to use, without waste.
The whole-animal butcher model works well for the farmers, who don’t have to butcher and package the animals themselves. “If there were more of those types of shops in the state of Maine, I could make it,” Caldwell said.
Willcox has already had to raise his prices even though his store has only been open since August. “We want this meat to be as accessible as it possibly can, and it already costs more than the stuff at the grocery store, so it’s a really tough decision,” he said. “But at the same time, things costs what they cost.”
“We’re trying to support our farmers and give them a fair price,” said Jarrod Spangler, butcher and co-owner of the whole-animal butcher shop Maine MEat in Kittery, where non-premium cuts of New England-raised beef sell for $12-$15 a pound. “So in the end, we have to turn around and up our prices a little bit just to make sure everyone’s being taken care of.”
A SUPERIOR PRODUCT
Local meat is far too pricey for many Mainers. But those who can swing it say the value is clear.
Matt Reece of Portland shops exclusively at Sawyer’s for his meat, about twice a week, citing how well the livestock is raised. “I want to trust the source, and I’m willing to pay to have that trust, and to help out the local farmers who are also facing price pressures.
“I can trust that the animal has been raised well, and at each stage it’s been treated with care,” Reece added. “You can really taste how much better it is when it’s local, even compared to the premium products I’ve bought at supermarkets.”
Chef Stephanie Brown said the quality of Caldwell’s ground beef makes her burgers at North 43 Bistro shine.
“It’s perfection, to me,” Brown said. “(Caldwell’s) prices for her meats are well-justified, because she’s offering an organic, high-quality product. Sometimes in the back office, I encourage her, like, ‘Look, if you need to charge more, charge more. You can’t take the hit.'”
“Stephanie told me, ‘You’ve got to put a fuel surcharge on. If you go out of business because you can’t buy gas to get me your product, that doesn’t do me any good either,’ ” Caldwell said. She now has a fuel surcharge of $8 per stop on her delivery route.
“But every single business is doing that to them,” Caldwell continued. “I feel bad that the economy is in such a way that there’s no break anywhere.”
Brown said that for the past few years, she’s been reckoning with substantial increases in meat costs, regardless of whether it’s local. Meat producers nationwide are affected by the same issues local farmers face. Beef prices in particular have been compounded by a cattle shortage stemming from 2023 snowstorms that wiped out much of the herd in the western United States.
It creates a budget and pricing quandary for Brown and other chefs. “Do you still want to serve the 12-ounce sirloin and charge them more, or do you want to give them a 10-ounce sirloin and charge them less?”
‘MAKE YOUR WORLD SMALL’
Dan Sullivan raises poultry and heritage-breed pigs on Broad Arrow Farm in Bristol. He saw his client list of restaurants and markets dwindle over the years because of price increases he needed to make.
So he shifted his business model. With a few exceptions, Broad Arrow no longer sells to restaurants, butchers and markets. They now turn two-thirds of the pork they produce into value-added products like dry-cured meats, which they sell — along with their fresh meat — direct to consumers through their farm store, at farmers’ markets and online.
Four years ago, Broad Arrow also opened The Rooting Pig restaurant on their property. The venue puts all the farm’s cured and fresh meats to use in various ways, including a top-selling charcuterie board.
“If you want to insulate yourself from how the global commodity markets are moving, make your world small,” Sullivan said. “Be hyperlocal, hyperseasonal, and that’s what we are.”
Sullivan and other farmers and purveyors said the state could use more meat slaughterhouses to prevent processing bottlenecks and keep farmers from having to travel long distances to get their meat processed.
Caldwell acknowledges that some of her high costs are voluntary. She said the wood shavings she uses for cattle bedding have become “astronomically” more expensive in the past couple of years. While she’s not required by law to do so, she insists on having clean, dry spaces for her cattle to rest.
‘NOT PAYING FOR ITSELF ANYMORE’
Quality of life for the farmers themselves is hard to come by these days.
“There’s a lot of suicide in the farming industry,” Caldwell said. “When you work 80 to 100 hours a week, and at the end of the week, you’ve got to figure out what bill you can pay, that wears on them over time.” Her father took his own life four years ago this month.
In the past couple of years, just to stay afloat, Caldwell has had to sell house lots from her land for the first time since her grandfather started the farm in 1944. Still, she tries to focus on the nonmaterial ways her farm pays off.
“If the weather’s good, I can see Mount Washington from where we are. There’s some pay in that. We have amazing sunsets. There’s pay in that.
“I’m very blessed to be where I am,” Caldwell said, her voice breaking as she choked back tears. “But it’s not paying for itself anymore, and we don’t have a lot of equity left to chew off. The next two years or less are make or break.”

title: How the IRS’ 2027 inflation adjustments change the standard deduction and child tax credit
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — The IRS released its annual inflation adjustments for the 2027 tax year, raising the standard deduction and the child tax credit. These adjustments will apply for tax returns filed in 2028.
Many of the increases, which the IRS released on Nov. 5, are routine and rise each year based on how much prices climbed. For 2027, that increase is about 3.2%. But several of the most popular tax breaks that Republicans included in their 2025 law remain fixed and do not adjust for inflation, meaning they will be worth slightly less each year.
The standard deduction for single filers will increase to $16,600 from $16,100. For married couples filing jointly the standard deduction will rise to $33,200 from $32,200. The standard deduction for heads of household will be $24,925, up from $24,150.
For a married couple earning $100,000 who use the standard deduction, their federal income tax bill would fall to $7,504 from $7,640, according to an Associated Press calculation. A single filer earning $60,000 would see their tax bill drop to $4,952 from $5,020. Those calculations assume the household’s income stays the same. Because these are inflation adjustments, workers whose pay increases with inflation will see their tax bills stay roughly unchanged.
The maximum earned income tax credit for a worker with no children will rise to $685 from $664. For a family with two children, the maximum credit will rise to $7,552 from $7,316.
The child tax credit will rise by $100 to a maximum of $2,300 per child, and the refundable portion will rise by $100 to $1,800. The 2025 law set the credit at $2,200 and tied future increases to inflation.
Several breaks from the 2025 law are not adjusted for inflation. Workers can still deduct up to $25,000 in tip income and up to $12,500 in overtime pay, or $25,000 for joint filers. People 65 and older will be able to claim an additional $6,000 deduction. All three tax breaks are set to end after the 2028 tax year unless Congress extends them.
The estate tax exclusion, which the 2025 law made permanent at $15 million, will rise with inflation to $15.48 million.
The top income tax rate stays at 37%, and in 2027 it will apply to income above $661,375 for single filers and above $793,650 for married couples filing jointly.

title: Wreaths Across America reveals schedule for 2026 Escort to Arlington
text:
Wreaths Across America reveals schedule for 2026 Escort to Arlington, which includes nearly a dozen stops in Maine
The Maine-based nonprofit organization Wreaths Across America has announced the schedule for this year's Escort to Arlington.
The convoy is scheduled to make nearly a dozen stops in Maine as it makes its way to Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia.
The annual journey started in 1992 when Morrill Worcester, the owner of Worcester Wreath Company in Harrington, Maine, decided to lay the surplus of wreaths his company had left over on the graves of veterans who are buried in Arlington.
Last year, more than 3.1 million sponsored veterans' wreaths were placed on headstones of U.S. service members at nearly 5,600 participating locations. Millions of volunteers helped place the wreaths, a third of whom were children.
This year's escort departs from West Quoddy Head Light in Lubec, Maine, where a sunrise service will be held on Dec. 12. The remaining scheduled stops for the 2026 Escort to Arlington are listed below.

title: US soldier arrested in Britain on suspicion of espionage linked to Russia
text:
LONDON (AP) — A member of the U.S. Army assigned to a NATO unit was arrested Tuesday in England on suspicion of espionage related to Russia, counterterror police and other officials said. The arrest comes during heightened concern over threats to American forces stationed in Britain and tension between Moscow and much of Europe.
The 41-year-old man, who was not named, was arrested near Gloucester on suspicion of violating two sections of the National Security Act 2023: assisting a foreign intelligence service and obtaining or disclosing protected information.
He was serving in NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps at Imjin Barracks near Gloucester, according to a U.S. official, a senior NATO official and a British government official. The man is an officer, the U.S. official said. All three spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military matters.
The Allied Rapid Reaction Corps is a multinational land unit within the NATO military alliance that is designed to quickly respond to crises or short-notice operations. According to the unit’s website, it is made up of forces from 20 nations but is led by the British and based in Gloucester, where the U.S. soldier was arrested.
U.S. Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, commanding general of the Army’s Counterintelligence Command, described the suspect as a senior soldier but offered no other details on his identity in a news release. Officials have not provided more information about the case.
The Metropolitan Police said its counterterror forces worked closely with the FBI and U.S. military. In the news release, FBI Director Kash Patel called it an “important arrest” dealing with allegations of espionage that are of “utmost concern” for the U.S. and its allies.
“This FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners,” Patel said.
The suspect was in custody at a London police station, officials said. Searches were conducted at two locations in Gloucestershire, a county about 90 miles (140 kilometers) west of London.
Police said the arrest was not related to other counterterrorism investigations, indicating no connection with a suspected terror plot linked to Iran in September at a U.S.-run base in Britain, RAF Fairford, near Gloucester.
After the threat, the U.S. Air Force withdrew bombers that had been used to strike Iran from RAF Fairford. The Air Force this week also relocated aircraft from another base in Britain — RAF Mildenhall — because of a threat, which The Wall Street Journal reported was related to Iran.
Tuesday’s arrest near Gloucester appears to be separate from those incidents, with authorities saying the case was related to Russia.
Several European nations have recently warned of the rising threat from Russian covert activity, including sabotage, espionage and drone incursions.
Denmark’s Defense Intelligence Service said Russian President Vladimir Putin may carry out military attacks against NATO only if he assesses NATO will not respond collectively and “especially if Russia assesses that the United States cannot or will not support the European NATO countries in a potential war against Russia.”
NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander, U.S. Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, said last month that the alliance is ready to fight if it is attacked. He made the comments in Poland as he outlined how NATO would defend itself from a Russian attack.
Since the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the AP has tracked more than 210 incidents of sabotage and malign activity across Europe blamed on Russia by Western officials that included organizing plots to set fire to warehouses, launching drones and trying to kill enemies abroad as well as stealing defense technology and carrying out cyberattacks on critical European infrastructure.
One of the most recent incidents was an attempted drone attack on a German airport in August that officials blamed on Russia. It prompted Germany to shut a Russian consulate.
___
Toropin reported from Washington. Associated Press writer Ben Finley in Washington contributed to this report.

title: NASA announces $1 million moon base challenge

The space agency announced a $1 million competition Sunday for high school and college students across the country.

title: Maine cites 6 fire departments after deadly Searsmont blast
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The state has cited six fire departments in the wake of the deadly Searsmont lumber yard explosion.
But the Maine Occupational Safety and Health program has waived nearly all $108,000 in penalties so that Appleton, Belmont, Lincolnville, Montville, Morrill and Searsmont can “prioritize their limited resources” to improve firefighter safety, according to Bureau of Labor Standards Director Kate Burkhart.
The Bureau of Labor Standards is a unit of the Maine Department of Labor.
“We are responsible for ensuring that people working for state, county, and municipal governments and other public employers have safe workplaces,” Burkhart said in a Tuesday statement. “We do that best when we balance enforcement with supporting public employers as they address violations to improve safety, mitigate hazards and reduce the risk of future harm to employees.”
The six departments were cited after they were unable to keep track of firefighters’ locations, while another five were cited for issues with personal protective equipment, including breathing apparatuses.
All the departments have resolved those problems, while the state is working to assist with training to improve systems for tracking the location of firefighters.
The fire broke out about 10:05 a.m. on May 15 at the Robbins Lumber campus off Route 131 in an area where wood shavings are packed in plastic bags and spread to a nearby silo.
At the time, the silo was about 20% filled with sawdust and wood shavings. The silo had a fire suppression system, but it failed to activate because the temperatures at the top had not become hot enough to trigger it.
Smoke could be seen coming from the base, and later an orange glow, prompting firefighters to pour water into the silo and the room at its base, which unbeknownst to them was adding oxygen and stirring up dust suspended in an “explosive mixture,” according to a federal investigation into the disaster.
Then the silo exploded without warning about 11 a.m., throwing, in a blast of pressure and fire, mill employees, firefighters and EMS providers who stood nearby.
Firefighters, many of them critically injured, rushed to pull survivors away from the inferno, as nearly 300 firefighters from 46 departments across four counties scrambled to the lumber yard to contain the blaze and tend to the wounded.
Morrill firefighter Andrew Cross, 27, died at the scene of the fire. Searsmont’s assistant fire chief, Wayne Woodbury, succumbed to his injuries on June 14. The blaze, one of the worst industrial disasters in recent Maine history, also killed one of the company’s co-owners, Alden Robbins, who died on July 2.
At least 10 other people, including first responders, a mill employee and another of the mill’s co-owners, were injured in the fire.
Robbins Lumber is a leading supplier of eastern white pine products, with roots in Searsmont that stretch back nearly 150 years. It employs more than 100 people.
The mill resumed operations on May 26.

title: NYC sightseeing helicopter makes emergency landing due to possible engine trouble
text:
NYC sightseeing helicopter makes emergency landing after reporting possible engine trouble
A New York City sightseeing helicopter on a maintenance flight made an emergency landing on Tuesday at a New Jersey cargo port after the pilot reported possible engine trouble.
Two people were aboard the Bell 206L-4 helicopter when it came down on a road at the Port Jersey Marine Terminal in Bayonne, across the Hudson River from Manhattan, around 8:55 a.m., the Federal Aviation Administration said.
No injuries were reported, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey said. Messages seeking comment were left for the helicopter’s operator, FlyNYON.
Video of the scene shows part of the helicopter’s tail sitting on the road about 30 feet from the aircraft, which was manufactured in 1999, according to FAA records.
In a recording of the air traffic control audio, the pilot can be heard saying, “mayday, mayday, mayday" and “we need to land outside of the airport.” The helicopter landed several minutes later, just outside of the container terminal, the Port Authority said.
Last year, a Bell 206L-4 sightseeing helicopter plummeted into the Hudson River, killing all 6 people on board. The National Transportation Safety Board said the remains of several geese were found on the helicopter, suggesting it may have struck several birds before crashing.
Last week, the U.S. Department of Transportation’s Office of Inspector General announced an audit of sightseeing helicopter regulations, citing “longstanding concerns regarding the industry’s safety and whether the current regulatory framework provides adequate safeguards."
Since 2008, there have been at least 58 helicopter crashes involving tourist helicopters in the U.S., including 11 that were fatal, Assistant Inspector General Marshall Jackson said.

title: What to know about the 'unexploded ordnance' off the coast of Portland
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
What to know about the 'unexploded ordnance' off the coast of Portland
The United States Coast Guard released a notice to mariners earlier this week regarding 'unexploded ordnance' found eight miles off the coast of Portland by mapping researchers with the Maine Department of Marine Resources.
Those working with the Gulf of Maine Research Institute say the image appears to show a shell from war equipment potentially dating back to World War II as Maine's offshore islands saw extensive naval training during that period.
They also stated that the shell appeared to be without a detonator.
"That being said, it's probably still full of explosives," said Zach Whitener, captain of GMRI's research vessel. "And so if it got mishandled, it could definitely still explode."
Whitener said it was found north of an area known to local fishermen as 'The Cod Ledges.'
He mentioned that it's not a heavily anchored area, especially by large boats. However, everybody should be aware and travel with caution. He placed emphasis on those who use dragging equipment, such as scallopers and lobstermen.
"We just want to make sure in this specific area that mariners stay away, make sure that they don't do any sort of anchoring or ground fishing or any kind of seabed disturbance in that area, just to make sure that we don't have any sort of incident there," said Lt. Amanda Barnett of the United States Coast Guard.
The notice released by the Coast Guard now alerts the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration to note the device on its maps used by mariners.
As for cleanup, researchers aren't sure it will be dealt with.
"Typically, these sorts of things aren't cleaned up," said Whitener. "Just because they've been there so long and it's so expensive to get it and deal with it with basically a bomb squad."

title: Cause of death revealed for 5-year-old Saylor Hayes 2 months after parents charged
text:
GEORGETOWN COUNTY, SC (WMBF/Gray News) - The investigation into the death of Saylor Hayes has concluded.
The Georgetown County Coroner’s Office determined the 5-year-old’s cause of death and announced it had concluded its investigation.
Saylor was reported missing in August while vacationing with her family in the Pawleys Island area. Her body was later found in the waters near where she was last seen.
Following an investigation, coroner Chase Ridgeway determined Saylor’s cause of death to be asphyxia due to drowning, with child neglect identified as a contributory factor.
The manner of death has been classified as undetermined. This classification reflects the inability to conclusively determine whether Saylor’s death was accidental or the result of a homicidal act, according to the coroner’s office.
According to the arrest warrants, Saylor, described as being severely nonverbal and autistic with a history of wandering and a known affinity for water, was left unsupervised near a body of water before she went missing.
Saylor’s parents, John Hayes III and Geordyn Hayes, were arrested after investigators alleged they misled deputies during the search for their daughter.
Washington County Sheriff Blake Andis said Saylor had been enrolled in the agency’s Project Lifesaver program since June 2024.
Project Lifesaver helps authorities find people who are at risk of wandering because of cognitive conditions or other special needs. People in the program wear a small transmitter that emits a radio frequency, helping authorities track missing people.
A helicopter equipped with the technology was even deployed to help locate her. However, Weaver said they couldn’t get a ping from Saylor.
Andis said it was discovered that Saylor did not have her transmitter when she went missing after wandering from her family’s rental home. Instead, investigators found the tracker in a vehicle on the property.
According to the warrants, John Hayes and Geordyn Hayes encouraged deputies to use Project Lifesaver, despite knowing Saylor did not have her transmitter.
The two also allegedly tried to divert the search efforts away from the nearby water.
“It is important to understand that Project Lifesaver is a voluntary program,” Andis said. “A parent, guardian or caregiver is responsible for ensuring the transmitter remains properly secured to the client. The transmitter is attached using a specialized band designed for continuous wear. It cannot simply be unclasped or removed by the client; the band must be physically cut in order to remove the transmitter.”
Andis reiterated that Project Lifesaver works and he believes that if Saylor had been wearing her transmitter, deputies could have found her much sooner.
John and Geordyn Hayes were arrested in Tennessee and charged with unlawfully placing a child at risk, or willfully abandoning a child, according to the Georgetown County Sheriff’s Office.

title: Maine to get another $190 million through federal rural health program
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine is set to receive more than $190 million in the second year of the federal Rural Health Transformation Program.
Sen. Susan Collins, who pushed for the $50 billion investment in the program during negotiations over the One Big Beautiful Bill, announced this year’s funding for Maine on Tuesday.
About $10 billion is to be distributed across all 50 states over five years as part of the program. Maine received $190 million in the first year and will get about $360,000 more in the second, which Collins credited to the state meeting program objectives.
Collins advocated for the funding in order to partially offset Medicaid cuts that are set to start in 2027. She and the rest of Maine’s congressional delegation, independent Sen. Angus King and Democratic Reps. Chellie Pingree and Jared Golden, voted “no” on the bill, partly because of the Medicaid cutbacks.
Maine stands to lose $5 billion in Medicaid funding under the bill.
“Funding from this program has already been used to protect the Penobscot Community Health Center from bankruptcy and will be crucial to helping rural health care providers in Maine innovate to lower costs and improve health outcomes for Mainers no matter where they live,” Collins said in a written statement.
It has yet to be determined how to utilize the funding. Earlier this year, Maine officials struggled to administer funds in ways that aligned with program guidelines, with the federal government previously vetoing two of the state’s proposed initiatives.

title: DOJ sues Lyft over alleged disability discrimination
text:
Department of Justice sues Lyft for alleged discrimination against passengers with disabilities
The U.S. Department of Justice said it is suing one of the nation’s largest rideshare companies.
The DOJ filed on Monday, Nov. 9, a federal lawsuit against Lyft, Inc., alleging the company discriminated against passengers with disabilities, including those who use service animals and mobility devices such as stowable wheelchairs.
Related video above: Traveling solo? Safety tips to avoid scams and costly mistakes
“Individuals with disabilities should be able to rely on rideshare services free of discrimination,” Acting Assistant Attorney General Jesus A. Osete of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division said in a statement on Monday. “We intend to uphold the ADA’s promise that people with disabilities are entitled to equal access in every part of public life, including essential transportation services.”
The Department of Justice said it is seeking $53 million for individuals with disabilities whom it claims Lyft discriminated against and added that those who were discriminated against submitted complaints to Lyft or the DOJ.
A spokesperson for Lyft provided Florida sister station WPBF with the following statement on Monday night:
"We disagree with the Department of Justice’s allegations. Discrimination has no place in the Lyft community. We have long-standing policies requiring drivers to accommodate riders who travel with service animals or use foldable mobility devices, and drivers who violate these policies face serious consequences, including permanent deactivation.
We’ve backed those policies with in-app tools, like letting riders tell drivers in advance that they’re traveling with a service animal and reminding drivers that refusing one is against the law. We’ve cooperated with the DOJ throughout its review and remain committed to serving every rider, including riders with disabilities."
The Department of Justice lawsuit, which was filed in the Northern District of California, alleges Lyft violated Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, which is also known as the ADA.
The law prevents discrimination by private transportation companies, like Lyft, that is based on disability.
Lyft and its drivers were accused of “routinely refuse service to individuals with disabilities; impose impermissible surcharges by charging fees such as cancellation fees to riders whom Lyft has unlawfully denied service; and refuse to reasonably modify Lyft’s policies, practices, or procedures where necessary to avoid discriminating against riders with disabilities, including by denying individuals with mobility disabilities the option to sit in the front seat when needed.”
CLICK HERE TO READ THE COMPLAINT
The DOJ wants the court to issue an order to force Lyft to stop discriminating against individuals with disabilities, modify its policies to comply with the ADA, and train staff and drivers on the ADA.

title: Maine voters could decide on three referendums in 2027
text:
Maine voters could decide on three referendums in 2027

Maine voters could decide on three referendums in 2027
The 2026 election is now behind us, and we're already looking ahead to 2027.
There are three potential referendums that citizens petitioners are hoping to get on the ballot in 2027.
Including, the Protect Girls Sports initiative that fell short of getting enough signatures to appear on the 2026 ballot.
The initiative, "An Act to Designate School Sports Participation and Facilities by Sex," would mandate that a student's participation in school sports and their use of facilities align with the sex on their birth certificate.
This spring, Secretary of State Shenna Bellows announced there were not enough valid signatures to move forward in 2026. The citizens petitioners have resubmitted the necessary signatures.
The Secretary of State's Office has also approved citizens petitioners for "An Act to Amend the Cannabis Legalization Act and the Maine Medical Use of Cannabis Act" to begin collecting signatures.
This proposal would repeal the current law that makes recreational marijuana legal in Maine. Petitioners have until June 8 to submit signatures for this proposal.
Another proposal that proponents are now collecting signatures for aims at creating a publicly funded health care system.
"Resolve, Directing the Development of Legislation Establishing a Publicly Funded System of Health Care Coverage for All Maine Residents" directs the legislature to develop a system for universal health care coverage in Maine. The deadline to submit signatures is April 24.
The 2027 election is on November 2.

title: Maine men’s basketball falls to Rhode Island
text:
Dylan Williamson scored eight straight points late in the second half and Rhode Island held on to beat the University of Maine 71-65 in a men’s basketball game on Tuesday night in Kingston, Rhode Island.
The Black Bears (1-3) lead by nine points with 10:06 left in the first half and by six early in the second. The Rams (3-0) took a 59-56 lead with 5:32 left on a 3-pointer by Williamson and never trailed again.

title: More ICE agents at Scarborough facility amid growing protests
text:
SCARBOROUGH — There are more Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents at the ICE facility in Scarborough, Rep. Chellie Pingree said in a written statement Monday.
ICE said the increase in agents is a response to the growing number of protesters outside the facility, including some who are armed, said Pingree, a Democrat representing Maine’s 1st District. On a windy Tuesday morning, there were six demonstrators.
The Maine Immigrants’ Rights Coalition said in a statement Monday that the additional ICE personnel at the facility are “focused on building security.” ICE did not immediately respond Tuesday to a request for comment or questions about the number of new agents in Scarborough and the reason behind the increase in personnel.
It is unclear how many new ICE agents are at the facility. Protesters said the agents arrived in cars with out-of-state license plates, accompanied by an armored vehicle that’s being stored in the garage.
Tensions have been rising at 40 Manson Libby Road, home to Maine’s only ICE facility. Protesters have stood watch on the road outside the facility for hours every day since an ICE agent killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford on July 13, and other groups have been organizing to push ICE out of Scarborough.
The Scarborough Police Department has been called to the facility more than 50 times since.
A protester who goes by K and asked not to be fully identified out of fear for her safety, has been openly carrying a camo AR-15 outside of the Scarborough ICE facility for weeks, ever since she heard a fellow protester say they were intimidated by agents in a nearby parking lot. A longtime gun owner, she had been carrying a concealed firearm while keeping a daily watch for months. Her belt has a hatchet, additional magazines, a medical kit and a racoon tail.
“If they want to start a firefight, I will return fire,” she said. Her hands rested on the handle of her weapon. “This is a civil war.”
Protesters say the increased ICE presence wasn’t a response to their guns, but rather they’ve witnessed ramped up activity at the facility for months, according to K.
Two other protesters have also started open carrying, she said, and both stood near two black pickup trucks parked just off the road in front of the ICE facility on a recent Tuesday morning. One demonstrator armed with a rifle wore a camo tactical vest and a matching buff covering their face. The other, also wearing a face covering and camo base layers, crossed their arms over their gun.
“Maybe one day, 100 people can show up with AR-15s,” K said. In her ideal world, there would be thousands of people mobilizing to the facility to physically force ICE out, she said.
K said she feels angry and disheartened by local, state and federal politicians, who have said they have limited oversight over this federal facility and its operations.
“We’re on our own,” she said. “What are we supposed to do?”
K said ICE agents are not directly engaging with or speaking to the handful of protesters who keep watch each day, except for an occasional wave.
“Please remember that many people in our community are already scared, anxious, and uncertain about what is happening,” Project Relief, a mutual aid group, wrote in a statement about the increased ICE presence shared on social media. “Seeing individuals openly carrying weapons, regardless of their intentions, can add to that fear.”
Pingree called on the U.S. Department of Homeland Security to withdraw the additional agents and close the facility.
“Their presence has left people scared to leave their homes, scared to send their kids to school, scared to go to work, and scared to go about their daily lives,” Pingree said in the statement. “The impacts — on families, on our communities, on businesses, on our economy — have been devastating.”

title: Trump moves to cut SNAP benefits for 6.3 million people
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Gray News) - The Trump administration proposed a rule that could cut food stamp benefits for 6.3 million people.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture proposal, released Monday, would limit automatic eligibility for SNAP to low-income households that receive cash assistance through the TANF program.
Households receiving noncash or nominal TANF services would no longer automatically qualify for SNAP under the proposal.
According to the proposal, the change would save $44.6 billion between 2027 and 2031. It is the Trump administration’s latest effort to curb SNAP spending, citing concerns about waste and fraud.
The proposal targets a policy known as “broad-based categorical eligibility,” which allows states to use TANF benefits such as child care or workforce training to qualify households for SNAP without applying the program’s standard income eligibility limit.
The changes would make SNAP eligibility more standardized and “preserve benefits for the truly needy,” the rule said.
The USDA also estimates that 1.8 million children would also lose eligibility for free school lunches under the proposed rule.
Nearly 18% of SNAP recipients, or about 6.3 million people, would lose benefits under the change.
The public will have 30 days to comment on the proposed rule.

title: Greta Thunberg warns ‘everything we love is at stake’ as she arrives at UN climate talks
text:
Greta Thunberg warns ‘everything we love is at stake’ as she arrives at UN climate talks
Climate activist Greta Thunberg arrived at U.N. climate talks on Tuesday, condemning the annual proceedings as hypocritical and urging leaders to put people and the planet ahead of profits and power.
The COP31 conference is being held in the Turkish resort city of Antalya following a year of deadly climate-related disasters, including heat waves and floods, and another energy shock caused by the Iran war.
“It’s a hypocrisy every year that the host countries are given an opportunity to whitewash themselves and we know that these negotiations are filled with lobbyists, paid by the very destructive industries which are benefiting from our extremely violent status quo,” Thunberg said as she arrived. “Our political and economic systems that have become incompatible with human nature.”
Related video above: More than 12 trillion tons of ice lost in climate change's big melt
COP31 co-hosts Turkey and Australia are promoting renewable energy and rooftop solar installations, but both still rely heavily on fossil fuels, especially coal, to generate electricity. Previous hosts, including Brazil, the United Arab Emirates and Azerbaijan, are major oil producers.
Climate change is “threatening everything,” Thunberg said, warning that “everything and everyone we love [are] at stake.”
“We should act to protect and benefit people rather than constantly sacrificing the global majority and the very planet we are all living on, for a fortunate few to keep making unimaginable profits and maintaining geopolitical power,” she said.
Thunberg blasts annual climate talks
This is the first climate summit Thunberg has attended since the 2021 talks in Glasgow, Scotland, where she dismissed world leaders’ promises as “blah, blah, blah.”
She rose to prominence in 2018 when, aged 15, she began a solitary “ School Strike for Climate ” outside the Swedish Parliament. In 2022, she published “The Climate Book,” outlining actions to address the climate crisis.
She has won multiple awards and advocated for other causes, including the Free Palestine movement. Last year, she was arrested in London while supporting hunger-striking pro-Palestinian activists. More recently, she supported French students protesting for more school resources.
In 2024, she joined a protest in Georgia against Azerbaijan’s hosting of COP29.
A key goal for Turkey is global electrification: shifting sectors such as transportation, buildings and heavy industry away from fossil fuels and toward electricity. Turkey wants electricity, preferably generated from renewable sources such as solar and wind, to account for 35% of global energy consumption by 2035, up from 23% today.
“We have to take the victories we have, of course, because we are so desperate in this situation that we have to take all the positive signs we can get to save as much as we can still save,” said Thunberg, who is expected to spend several days at COP31.
Youth activists rally around Thunberg
Thunberg's arrival at the conference created excitement among many youth climate activists.
“In this time of heightened geopolitical tensions, I hope that Greta’s presence here reminds us of why we started this work in the first place: to push for meaningful change, hold decision-makers accountable, and work towards a better future for all of humanity,” said Amber Turner, a 26-year-old fellow with the Alliance of Small Island States.
“Worsening climate change impacts make it challenging for young people to be sure of a safe and thriving future,” Turner added.
Protests at COP31 demanded more climate finance and criticized growing interest in nuclear energy.
“The presence of such a headline climate activist at one of the world’s biggest conferences on climate is symbolic, and I hope that it will put pressure on the COP itself to deliver real action and implementation,” said Kamori Osthananda, a youth negotiator with Thailand’s COP delegation.
Qiyun Woo, a youth environmentalist from Singapore, said Thunberg's “powerful” presence "adds to calls from a generation that inherits the consequences of these negotiations.”
“Besides her, there are many youth activists from around the world who are also on the ground ... actively fighting for their communities, home and collective future,” she said.
The U.N. talks in Antalya run until Nov. 20. COP32 is scheduled to take place in Ethiopia’s capital, Addis Ababa, in November 2027.

title: Bread & Friends opening bakery and cafe in former Belleville spot
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Bread & Friends restaurant is launching a bakery and cafe this Saturday in the former Belleville Bakery.
Co-owner Maggie Rubin said Bread & Friends moved all of its pastry production to the space at 767 Forest Ave. in mid-October.
For now, the bakery will be open Saturday-Sunday from 7 a.m. to noon, offering all the same pastries and breads available at Bread & Friends’ Fore Street location, along with teas and drip coffee from Enjoy Coffee Roasters in Providence, R.I.
The Forest Avenue space is takeout only for now, though Rubin said they hope to add seating after renovations next year. She said they also aim to expand their coffee program and be open more days by spring or summer.
Moving production to Forest Avenue allowed Bread & Friends to make their wholesale program three times bigger. They provide pastries and bread for as many as 30 coffee shops, restaurants and grocery stores; Rubin said Belleville passed a number of their former clients on to Bread & Friends.
“We’re excited to have an outpost off the peninsula,” Rubin said. “Sometimes for locals, going to the Old Port is such a slog. Our hope is that everyone can get their sweet treat or their loaf for the week a little easier.”

title: ‘Most rewarding’: 97-year-old who left school to take care of her family receives honorary diploma
text:
BAY ST. LOUIS, Miss. (WLOX/Gray News) — A Mississippi woman received her long-awaited high school diploma this week.
Etta Mae Williams, 97, received an honorary diploma from the Bay-Waveland School District on Monday.
Williams put on her cap and gown and accepted the diploma as a member of the Class of 2026.
“Good things come to those who wait, and I patiently waited,” Williams said. “I’ve been waiting for this for a long time. But I got it.”
Williams left school when she was young to help support her family. Years later, she tried to go back to school, but COVID-19 derailed those plans.
“I finally got this piece of paper I always wanted,” Williams said. “I worked the whole way through it. Thank the Lord I got it.”
Her great-niece, Britney Williams, has admired that determination.
“She had to drop out of school to help out. She had to work. She had to help provide for the family when her father passed,” Britney Williams said. “And so, just to keep striving. Just to keep going on. To fulfill her education means a lot.”
Etta Mae Williams’ dream came true after a community member asked Superintendent Sandra Reed if the district could help make it happen.
Reed said the decision was easy, especially after she learned all eight of Etta Mae Williams’ children graduated from Bay High School.
“I can honestly say that this was the most rewarding diploma that I’ve ever handed out,” Reed said. “Just the joy, the love, the grace were just overflowing from her. And it was just my honor.”
Mississippi Rep. Jeffrey Hulum III also presented Etta Mae Williams with a proclamation honoring her hard work.
“You’re never too old to learn,” Etta Mae Williams said. “I tried, I tried, I tried, and I succeeded. Thank you.”

title: US-mediated talks on ending Russia-Ukraine war begin in Abu Dhabi
text:
US-mediated talks on ending Russia-Ukraine war begin in Abu Dhabi
Three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States opened Tuesday in the United Arab Emirates, as Washington renews its push to end the war that followed Moscow's all-out invasion nearly five years ago.
The two-day session in the UAE's capital, Abu Dhabi, is the first such meeting since February. It will focus on security guarantees, the White House said before the discussions. Russia sees NATO as a threat, and Ukraine wants to prevent future Russian invasions.
Hopes of progress in ending Europe’s biggest conflict since World War II are tempered by the absence of any significant breakthroughs in three previous rounds of talks early this year. The war has already killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of civilians, analysts and humanitarian organizations say.
Related video: President Trump says he'll work with Democrats as White House warns against investigations
There are no signs the fighting is abating, and the talks took place against a backdrop of new long-range strikes between Russia and Ukraine. The two armies are largely deadlocked on the front line.
Russia launched 162 drones of various types and a ballistic missile at Ukraine overnight, Ukraine’s air force said.
Meanwhile, Russia’s Ministry of Defense said that its forces shot down 155 Ukrainian drones overnight above eight Russian regions, as well as the Crimean Peninsula, which Russia annexed from Ukraine in 2014.
Ukrainians meet first with European and NATO officials
U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, said on X that he and fellow envoy Steve Witkoff were working on a “negotiated solution that can deliver lasting peace and create the conditions for a sovereign, secure, and prosperous Ukraine within a more stable European security environment.”
The head of the Russian delegation, Vladimir Medinsky, noted at the start of the talks that the Russian delegation “has become bigger and more professional.”
He expressed hope that the meeting “will allow us to advance on the path towards peace in the interests of the people of Russia and the people of Ukraine.”
Rustem Umerov, the head of Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service who is leading Kyiv's delegation, said that the day began with a meeting between the Ukrainian team, the U.S. envoys and representatives from the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, NATO and the European Commission.
Russia and Ukraine hold to their divergent demands
The Russian and Ukrainian governments remain far apart on key elements of any prospective deal.
Russian President Vladimir Putin wants Ukraine to pull its troops back from Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson — the four regions that Moscow annexed in September 2022, but never fully captured. He also demands that Ukraine abandon its bid to join NATO, accept strict limits on its military and drop restrictions on the Russian language and the Moscow-affiliated Orthodox Church in Ukraine.
Putin wants a comprehensive peace deal on those conditions and won’t agree to a general halt in hostilities, arguing that it would only allow Ukrainian troops to rest and replenish their weapons stockpiles. He has warned that Russia will achieve its goals by force if Kyiv refuses to meet its conditions for peace.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who was visiting Denmark on Tuesday, rejects Putin’s demands to voluntarily cede territory that Russia hasn't been able to take on the battlefield. Zelenskyy also rejects any limits on Ukraine's military or its arrangements with Western partners, which Kyiv sees as essential security guarantees to stop Moscow from invading again.
Ukraine argues that an immediate ceasefire is the necessary first step toward negotiating a wider settlement and says a direct meeting between Putin and Zelenskyy is the only way territorial issues can be settled.
Russia and Ukraine send experienced negotiators
The Russian and Ukrainian delegations include senior officials who have attended previous rounds of talks.
Russia’s chief negotiator is Medinsky, a Putin aide who has led Moscow’s team since the first direct peace talks with Ukraine in Istanbul in March 2022. The Russian delegation also includes deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov and deputy chief of the General Staff’s operational department, Yuri Zhigarlovsky.
Apart from Umerov, the Ukrainian delegation also reportedly includes Zelenskyy’s chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov, his deputy, Sergiy Kyslytsya, and Davyd Arakhamia, the parliamentary faction leader of Zelenskyy’s Servant of the People party.
U.S. says broader European security deal in the works
Last week, Trump declared that some kind of grand deal about European security was in the works, describing it as “a big agreement” that is “going to involve more than Ukraine.”
Kushner said Monday on X that a “comprehensive and lasting settlement will also require direct engagement between Russia and our European partners on the broader security arrangements that affect them.” The discussions in Abu Dhabi will set the stage for “that engagement to begin in the near future, as part of a broader multilateral process,” he said.
Moscow has praised the broad approach.
“We can only welcome the (U.S.) negotiators on President Donald Trump’s request proposing to put the issue of collective security on top of the agenda of the talks on a Ukrainian settlement,” Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said.
Just before Moscow launched the full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, it demanded that NATO roll back its deployments in the trans-Atlantic alliance’s member countries in Central and Eastern Europe, seeing their presence as a security threat. Similar demands will likely be part of any comprehensive peace deal proposed by Russia.
Kushner said that before the start of the three-way talks, he and Witkoff would meet separately with envoys from Ukraine, the European Union, NATO, Germany, France, the United Kingdom and Italy to “continue the close consultation and coordination we have undertaken on European security and Ukraine’s postwar future over the past several weeks.”
Some in the EU see Washington's proposals as too accommodating to Moscow.
Russia has objected to the Europeans’ involvement in the three-way talks, but said that EU representatives could join at a later stage.
Russia and Ukraine have escalated aerial attacks
While the ground battles have morphed into a war of attrition along the 1,200-kilometer (about 750-mile) front line, Russia and Ukraine have ramped up their long-range strikes with drones and missiles.
Russia has intensified its air campaign against Ukraine’s power grid, seeking to weaken the country’s resolve as winter sets in. Moscow has relied on ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones, taking advantage of Ukraine’s shortage of U.S.-made Patriot interceptors.
Ukraine, meanwhile, has escalated its drone strikes on Russian oil refineries.

title: Dreams, desks and selfies: Newly elected members of Congress learn their way around
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack, a community organizer who stunned her own Democratic Party by defeating a well-know North Carolina Republican on her shoestring $56,000 campaign budget, said she’s excited to arrive in Washington and show what’s possible.
Rep.-elect Brian Poindexter said his win over incumbent GOP Rep. Max Miller ensures Ohio remains a very swing state.
And Rebecca Bennett, a former Navy helicopter pilot in New Jersey who said she’s spent her whole life “trying to find the biggest, hardest problem to throw myself at,” was ready to give Congress a try. “There’s always the unknown.”
They were among more than 100 newly elected members of Congress arriving in Washington this week for the start of freshmen orientation — the crush of new Democrats, many bringing a new sense of urgency after the party’s sweep of the midterm elections, and the slim new class of freshmen Republicans.
“People were just looking for somebody who’s going to listen to them,” said Womack, who said she won by simply showing up and talking with voters.
“I’m a single mom and so I know what it’s like to have to live on a budget and figure out how am I going to feed my family,” she said. “And that’s what people want to fight for them in Washington right now.”
New-member orientation creates an unusual mash-up on Capitol Hill, as the newcomers are arriving and the exiting lawmakers begin to clear out, all in preparation for the peaceful transfer of power on Jan. 3, when lawmakers are sworn in and the new Congress begins.
This week’s orientation includes training sessions and ritzy receptions for the newcomers, and for the defeated or retirees it’s the start of figuring out what’s next. Briefing rooms are filled with information about office set up, payroll and benefits, and there’s a room to take officials portraits.
It’s also the time for the House and Senate to hold internal party elections for their new leaders, ahead of a public vote in January for the speaker of the House.
“I’m looking forward to learning as much as I can and being the best representative I can be for my district,” said Poindexter as he arrived at the nearby Navy Yard hotel where lawmakers are temporarily housed.
Selfies, besties and tough votes ahead
The Capitol was a changed place as the members-elect started meeting up with their colleagues and getting to know their way around the place.
Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan was swarmed by young people in the Capitol basement, taking pictures with the progressive star who is also the first Muslim in the Senate.
Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico paid a visit to the outgoing Texas Republican Sen. John Cornyn, who lost his own primary for reelection when President Donald Trump backed his rival, Ken Paxton, who was defeated.
“I’m so grateful for his advice and his guidance as I try to fill his big shoes,” Talarico said of Cornyn as he walked through the Senate between orientation events. He said he wants to meet with Republican Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas as well.
And Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton of Illinois snapped a photo with new Democratic senators-elect including Talarico, El-Sayed, Annie Andrews, Roy Cooper, Peggy Flanagan, Josh Turek and others.
“First Freshmen Senator selfie! Couldn’t ask for a better team,” she posted as the caption.
Among them was former Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, who defeated Republican Sen. Jon Husted, a Trump-backed favorite, for a comeback. Brown was in the Senate for 18 years before he lost two years ago to GOP Sen. Bernie Moreno, but he still joined his freshmen colleagues for their orientation.
“I’ve actually learned some things,” said Brown, who was celebrating his 74th birthday on Monday. “I’ve gotten to know my colleagues.”
Leadership elections test the new members
One of the first decisions the incoming lawmakers will make happens even before they’re sworn into office, as they huddle with their parties in private meetings to choose House and Senate leadership.
Congressional offices are being bombarded with phone calls and social media messages pushing Democrats to dump their current choices – House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer – in favor of a fresh start.
Jeffries scoffed when questioned Monday if he had support— the typically low-key leader flashing confidence he would have the votes. He is on track to make history as the nation’s first Black American to become speaker of the House.
Progressive lawmakers, in particular, are agitating for change reflective of voters’ sweeping turnout for Democrats, especially in the Senate.
Sen.-elect Chris Pappas, D-N.H. — who was darting back and forth between his day job as an outgoing member of the House and his new one as an incoming senator — said their class is “a new generation of leadership that wants to do things differently and shake up Washington.”
He said he wants to meet with Schumer and will later decide who he will support, if anyone challenges him.
Republicans will also choose their new leaders after House Speaker Mike Johnson decided to step aside following the party’s election defeat. Tuesday’s closed-door race between the No. 2 Republican Rep. Steve Scalise of Louisiana and Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan is a repeat of the contest in 2023, before Johnson rose to power.
Rep. Richard Hudson, the House GOP campaign chairman who lost his own reelection bid in North Carolina, hesitated to assess the outcome.
Besides, he said, he doesn’t have a vote in the matter — the exiting lawmakers are blocked from the GOP meeting.
A diverse new class arrives
As the week began, the House Chaplain Margaret Kibben opened Monday’s session with a prayer, “some of us enjoying victories and others enduring disheartening defeats.”
On the Democratic side, the new Congress will see many milestones – Flanagan will be the first Native American female U.S. senator, Pappas the first gay male senator, and more.
Rep. Suzan DelBene, the House Democrats campaign chief, called the party’s candidates “all very unique.”
“We had firefighters, ministers, mayors, veterans, teachers, farmers, prosecutors, union leaders, law enforcement, doctors, journalists and even a Grammy-award winning musician,” she said earlier.
“They understand that their job title is representative, not rubber stamp.”
Johnson, the outgoing speaker, hosted a reception in the Capitol’s stately Statuary Hall for the House Republicans, whose shrinking numbers left the party lopsided, their minority made up of mostly white men.

title: LIV Golf files bankruptcy plan and sets sight on January liquidation
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(AP) - LIV Golf filed a Chapter 11 bankruptcy plan with a New Jersey court Tuesday, along with a proposed schedule for a final hearing on its disclosure statement on Jan. 7 that would begin liquidation.
LIV Golf filed for bankruptcy on Sept. 8 after the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia, which had bankrolled the breakaway league from the start, said a change in strategy meant it would no longer pay for LIV after the 2026 season.
The bankruptcy plan is for an orderly wind down of LIV. The restructuring agreement with BC Partners Credit, which had pledged $300 million, failed to garner enough support for a LIV 2.0 version that would have kept the league going in 2027.
“Debtors have determined that no viable restructuring transaction remains available due to lack of player participation and BC Partners’ termination of the Restructuring Support Agreement,” LIV said in a summary of the bankruptcy plan.
It said PIF invested approximately $5 billion in equity capital and that LIV Golf continually operated at a loss and was years away from profitability. The filing also revealed LIF laid off 289 employees and furloughed 22 others roughly a week before filing for bankruptcy.
This was about a month after it finished paying $15.6 million in retention bonuses to seven executives LIV said was essential to finishing the 2026 season and making plans for restructuring.
A hearing is scheduled for Nov. 24 to conditionally approve the disclosure statement, which requires adequate information for those to whom LIV owes money and begins the wind-down phase of LIV operations.
The six weeks in between the Jan. 7 hearing to approve the statement are to determine voting rights and take any objections from those who have claims. A wind-down trust would oversee payments to creditors, resolve legal claims and handle other financial matters.
The judge last week approved Jon Rahm’s separation from LIV, which cost the two-time major champion a reported $100 million he was owed from when he joined the Saudi-funded league at the end of 2023. Rahm won last week in Abu Dhabi for his first regular European tour title since 2022.
The other LIV players, who have been banned by the PGA Tour, now must figure out where to play. Some have European tour membership or can try to get sponsor exemptions to tournaments, though not the strongest events on the schedule.
The PGA Tour has not indicated a path back for players and likely won’t until the bankruptcy proceedings are over.

title: NYC sightseeing helicopter makes emergency landing after reporting possible engine trouble
text:
BAYONNE, N.J. (AP) — A New York City sightseeing helicopter on a maintenance flight made an emergency landing on Tuesday at a New Jersey cargo port after the pilot reported possible engine trouble.
Two people were aboard the Bell 206L-4 helicopter when it came down on a road at the Port Jersey Marine Terminal in Bayonne, across the Hudson River from Manhattan, around 8:55 a.m., the Federal Aviation Administration said.
No injuries were reported, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey said. Messages seeking comment were left for the helicopter’s operator, FlyNYON.
Video of the scene shows part of the helicopter’s tail sitting on the road about 30 feet (9 meters) from the aircraft, which was manufactured in 1999, according to FAA records.
In a recording of the air traffic control audio, the pilot can be heard saying, “mayday, mayday, mayday” and “we need to land outside of the airport.” The helicopter landed several minutes later, just outside of the container terminal, the Port Authority said.
Last year, a Bell 206L-4 sightseeing helicopter plummeted into the Hudson River, killing all 6 people on board. The National Transportation Safety Board said the remains of several geese were found on the helicopter, suggesting it may have struck several birds before crashing.
Last week, the U.S. Department of Transportation’s Office of Inspector General announced an audit of sightseeing helicopter regulations, citing “longstanding concerns regarding the industry’s safety and whether the current regulatory framework provides adequate safeguards.”
Since 2008, there have been at least 58 helicopter crashes involving tourist helicopters in the U.S., including 11 that were fatal, Assistant Inspector General Marshall Jackson said.

title: Jimmy Carter's family farm to be preserved and opened to the public
text:
The family farm where President Jimmy Carter tended peanuts, corn and sugarcane as a boy and later returned throughout his life will be preserved and opened to the public.
Preservation group The Conservation Fund said Monday that it has acquired the farm as part of a 2,458-acre (995-hectare) purchase. The farm is just outside Plains, Georgia, the 39th president’s hometown. Carter spent his youth exploring the woods around the farm and returned many times as an adult to walk with his wife Rosalynn and hunt, the fund said.
Near the end of his life, Carter, who died in 2024 at 100, returned to the farm for one final fishing trip to its pond. Rosalynn Carter died in 2023.
“For our family, this land was always about more than a farm. It was home — a place my grandparents treasured. We’re grateful to The Conservation Fund and to everyone working to make sure it’s protected for generations to come,” Jason Carter, a grandson of the Carters, said in a statement.
The farm should be open to the public for hunting, fishing and outdoor recreation as soon as next year, The Conservation Fund said. The fund said it plans to transfer the land to the Georgia Department of Natural Resources the following year. The purchase price was $8.5 million, The Washington Post reported.
The family kept a stand of mature longleaf pines at the farm at Carter’s request, The Conservation Fund said. One of his final decisions about the property was to replant much of it with young longleaf pines, the fund said.
The replanting effort means the property is a natural fit to expand Georgia’s Lanahassee Creek Wildlife Management Area, which will grow to almost 7,000 acres (2,833 hectares), the fund said. The Plains area is also home to Jimmy Carter National Historical Park, which includes Carter’s boyhood home.
“Long before Jimmy Carter protected millions of acres across America, he was a boy working the fields and roaming the woods of southwest Georgia,” said Stacy Funderburke, vice president of the central Southeast region at The Conservation Fund. “This land shaped him and his legacy, and he never stopped coming home to it. We’re honored to help ensure this land remains healthy habitat for wildlife, and we look forward to the day it is open to everyone who wants to experience it.”

title: Husson women’s soccer prepares for NCAA Tournament run
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Husson won its sixth NAC women’s soccer championship in team history when the Eagles defeated Lesley, 2-0, on Saturday.
Husson has earned a trip to the NCAA Tournament by winning the conference title.
They’ll be facing No. 3 Tufts on Saturday at 11 a.m. at Vassar College in Poughkeepsie, N.Y.
“It was really exciting to be back. We were there in 2024, and a lot of us remember it. We’re just really excited to be a part of it again,” said Thea Gerfen, redshirt sophomore defender.
“We worked really hard to bond as a team this year. (We) put our heads down and just grinded it out to get to where we are today,” said Hailey Tarbox, junior midfielder.
“It’s always such a crazy feeling to hear Husson’s name being called out, and I think that being able to play a team like Tufts is going to be very, very fun. It’s going to challenge us a lot, but I think that we definitely have the people to give them a good fight,” said Marila Corletto, fifth year midfielder.
The Colby Mules also made the NCAA Tournament after their 2-1 double-overtime loss to Middlebury in the NESCAC Championship.
Colby will face Mary Washington on Saturday at 1:30 p.m. at The College of New Jersey.
