title: Rock & Roll Hall of Fame 2026: Who will perform, who will skip the ceremony and what to expect
text:
The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame ceremony is this weekend. Here's who's getting in, and who's honoring them?
Billy Idol, Oasis, Wu-Tang Clan, Phil Collins, Sade, Queen Latifah, Iron Maiden, Joy Division/New Order and the late Luther Vandross will be inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame on Saturday.
That's been established since the announcement six months ago. But not much has been revealed about who will show up, who will perform, who will induct them, and who will give musical tributes to the new members.
Related previous coverage in the video player above: New Edition snubbed from Rock & Roll Hall of Fame
Fans learned Monday that Oasis will be a no-show. Iron Maiden previously revealed they won't be there either. A few more answers are likely to trickle out this week, but the Rock Hall likes to keep most of the show a surprise.
For the second straight year, the ceremony that moves between Cleveland, New York and Los Angeles will be held at the Peacock Theater in downtown LA. After two years of streaming it live, the Rock Hall is returning to its previous model, where the public won't see it until an edited version airs in December.
The list of 2026 honorees also includes MC Lyte, Celia Cruz, Fela Kuti and Gram Parsons, along with music producers Rick Rubin, Linda Creed, Arif Mardin and Jimmy Miller and variety show host Ed Sullivan.
Here's a closer look at the nominees and what we know about the show.
Performer inductees
Eight of this year's inductees came in through the main entrance — the performer category. A nominating committee put them up for a vote from more than 1,200 people, including music industry figures and historians. Artists become eligible for the hall 25 years after their first music release, but it can take much longer for them to be nominated.
Phil Collins
The 75-year-old English singer, songwriter and drummer is already in the hall as a member of Genesis and now gets in again for a solo career that brought some of the biggest hits of the 1980s.
The eight-time Grammy winner got in with his first solo nomination and had been eligible since 2006.
Will he perform? No. Collins has said the health problems that have kept him off the stage since 2022 will keep him from performing Saturday. It’s not clear whether he’ll appear to accept the honor.
Key songs: “In the Air Tonight,” “Against All Odds,” “One More Night,” “You'll Be in My Heart,”
Billy Idol
The 70-year-old punk-coded English rock singer had also been eligible for the hall since 2006, and voters put him in after his second nomination.
Will he perform? Yes. Idol, who toured the US in summer and had a residency in Las Vegas, plans to play and says he’s going to “bring it” when he does.
Key songs: “Dancing With Myself,” “White Wedding,” “Rebel Yell,” “Eyes Without a Face.”
Wu-Tang Clan
The epic hip-hop coalition from Staten Island — made up of RZA, GZA, Method Man, Raekwon, Ghostface Killah, Inspectah Deck, U-God, Masta Killa and previously, the late Ol’ Dirty Bastard — got into the hall with their first nomination. They had been eligible since 2017.
They've been hip-hop innovators since their 1993 debut album, “Enter the Wu-Tang.”
Will they perform? Maybe. They toured together just last year on what was billed as a farewell tour.
Key songs: “C.R.E.A.M.,” “Protect Ya Neck,” “Wu-Tang Clan Ain’t Nuthing Ta F’ Wit,” “Gravel Pit.”
Oasis
The famously feuding brothers of Brit pop, Noel and Liam Gallagher, enter the hall with their second nomination. They've been eligible since 2019. At 54, Liam Gallagher is the youngest inductee of the class of 2026. They enter the hall a year after a reunion tour that brought them back together for the first time in 16 years and they've announced they'll do it again next year.
Will they perform? No. Noel Gallagher has announced a solo set at a London jazz festival on Saturday. And Rolling Stone reports that his little brother, who has sneered at the idea of the hall since becoming eligible for it, won't be there either.
Key Songs: “Wonderwall,” “Live Forever,” “Don’t Look Back in Anger,” “Champagne Supernova.”
Joy Division and New Order
The two British rock bands will get a rare joint nomination that makes sense given their members and circumstances.
Joy Division was a dark and seminal post-punk band formed in 1976. When their charismatic lead singer, Ian Curtis, died in 1980, the remaining members formed New Order, which went in the direction of electronic and dance music.
Will they perform? Maybe. Bassist and key member of both bands, Peter Hook, has been estranged from his mates for many years. Whether they'll bury the hatchet for a moment is one of the night's biggest questions.
They had been eligible since 2003 and got in with their third nomination.
Key songs: “Love Will Tear Us Apart,” “Disorder,” “Blue Monday,” “Bizarre Love Triangle.”
Iron Maiden
The scorching rock band who led the new wave of British heavy metal starting in the late 1970s got an induction that many thought was long overdue.
Will they perform? No. Iron Maiden are together and thriving, but so much so that they’re on tour in Australia and won’t be appearing to accept or to play.
Voters installed them on their third nomination. They'd been eligible since 2005.
Key songs: “The Trooper,” “Fear of the Dark,” “Run to the Hills,” “Aces High.”
Luther Vandross
The love songs of Luther Vandross, delivered with a voice of velvet, made him one of the definitive R&B singers of his era.
The solo career of the New Jersey-born Vandross began in the early 1980s, and he went on to win eight Grammys and have 11 consecutive platinum albums.
He was also a songwriter, producer and one of pop music's great collaborators with artists including Rock Hall members David Bowie and Aretha Franklin.
Vandross was 54 when he died in 2005.
He's been eligible since the year after his death, but did not get a nomination until this year, and was voted in on the first ballot.
Key songs: “Never Too Much,” “Dance With My Father,” “I'd Rather,” “Here and Now.”
Sade
First, a head-scratching fact that even big fans may not know. Sade is the name of the band. For real. It is also the first name of its Nigeria-born, England-raised lead singer Sade Adu, making many think she's a solo act.
But she'll be inducted along with the members of her band, who entranced audiences with their blend of jazz, smooth-and-sultry R&B and sophisti-pop when they launched in Britain in the mid-1980s.
Will they perform? Maybe. And it’ll be momentous if they do. Adu is famously media-shy and the band hasn't played on stage since 2011.
Key songs: “Smooth Operator,” “No Ordinary Love,” “Like a Tattoo,” “Kiss of Life”
Early influencers
Some inductees are brought in through a sort of side door, getting awards handed out by committees. But they're still considered full-fledged hall members. Rubin and the other three producer-inductees are all recipients of the Musical Excellence Award. Sullivan is getting the Ahmet Ertegun Award for nonmusicians.
And the following five artists are getting in by receiving the Early Influence Award.
Queen Latifah
The 56-year-old New Jersey-born Queen Latifah achieved unprecedented success for a female rapper, becoming a star at age 19 with the release of her 1989 album “All Hail the Queen” and the single “Ladies First.”
She later became known more for her acting in film and television, including a role in “Chicago” that got her an Oscar nomination.
Will she perform? Probably. It hasn't been made official, but all signs point to yes.
Key songs: “U.N.I.T.Y.,” “Ladies First,” “When You're Good to Mama.”
MC Lyte
About two years before Latifah in nearby Brooklyn, MC Lyte did her own trailblazing, becoming the first female rapper to release a full solo album, “Lyte as a Rock.”
Her hard-edged rhymes brought a political consciousness that was growing in hip-hop at the time.
Will she perform? Almost certainly. The 56-year-old has been doing a “Road to the Hall” concert tour in the run-up to the ceremony.
Key songs: “Keep on Keepin' On,” “Cold Rock a Party,” “Ruffneck.”
Celia Cruz
The queen of salsa and innovator and spreader of Afro-Cuban sounds and one of the most popular Latin artists of the 20th century, the Havana-born singer Cruz becomes the first member of the Hall of Fame who sang primarily in Spanish.
She was 77 when she died in 2003.
Key songs: “Vasos Vacíos,” “La Vida Es Un Carnaval,” “El Último Adiós.”
Fela Kútì
The Nigerian saxophonist, bandleader, progenitor and activist who died in 1997 at age 58 becomes the first African-born artist to enter the Hall of Fame in the same year he became the first African artist to receive the Grammys' Lifetime Achievement Award.
He was born in 1938 in colonial Nigeria. His music career, which spanned the late 1950s up to the 1990s, is a signature blend of high-octane horn, jazz, and funk with Yoruba rhythms.
Key songs: “Water No Get Enemy,” “Zombie,” “Let's Start.”
Gram Parsons
Arguably the most important figure in rock's turn toward country in the late 1960s and early '70s, Parsons joined the Byrds for their very country “Sweetheart of the Rodeo,” was a founding member of the Flying Burrito Brothers, and made a pair of solo records where he duetted with a folk singer he discovered named Emmylou Harris, launching her storied country career.
He was 26 when he died in 1973.
Key songs: “Hickory Wind,” “Love Hurts,” “Return of the Grievous Angel.”

title: Andersson: Wiscasset’s cost per student not in ‘outer space’ for region
text:
Richmond's the outlier, Wiscasset Superintendent of Schools Dr. Kim Andersson told selectmen and her other fellow residents Oct. 6. She was addressing recent months' public comments comparing Wiscasset's per student cost to Richmond's.
By outlier, Andersson was referring to Richmond's being lower than not just Wiscasset's, but Boothbay-Boothbay Harbor Community School District's and Bath-based Regional School Unit 1's, too.
“Over the past few months, there have been many public comments about the cost per student of Wiscasset schools compared to other area schools, and often with Richmond, with Richmond being identified as something we should (aspire) to be. And that Wiscasset was somehow in outer space with our cost per student.”
Then Andersson said she just wanted to share some information “that dispels that notion.”
Andersson said, for fiscal year 2024-25, the most recent one on Maine Department of Education’s data dashboard, Richmond's per student cost was $18,412, “which is indeed very low”; Boothbay-Boothbay Harbor CSD's, $27,320; RSU 1's, $25,424; and Wiscasset's, $25,060.
“And I just wanted to get that out there because, while we are often compared to Richmond, I want it to be very clear that Richmond is in fact an outlier," Andersson said in the selectboard meeting's public comment period.
Nov. 3, voters consider the school department's third try at a 2026-27 school budget.
After the second try lost Sept. 1, Andersson also addressed the Richmond-Wiscasset comparison. She told the school committee she went through Richmond's school budget line by line and found its special education budget is more than $1 million less than Wiscasset's. She explained, Richmond has fewer out-of-district placements. And she said Richmond budgets about half a million dollars less for facilities than Wiscasset does. School committee member Doug Merrill said Richmond's facilities are "much newer."
Andersson said at the time, if the school budget process does not keep being repeated multiple times a year, she "could see a future where my position might be able to scale down to three or three and a half days a week." Richmond's superintendent is contracted for three days a week, she said.
Also Oct. 6, selectmen nodded tapping the Larrabee Fund for $110,100 for the school department's band program: $78,280 for a band director's salary and benefits; $920 for music books; $4,040 for dues and fees; $3,060 for transportation to district and all-state competitions; $3,700 for instrument repairs and contracted services; and $20,000 for instruments.
Resident Steve Christiansen said he thought the Fund was for band equipment and functions, not a band director's salary. Town Manager Dennis Simmons said the fund states it is to be used for the maintenance of a band. "That's all it said." He ran it by the town attorney last year, when the director's pay was also included in the request. "And the attorney says, 'It says maintenance of a band; you can't have a band if you don't have a band instructor.'"
Simmons added, "'Maintenance' is pretty ambiguous, so there's a lot of room for interpretation in that."
Selectmen nodded this year's request, 5-0.

title: GOP lawmaker introduces articles of impeachment against Hegseth
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) introduced eight articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth Monday, the first day of the U.S. House session after the midterm elections.
Massie mentioned Hegseth’s role in military actions in Venezuela and Yemen, but the main focus of the impeachment resolution is Hegseth’s handling of the war with Iran.
“We’re not indicting him for being bad at his job. In fact, he was very effective at killing school children in Iran. He was very effective at extrajudicial killings,” Massie said during a press conference outside the Capitol building. “There’s no argument in these impeachment articles that he’s ineffective. The argument here is that he’s broken laws and he’s violated the Constitution.”
Massie previously attempted to impeach Hegseth in September. House Speaker Mike Johnson sent lawmakers home early to avoid the vote.
Johnson could do something similar this week, but Massie is pushing for Johnson to bring the resolution to the floor.
“We’re still in the majority,” he said. “They can still do the right thing.”
If there is a vote on the resolution, Democrats would likely support it. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said he is a “hard yes.”
“Pete Hegseth has abused his power, undermined America’s national security, and he’s the architect of the reckless and costly failed war of choice in Iran,” Jeffries said Monday.
Massie, an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump, was defeated in May by Trump-endorsed primary challenger Ed Gallrein.
Trump responded to the impeachment call during an impromptu press briefing at the White House Monday. He said he would stand by Hegseth and called on Congress to do the same.
“Massie is a loser,” Trump told reporters. “He shouldn’t be taking up the time of Congress or the Senate or anything that he’s doing. The guy’s a stone-cold loser.”
Hegseth will likely respond Tuesday morning, when he’s scheduled to hold a press briefing at the Pentagon. It will be his first in more than 180 days.

title: Obituary: Byron S. “Bud” Philbrick Jr.
text:
WILTON – Byron S. “Bud” Philbrick Jr., 87, of Wilton, Maine, passed away on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. Bud was born on April 10, 1939, in Freeman Township, the son of Byron S. Philbrick Sr. and Clara (Thompson) Philbrick. He was raised in Kingfield, where he excelled on the basketball court and graduated from Kingfield High School with the Class of 1957.
Following high school, Bud proudly served his country in the United States Army from 1959 to 1965 as a photographer. He completed Airborne Paratrooper training at Fort Benning, Georgia. During his military service, he was stationed in Germany, Iceland, and Alabama, gaining experiences and memories that remained meaningful throughout his life.
After returning to Maine, Bud built a successful career as an automobile salesman, working for many years at dealerships throughout the Farmington and Skowhegan areas. He was known for his friendly personality and ability to connect with people.
Bud was a devoted member of the Benevolent and Protective Order of Elks for many years. His dedication to the organization earned him numerous honors as he served as Exalted Ruler, District Deputy and served on committees of the Maine Elks Association. His commitment to community service and fellowship left a lasting impact on many fellow Elks throughout the state.
Bud enjoyed an active and fulfilling life. He loved playing and officiating sports, dancing, and reading. He cherished time with family and friends and was always ready to share a story, a laugh, or words of encouragement.
He is survived by his loving companion, Candace Clark; his children, Stephanie Philbrick and her husband, Maurice Dubreuil, of Bowdoin; Byron Philbrick III and his wife, Ginny, of Durham; and Casey Philbrick and her companion, Jay Roy, of Standish. He is also survived by his siblings, Louise Lovejoy of Kingfield; Verna Sepe of Florida and Rhode Island; Sandra Niemi and her companion, Dennis, of Florida; and Rodney Philbrick and his wife, June, of Florida; as well as many beloved nieces, nephews, extended family members, and dear friends.
He was predeceased by his parents, Byron S. Philbrick Sr. and Clara (Thompson) Philbrick; his daughter, Valerie Philbrick; and his brothers-in-law, Richard Lovejoy, Luke Sepe, and Lawrence Niemi.
Bud will be remembered for his warmth, quick wit, unwavering dedication to his family, and the friendships he built throughout his life. His legacy of service, kindness, and love will continue to live on in all who knew him. Funeral and memorial service information will be announced at a later date.
Arrangements are under the care of Dan & Scott’s Cremation & Funeral Service, 488 Farmington Falls Rd., Farmington, Maine, where memories, photos and condolences may be shared at http://www.dsfuneral.com

title: Air Force veteran helps service members navigate life after the military
text:
Air Force veteran helps service members navigate life after the military
Heading into Veterans Day, Federal VA data shows Maine has one of the highest rates of veteran suicide in the country.
The struggles service members face after leaving the military continue to show up in statistics, with more than 50 Maine veterans dying by suicide in 2024.
Air Force Veteran Christina Kang is helping other veterans who are navigating life after military service. She's working on the Warrior PATHH Program, which she once enrolled in when she says she was struggling.
"My life has definitely changed in a positive way," Kang said. "I still experience a lot of struggles, you know, I'm still human, I still make a lot of mistakes, but I've really learned how to have these new practices that give myself grace and compassion and understanding."
The Warrior PATHH Program helps veterans nationwide learn how to thrive after facing trauma. In Maine, veterans can participate in the program through the Travis Mills Foundation. Kang says the guides running the program are all peers who have experienced similar situations.
"Taking that first step of admittance takes a lot of courage and bravery," Kang said. "I'm very thankful to look back and have people, my support system, who made it feel safe for me to say, 'Hey, I'm struggling.'"
The Warrior PATHH program is one of many services available to Maine veterans seeking help and a resource to remember heading into the federal holiday.
Veterans in Maine who are seeking mental health support can connect with the VA Maine Healthcare System through the Togus VA Medical Center in Augusta, community-based outpatient clinics and Vet Centers across the state.
Sweetser also offers adult behavioral health support and works with community partners, including the VA, to coordinate care for uniformed service members and veterans.
Those who are in need of crisis support can contact the Veterans Crisis Line by calling 988 and pressing 1, texting 838255, or chatting online at VeteransCrisisLine.net/Chat. The Veterans Crisis Line is available 24/7, and you do not have to be enrolled in VA healthcare to reach out.

title: Trojans fall to Old Town in 8-man North Regional Championship
text:
OLD TOWN — The 2026 MDI High School football season came to an end on Saturday, Nov. 7, when the Trojans fell to Old Town 56-6 in the 8-man Northern Maine Regional Final.
The setting for the contest was almost certainly described on a number of separate occasions by spectators and participants alike as “football weather,” with sheets of chilly rain before and during the game turning the field into a mud pit. The Trojans were perhaps hoping that nature would turn the dial up even farther, however, as they would have welcomed any help slowing down Old Town’s explosive offense — a unit that had averaged a little over 51 points per game during the team’s 8-1 regular season, plus the Coyote’s 60-2 playoff win over Houlton the week prior.

title: Chellie Pingree says ICE is beefing up security at its Scarborough office
text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has deployed more personnel to its Scarborough field office, according to U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree. She said it appears to be in response to protests outside the building.
A group of people have staked out the ICE office for months in an effort to track the agency’s operations, and on Monday, they reported the arrival of several new agents and vehicles, including an armored truck.
An ICE spokesperson declined to share specifics, but Pingree said in a statement Monday that ICE cited the “growing number of protestors — and armed protestors specifically — as a reason for deploying more personnel to the facility.”
The Maine Immigrants’ Rights Coalition added in its own statement that it appears the new officers are assigned to “building security, not immigration enforcement activity.”
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.

title: Average price of gas falls below $4 a gallon across the US
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(CNN) - The average price of gas is now below $4 a gallon.
According to AAA, the national average is $3.98.
Although the number doesn’t mean anything specific economically, $4 acts as a psychological threshold for gas prices. Falling below that makes the price seem much cheaper.
Prices are trending down primarily due to falling demand caused by the end of summer driving and the return to standard time.
Long term, gas prices still face serious headwinds. Fighting in Russia and the Middle East has damaged refineries there.
Many in the United States will have to go offline in the near future for maintenance.
They’ve been deferring maintenance this year to keep supplies steady.

title: French speakers gather at UMA for annual immersion weekend
text:
Annual event gives students, educators and heritage speakers a chance to connect through a shared language
AUGUSTA — French speakers from across Maine gathered at the University of Maine at Augusta on Saturday, Nov. 7, for a day of conversation, cultural activities and workshops conducted entirely in French.
The university’s annual French Immersion Weekend welcomed more than 65 participants, with 15 workshop leaders guiding the activities, bringing together a diverse group of high school and college students, community members, French teachers and speakers from various parts of the Francophone world, including Mali and the Democratic Republic of Congo, North America, France and Cambodia. Registration reached capacity before the event, with additional participants joining a waitlist.
The program gives people of different ages, backgrounds and levels of experience an opportunity to speak French outside the classroom. For students learning the language, it offers a chance to practice with experienced speakers. For those who grew up speaking French, it provides an opportunity to share their language and connect with others who speak it.
The weekend began Friday, Nov. 6, with a free public performance by Crocodile River in UMA’s Farber Forum. The performance featured music and dance from African countries, followed by a question-and-answer session with the audience. On Saturday, participants experienced these dances in a different way, through a step-by-step dance lesson that featured rhythmic and energetic moves.
Saturday’s program also featured interactive workshops and discussions exploring French language and culture in Maine and around the world. Workshop highlights included: a Congolese beignets workshop, where participants got to reminisce about their own childhood favorite foods; a folklore music workshop that included songs from Acadia, Louisiana, and Quebec; a presentation that highlighted Francophonie in Cambodia; and French students from the University of Western Brittany giving their perspective on the current protests by young people in France.
“French is an important part of Maine’s history, but it’s also a language that people across the state continue to speak and learn today,” Chelsea Ray, a professor of French language and literature at UMA and the coordinator of the event, said. “This weekend gives people a chance to use French in a setting where everyone is encouraged to participate, whether they’ve been speaking it their whole lives or are still learning. We especially want to welcome new Mainers who bring French from their country, such as the Democratic Republic of Congo. It is a richness that we can all share.”
The French Immersion Weekend is organized by Ray, Nathalie Gorey, president of the Maine chapter of the American Association of Teachers of French, and a committee of French educators. The event is sponsored by French at UMA and the Maine chapter of the American Association of Teachers of French.
The annual program provides opportunities for students, educators and community members to practice French while exploring the language’s place in Maine’s Franco-American heritage and the cultures of French-speaking communities around the world.
Reflecting on the weekend, Ray described the importance of learning other languages, “Language teaches us that it is all part of one story: the human story. We have more in common than you think. The struggles and efforts of the previous generations are within us, as well as their triumphs. We are standing on their shoulders. We pay it forward when we learn the language and culture of someone else. Without directly saying it, we communicate: I see you. I value you and I want to learn more about your life and who you are.”
UMA offers French language courses, minors and a certificate for students interested in studying the language and its cultures.
For more information about French at UMA and future immersion events, visit uma.edu/frenchimmersion.

title: Good Samaritan breaks window to free 3-year-old girl from car sinking in pond
text:
ST. PETERS, Mo. (KMOV/Gray News) - A Missouri mother is extremely grateful to a good Samaritan who rescued her 3-year-old daughter after the family’s SUV rolled into a pond.
Austin Collins was dropping his kids off at a school bus stop Thursday morning in St. Peters when he saw an SUV roll from a parking lot, down a hill and into a pond. A 3-year-old girl named Melody was inside at the time.
“I just saw a big ol’ splash, and immediately, everyone just ran over and took action,” Collins said.
He called 911 then jumped into the pond to help the toddler.
“I was honestly holding onto the vehicle to stay afloat,” Collins said. “I didn’t know how deep it was at the time.”
Collins said someone handed him a hammer, and he used it to break a window to free Melody. He cut his hand on the broken glass in the process.
“I knew that as soon as I grabbed the little girl, she would potentially get cut,” he said. “So, I ended up just taking my hand and clearing as much glass as I could before I grabbed her.”
Mom thankful her little girl is still alive
Melody’s mother, Megan Kohlhaas, was helping her other kids get on the bus when the incident happened.
“So, I’m just waving bye to them, making sure he gets on the bus, and next thing, I know, the kids are all screaming, ‘The car! The car!’ And it just rolls backwards,” Kohlhaas said.
She said the quick response from others helped save her daughter’s life.
“Even just finding the hammer and how fast someone was able to pass it on to someone in the water and break in and that we had that time is just a miracle,” she said.
Kohlhaas said she is thankful Melody is still alive.
“I’m just thankful she’s alive, and I can’t stop thinking about the man and all the people that helped,” Kohlhaas said. “Without him, we would’ve lost her.”
Collins credited Kohlhaas for how the group responded.
“Kudos to the mom. She definitely created that urgency early on so that we all could pull together,” he said. “It really outlines what we can do as a community when somebody is in need: we just all pull together.”
Melody is doing just fine after the incident. A GoFundMe has been created to help Kohlhaas replace her car.
Information from investigators on why the SUV was able to roll away is pending.

title: Rep. Jim Jordan elected new House GOP leader
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) will be the next House Minority Leader after House Republicans voted to pick new leadership, one week after voters returned the majority to Democrats.
Jordan defeated Rep. Steve Scalise (R-La.), the current House Majority Leader and #2 Republican, 106 to 73.
“Democrats offer more government, we offer more freedom,” Jordan said.
The Republican caucus is down 30 seats, and the number could grow. Fourteen races have yet to be called.
Rep. Kat Cammack (R-Fla.) described what she is looking for in a leader.
“Someone who is really going to be highlighting the stark differences and the vision that Republicans have vs. Democrats and the stark differences about how we navigate not just the next two years, but the next 10,” Cammack said.
Jordan is chair of the House Judiciary Committee. As minority leader, he will lead House Republicans as Democrats have promised investigations into the Trump administration.
This is Jordan’s third attempt to lead his party in the House. He tried and failed in 2018 and again in 2023.
Jordan begins his tenure as leader Jan. 3, 2027.

title: Men’s Club Soccer Overcomes Financial Hurdles to Compete in National Championship in Florida
text:
After a successful season, for the first time in history, Bates Men’s Club Soccer qualified to compete in the U.S. College Club Soccer (UCCSC) National Championship in Bradenton, Fla. Aside from the talent on the field with experienced seniors, an eager freshman class, and former Bates varsity soccer players, the team’s organizational structure and chemistry contributed to an exceptional season.
In addition to this being the first time the Bobcats have made the tournament, this is their first season in the UCCSC New England North Division, where they formally competed in the National Intramural-Recreational Sports Association (NIRSA). Given strong past season performances, the Bobcats were invited among other colleges to compete in UCCSC New England North as this would give them the opportunity to contend in a more competitive league and qualify for a national championship.
The Bobcats finished third overall in their conference’s standings with notable wins, specifically beating Colby College 1-0 on Oct. 24.
“Our 1-0 win against Colby was the biggest result for us,” Club President Kelyn Kiezca ‘27 said. “They were at the top of the table, so by beating them, we essentially secured a spot at nationals.”
However, despite the excitement of clinching a tournament spot and the opportunity to travel to Florida, financial obstacles threatened to derail the team’s plans.
“Club sports are student-led organizations supported through a combination of department funding, fundraising, and student contributions when applicable,” said Mike Milliken, manager of Community Well-Being and Coordinator of Club Sports. “Because national championship opportunities and associated travel expenses vary from year to year, these costs are not typically included in annual funding allocations.”
This presented a substantial obstacle for the team.
“Mike Milliken told us we need to raise $25,000 for nationals, and we had a week and a half to fundraise,” Kiezca said.
Faced with a short timeline, the team began exploring ways to raise the necessary funds and make the trip possible.
“We’d heard, originally, at the start of the season, that there’s a chance we might not be able to go,” said Kiezca. “But it was something that everyone on the team wanted…[and] we really pushed for it.”
Kiezca stated that the team had taken a strong initiative to keep in contact with Milliken, Athletics, and Campus Life. The team also created a GoFundMe to support the trip and spoke to alumni that provided generous contributions.
“Recognizing the significance of this opportunity, Athletics worked with the team to identify solutions that would make participation more financially accessible,” Milliken said. “Through team fundraising, student contributions, and direct financial support from the Athletics budget, we were able to help make this experience possible.”
“It wouldn’t have been possible without any one of those groups of people,” said Kiezca.
As club president, Kiezca serves as the team’s primary liaison with Athletics, oversees scheduling and financial logistics, and helps coach the team, while also playing on the field.
Kiezca said the team operates without a designated coach, with more experienced players taking on coaching opportunities. With the possibility of traveling to nationals in sight, Kiezca took on a greater role in ensuring this would happen.
“It’s been the craziest week of my life,” he said. “It’s been a lot of meetings and figuring out logistics of what things will cost. I’d say that was the thing most on my mind this week, more so than school in some ways.”
After overcoming financial obstacles and navigating negotiations to make the trip possible, competing at nationals takes on a significance beyond the tournament itself, but represents a culmination of the team’s hard work and collective effort.
“I’m excited that this is new for club soccer, that we made this happen, we’re going to play soccer in Florida, and we’re going as a team,” said Kiezca.
“We are incredibly proud of our men’s club soccer team for earning a spot in the nationals tournament during its first season competing in a new league,” said Milliken. “This is an exciting accomplishment and a testament to the dedication and hard work of our students.”
The Bobcats head to Fla., Thursday, Nov. 12th, ahead of their first matchup against Clemson University Tigers on Friday, Nov. 13th, as they begin their pursuit for a national championship.

title: Portland Hearts of Pine soccer team kicking retail reach into Bangor
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Two hours north of its home base in Maine’s largest city, the Portland Hearts of Pine soccer club aims to reach even more fans with the opening of a pop-up store in Bangor, its second retail location.
The 700-square-foot store, located at 22 State St. in downtown Bangor, will be open for business from Nov. 13 through Jan. 3, according to Kate de Oliveira, senior director of consumer goods for the organization.
The pop-up site will sell clothing and team memorabilia for both the Hearts of Pine men’s pro team and the Maine Wildness women’s pre-professional squad, similar to the merchandise available at the organization’s much larger store located at 127 Marginal Way in Portland.
The Bangor location, next to Orono Brewing, is expected to score well with fans.
De Oliveira said the pop-up is designed to serve a wider audience across the state.
“The reason we’re here is we want to engage with the entire state of Maine,” she told Mainebiz. “We’re the soccer club for the whole state, not just for Portland, and we want to show up for our fans like they’ve shown up for us”.
Community hub
The 3,000-square-foot Portland store, across the parking lot from Trader Joe’s, has been a busy location for the organization since it opened in May. It serves as the team’s inventory hub, supplying merchandise to Fitzpatrick Stadium on game days, and as a place for fans to connect with one another.
“We’ve been seeing shopping patterns change a bit. In the beginning, it was very transactional. But now we’re seeing more browsing, which fosters community, which is what we’re all about,” de Oliveira said.
Merchandise for both the men’s and women’s teams has been selling well, she said.
‘Showing up’ for fans
De Oliveira said that while there are no immediate plans to open a permanent store in Bangor, “something that is always top of mind is how we can show up through community engagements outside of Portland.”
The Bangor store will be open six days a week — closed Tuesdays — and will have five part-time employees and a store manager.
Hearts of Pine men’s soccer team was founded in 2023 by Gabe Hoffman-Johnson and is led by President Kevin Schohl. The women’s team will play its inaugural season in 2027.

title: Ohio State fraternity placed on interim suspension after video shows two people on fire
text:
Ohio State fraternity placed on interim suspension after video shows two people on fire
An Ohio State fraternity has been temporarily suspended after a widely circulated video captured two people whose clothes were engulfed in fire, surrounded by a crowd of onlookers in university jerseys in an incident that police believe happened over the weekend.
Video above: Ohio State University student reacts to fraternity suspension
The school’s Sigma Alpha Epsilon chapter is suspended while authorities investigate the “extremely concerning” incident, the university said Monday. The university says it alerted the incident to Columbus police, which says it appears to have taken place Saturday in a neighborhood dotted with Greek life houses, including the large, four-story brick home of Sigma Alpha Epsilon.
The video begins with a person in gray sweatpants kicking on the ground while their legs are engulfed in flames. A bystander appears to try to put out the fire with an extinguisher but struggles to deploy the fire retardant. The person on fire gets up and runs across the dry, leaf-strewn grass and collides with another person whose pants also appear to be on fire.
A large circle of onlookers in Ohio State jerseys and colors watch as the chaos unfolds, then several people step in to try to extinguish the flames by stomping and pulling the clothes off their bodies.
Both people are “receiving needed medical care,” the university said. The men in the video were rushed to a hospital in a private vehicle with burn injuries and were in stable condition, a Columbus fire spokesperson told WSYX in a story published Monday.
Saturday was a day when Ohio State’s football team played Oregon at home, a game OSU lost 41-28. Though police said the incident happened in a neighborhood with Greek life houses, the exact location isn’t clear. Details about what led to the incident weren’t immediately available.
The university’s action comes amid intensified scrutiny of fraternity conduct – and college administrations’ handling of it – in the fallout from allegations of gang rape at a Cornell University fraternity in New York. A lawsuit filed by a former Cornell student in September returned a spotlight to long-standing concerns about alleged misconduct in Greek life and how schools, investigators and prosecutors respond.
“Ohio State is committed to a safe and healthy environment and expects students and student organizations to uphold that commitment and the university’s values,” Ohio State said Monday.
Police did not receive any calls about the incident on Saturday, but they were alerted on Sunday as the video began proliferating online, Columbus police Sgt. Joe Albert said Monday.
“We will be working with the Ohio State University, as well as the Columbus Division of Fire’s Arson Unit, to determine if any criminal acts occurred,” Albert said.
The national Sigma Alpha Epsilon organization takes “this matter seriously and are actively investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident while working closely with university officials and local law enforcement,” Steve Mitchell, the fraternity’s national CEO, said in a release.
Ohio State’s chapter represents a national fraternity with a mission of “advancing the highest standards of friendship, scholarship, leadership, and service.”
“Sigma Alpha Epsilon holds its collegiate members to high standards of conduct and accountability,” Mitchell said. Behavior that violates these standards has no place in our organization. We are committed to holding those responsible accountable and will take appropriate action based on the findings of the investigation.”

title: Maine cites fire, rescue departments after deadly Searsmont sawmill explosion
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - The Maine Department of Labor has cited six fire departments for lacking an effective system to track firefighters at the scene of the deadly May fire and explosion at Robbins Lumber in Searsmont.
The department also cited four of those fire departments, Searsmont, Morrill, Montville, and Belmont, as well as Searsmont Rescue over personal protective equipment protocols. Morrill was cited for 11 items in all.
The findings follow workplace safety investigations involving the Searsmont, Morrill, Montville, Belmont, Appleton and Lincolnville fire departments, as well as Searsmont Rescue.
Firefighter tracking and protective equipment
Firefighters from across the region responded to a silo fire and subsequent explosion at Robbins Lumber on May 15. Morrill volunteer firefighter Andrew Cross, 27, was killed, and more than a dozen other people were injured.
Searsmont Assistant Fire Chief Wayne Woodbury, 76, died in June from injuries he sustained while responding to the incident. Mill co-owner Alden Robbins died from his injuries in July.
A federal report released in August found officials did not realize Cross was missing until two hours after the incident.
The state cited all six fire departments over the lack of an effective accountability system for tracking firefighters’ locations at the scene. Searsmont Rescue was cited for actions including the setup of a firefighter rehabilitation area within 50 feet of the silo fire.
Kate Burkhart, director of the Bureau of Labor Standards, said every department and town worked with the state on plans to correct the issues.
“It’s not enough just to point out when there is a workplace safety or health violation. It’s really important to support the employer as they fix the problem and move forward,” Burkhart said.
“They are all invested in improving the safety for their employees and their volunteers. That’s really important here, is a lot of these fire departments rely on volunteers.”
Penalties and training
The labor department is suspending nearly all of the $108,000 in penalties it issued. Montville must pay $1,000 because of a record of one repeat fit-testing violation.
“We believe that it is more important for these towns and departments to allocate their resources toward the improvement efforts than it is to pay a civil penalty,” Burkhart said.
Those efforts include implementing or improving accountability systems. Most of the departments are moving toward the same system.
“If we have a standardized procedure and a standardized system, then it makes it that much easier for everybody,” Ron Harford said.
“We know what we got to do better next time,” Harford said.
The Maine Department of Labor is coordinating with the Maine Fire Chiefs’ Association and the Maine Fire Service Institute to provide training for the departments’ chiefs and officers. It will be held in Belmont in February.

title: Former police officer, teacher’s aide arrested in stabbing death of jogger
text:
NEW YORK (WCBS) — A man is in custody and charged with the murder of a jogger in New York City.
Police arrested Sayed Mohassib at his home on Saturday.
Detectives said evidence collected at the Brooklyn murder scene in October led them to Mohassib. He is accused of killing 28-year-old Katie Suarez.
Search along the waterfront
Suarez was out for a run along a popular waterfront path. She routinely jogged on the path, but she did not come home on Oct. 30. That’s when her father went searching for her.
He found her with two stab wounds to the neck. She died several days later at a hospital.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani spoke about the case.
“This is something that leaves, not only our hearts with her loved ones and her friends and her family who have been shattered by this, but also to emphasize our commitment to hold the individual responsible fully accountable,” Mamdani said.
Suspect’s background
Investigators said Mohassib is a former Marine and briefly worked for the New York City Police Department.
Mohassib recently worked as a teacher’s aide in a New York City school.
“We know that when it comes to this specific case, New York City Public Schools has suspended the individual and is moving to terminate his employment pending the outcome of this case,” Mamdani said. “We are also making counseling and support available to all the students and families at the school, and just when we speak about this case at large, this attack on Katie Suarez was horrific.”

text:
Sandwich shop partners with homeless shelter to help rebuild lives
The South O Sandwich Company, a unique restaurant concept in South Omaha, is partnering with the Stephen Center homeless shelter to help individuals re-enter the workforce through training and employment opportunities.
Nick Bartholomew, general manager of the South O Sandwich Company, said the restaurant is unlike any other concept he has worked with.
"I've been doing [work] in restaurants a long time. And this is unlike any concept that I've been a part of," Bartholomew said.
The partnership aims to provide a pathway for Stephen Center guests who have completed their programs to find employment and stability.
"The idea there was that guests from the Stephen Center who were coming through the program, graduating their programs, could find a leg up, find a way to get back into the workforce," Bartholomew said.
Bartholomew said workforce challenges are a major issue for metro restaurants, but the South O Sandwich Company hopes to address this through training.
"Once that community is brought back up and taught things like money handling, customer service, preparatory needs and things like that, they become not only more valuable to themselves, but they become more valuable to our community as a whole," he said.
One of the employees benefiting from the program is James Sova, who needed a job and a place to stay after his father was placed into assisted living.
"The Stephen Center was kind enough to help me out with that. And through that, I found out about this program and I thought, well, maybe that's a calling that a restaurant that needs a guy like me. I think it's a good fit," Sova said.
Sova, who describes himself as a "food geek," said the South O Sandwich Company offers a chance for people to rebuild their lives.
"Some people don't get a fair shake in life. Some people have a jaded past, and they're trying to get their life back together, and they need a break. And this is the kind of place where you get that kind of break," he said.
Sova also praised the restaurant's menu, which features unique sandwiches like the Dr. Pepper BLT and Peach of Mind.
"This is not a Subway or a or a Jimmy John's, you know ... we had our bread fresh every day," Sova said.
After operating as a pop-up downtown over the summer, the restaurant has now found a permanent home within 'The Daily' on 120th and Center.
"The hope is that within a year's time, the proof of concept is in place where this now can become a local Omaha concept that translates just about anywhere," Bartholomew said.

title: A note to ‘46’: Donald Trump’s private message to Joe Biden revealed in new memoir
text:
(AP) - President Donald Trump, who for years disputed his loss in the 2020 election and publicly decried the result having been stolen from him by Democratic forces, privately lauded incoming President Joe Biden as someone he believed “will be true to yourself and the American people.”
That sentiment, along with others, was part of the letter Trump left for Biden upon leaving office in January 2021. Biden showed the note to some members of his staff after his inauguration in 2021 but didn’t let anyone read it, describing it later that day as “very generous” but otherwise saying he considered it to be private.
Inclusion of the letter in Biden’s “Promise Me, America,” his White House memoir slated for release Nov. 17, was first reported Tuesday by The New York Times. The Associated Press has reviewed a photocopy of the two-page letter, handwritten in Trump’s trademark black Sharpie on White House stationery and addressed “To ‘46,’” denoting Biden’s place as the 46th U.S. president.
“Many presidents have come and gone who simply governed as Republicans or Democrats,” Trump wrote. “Largely, they did not change history, they were just swept along in its relentless tide. This will not happen to you because I know how much you love the American people.”
At the time of transition, Biden was said to have been surprised by how gracious he thought the letter was, given the animosity between the political rivals. Trump had opted out of other presidential traditions, like attending Biden’s inauguration, or hosting the incoming president and first lady for tea at the White House.
Trump has said he thought it was up to Biden to share the letter, calling it “a nice note” during a September 2023 interview with NBC’s “Meet the Press,” adding, “I took a lot of time in thinking about it.”
Elsewhere in the memoir, the first excerpt of which was published Monday by the Atlantic, Biden wrote of the deep damage Trump has inflicted, with an administration determined to “tear down institutions and inflame hatreds.”
Lamenting Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency and his aggressive reversal of many of his policies, Biden wrote of Trump’s “dismissive and destructive nature,” describing his predecessor and successor as someone “who seemed unable to tolerate the idea that someone else’s accomplishments might be worth building on rather than tearing down.”
But Biden’s harshest characterization so far was focused on Trump’s role in the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol, as Congress met to certify the 2020 election, which Biden had won. Writing that Trump “led an insurrection,” Biden said Trump’s ”goal was to remain in power after the American people had voted him out of office."
“What Trump did on January 6, 2021, should never be forgotten,” Biden wrote. “It should follow him to his grave.”
Asked for comment on both the letter and Biden’s memoir, White House communications director Steven Cheung called the former president “a disgrace” who “should have heeded the President’s wise words, but instead he tried to destroy this country and weaponize the justice system against his political enemies.”
___
Meg Kinnard can be reached at http://x.com/MegKinnardAP

title: Obituary: Beverley Jane Andrews
text:
OAKLAND – Beverley Jane Andrews, of Oakland, Maine, passed away peacefully on the afternoon of Oct. 20, 2026, just shy of her 86th birthday, surrounded by the love of her family.
Beverley (“Bev”) was born on Nov. 10, 1940, at Friendship Hospital in Bangor, Maine, to Natalie and Everett Stimpson.
Bev spent her early childhood in the Old Town area and loved to tell stories about her time at her grandparents’ Cunningham family farm. There she learned the value of hard work and formed a special bond with her grandfather. It was also there that her love of animals began, and it grew throughout her life. From the pony she had as a child, to the many cats and dogs that followed, each held a special place in her heart. Her lifelong love of gardening began on the farm as well. Planting beautiful flowers brought her great joy, and everything she planted seemed to thrive under her care.
Beverley, spelled with “ley,” as she would often remind everyone, attended elementary and high school in Old Town. Her treasured keepsakes reflect her dedicated involvement in many booster clubs and school spirit activities.
Bev met her future husband, Wayne Gary Andrews, on a blind date at a friend’s house near the Stillwater Bridge. After a brief courtship and engagement, they were married in Old Town in 1961. In 1970 they moved to Oakland, where they made their home for the rest of their nearly 64 years of marriage.
Bev worked in retail in the Old Town–Bangor area and embraced opportunities to model clothing. She later worked with special-needs adults in the Waterville area, as well as at several local nursing homes and a hotel, before settling into long-term employment at Hannaford Supermarket in Waterville.
Bev was always fun to be around, always willing to help when help was needed, always considerate and appreciative of others, and always showed how deeply she cared. She worked hard to reach her own goals and to help her children achieve theirs. She was a selfless and devoted mother, grandmother, and friend. She loved to shop and bake, and she sent gifts to family and friends all year long, always going above and beyond. Every card and package was decorated with elaborate stickers and stamps, and prepared with the utmost care.
Known to many as “Nana,” Bev raised her two children and helped raise two grandchildren into happy, healthy, and successful adults. She supported her family in a strong, no-nonsense, yet gentle way. She often offered “pocket money,” and when someone tried to refuse, she would warn, “Never refuse an offer of money, as it may not happen again…” or simply insist, “I want you to take it!” She sure loved to talk about her family, and was so proud to share their adventures and accomplishments. Those who knew her were lucky to have her as an inspiration and role model.
Bev had a gift for conversation, and we were always amazed by the stories of the people she met. She would come home from medical appointments and share the family histories of her providers, recalling every detail with a memory as sharp as a tack. She truly loved socializing, and many of the people she met over the years became her friends.
Bev faced health challenges in later years that limited her ability to drive, travel, and experience new places. Through it all, she remained resilient, kept a great sense of humor, and stayed optimistic.
Bev was predeceased by her parents, Natalie and Everett Stimpson; her son, Wayne Gary Andrews II, in 2021; her husband, Wayne Gary Andrews, in 2025; her sisters, Ruth Boucher and Rosemary Stone; and many beloved pets.
She is survived by her daughter, Deborah Luce and Deborah’s husband Brian, her grandchildren, Neil and Katie Luce, all of Sidney, Maine; and her sister-in-law, Shireen Burse, and niece, Lisa Burse, both of Eastport, Maine.
She will be greatly missed and lovingly remembered by her family and the many who knew her.
The family extends special thanks to the MaineGeneral Hospice team for the care and support given to Beverley and her family. Their compassion and understanding are deeply appreciated.
Interment services will be held on Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026, at 11:30 a.m. at Lewis Cemetery on Cottle Road in Oakland, Maine. A memorial gathering will follow at Governor’s Restaurant in Waterville.
Services are under the care of Wheeler Funeral Home in Oakland Maine. Please visit wheelerfh.com to sign an online guestbook or share a memory.
In lieu of flowers,
donations may be made to:
Waterville Area
Humane Society

title: Gunman wishes woman ‘a blessed day’ after church parking lot robbery, police say
text:
SPARTANBURG, S.C. (WHNS/Gray News) - Police in South Carolina say a woman told them a man wished her a “blessed day” after robbing her at gunpoint in a church parking lot.
The woman was attending a dance recital at a Spartanburg church Thursday when she walked to her car in the parking lot, according to a Spartanburg Police incident report. She said she noticed a silver Chevy Malibu with dark-tinted windows backed into a space two spots away from her car. Its lights were on.
The woman told police she approached the Malibu to see who was inside but changed her mind and turned around to walk back into the church. That’s when she heard a door open and turned around to see a suspect wearing a gray hoodie running toward her, according to the report.
The suspect had a gun and said, “Give me your money, or I will kill you,” and “I already killed two people; there are no cameras here,” the report said.
The woman told the suspect her purse was inside and offered to leave her car keys while she retrieved it, according to the report. She then returned and handed the suspect money.
The suspect returned her keys and told her, “Have a blessed day,” before getting back into his car and driving away, the report said.
Police said the woman memorized the car’s license plate, which helped officers identify the suspect as 26-year-old Demarieia Quartez Collins. Collins was taken to the Spartanburg County jail and charged with armed robbery, officials said.
The Rev. Heather Humphries of St. James United Methodist Church made the following statement after the incident:
“Our hearts are deeply troubled by the armed robbery that occurred in the parking lot of St. James United Methodist Church on Thursday. An act of violence in a place dedicated to worship, fellowship, and service is especially unsettling for our congregation and our community. Our immediate concern is for the victim of this frightening incident. We lift her and her loved ones in prayer, asking God to surround them with peace, comfort and healing. The safety and well-being of everyone who enters our church property remains our highest priority. We take this incident seriously and are committed to working with law enforcement by, among other actions, providing access to recordings made by our security cameras. We also are already reviewing our own security measures and taking appropriate steps to help ensure that St. James remains a safe and welcoming place for all. We ask for your continued prayers for all who have been affected, including the young man arrested in connection with this incident. Even in moments of fear and uncertainty, we remain steadfast in our faith and our calling to be a community of love, hope, and peace.”

title: Thune, Schumer face questions about Senate leadership in aftermath of elections
text:
Thune and Schumer face questions about Senate leadership in aftermath of elections
Senators from both parties returned to Washington on Monday with questions about the future of their leadership after last week's election decisively gave Democrats a significant new majority.
Republicans who are losing around a quarter of their conference to election losses and retirements are debating whether to immediately reelect South Dakota Sen. John Thune as leader in votes scheduled for Tuesday. Across the aisle, Democrats who could hold as many as 56 seats next year are having private discussions about whether New York Sen. Chuck Schumer is still the right person to lead them, even as he carried the party to historic wins.
Both men are expected to easily win the backing of a majority of their members in closed-door, secret-ballot elections — the Republicans this week, and Democrats likely in December. But the internal discussions on both sides could prove consequential to their parties' effectiveness in the next Congress and how voters perceive them leading into the 2028 presidential election.
The soul-searching comes as lawmakers are trying to wrap up the year's work — funding the government and seeing if there are some issues they can work together on, including national security money and energy permitting. Republicans will try to confirm as many of President Donald Trump's nominees as they can before the new Congress begins Jan. 3, and Democrats will strategize on how to best keep up their momentum into next year.
"The American people are not looking for socialist government and leftist fantasies," Thune said on the Senate floor Monday, reflecting on his party's "tough night" last week and how Republicans will handle minority rule in the Senate. "We will oppose any attempt to balloon the size of government or tear down American institutions."
Schumer said Democrats will prioritize affordability issues and "spend every second of every day striving to prove ourselves worthy of Americans' trust."
Some Republican senators push for delay in leadership elections
Thune, who replaced Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky as leader two years ago, has broad support among Senate Republicans and is expected to win reelection. Trump called him "a very fine man" on Monday, but said his reelection as leader "is up to the Senate."
Still, some in his conference say Tuesday's election is too soon and a lengthy conversation about the future is necessary.
A small group of senators has publicly called on GOP leadership to delay Tuesday's election. Pennsylvania Sen. Dave McCormick in a statement over the weekend said Republicans shouldn't choose a leader until the lessons of the election have been "digested and debated."
Republican Sen. Mike Lee of Utah, one of several senators who signed a letter from Wisconsin Sen. Ron Johnson asking for a delay, said any leadership contest should come after the two outstanding Senate elections in Alaska and Mississippi are decided. Neither of those races have yet been called, and it's unclear if Republican Sens. Dan Sullivan of Alaska and Cindy Hyde Smith of Mississippi will be returning next year.
Thune made clear Monday that leadership is moving ahead with the election, but senators could seek a vote to delay at the Tuesday morning meeting.
He said the conference will have a "very fulsome, robust conversation about where we go from here and then we'll see what the consensus of the conference is."
"Ultimately that's a decision made by Republican senators," Thune said.
Thune has at times been at odds with Trump, and some in the Republican base have criticized Thune for the chamber's failure to pass voting legislation that would require proof of citizenship for all voters.
Schumer faces critics on all sides, but still has support
Schumer has found critics on the left and the right as candidates from both sides of the party declined to say on the campaign trail whether they would support him as leader. Many in the party have said it's time for generational change after Schumer's 12 years leading the Senate Democratic caucus.
Still, Schumer appears to have widespread support from his members after carrying his party to massive wins in Tuesday's elections.
Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, Schumer's New York colleague and the head of the Democratic Senate campaign arm this cycle, said he not only won the Senate back but he "cares deeply, and he understands politics well."
Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen is considering a challenge to Schumer, according to a person familiar with his thinking, and he is open to a run. But it is unclear how much support he would have. Leadership elections are done via secret ballot and it requires only a majority to win.
Visiting the Capitol for the first time Monday, Democratic senators who will be sworn in next January were split on how they will vote. Incoming senators vote in party elections, even though they are held before they are seated.
Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan said he will support Van Hollen, whom he endorsed during his campaign. "I think he'd do a great job," El-Sayed said.
Former Sen. Sherrod Brown of Ohio, who beat Republican Sen. Jon Husted to return to the chamber, said he is supporting Schumer, but declined to elaborate.
Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan of Michigan said she's not ready to make any commitments.
"I think it's a moment where there are a lot of new voices, and making sure those voices are incorporated into the future of the Senate is really important," she said.

title: Defense secretary calls impeachment effort 'political spectacle'
text:
Defense secretary calls impeachment effort 'a political spectacle'
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has responded to articles of impeachment drafted by Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, defending his actions and calling the effort "a political spectacle."
"As for the articles themselves, Iran, the cartels, Maduro, Yemen, everyone was a lawful operation ordered by the commander-in-chief, then ordered by myself, notified to Congress and executed by American warriors who did their jobs," Hegseth said.
The resolution primarily focuses on Hegseth's role in military actions related to the Iran war but also includes references to military operations in Yemen and Venezuela.
Massie claims Hegseth's actions amount to "high crimes and misdemeanors" and argues that his leadership at the Pentagon warrants impeachment.
Hegseth is also calling this effort an attack on American troops.
"On the eve of Veterans Day," Hegseth said, "these resolutions tell every one of them that their service was a crime."
The House could vote on the resolution as soon as this week.

title: Maine Attorney General joins veterans abortion care lawsuit
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - Maine Attorney General Aaron Frey is joining a multi-state lawsuit challenging a new rule restricting veterans’ and their families’ access to abortion care.
According to the lawsuit, the Department of Veterans Affairs rule, finalized in December of 2025, denies abortion care to 90% of previously eligible veterans.
It reverses a 2022 rule that allowed abortion care in cases of rape, incest, or a life-threatening emergency.
The states argue the new rule could leave veterans and their families with expensive medical bills and confuse providers during life-threatening emergencies.
Attorneys General from more than 20 other states have joined the lawsuit.

title: Hogtied by rising costs, Maine meat farmers rely on loyal clients
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Deedee Caldwell makes weekly beef deliveries to markets and restaurants. Between stops one recent Thursday, she recounted the growing challenges her cattle farm in Turner faces.
Nearly every input, from her electric bill to the cost of wood shavings for cattle bedding, has shot up dramatically in price. Caldwell Family Farm used to be able to get a load of chicken manure fertilizer from Hillandale egg farm in Turner for as little as $275. But Hillandale went out of business in 2024, and a truckload of pelletized chicken manure from Connecticut now costs Caldwell $9,000.
Because of the drought, her land couldn’t produce as much hay and silage as Caldwell needed in 2025 to feed the cattle, so the farm had to buy $45,000 of corn silage last winter.
At the end of summer, it cost Caldwell $350 for diesel to fill her delivery truck. A week later, it was $450, and that was before diesel jumped to more than $6 a gallon. The petroleum-based plastic bags her farm uses to package its meat cost 45 percent more this year.
Last year she bought 75 fewer head of cattle than she needed because the cost had more than doubled in two years. “There will be some businesses that, for the first time in two decades, I won’t be able to deliver to this winter, because I don’t have the beef,” she said.
Caldwell has raised prices on her animal welfare-certified, pasture-raised beef as little as possible, but still lost a few lucrative restaurant accounts in Portland this year, as restaurateurs face their own financial struggles.
“We’ve been going drastically behind in terms of making a living for a couple of years,” Caldwell said. “My grandpa told me when I was a little girl, ‘Deedee, if you get up a little earlier, work a little harder, go to bed a little later, you’ll always be able to pay your bills.’ And it doesn’t work that way anymore.”
Wholesale and retail prices of local meat are creeping upward as Maine meat farms grapple with these unprecedented burdens. As some grocers and restaurateurs balk at the price hikes and switch to cheaper commodity meats, local meat farmers are now more reliant on — and grateful for — the chefs, shop owners and residents who remain loyal customers.
“There’s a really wonderful network in Maine of restaurants, small stores and butcher shops that are really committed to supporting these products,” said Mark Law, CEO of Rosemont Market & Bakery. “They believe it’s the right thing to do, but they also recognize that the quality of the product is superior, and it makes a difference for their customers.”
‘DEATH BY A MILLION CUTS’
“We want to make sure our farmers are getting the volume they need to sustain their business,” said Jack Barber, co-owner of Barber Brothers Meat & Provisions in South Portland. “And if they need to make another price increase, we’ll absorb as much as we can into our costs and try not to pass it on to the customers, because not having local meat would be a travesty.”
Law said Rosemont has absorbed some farm price increases as well, like with their holiday turkeys. “This year, we’ve made a conscious effort to lower our margin a little bit so we can keep our prices the same and commit to volume for (the farmers),” he said. “They’ve been under such duress economically, we want to really support them by selling as much as possible.”
Gabe Clark, co-owner of Cold Spring Ranch in New Portland, has seen costs at his cattle and pig farm jump 30 percent since 2024.
“This seems like a unique, tough situation this year,” Clark said. “I don’t think there’s a single part of our production costs that has gone down in price, and usually we see some give and take. It’s death by a million cuts.”
Clark usually raises his meat prices just once a year. Last year, for the first time, he had to increase prices three times. “The only way to address these increases in costs is to pass it on to consumers,” he said. “And it’s hard because consumers are facing higher costs across the board themselves.”
Pork chops go for around $2 a pound at the supermarket. Chris Wilcox, owner of Sawyer’s Butcher & Delicatessen in Portland, pays twice that much per pound for whole local pigs. After Wilcox and his team of skilled whole-animal butchers break down the carcasses, chops sell for about $14-$15 a pound.
Sawyer’s can offer specialty cuts you won’t find at supermarkets, like coppa pork roasts and beef steak cuts like Denver, merlot, hanger and flat-iron. Sawyer’s sells other parts wholesale to local restaurants — pig heads, jowls, marrow bones — putting the entire animal to use, without waste.
The whole-animal butcher model works well for the farmers, who don’t have to butcher and package the animals themselves. “If there were more of those types of shops in the state of Maine, I could make it,” Caldwell said.
Willcox has already had to raise his prices even though his store has only been open since August. “We want this meat to be as accessible as it possibly can, and it already costs more than the stuff at the grocery store, so it’s a really tough decision,” he said. “But at the same time, things costs what they cost.”
“We’re trying to support our farmers and give them a fair price,” said Jarrod Spangler, butcher and co-owner of the whole-animal butcher shop Maine MEat in Kittery, where non-premium cuts of New England-raised beef sell for $12-$15 a pound. “So in the end, we have to turn around and up our prices a little bit just to make sure everyone’s being taken care of.”
A SUPERIOR PRODUCT
Local meat is far too pricey for many Mainers. But those who can swing it say the value is clear.
Matt Reece of Portland shops exclusively at Sawyer’s for his meat, about twice a week, citing how well the livestock is raised. “I want to trust the source, and I’m willing to pay to have that trust, and to help out the local farmers who are also facing price pressures.
“I can trust that the animal has been raised well, and at each stage it’s been treated with care,” Reece added. “You can really taste how much better it is when it’s local, even compared to the premium products I’ve bought at supermarkets.”
Chef Stephanie Brown said the quality of Caldwell’s ground beef makes her burgers at North 43 Bistro shine.
“It’s perfection, to me,” Brown said. “(Caldwell’s) prices for her meats are well-justified, because she’s offering an organic, high-quality product. Sometimes in the back office, I encourage her, like, ‘Look, if you need to charge more, charge more. You can’t take the hit.'”
“Stephanie told me, ‘You’ve got to put a fuel surcharge on. If you go out of business because you can’t buy gas to get me your product, that doesn’t do me any good either,’ ” Caldwell said. She now has a fuel surcharge of $8 per stop on her delivery route.
“But every single business is doing that to them,” Caldwell continued. “I feel bad that the economy is in such a way that there’s no break anywhere.”
Brown said that for the past few years, she’s been reckoning with substantial increases in meat costs, regardless of whether it’s local. Meat producers nationwide are affected by the same issues local farmers face. Beef prices in particular have been compounded by a cattle shortage stemming from 2023 snowstorms that wiped out much of the herd in the western United States.
It creates a budget and pricing quandary for Brown and other chefs. “Do you still want to serve the 12-ounce sirloin and charge them more, or do you want to give them a 10-ounce sirloin and charge them less?”
‘MAKE YOUR WORLD SMALL’
Dan Sullivan raises poultry and heritage-breed pigs on Broad Arrow Farm in Bristol. He saw his client list of restaurants and markets dwindle over the years because of price increases he needed to make.
So he shifted his business model. With a few exceptions, Broad Arrow no longer sells to restaurants, butchers and markets. They now turn two-thirds of the pork they produce into value-added products like dry-cured meats, which they sell — along with their fresh meat — direct to consumers through their farm store, at farmers’ markets and online.
Four years ago, Broad Arrow also opened The Rooting Pig restaurant on their property. The venue puts all the farm’s cured and fresh meats to use in various ways, including a top-selling charcuterie board.
“If you want to insulate yourself from how the global commodity markets are moving, make your world small,” Sullivan said. “Be hyperlocal, hyperseasonal, and that’s what we are.”
Sullivan and other farmers and purveyors said the state could use more meat slaughterhouses to prevent processing bottlenecks and keep farmers from having to travel long distances to get their meat processed.
Caldwell acknowledges that some of her high costs are voluntary. She said the wood shavings she uses for cattle bedding have become “astronomically” more expensive in the past couple of years. While she’s not required by law to do so, she insists on having clean, dry spaces for her cattle to rest.
‘NOT PAYING FOR ITSELF ANYMORE’
Quality of life for the farmers themselves is hard to come by these days.
“There’s a lot of suicide in the farming industry,” Caldwell said. “When you work 80 to 100 hours a week, and at the end of the week, you’ve got to figure out what bill you can pay, that wears on them over time.” Her father took his own life four years ago this month.
In the past couple of years, just to stay afloat, Caldwell has had to sell house lots from her land for the first time since her grandfather started the farm in 1944. Still, she tries to focus on the nonmaterial ways her farm pays off.
“If the weather’s good, I can see Mount Washington from where we are. There’s some pay in that. We have amazing sunsets. There’s pay in that.
“I’m very blessed to be where I am,” Caldwell said, her voice breaking as she choked back tears. “But it’s not paying for itself anymore, and we don’t have a lot of equity left to chew off. The next two years or less are make or break.”

title: Obituary: Lynda Yarborough Giard
text:
PORTLAND – Lynda Yarborough Giard passed away peacefully at home on Nov. 4, 2026. She was 84.
Lynda was born and raised with her brother Bill in Tylertown, Mississippi, the daughter of William and Katherine Yarborough.
She is survived by her husband of 61 years Richard Giard; her children, David Giard, Michael Giard, and Susan Peters; six grandchildren, Christopher, Charles, Austin, Lilah, Jack, and Penn; and one great-grandchild, Lucas; and brother William.
She was proud to have moved many times with her husband, including spending a couple of years in Turkey.
Lynda graduated from Millsaps College with a degree in mathematics and taught high school math for several years before having children and moving around the country with her husband.
Lynda loved books and managed several bookstores before spending nine years as a pastor at Shorey Chapel in Industry.
A celebration of life will be scheduled for Shorey Chapel.
