title: Jayson Tatum gets better of Jaylen Brown as Celtics beat 76ers
text:
PHILADELPHIA — Jayson Tatum scored 21 points and outplayed former Boston teammate Jaylen Brown, and Paul George hit six 3-pointers and scored 36 points in his return to Philadelphia, leading the Celtics past the 76ers 123-101 on Tuesday night.
Brown ran into early foul trouble and scored only 13 points in his first game against Boston since the 2024 NBA Finals MVP was traded over the summer to the Sixers. His head-to-head showdown with Tatum was one of the more anticipated early-season matchups with both players refusing to say much about their frosty relationship.
Tatum tried to dap up Brown before the opening tip with a tap on the shoulder and thump on the chest that his former teammate ignored. Tatum shook hands and exchanged a big hug with LeBron James.
Brown picked up two quick fouls in the first quarter and was whistled for his fourth early in the second half.
George, traded for Brown after two seasons with the 76ers, enjoyed the homecoming. He appeared to give the finger in a bowling motion near the visitor’s bench after he sank his fourth 3 of the game for a 100-82 lead that pushed the Celtics to their ninth win in 10 games.
The Sixers survived a scare late in the second half when Joel Embiid landed awkwardly and hit the court on a missed layup attempt. The oft-injured big man curled up on the court while VJ Edgecombe dunked over him.
Embiid gingerly ran down the court and hunched over as the halftime horn sounded with the Celtics up 62-51.
Embiid’s health has been a career-long issue for him, and the Sixers have declined to play him in back-to-back games. A two-time NBA scoring champion, Embiid has slumped with his shot this season, with no game worse than last Friday in Cleveland when missed all nine shots from the floor and scored only two points.
He had missed 27 of 30 (and 20 consecutive) 3-pointers entering the game. Embiid missed two 3-point attempts in the first half but opened the second with his first 3 since the second game of the season.
Tyrese Maxey led the Sixers with 24 points.
Up next
Boston completes a back-to-back at Toronto.
The Sixers host the Raptors on Thursday.

title: AI scanners at rental car lots are ‘definitely not perfect,’ watchdog says
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Several rental car companies are now using AI scanning systems to check vehicles for damage, and a consumer watchdog says renters should document the car themselves to avoid a surprise bill.
The scanners look like a car wash at pick-up or drop-off. Cameras take photos and videos from different angles, looking for damage.
Teresa Murray, consumer watchdog director with the U.S. Public Interest Research Group, said the technology comes with both benefits and drawbacks.
Murray said artificial intelligence can make mistakes that matter in a rental car setting.
“We know that artificial intelligence can hallucinate. We know AI can fabricate data, misinterpret data, and in the case of damage in a rental car, it could mean that a splotch of dirt gets mistaken for a dent. You know, some kind of shadow could look like some pretty significant damage. So, it’s definitely not perfect,” Murray said.
Murray’s advice is the same whether a company uses AI or an employee looks the vehicle over: take a few minutes to inspect the car closely before leaving the lot.
“People should take pictures of every single thing and they should take walk around video. If you need to crouch down on the ground to get up under it, you know, the wheels and all that kind of stuff. The hubcaps, the interior, the trunk, you know, the glass, I mean everything. Do it. And I mean, if you’re going to rent a car, you need to allow 5 to 10 minutes to do this, depending on whether it’s with a live worker or without,” Murray said.
If a company uses an AI scanner, Murray recommends doing the same inspection before and after the trip. Having your own photos gives you a way to challenge a charge if a damage bill arrives later.

title: Many defectors see daughter of North Korea's Kim as heir apparent
text:
‘Like gods reigning over humans’: Many defectors see daughter of North Korea's Kim as heir apparent
Until she fled North Korea three years ago, Kim Yumi felt deeply frustrated whenever state TV showed leader Kim Jong Un with his young daughter. The message, she felt, was clear and worrying: North Korea was laying the groundwork for an eventual hereditary transfer of power, this time to Kim's daughter.
Publicly questioning the Kim dynasty's hold on power would mean severe persecution. Already angered by draconian pandemic regulations that ruined her family’s fishing business, she defected to South Korea by boat with her family.
“My husband and I didn’t want our children to live under a fourth-generation dictatorship. As parents, we thought the best thing we could do for our children was to give them freedom,” said Kim Yumi, 32, who now lives in Seoul.
North Korea allows no dissent and harshly punishes attempts to flee the country. Established in 1948, the nation is nominally a socialist republic, but in reality it is an authoritarian dynasty, with three generations of the Kim family ruling in succession. There was no known public resistance during its previous two successions — from state founder Kim Il Sung to his son Kim Jong Il in 1994, and then from Kim Jong Il to his son Kim Jong Un in 2011.
This time, North Korea is apparently trying something radical.
Kim Jong Un's repeated public appearances with his daughter over the past four years have led to speculation that she’s being groomed as her father’s heir.
The question of who will become North Korea's next leader is crucial because that person will face a huge challenge — governing an impoverished, nuclear-armed nation whose 26 million people have little political freedom and live under strict state surveillance while being cut off from much of the outside world.
North Koreans have no say in the selection of their future leader, and analysts and defectors say they will passively accept a third dynastic succession — at least publicly.
To gauge North Koreans' private views, The Associated Press spoke with nearly a dozen defectors who still have contacts in North Korea or witnessed the country’s previous power successions, as well as several experts.
Most defectors believe the girl is Kim’s heir
Not much is known about Kim’s daughter except that she’s reportedly about 13 and named Kim Ju Ae.
Since late 2022, she has made dozens of public appearances, all of them with her father at big events like weapons tests and military parades. State media has called her Kim’s “most beloved” and “respected” child. Her status has been emphasized by images showing an elderly general kneeling before her and her standing in front of her father.
South Korea’s spy agency says she is Kim’s likely heir. Eight of the 11 defectors interviewed by the AP shared that view; the others disagreed, citing the North's deeply patriarchal culture.
“During her visits to missile launch sites and factories, the way senior North Korean officials treat Kim Ju Ae involves protocols reserved for a successor, not the ones simply for a daughter of Kim Jong Un,” said Tae Yongho, a former minister at North Korea’s Embassy in London who defected to South Korea in 2016. “They are repeating the same protocol and treatment they provided for Kim Jong Un,” when he accompanied his father as his heir.
Kang Mi-Jin, a defector who runs a company analyzing North Korea’s economy, said her contacts inside the North told her over smuggled phones that they think Kim Ju Ae is in line to succeed her father.
Jung Gwang-il, a defector who specializes in smuggling outside information to North Korea, said the North Koreans he meets as they visit Chinese border towns also hold the same belief.
Former NBA star Dennis Rodman was the first to reveal her identity, holding her as a baby during a 2013 trip to Pyongyang.
Doubts remain about a woman becoming North Korea's leader
Much of the skepticism about Kim Ju Ae as a potential leader stems from her being female. South Korean officials believe she has a younger sibling whose gender hasn't been confirmed.
Women in North Korea remain deeply underrepresented in senior posts. Only one of 17 department directors for the ruling Workers' Party is a woman. That woman is Kim Jong Un’s influential younger sister, Kim Yo Jong, according to South Korea's Unification Ministry.
“My contacts in North Korea say it would be nonsensical to revere that little girl as their supreme leader,” said Kim Jeong-Ah, a former North Korean army officer who resettled in South Korea in 2009.
Lee Si-young, a defector who heads the Seoul-based Free North Korea Radio station, said that some of her older contacts in North Korea aren't happy with a woman taking power. But she said members of the Kim family “are like gods reigning over humans so gender really doesn't matter.”
Kim's push for hereditary power transfer faces little resistance at home
Whether or not the girl succeeds her father, observers agree that Kim Jong Un, 42, is likely to designate one of his children to prolong his family's rule, a move they expect would face little resistance at home. South Korea’s spy agency recently assessed that Kim is extremely obese and at high risk of cardiovascular disease but shows no other signs of poor health.
North Koreans will passively “accept a hereditary succession as something that they should go along with,” said Ahn Chan-il, a defector and scholar who heads the World Institute for North Korean Studies in Seoul.
During North Korea’s first leadership transition, in 1994, the new leader, Kim Jong Il, then 52, had already spent two decades as the official successor working alongside his father to run the country.
The second succession, in 2011, was more uncertain. Kim Jong Un, who was then 27, was seen by outsiders as too young and inexperienced. He quickly consolidated his grip on power, however, by orchestrating high-profile executions and purges, including the 2013 killing of his powerful uncle Jang Song Thaek.
“A hereditary power succession system has been institutionalized in North Korea, just like presidential elections in our system,” said Oh Gyeong-seob, an analyst at Seoul’s Korea Institute for National Unification. “North Korea’s ruling elite accepts it as a matter of course. So do its general citizens.”
Choi Song-juk, who fled North Korea in 2015, said she had been so brainwashed that she had no complaints about the North's two earlier power successions. She now calls them “nonsense.”
Defector Jeon Jae-hyun said North Korea's pervasive surveillance apparatus keeps people from voicing their discontent with the government and helps enforce political loyalty.
Defector Kim Yumi said she had never heard about the girl until Kim Jong Un publicly introduced his daughter at a long-range missile launch site in November 2022.
“Ordinary people know absolutely nothing about private lives of the Kim family,” said Kim Yumi, who now runs a YouTube channel on North Korea. “They don't really try to know about it and don't pay attention to it because doing so could put them in danger.”

title: Another country star says he was denied CMA Awards red carpet access
text:
NASHVILLE (KALB/Gray News) - Days after Sammy Kershaw made waves across the country music world, a fellow alum of the 90s and 2000s country scene announced Saturday that he, too, was snubbed by the Country Music Association after requesting red carpet access to the upcoming 2026 CMA Awards.
Rodney Atkins, known for country hits like “Honestly (Write Me a List),” “If You’re Going Through Hell (Before the Devil Even Knows)” and “Watching You,” expressed his frustration with CMA on social media, writing:
“After more than 20 years as a CMA member and countless CMA Fests I’ve played for free, Rose and I were denied red-carpet clearance just like Sammy Kershaw. So we’ve decided not to attend this year’s CMA Awards.”
Atkins also posted a video message to fans, explaining that he felt sympathetic toward Kershaw after news began to spread, only to find out later that he and his wife, fellow country artist Rose Falcon, had also been denied access to this year’s awards.
Nineties hitmaker Kershaw says he was delisted from the red carpet in a post to social media Thursday, which drew an outpouring of support from fans and fellow musicians.
The Country Music Association has not yet publicly responded to either Kershaw’s or Atkins’ comments.

title: An Idaho man gets 18 years in prison for an Islamic State support plot
text:
BOISE, Idaho (AP) — An Idaho man has been sentenced to 18 years in federal prison for attempting to provide material support to the Islamic State group.
Alexander Scott Mercurio, 21, pleaded guilty to the federal terrorism charge last month. U.S. District Judge David C. Nye sentenced him Tuesday and said Mercurio would be placed on lifetime supervised release after completing his prison term.
Prosecutors said Mercurio had pledged his allegiance to IS and planned to attack churches in Coeur d’Alene on the group’s behalf, using explosives, knives, firearms and other weapons. He was arrested by the FBI on April 6, 2024, one day before the planned attack, according to prosecutors.
Idaho U.S. Attorney John Shirts said the sentence “sends the clear message that where individuals intend to pursue acts of terrorism against the United States — whether in Coeur d’Alene, or any other community — they will be brought to justice.”
Mercurio’s defense attorneys, Carter Powers Beggs and J. Stephen Roberts Jr. with the Federal Defenders of Eastern Washington and Idaho, declined to comment on the case. But in a court document, they described Mercurio as a depressed teen when he was arrested who was raised in a dysfunctional family that exposed him to white supremacist ideology at a young age.
Mercurio was dealing with family trauma and isolated from the outside world when he was befriended online by a government informant, his attorneys wrote. He had already bounced between multiple political ideologies by that time, ultimately embracing radical Islam when the COVID-19 pandemic hit in 2020, they said.
“Starting when he was just seventeen years old, Mr. Mercurio spent his days holed away in his basement bedroom, talking with his best friend about increasingly radical terrorist ideologies,” his attorneys wrote. “Together they brainstormed a plan that was as horrific as it was unlikely to succeed: a suicidal attack on local churches using his father’s firearms and an untested improvised explosive/flamethrower.”
Mercurio has since renounced his extremist views, and has been assessed as a low risk of future danger, his attorneys said. They asked the judge to impose a sentence of nine years in prison.
According to court records, Mercurio created an online repository for pro-IS content and originally wanted to travel overseas to support the organization but lacked the money and resources to make the trip. Shortly before his arrest, he gave the informant an audio recording pledging his support for IS, along with a photo of himself holding a knife in front of an IS flag.
The Islamic State group, which the U.S. government designates a terror group, took control of a large swath of territory in Syria and Iraq in 2014 and declared the territory to be a caliphate. The group had been largely defeated in both countries by 2018, but still has sleeper cells that carry out deadly attacks in both countries, and IS affiliates also operate in West Africa.

title: How a routine robotic surgery turned into a nightmare
text:
ATLANTA, Ga. (InvestigateTV) - An Atlanta mother checked into the hospital for a hysterectomy, expecting to be home from that same day. Instead, she didn’t leave for nearly three months.
Doctors confirmed the issues stemmed from fibroids, or noncancerous tumors. To get rid of them, Button opted for a robotic hysterectomy at Southern Regional Medical Center. The procedure surgically removes the uterus.
What a robotic hysterectomy is
A robotic hysterectomy is considered the least invasive and quickest for recovery because doctors use the device to make very small incisions in the abdomen. Once inside, the robot’s tiny arms are controlled by the surgeon who is standing feet away.
“I wasn’t actually going to the hospital initially thinking I was going to be a resident in its ICU following this procedure,” Button said.
Photos documented Button’s journey of days in a coma and nearly three months awake in the ICU battling blood loss and infections.
Button is now suing both Southern Regional Medical Center and the physician, Dr. Beverly Love, for negligence. The lawsuit alleges the hospital failed to maintain its equipment and the doctor “failed to exercise degree of care and skill.” The lawsuit also claims Dr. Love wrongfully removed her right ovary.
An expert hired by Button’s attorneys to review the case wrote the incident required doctors to “recognize and treat active bleeding” but they “failed to adhere to standard of care.”
Although Dr. Love has since passed, lawyers for his estate deny all wrongdoing, blaming Button’s own medical history for complications.
Surgeon describes technical challenges and conversion mid-procedure
In cellphone video recorded after the procedure, Dr. Love told Button’s husband about issues during surgery.
“Well, what happened was we had some technical challenges and I couldn’t manipulate the uterus the way I wanted to so I couldn’t really get to the blood vessels the way I wanted to so I said uh…we just converted to just going straight taking it out through the vagina and we stopped the robot," Dr. Love said.
Button said the robot used was the Da Vinci, a robotic surgical system that has been used in millions of various surgical procedures globally. However, Da Vinci and its manufacturer, Intuitive Surgical, are not mentioned or named as a defendant in the lawsuit.
From 2016 to 2025, Atlanta News First Investigates uncovered at least 434 “adverse events” — like death, injury, or malfunctions — reported to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) related to any Da Vinci device used in any surgery. At least 49 of those reports specifically involved devices used in hysterectomies. The Da Vinci device has been used in millions of various surgical procedures globally.
Manufacturer emphasizes safety record, notes limits of FDA database
“Patient safety is our highest priority,” an Intuitive Surgical company spokesperson said. “More than 20 million procedures have been performed globally using Da Vinci systems. The safety and effectiveness of our systems are supported by more than 48,000 peer‑reviewed publications, which, in aggregate, demonstrate positive clinical outcomes for patients."
The FDA maintains a database that tracks adverse events involving medical devices. “As the FDA itself recognizes, reports in the database have significant limitations and are not intended to evaluate device-related adverse event rates or establish causality between use and a potential injury,” the spokesperson said.
Dr. Love practiced for more than 40 years. Although he was in good standing with the Georgia Composite Medical Board, the agency said there was no medical malpractice insurance on file for him.
Malpractice insurance protects both doctors and patients who want to seek financial damages, but Georgia does not require doctors to carry it. Only seven states currently mandate it: Colorado, Connecticut, Kansas, Massachusetts, New Jersey, Rhode Island and Wisconsin.
“I need insurance to drive my car,” Button said. “But with the hospital, in that sense, when it crashed and burned, they started pointing fingers.”
OBGYN: robot can be safer, but surgeons must be ready without it
Dr. Timothy Cowthorn said his local hospital required him to carry medical malpractice insurance to operate at its facility. Cowthorn is not connected to Button’s case, but the OBGYN just completed his 1,000th robotic hysterectomy.
Asked whether the robot adds risk, Dr. Cowthorn said that even if it malfunctioned, he would still have to complete the surgery, so he must be prepared to operate without it.
With his experience at a local hospital and his private practice at Greystone, Dr. Cowthorn said the device transformed healthcare.
“These cutting instruments, which on the robotic arms are wristed so they can turn like your wrist of your own hand,” he said. “Going to the platform or going to the console where we manipulate those instruments is literally like being inside a patient. To me, it’s safer.
“Not only is it more precise, but I have less complications and less infections. Over the years, this has been one of the greatest technologies for women.”
What Button wants now: damages and policy change
Button’s complications didn’t stop when she left the hospital.
She said the medical bills eventually forced her out of her home; the long recovery cost her job; and her marriage did not survive the ordeal. Button described the ordeal as devastating, and said the severe PTSD, health issues, and ongoing sepsis have made it an uphill battle to rebuild her life.
Button is hoping her lawsuit does more than recover damages. She wants it to change how hospitals protect patients and how Georgia protects them from doctors without insurance. She started a fundraiser to help with legal costs.
Southern Regional Medical Center declined to answer questions about insurance requirements and what happened in this case. “Our focus remains on providing high-quality, compassionate care and serving the patients and communities who rely on us every day,” it said. “Due to pending litigation, we are not able to comment on this matter.”
Attorneys for Dr. Love’s estate did not respond to requests for comment.

title: Former police officer, teacher’s aide arrested in stabbing death of jogger
text:
NEW YORK (WCBS) — A man is in custody and charged with the murder of a jogger in New York City.
Police arrested Sayed Mohassib at his home on Saturday.
Detectives said evidence collected at the Brooklyn murder scene in October led them to Mohassib. He is accused of killing 28-year-old Katie Suarez.
Search along the waterfront
Suarez was out for a run along a popular waterfront path. She routinely jogged on the path, but she did not come home on Oct. 30. That’s when her father went searching for her.
He found her with two stab wounds to the neck. She died several days later at a hospital.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani spoke about the case.
“This is something that leaves, not only our hearts with her loved ones and her friends and her family who have been shattered by this, but also to emphasize our commitment to hold the individual responsible fully accountable,” Mamdani said.
Suspect’s background
Investigators said Mohassib is a former Marine and briefly worked for the New York City Police Department.
Mohassib recently worked as a teacher’s aide in a New York City school.
“We know that when it comes to this specific case, New York City Public Schools has suspended the individual and is moving to terminate his employment pending the outcome of this case,” Mamdani said. “We are also making counseling and support available to all the students and families at the school, and just when we speak about this case at large, this attack on Katie Suarez was horrific.”

title: Bob Boone, legendary MLB catcher and Gold Glove winner, dies at 78, son says
text:
(Gray News) — Legendary MLB catcher Bob Boone has died, according to his son. He was 78.
“My dad- He was my mentor, my coach, my rock. He taught me how to be a pro and more importantly, how to be a man. He was one of the highest integrity people I’ve ever known and I’m going to miss him dearly. Baseball lost a great one yesterday. R.I.P dad, I love you,” Boone’s son, former MLB player Bret Boone, wrote on X.
According to Sports Illustrated, Bob Boone won four Gold Glove Awards in seven seasons as the California Angels’ catcher in the 1980s. He won the award in 1982, 1986, 1987 and 1988.
Bob Boone was originally from San Diego and played college baseball at Stanford University.
His MLB debut was with the Phillies in 1972. He helped the team win its first-ever World Series in 1980, according to Sports Illustrated.
Bob Boone spent his first 10 seasons with the Phillies before playing seven seasons with the California Angels, followed by two seasons with the Kansas City Royals. He also went on to manage the Royals from 1995-97 and the Cincinnati Reds from 2001-03, according to ESPN.
According to MLB, Bob Boone played an integral part in “one of baseball’s most historic families.”
“Along with his father Ray, and his sons Bret and Aaron, the Boones became the first family to field three generations of Major League players, all of them All-Stars,” MLB wrote on X.
A cause of death was not yet given.

title: VA data shows Maine veterans face a higher risk of suicide
text:
VA data shows Maine veterans face a higher risk of suicide than others across the country
Data from the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) shows that in 2024, 54 Maine veterans died by suicide, and the state's veteran suicide rate was significantly higher than the national rate.
Sweetser adult residential clinical director Doug Weaver, an eight-year Army veteran who served in Iraq, joined Maine's Total Coverage to speak about how returning home brings its own set of challenges to veterans.
Weaver said that when veterans come home, the mission changes to their family, career and responsibilities, but their selfless mindset stays the same, as veterans often put everyone else's needs first and push their own needs aside.
"What's important is to recognize that we need to make it a priority to take care of ourselves," he said.
Weaver added that veterans do not want people to know that they are struggling and will sometimes suffer in silence.
"Veterans can be extremely prideful and self-reliant. They handle everything themselves, so asking for help can feel like a weakness, and the reality is it's a strength," Weaver said. "It takes a lot of courage to say, 'I'm struggling and I need support.' Really, no veterans should have to fight those battles alone."
Weaver encouraged people to reach out to a veteran in their life if they have not heard from them in a while.
"Give them a call. Send them a text. You don't need to know what to say or how to help, but just knowing somebody is thinking of you can make a huge impact," Weaver said.
Veterans in Maine who are seeking mental health support can connect with the VA Maine Healthcare System through the Togus VA Medical Center in Augusta, community-based outpatient clinics and Vet Centers across the state.
Weaver said Sweetser also offers adult behavioral health support and works with community partners, including the VA, to coordinate care for uniformed service members and veterans.
Those who are in need of crisis support can contact the Veterans Crisis Line by calling 988 and pressing 1, texting 838255 or chatting online at VeteransCrisisLine.net/Chat. The Veterans Crisis Line is available 24/7, and you do not have to be enrolled in VA healthcare to reach out.

title: Louisiana’s wetlands are vanishing, threatening a haven for migrating birds
text:
PLAQUEMINES PARISH, La. (InvestigateTV) — At the first sign of some potential threat, goose necks stretch in unison before the sky fills with a blizzard of white and black wings.
In one of North America’s great migrations, snow geese and ducks descend on the south Louisiana delta by the hundreds of thousands, most often in places far from city life.
One of the busiest migration spots is near the mouth of the Mississippi River in the Bird’s Foot Delta.
“When you come to the Bird’s Foot Delta, this is the terminal end of the Mississippi Flyway in North America,” said Todd Baker, a wildlife biologist and project manager for the Louisiana Coastal Protection and Restoration Authority.
“This time of year, you get birds from Canada, the Arctic, all over North America, migrate down to the mouth of the river,” Baker said.
In the winter months, birds journey down the Mississippi Flyway, a migratory superhighway for more than 300 species. Annual surveys estimate 3 million snow geese choose Louisiana and Texas for their wintertime retreats.
“You can look over your shoulder and see something at every turn,” Baker said.
Yet no place on the continental U.S. loses wetlands at the rate Louisiana is shedding its coast.
The U.S. Geological Survey estimates, on average, Louisiana loses the equivalent of a football field of land every 90 minutes.
Historic shipping channel now unusable
Baker steers down Pass-a-Loutre, one of three main arteries running from the river to the Gulf.
“This used to be the original navigation channel for the state of Louisiana, for the Mississippi River,” Baker said. “For commercial traffic (today), it’s pretty much unusable. Recreational boating still gets out here.”
Over time, the channel silted in, partly from material the Army Corps dredges and deposits to keep the modern channel open for shipping.
“Anytime you cut the river off from its marshes, it goes into retreat pretty quick and this is a pretty fluid example of that right in front of you,” Baker said. “The river doesn’t make it out here anymore; the sediment doesn’t make it out here anymore. So, it’s starting to retreat.”
Lighthouse tells story of land loss
For decades, the Pass-a-Loutre Lighthouse guided mariners home. The lighthouse had stood in that spot since 1855, until Hurricane Katrina bulldozed over the area and decapitated the structure.
Baker said what has been dubbed “the loneliest lighthouse” was situated about a mile or so inland 25 years ago. Today, it is isolated several hundred feet offshore.
Five years after the hurricane, a man-made disaster inflicted more harm. The Macondo oil well blowout belched millions of gallons of oil for 87 days until crews finally capped it.
“BP had a tremendous impact on this landscape,” Baker said. “This is the closest landmass to the oil spill. It was the first land mass hit by the oil spill, and it was hit multiple times. And it’s very difficult to get out here. So, cleanup was pretty slow. The impacts were pretty severe.”
The wetlands surrendered more land after the spill.
“The oil spill greatly sped up the rate of erosion down here, leading to the loss of a lot of the property,” Baker said.
Southwestern Louisiana also faces land loss
Other parts of Louisiana’s coast face their own challenges. A similar population explosion plays out southeast of Lake Charles in the marshes of the Rockefeller State Wildlife Refuge. The Rockefeller family donated the 86,000-acre refuge to Louisiana over a century ago.
Today, 70,000 acres remain. And during some years, the Gulf chews away 300 feet of beach.
“The outlook for the future is trying to maintain what we have,” said refuge manager Scooter Trosclair.
In several phases, the state has installed shoreline protection, which has stopped some of the bleeding.
Trosclair said they are like “farmers of the marsh.” There are 52 large structures that control water levels and salinity, providing an added bonus of flood protection for populated areas to the north.
“Is it going to prevent all flooding? No, but it’s going to get water out quicker,” Trosclair said.
Trosclair explained that lowering water levels to just the right depth makes the water shallow enough for birds to feed.
A series of hurricanes over the last couple decades walloped the surrounding area and the Rockefeller Refuge. They’re in the process of repairing the damage.
“With all these water control structures, levee systems, it’s taken 100 years to build this,” Trosclair said. “And so, here we’re basically trying to rebuild all this infrastructure in a few years. So, it’s going to be a challenge.”
Wildlife Viewing Area
Southwestern Louisiana also offers some of the best opportunities to see birds up close, including a three-mile driving loop in the Lacassine National Wildlife Refuge, southeast of Lake Charles.
The Lacassine Pool Wildlife Drive takes motorists along the perimeter of a 16,000-acre freshwater impoundment. Common species in the fall and winter include gadwall, American wigeon, mallard, mottled duck, blue-winged teal, northern shoveler, northern pintail, green-winged teal, ring‑necked duck, lesser scaup and ruddy duck.
Hydrologic Restoration Project
Near Pass-a-Loutre, Baker pushes an idea to buy these wetlands some time.
The Bird’s Foot Delta Hydrologic Restoration Project would dredge Pass-a-Loutre, South Pass, Southeast Pass and a small portion of the Pilottown anchorage.
According to Baker, dredging the anchorage -- a natural pinch point in the river -- would open the river channel a bit more to allow more sediment to flow.
“We’re just going to open it up and get that sediment pumping back out to the marshes and let it build,” Baker said.
Contractors would dredge two-thirds of the channel in Pass-a-Loutre, sucking 16 million cubic yards of sediment from the river, the equivalent of 3½ Superdomes of sand and dirt.
“It’s going to clean out Pass-a-Loutre, clean out South Pass and let Mother Nature build marsh like it used to out here,” Baker said.
The state Coastal Protection and Restoration Authority, which still must apply for federal and state permits, hopes to fund the $176 million project with settlement money from the 2010 oil spill.
Navigation interests generally support the concept but have raised questions about how the Corps and the state would handle the possible buildup of sand in the channel downstream of the project.
Sending more water down Pass-a-Loutre would slow the flow in the main Mississippi River channel, allowing for shoaling to occur.
The state estimates the project would result in only a 2 percent increase in sand buildup in Southwest Pass and would also decrease sediment buildup north of the project.
Baker also concedes there are doubters, who question whether the rapidly sinking delta is doomed to future sea level rise and subsidence.
“So, we get that a lot of times. Why bother? Well, this is a habitat that’s unique to North America,” Baker said. “We don’t have a delta like this anywhere else in North America. So, to go with that line of thinking, we’re saying it’s OK to take that ecosystem and say it’s functionally extinct. We’re not going to do anything anymore.”
If Mother Nature had her way, the river would have shifted course long ago.
“We, as human beings, have locked this system into where it’s at,” Baker said. “So, it’s not a natural system anymore.”
Rather than abandon the delta, he argued, “it’s important to preserve that habitat where we have it.”

title: Woman credits free BRCA gene study with catching her cancer risk early
text:
OMAHA, Neb. (Aging Untold) — A Nebraska nurse practitioner says a free genetic research study likely saved her life after she learned she carries a BRCA2 gene mutation, despite having little family history of cancer.
Erin Thoman, a 34-year-old mother of four, said cancer was not something she had considered a personal risk. That changed after her sister, also a nurse, participated in the Genetic Insights Project at Nebraska Medicine.
“She didn’t really think much of it and so offered to do it to kind of help out with the study,” Thoman said. “Then she found out that she had the BRCA2 gene mutation.”
Thoman and her mother were then tested through the same study and both learned they also carry the mutation.
“We definitely were all surprised,” Thoman said.
Preventive surgeries ahead
Everyone carries two types of BRCA genes. When functioning properly, they repair DNA, keep other genes healthy and prevent cancerous changes in cells, according to Johns Hopkins Medicine.
When a mutation damages either gene, a person’s risk of developing cancer increases.
Inheriting damaged copies of the BRCA genes can increase the risk for breast and ovarian cancer in women, and breast and prostate cancer in men.
For Thoman, the path forward was clear.
“I wanted to not have that stress of wondering, is today the day I find out I have cancer?” Thoman said.
She has met with a breast surgeon at Nebraska Medicine and has additional appointments scheduled with a surgeon who would remove her ovaries and fallopian tubes.
The double mastectomy is expected to drop her breast cancer risk from around 60% to less than 10%.
“I’m very fortunate that I have four healthy kids, I no longer need those parts, so let’s just get rid of them,” Thoman said. “Honestly, I feel like this is a blessing. I have the opportunity to prevent it and be around a long time to watch my kids grow up.”
About the Genetic Insights Project
Thoman is one of 15,000 people in the Omaha metro area to receive genetic results through the free study. Researchers want to enroll up to 100,000 people in Nebraska and 3 million nationwide.
Participants provide a blood sample or complete an at-home saliva kit, which is sent to Helix, a genetic testing company. The screening looks for three gene mutations known to increase risk for several diseases, including multiple types of cancer.
Dr. Doug Stoller, a cardiologist involved in the study, said the goal is early detection.
“The goal here is to detect as early as possible and prevent even the possibility that cancer could ever start,” Stoller said.
About one in 75 people screened learn they carry a genetic mutation.
“Many participants that find that they carry one of these variants actually are found to have very early-stage disease already by the time that they actually get their screening done,” Stoller said.
More than half of those who test positive did not know they were at risk.
Thoman said she is now encouraging others to sign up.
“It’s free, it’s super easy and it’s just nice to know if you have that risk,” she said.

title: Michigan’s El-Sayed said Israel aid violates law. Does it?
text:
Abdul El-Sayed said US aid to Israel violates Leahy laws. What are they, and is he right?
After campaigning to end U.S. aid to Israel, Michigan’s U.S. Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed found a rare point of agreement with President Donald Trump.
This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.
El-Sayed, a Democrat, said in a CNN interview he agrees with Trump’s call to end $4 billion in annual U.S. military aid to Israel. El-Sayed said he wants to take that further and prohibit all weapons transfers to Israel.
“I don’t know why we are engaged in weapons transfers against the Leahy laws, our own policy, with a government that has engaged in war crimes and the worst with our weapons,” El-Sayed said Nov. 5.
The Leahy laws prohibit the federal government from providing military assistance or training to foreign security forces credibly implicated in gross violations of human rights. They’re named after former U.S. Sen. Patrick Leahy, D-Vt., who introduced the laws in the 1990s.
El-Sayed has a point: Human rights experts have said the U.S. has essentially ignored the Leahy requirements for Israel funding and slow-walked investigations to avoid sanctioning Israeli forces.
The U.S. government has never used the law to restrict aid to Israel’s military, despite State Department-documented evidence of human rights abuses by Israeli soldiers. The Leahy law process for investigating alleged human rights abuses by Israeli forces, however, is opaque and marked by frequent delays. Critics say the U.S. has given special treatment to Israel despite the law.
The U.S. provides about $3.8 billion in annual aid to Israel, and Trump provided little detail about how he would phase it out.
If that aid does end, Israel could continue buying weapons from the U.S., which would not be subject to Leahy rules.
What are the Leahy laws?
The Leahy laws apply to both the State Department and the Defense Department. Leahy law violations include “torture, extrajudicial killing, enforced disappearance, and rape,” according to the State Department.
If the secretary of state determines that the foreign government has addressed the conduct, the U.S. can resume its assistance. The U.S. government can also continue sending military funding to a country and its other military units, even if a unit in the country becomes ineligible. The law doesn’t apply to weapons purchases made with the foreign country’s money, rather than U.S. aid.
How is Israel aid handled under Leahy laws?
The U.S. has a unique process for ensuring Israel military aid follows the Leahy laws that critics have called secretive and ineffective.
Most military funding to Israel isn’t traceable to a specific military unit. For nontraceable funding like that, Congress updated the Leahy laws in 2019 to require the secretary of state to create a list of foreign military and police units that aren’t eligible for funding. The department must provide the list to the foreign government receiving funding and work with it to ensure that the funding doesn’t reach those groups.
In response to that change, the State Department in 2020 established the Israel Leahy Vetting Forum — a panel of Middle East and human rights experts in the State Department — to investigate potential human rights abuses by Israeli soldiers and determine eligibility for U.S. military funding. Yet, the panel appears to have moved slowly. The State Department’s inspector general found in 2025, two years after the start of the Israel-Hamas war, that the panel had not finalized standard operating procedures, which led to delays in investigating and deciding on potential human rights abuses by Israeli units.
The report said it would take 12.5 years for the panel to go through the backlog of alleged violations. The report did not say how far back the cases go, but it said the human rights abuse allegations have grown since the start of the Israel-Hamas war in October 2023. These delays and lack of clear rules “raised the risk that security assistance could be provided to an ineligible unit,” the report said.
The U.S. government has never publicly said an Israeli military group is ineligible for aid under the law, and there’s no record it has provided a list of ineligible units to Israel. Charles Blaha, who oversaw the State Department’s Office of Security and Human Rights from 2016 to 2023, said the failure to provide a list of ineligible units to Israel violates the Leahy law.
“What all this shows is that the State Department is violating the law by basically refusing to adjudicate units for Israel,” he said.
Blaha is a senior adviser for DAWN, a human rights advocacy organization focused on the Middle East. DAWN is involved in an ongoing lawsuit accusing the U.S. State Department of violating the Leahy law by not investigating violations or providing a list of ineligible units to Israel.
“This is mostly an issue of law, but one where most experts and Leahy Law authorities agree that the Leahy Law has not been applied to Israel in the manner that it is normally applied to other countries,” said John Ramming Chappell, a senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy.
The State Department under President Joe Biden said it applied the same standards to Israel as other countries under Leahy laws. Lawyers for the State Department under Trump have argued that decisions about cutting off aid are under the secretary of state’s discretion. A State Department spokesperson told PolitiFact the department is continuing to implement the Leahy laws, and did not provide additional details.
Biden administration identified violations
Under President Joe Biden, the State Department announced in 2024 that it had found five Israeli units had committed gross human rights violations in incidents before the start of the Israel-Hamas war on Oct. 7, 2023.
Department officials said four units had addressed the violations, and a fifth — the ultra-Orthodox Netzah Yehuda Battalion — was in the process. There was no pause in weapons transfers, and Netzah Yehuda wasn’t formally sanctioned.
The four resolved incidents involved cases of extrajudicial killing and rape, with punishments ranging from long prison sentences to community service.
The Netzah Yehuda incident involved the death of 78-year-old Omar Assad, an American citizen and Palestinian. In 2022, soldiers detained Assad in the West Bank and left him bound and gagged at a construction site, where he died of a heart attack. Two officers were disciplined, but no one was charged.
Blaha wrote in a 2024 article that the State Department wouldn’t consider the response to the Netzah Yehuda incident as adequate remediation if it were done by another country.
Leahy, who left the Senate in 2023, criticized the State Department’s handling of those cases in 2024. He said the State Department’s ruling that only five Israeli security forces had committed gross human rights violations “makes a mockery of the law.”
This story was originally published on PolitiFact.com.
It is republished here as part of a reporting and fact-checking partnership between PolitiFact and Hearst Television.

title: White Sox’s Will Venable beats out Red Sox’s Chad Tracy for AL Manager of the Year
text:
Will Venable won the AL Manager of the Year award after the Chicago White Sox made the playoffs this year following three 100-loss seasons in a row.
The White Sox became the first team in major league history to reach the playoffs after consecutive 100-loss seasons. Only the third of those came under Venable after he took over in 2025. Chicago went 84-78 this year.
Pat Murphy from first-time World Series champion Milwaukee was among the NL finalists along with Philadelphia’s Don Mattingly and Atlanta’s Walt Weiss. Murphy was seeking later Tuesday night to become the first manager in either league to win the award three years in a row. The Brewers had an MLB-high 103 wins during the regular season.
Venable got 15 of 30 first-place votes and 111 points in balloting by the Baseball Writers’ Association of America that was conducted before the postseason and announced Tuesday night. The other AL finalists were two-time winner Kevin Cash of the AL champion Tampa Bay Rays, who got 12 first-place votes and 98 points, and Chad Tracy, who took over the Boston Red Sox in April and led them to the playoffs.
Venable, a former big league outfielder, got his first managerial job when the White Sox were coming off 121 losses in 2024 and 101 the previous season. They went 60-102 in Venable’s debut and followed that this season by making the playoffs for the first time since 2021.
After sweeping Houston in two games on the road in the AL Wild Card Series, they had a 2-0 series lead before losing a five-game AL Division Series to Cleveland.
Before he was hired by the White Sox, Venable was on manager Bruce Bochy’s staff in Texas and was part of the Rangers’ only World Series title in 2023.
Venable is first White Sox manager to win the award since Ozzie Guillen in 2005.
Tracy went 77-58 after taking over when the Red Sox fired Alex Cora on April 25. Boston struggled early in Tracy’s tenure before a 27-3 stretch from July 3-Aug. 8 vaulted it into playoff contention. That stretch included a franchise-recording tying 15-game winning streak.
Boston removed the interim tag and gave Tracy a three-year contract on Sept. 22.
Venable earned 15 first-place votes and finished with 111 total. Cash was second with 12 first-place votes. Tracy earned three first-place votes and finished third.

title: Democrats plan to use new power to rein in Trump’s education agenda, but their tools are limited
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Democrats in Congress are preparing to flex their soon-to-be majorities in opposition to some of President Donald Trump’s marquee education policies, starting with the dismantling of the U.S. Education Department. But with Trump threatening to use his veto power, they may be limited to opening investigations and using federal funding as leverage.
The White House has given no sign of backing away from its campaigns to close the department and to end diversity, equity and inclusion policies. But Democrats are preparing to use their oversight and appropriations powers to push back against Trump administration decisions that have reverberated through schools and universities.
Rep. Bobby Scott of Virginia, the top Democrat on the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, said he plans to “leave no rock unturned” as he takes the helm of the panel’s investigative powers, which include authority to issue subpoenas and hold hearings.
The committee is preparing to explore the Trump administration’s dismantling of the Education Department, its oversight of federal student loans and its anti-discrimination policies, Scott said. Under Trump, the Education Department has prioritized investigations into transgender issues while backing away from addressing systemic racism in schools.
A day after the midterm elections, Scott sent a letter to 10 federal agencies reminding them to preserve records that might become part of a congressional review.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, called on Democrats to “hold the Trump administration accountable for dismantling the Department of Education and turning its back on students.”
Trump officials denounced Democrats’ plans, with Education Department spokesperson Savannah Newhouse saying they’re plotting to “prematurely sabotage” Education Secretary Linda McMahon. White House spokesperson Liz Huston accused Democrats of failing American students with “disastrous leadership” before Trump returned to office.
Investigations aren’t likely to stop Trump agenda
Congressional investigations can be used to apply political pressure and uncover how decisions were made, but they are unlikely to present a substantial brake on Trump’s education policies that have outraged Democrats over the last two years. And with Trump pledging to veto Democratic bills he sees as harmful, there’s little optimism for legislative countermeasures.
“We’re very happy that this Congress is unlikely to pass legislation like the legislation that was passed last year,” said Diana Autin, executive director of the SPAN Parent Advocacy Network, a nonprofit based in Newark, New Jersey.
Still, she said, “it’s not very likely that they will be able to undo the harm that’s already been done.”
Democrats on the Senate Appropriations Committee are exploring harder checks through the budgeting process. Some are planning to add conditions to spending bills aimed at reining in the Trump administration’s education agenda.
“I think there will be an interest in using the power of the purse to establish guardrails and prevent these abusive practices,” Sen. Chris Van Hollen, a Maryland Democrat on the Appropriations Committee, told The Associated Press.
Last year, Democrats failed to secure broad language in a funding bill to block further dismantling of the Education Department. Now, with majorities in both chambers, they’re preparing to try again. Van Hollen described it as one avenue to “stop the bleeding” but not necessarily to reverse the dismantling that has been done.
“It’s a little harder to try to rebuild an entity just through an appropriations bill,” he said. “But we can certainly try to prevent further damage and then seek to reverse the harm that’s been done.”
There’s also interest in conditioning federal funding to rein in Trump’s battle to reshape higher education, Van Hollen said, including the White House’s repeated efforts to cut funding at Harvard and other prestigious universities. “That said,” he added, “we’re dealing with an administration that has demonstrated no respect for the law.”
Education advocates are pushing Democrats to go a step further. Some hope to see appropriations language ordering the administration to reverse decisions moving Education Department functions to other agencies, including one that put special education programs under the Department of Health and Human Services, and another that put the investigation of school discrimination claims under the Justice Department.
“I think it’s going to become more and more apparent that they don’t have the authority just to keep dismantling some of these offices,” said Aaron Ament, president of the advocacy group Student Defense, which is representing plaintiffs in a lawsuit challenging the dismantling of the Education Department.
Some want Democrats to pass bills, despite veto threat
Some advocates are hoping the next Congress will be in place in time to approve the nomination of a replacement for Harmeet Dhillon, an assistant attorney general who spearheaded the Justice Department’s sweeping investigations into elite universities. She announced her resignation last Thursday in the wake of the midterms. Alarming to some education advocates, however, is Trump’s decision promoting Stephen Miller, the architect of some of Trump’s most hard-line policies, to chief of staff.
Todd Wolfson, president of the American Association of University Professors, said that the higher education environment was so tough that the organization endorsed candidates for the first time during the midterms. Those candidates included Abdul El-Sayed, a former professor, who won a bitter campaign for Michigan’s open Senate seat. Now, Wolfson is looking not just at reversing some of what has happened during the Trump administration, but building a campaign for a free public higher education system.
“Most other countries have figured this out, and we can too,” Wolfson said.
But with Trump’s veto power, such a change is unlikely in the next two years.
Trump’s second term in office has been marked by seismic change in education policy. Trump officials cut the Education Department’s staff by nearly half and signed intergovernmental agreements parceling its top duties to other agencies. In higher education, the administration has mounted a battle to eliminate DEI practices and curb international enrollment, using federal funding as leverage to advance policies favored by the White House.
Yet education issues receded to the background in midterm elections that became a referendum on Trump’s deeply unpopular economic policies and the Iran war. As Democrats sort out a vast oversight agenda, education is expected to fall farther down the list of priorities, behind big topics like Trump’s self-enrichment and federal immigration raids.
Despite their new power, there’s little optimism that Democrats will be able to override Trump’s veto on big education bills. Some advocates want lawmakers to try anyway.
“Even if he vetoes them, let’s put the pressure on to get it to his desk, and then you see what the contrast is,” said Randi Weingarten, president of the American Federation of Teachers union.
Some on the right are pushing for last-minute legislation to advance Trump’s agenda. A day after the midterms, the Heritage Foundation asked Republican lawmakers to propose a bill to close the Education Department and strip any mention of it from federal law. In what amounts to a political Hail Mary, the group argued the agency has failed to prove its value since it opened in 1980.
The letter asked Republicans to collaborate with McMahon “to sunset this failed bureaucracy.”
___
Hollingsworth reported from Mission, Kansas.

title: Obituary: Madeline K. Whitney
text:
KNOXVILLE, Tenn. / PORTLAND – Madeline K. Whitney, 88, passed away on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026, at Fort Sanders Regional Medical Center in Knoxville, Tenn.
Born in 1938, Madeline grew up on a small farm in St. Vincent, Ark., as the ninth of 10 children. She graduated from Wonderview High School and began a life journey that first took her to Little Rock, Ark., where she found employment as an operator for the Bell Telephone Company. It was there that she met and married Jack Whitney, her husband of 60 years.
In 1962, Jack and Madeline moved to Bangor, where she continued her career with the telephone company, eventually advancing to the position of group manager. They later moved to Portland in 1980, where Madeline eventually retired from Verizon.
Madeline was an avid runner, winning age-group state championships in multiple events. Always willing to lend a hand to those in need, she volunteered tirelessly in her church and community.
Madeline was preceded in death by her devoted husband of 60 years, John “Jack” Whitney.
She is survived by her sister, Marie Labrie; her son, Joe Whitney, her daughter-in-law, Linda Whitney; her granddaughter, Samantha Teixeira, and her husband, Brian; two great-granddaughters, Alice and Emma; her lifelong best friend, Rose (Rodie) Rohlman; and numerous cousins, nieces, nephews, and friends in both Maine and Arkansas.
Services are being planned, with details to be announced at a later date.

title: Maine football returns from bye week to face No. 25 UAlbany
text:
ORONO, Maine (WABI) - Maine football is back after a bye week for the home stretch of the regular season.
The Black Bears spoke about how they spent the bye week to improve.
“I took the bye week, get some extra prep, watch a little bit of extra film. Saturday morning, we got to turn on and watch the Albany-Bryant game. It was good to get a little leg up, not only in the preparation, but also getting some rest and recovery, catching up on maybe some missed sleep and just taking care of your body,” said Anthony Iliano, redshirt junior offensive lineman.
Maine returns to action after a 14-13 road loss to Rhode Island where a blocked extra point cost them the game in overtime.
“After any game, you’re just excited for the next game, especially the way that one ended. You want to get back out there and compete again,” said Jordan Stevens, head coach.
The Black Bears leave Alfond Stadium for the last time this season when they go to UAlbany on Saturday at Noon. The Great Danes are 6-4, but ranked No. 25 in the country.
“(They’ve got a) great offensive line, good running backs, and just a solid offensive room overall. We’ve got to just bear down and be ready to fight,” said Kye Pressley, redshirt junior defensive lineman.
“These guys have just continued to work extremely hard this year, practice hard, and have a positive attitude towards going to play Albany. (We’ve) got to do a great job just fundamentally and can’t put ourselves in positions where we beat ourselves. How do you beat yourself? It’s when you turn the ball over. We’ve got to take care of the football. They’re probably one of the best teams I’ve seen this year at forcing takeaways on their defense,” said Stevens.
Maine will try to end its eight-game losing streak with a road win over a ranked team.
The Black Bears finish the regular season after the UAlbany trip by hosting New Hampshire in the Battle for the Brice-Cowell Musket on Saturday of next weekend at 1 p.m.

HALLOWELL, Maine (WABI) -The Quarry Tap Room will keep its liquor license after a vote by the Hallowell City Council on Monday night.
The council approved the license with one member recusing themselves.
Police chief reverses recommendation
Police Chief Zachary Kindelan said officers have responded to 15 incidents at the Tap Room. Eleven of them ended in an arrest or summons.
Kindelan had originally recommended against renewing the license. He reversed course after meeting with bar staff Monday.
Supporters fill meeting
Supporters filled the Community Theatre, where the council meeting was held. Employees and residents spoke about what the establishment means to them and its impact on the community.
“We feel great. You know, all along we felt we didn’t really do anything wrong. It was unfortunate. Social media kind of took over the firestorm and created a whole lot of buzz,” said Steven Lachance, co-owner of the Quarry Tap Room.
No one spoke against the license renewal during the public comment period.

title: Letter to the Editor: The Governed have spoken
Missing 11-month-old found, survived 24 hours after father buried him alive in a dog crate, sheriff says
text:
LEXINGTON COUNTY, S.C. (WIS/Gray News) — Authorities in South Carolina said an 11-month-old baby miraculously survived after they believe his father buried him alive in a dog crate.
Koah Sharpe was found alive Tuesday afternoon just over 24 hours after he was last seen with his father, 25-year-old Michael Comer.
Lexington County Sheriff Jay Koon said Koah was found buried in a dog crate wrapped in a towel.
“By the grace of God, [it] probably provided enough air for him to survive an estimated 24 hours under that dirt,” Koon said.
The sheriff said Comer’s mother was caring for the child when Comer arrived at the home on Monday. She then left Koah in Comer’s care while another caregiver was on the way.
“By the time the caregiver got there, Michael was gone and Koah was gone with him,” Koon said.
Other members of Koah’s family filed a missing persons report Monday afternoon. Koon said authorities went to the nearby home of Comer’s father, where they found both doors open and Koah’s belongings, but no sign of either Comer or Koah.
Authorities also believe Comer was in multiple locations across Lexington County on Monday, but they said that he does not have access to a vehicle. That is why an Amber Alert was never issued.
“To be able to issue an Amber Alert, you have to have a known description of a car and a license plate to put that out,” Koon explained Tuesday.
The sheriff said it’s believed Comer asked for rides to get from place to place. Video footage also pointed to Comer being in the Batesburg-Leesville area, but with no baby.
Authorities arrested Comer Monday night on a burglary charge after finding him in a shed in Batesburg. Koah, however, was not with him.
The search for the 11-month-old extended into Tuesday, with local, state and federal agencies joining the search.
Koon said it wasn’t until authorities looked near Comer’s father’s house that they found pine straw and “freshly disturbed dirt.” Once they started digging, they heard Koah crying.
“So, as you imagine, the race was on,” Koon said. “Everybody’s getting down there trying to get him out.”
Koon said it’s believed that Koah was buried for around 24 hours.
“It [the dog crate] was buried, and it was wrapped with a towel. So probably created an air pocket, if you can imagine,” Koon said.
The sheriff said Koah is being treated at a hospital. Comer, meanwhile, remains in custody as of Tuesday afternoon.
Comer’s arrest comes just over a month after he was placed on probation following a guilty plea for aggravated breach of peace, according to public court and state records.
Court records also show Comer had previous arrests earlier this year for domestic violence, as well as a weapons-related charge.

title: Wild River Fire in the White Mountains is now more than half contained
text:
White Mountains wildfire now more than half contained
The Wild River Fire in the White Mountains is now more than half contained, officials announced on Tuesday morning.
The update from the White Mountain National Forest said the fire was 53% contained and was listed at 821 acres. The Wild River Fire was first reported the afternoon of Nov. 1, just southeast of Gorham, New Hampshire, and just south of Gilead, Maine, near Evans Notch.
Firefighters said on Tuesday that their lines were holding along more parts of the perimeter and they were working to secure and tie together the containment line. Crews continued to monitor and evaluate more hot spots and conduct mop-up operations.
A total of 88 personnel were still battling the fire, down from more than 140 at one point.
On Wednesday, the Forest Service issued a closure order that was still in effect on Tuesday. Click here to see a map of the closure.
On Thursday, officials revealed that they believed the fire was caused by humans. A community meeting was held that evening to share information with people who live in the area and to answer questions.
Another public information meeting about the Wild River Fire is scheduled from 6 to 7 p.m. Tuesday at Shelburne Town Hall at 74 Village Road in Shelburne, New Hampshire. People can also attend the meeting virtually through Microsoft Teams. Click here for the Teams link for Tuesday's meeting.

title: InvestigateTV+: Vanishing wetlands threaten haven for migrating birds
text:
(InvestigateTV) — InvestigateTV+ takes you to the mouth of the Mississippi River for an in-depth look at the multi-million-dollar fight to save a disappearing coastline.
Plus, a surgical nightmare that left one Georgia mother fighting for her life, and the questions her case raises about medical accountability.
Then, the inspiring story of an artist creating miniature wonders that bring big joy.
A threatened migration
In the winter months, birds journey down the Mississippi Flyway, a migratory superhighway for more than 300 species. Annual surveys estimate 3 million snow geese choose Louisiana and Texas for their wintertime retreats.
Yet no place on the continental U.S. loses wetlands at the rate Louisiana is shedding its coast.
Robotic surgery leads to lawsuit
An Atlanta mother checked into the hospital for a hysterectomy, expecting to be home from that same day. Instead, she didn’t leave for nearly three months.
Star Button had persistent pain and excessive bleeding for years. The chronic issues interrupted every part of her life, including work.
Doctors confirmed the issues stemmed from fibroids, or noncancerous tumors. To get rid of them, Button opted for a robotic hysterectomy at Southern Regional Medical Center.
Side hustle apps
Apps that let people rent out things they already own are offering users a way to earn extra cash without taking on an in-person part-time job.
Hand-painted seashells
An ordained minister, Gil Ames has not let anything get in the way of his passion for painting. He volunteered with the Red Cross at 52 national disasters, including ground zero in New York.
He also spent 25 years as a long-haul truck driver. He pivoted to something more portable to paint on during that time.

title: Maine men’s basketball falls to Rhode Island
text:
Dylan Williamson scored eight straight points late in the second half and Rhode Island held on to beat the University of Maine 71-65 in a men’s basketball game on Tuesday night in Kingston, Rhode Island.
The Black Bears (1-3) lead by nine points with 10:06 left in the first half and by six early in the second. The Rams (3-0) took a 59-56 lead with 5:32 left on a 3-pointer by Williamson and never trailed again.
Williamson’s layup with 3:26 left started his run that stretched URI’s lead to nine.
The Black Bears closed to within five on a 3-pointer by Darius Lopes with 12 seconds left, but didn’t score again.
Williamson finished with 18 points, including 15 in the second half, and five assists. Jason Fontenet II added 13 points and 12 rebounds.
Deandre Williams and Lopes each scored 13 points for Maine. Ayden Evans added 10 points. Newport native Ace Flagg scored seven points.

title: Precautions Urged Amid Rising Heating Costs
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AROOSTOOK COUNTY, Maine (WAGM) -As county residents look for ways to manage heating costs, county officials are reminding locals to make safety a priority. Rising heating costs are driving more people to alternative heating methods. Whether you rely on a furnace, a woodstove or a space heater, local emergency officials say taking precautions can help protect your home from a fire.
Derrick Lamothe, a Firefighter and EMT for Caribou Fire & Ambulance says: “You need to make sure that the way you’re gonna do it is safe and get your furnace, get whatever heating source you’re gonna have tuned up to make sure that it’s gonna run properly and safely.”
Officials say there are several precautions to keep in mind when using alternative heat sources.
“Making sure your chimney’s clean. We see a lot of chimney fires due to not cleaning your chimney and that can turn into a full-blown house fire very quickly. Making sure that there’s no kids or anything playing around the woodstove. You know, some people will put stuff over the woodstove to dry. I would not recommend doing that. If something falls on the stove it can turn catastrophic very quickly,” continued Lamothe.
“Space heaters, make sure you’re not plugging those into extension cords. They should be directly plugged into the wall and then make sure you’ve got a good space around them. We see all the time people that have items too close to space heaters as well as things like wood stoves, kerosene stoves. So, make sure that you have adequate spacing around them. So, you don’t cause a fire inadvertently in your home,” added Darren Woods, Director of the Aroostook E.M.A.
Officials say winterizing your home can also help reduce heating costs.
“We’re all looking at these high fuel prices. We’re all trying to find ways that we can survive through a winter where we have high costs. Anything you can do in your home that would reduce the need for more heat. Things like putting plastic on your windows, putting foam covering over your pipes. Anything you can do to winterize your home that would make it a little bit more efficient would certainly help you be more comfortable and save you a few dollars,” continued Woods.
I asked Caribou fire officials if they expect more fires this season as residents look for more ways to stay warm. Lamothe said: “We hope not but it’s always kind of on our mind that people are gonna do whatever they can to stay warm.”
Emergency officials say keeping these safety tips in mind and paying close attention to your heat sources could help prevent fires this winter.
