title: Aroostook educator’s YA novel teaches inner resilience
text:
When Aroostook teacher Sara McQuarrie was a kid, she was always drawn to survival stories. But when she wrote a young adult novel, she wanted it to be more than that.
She wanted kids to know they could do hard things.
“I especially wanted the story to speak to young people who may have experienced difficult circumstances or have been made to feel that somehow they weren’t enough,” McQuarrie said. “Sometimes children carry burdens that were never theirs to carry, and I wanted to convey that those experiences don’t diminish who they are.”
Rooted in a lifelong love of the outdoors, McQuarrie’s debut novel, “Strength Hidden,” is set in the rugged Maine woods, weaving the details of Maine’s natural history with themes of wilderness survival and personal resilience. As kids struggle with personal challenges, internet-created isolation and a tumultuous world, such lessons can be helpful, she said.
McQuarrie, a certified interpretive guide with the National Association for Interpretation, a Maine master naturalist and a Houlton middle school teacher, took five years to write the book. The story details the survival story of Andromeda, better known to young readers as Andy.
She worked to give the tale layers so kids could learn about why survival was important to Andy. She wanted readers to care about her and to have an emotional response to what they were reading, she said.
Andy’s harrowing story of surviving in the deep wilderness after running from an abusive foster home lets kids know that the strength, courage and worth they need are already within them, even if they haven’t discovered it yet, McQuarrie said.
Throughout the story, Andy learns that she has more strength and courage than she thinks and that she was treated poorly because of the people who were doing it, not because she deserved it, she said.
“I think in situations where children are abandoned, they often take it to heart and assume it was their fault,” McQuarrie said. “I wanted kids who were reading it to start thinking, ‘Maybe it wasn’t my fault. Maybe I can do hard things.’”
After many edits over the years, McQuarrie showed the story to a small group of family and friends who encouraged her to publish it, she said.
Published by Maine Authors Publishing in September 2025, “Strength Hidden” was just honored with the Gold Medal in Young Adult Fiction at the Independent Publisher Book Awards and the Moonbeam Children’s Book Awards Outstanding Book of the Year.
The Independent Publisher Book Awards were created to bring increased recognition to exemplary independent, university, and self-published books. A panel of judges — including librarians, booksellers, reviewers and designers — evaluated thousands of entries from around the world. The awards, known as IPPYs, spotlight books that break new ground and make meaningful contributions to literature and culture, according to a release.
The Moonbeam Children’s Book Awards honor exceptional new titles that ignite imagination, promote a love for reading and celebrate artistry and innovation in children’s literature. The awards showcase books that serve as invaluable resources for fostering creativity, empathy, and critical thinking, the release stated.
“I was wicked excited,” McQuarrie said when she first heard about the awards, never expecting to win.
At the time, the McQuarries were on vacation this summer and she ran down the hall to her daughter, saying, “Guess what?”
“Strength Hidden” is available online through major retailers and select local booksellers. To learn more about Sara McQuarrie, her books, or upcoming local events, visit saramcquarrie.com.
Beyond writing and teaching, McQuarrie shares her passion for nature through the Twin Ponds
Nature and Discovery Center on her property in Hodgdon, where she hosts hands-on nature
programs for local youth.
“Nature has always been a central part of my life, and sharing that connection to the outdoors through story is wonderfully rewarding,” she said. “I hope ‘Strength Hidden’ encourages readers to step outside, embrace challenges and discover their own inner resilience.”

title: Tennessee seeks to block Christa Pike's attorneys from inspecting drug used in failed execution
text:
Tennessee is seeking to block Christa Pike’s attorneys from accessing the lethal injection drug used in her failed execution on the grounds that it would reveal the supplier in violation of state law, court filings show.
The request follows a judge’s order to preserve evidence in a lawsuit filed by Pike’s attorneys and reflects the secrecy surrounding execution drugs, which states often argue is necessary to protect access to the drugs and the safety of suppliers.
Pike, 50, survived two doses of pentobarbital in September, which her attorneys say probably did not enter her bloodstream correctly and instead pooled in her arms, leaving them burned and blistered. The state has said it is complying with a broader order by Judge I’Ashea L. Myles requiring the preservation of evidence.
But in a Friday court filing, the state asked the judge to rescind the part of her order allowing Pike’s legal team to inspect, collect and test any leftover pentobarbital from the execution attempt.
Tennessee Department of Correction fears it will lose its lethal drug supplier
In an affidavit cited in the state’s filing, a Tennessee Department of Correction employee said the drug supplier would become identifiable if Pike’s legal team is allowed to handle vials of pentobarbital left over from the execution attempt, or review the vials’ labeling. The employee, whose name was not disclosed, wrote that residue of the pentobarbital used in Pike’s botched execution is “most likely to be found” in vials of the substance used in the attempted execution.
The employee stated the state’s supplier was concerned that even with redactions on the labels, the source of the pentobarbital would be identifiable. The employee said that another supplier had stopped communicating with the department in 2024 after its identity was exposed and that the state would likely be unable to find other providers if it lost access to its current source for the drug.
“Pike’s counsel and experts cannot be allowed to see, handle, or otherwise get the information on the leftover vials of pentobarbital from Pike’s attempted execution,” Tennessee Attorney General Jonathan Skrmetti wrote in a court filing.
Tennessee law prohibits the public disclosure of any individual or entity involved in procuring lethal substances or carrying out executions.
Pike’s attorney says accessing the lethal drug is key
Luke Ihnen, a lawyer representing Pike, said that publicly identifying the state’s lethal injection drug supplier “has never been the goal” of the litigation.
He said that it is important for Pike’s legal team to be able to review how the pentobarbital used in her botched execution was labeled and stored to understand if there were issues with how it was mixed, transported or handled, and whether it was expired.
“We still don’t know exactly what happened that night,” Ihnen said. “Those types of things are all valuable pieces of information about what went wrong.”
Tennessee Department of Correction spokesperson Dorinda Carter declined to comment, citing pending litigation.
Governor-elect calls for alternative methods of execution
Pike was hospitalized on a ventilator for days following the failed execution. She has returned to prison and said she remains in constant pain.
Pike and her boyfriend tortured and stabbed a 19-year-old classmate, Colleen Slemmer, to death in 1995. Pike was 18 at the time, making her one of the youngest women sentenced to death. Slemmer’s mother had traveled from Florida to witness Pike’s execution.
Frank Strada, commissioner of the Department of Correction, announced his resignation in the wake of Pike’s failed execution. The governor named Christopher Hansen as interim commissioner.
Pike’s attorneys want Republican Gov. Bill Lee, who is set to leave office in January, to change her death sentence to life in prison. He has said that she will remain on death row unless a court determines otherwise. U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the state’s Republican governor-elect, has called for the state to explore alternative methods of execution, including the electric chair.
The governor has tapped a former U.S. attorney to conduct an independent review of the failed execution, and postponed the state’s other lethal injection scheduled for this year.
___
Brook is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues

title: ‘A lot of people knew her’: 18-year-old college freshman found dead in her dorm room
text:
WICHITA, Kan. (KWCH/Gray News) - A first-year student-athlete has been found dead in her dorm room over the weekend at Newman University.
According to the university, a resident found 18-year-old McKenzie Rohr, a member of Newman’s new track and field team, in her room on Sunday.
First responders were called to the scene where she was pronounced dead.
The Sedgwick County Medical Examiner’s Office said it was working to determine the 18-year-old’s cause of death.
Newman University President Kathleen Jagger noted there was no indication of suicide and that an investigation is underway.
Jagger said the university did not have all the details surrounding Rohr’s death.
“It’s just a tragedy. And whenever you lose a young person, no matter the age, you know it seems premature, and no one’s ready for it,” Jagger added.
First-year student Vincent Cuhlman said Rohr was dedicated to athletics and her studies.
“A lot of people knew her as a good friend to be around,” he said.
A candle was burning in the university chapel in Rohr’s memory. Newman staff said they were also providing additional therapists and religious resources for students who needed support.
“It’s a big change, and it’s a lot to unpack,” Ba Nguyen, a second-year Newman student, said. “That’s why it’s really necessary to talk to people about it.”
The university confirmed a memorial service for Rohr has also been planned for Wednesday night.
Jagger asked for prayers for Rohr’s family, friends and the university community.

title: Bar Harbor Historical Society to restructure following layoffs
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BAR HARBOR — It has been nearly two weeks since the Bar Harbor Historical Society laid off its entire staff. What lies ahead for the 80-year-old nonprofit now?
The simplest answer is that the organization is restructuring, explained board president Dick Cough, but it was not a simple or pain-free process to get there.
In total, five positions were eliminated. Three were full-time, and two were part-time. The board hired a human resources professional to guide them through the process, said Cough, “to ensure we handled things as thoughtfully as we could under the circumstances and to assure our employees had the best advice upon departure.” Cough said that each employee was given the equivalent of two weeks’ pay as severance.
The board will spend its winter working on a restructuring plan and has every intention of opening the doors to its historic mansion-turned-museum in the spring, said Cough. Any spring hiring decisions would be made after an operational assessment is conducted. In the meantime, the board will run the day-to-day operations.
“We have a strong team of board members made up of successful business leaders and those with extensive experience overseeing organizations with large archival collections, as well as decades of experience in museum operations, management, and marketing,” said Cough. “Over the winter, board members will be monitoring the museum and ensuring the protection of our collection of more than 20,000 objects and the mansion.”
The board will also lean on its large volunteer base to help it open in the spring. “Our exhibits will remain relevant, authentic and of great interest to locals and tourists alike as usual.”
The society, which operates from May through October, relies primarily on grant and foundation money, as well as donations, rental fees and ticket sales to meet its bottom line.
Over the last few years, it has become more of a challenge to maintain the organization in the present form, explained Cough. “The world around us has changed significantly over the years, impacting how people spend their time and museum visitation.” He said that under the present model, the organization has lost money year over year and “it is our fiduciary duty as Directors to all who support us to run a fiscally responsible business.”
The organization’s tax filings bear that out. In 2024, the most recent year that IRS Form 990 figures are available, the organization reported an operating loss of $128,000. The year before, the organization reported an operating loss of $63,000. Those numbers have not improved in the last two years, confirmed Cough, leading to what he describes as the “painful decision” to eliminate its staff.
“We recognize the very real impact this has on the individuals affected and are deeply grateful for their contributions to BHHS over the years,” said Cough.
In 2024, the organization listed its highest-paid employee at $70,000. That year, it also reported approximately $230,000 in other salaries, benefits and payroll taxes, bringing its total staffing spend to $300,000.
The society moved into La Rochelle in 2019, purchasing the 41-room, 13,000-square waterfront mansion for $4.75 million from Maine Seacoast Mission. Originally built in 1903, the building was donated to the Mission by Tristram and Ruth Colket in 1972.

title: Hallowell passes data center moratorium
text:
HALLOWELL — The city has joined a slew of Maine cities and towns enacting moratoriums on data center development following a unanimous City Council vote Monday.
The new ordinance will ban any data center developments for 180 days as city officials work to develop a longer-term plan regulating — or completely banning — the facilities.
Only one person spoke during the ordinance public hearing, voicing support for the moratorium.
John Merrill, owner of Merrill’s Bookshop, said he supported the moratorium and urged councilors to next adopt a total ban on data centers, citing problems with air and water pollution and water usage.
“The more you learn about them, the more concerned you are and the more you realize they don’t make good neighbors,” Merrill said. “Any community that agrees to allow these into the neighborhood, you’re allowing your neighbors to suffer a lot of problems.”
After Gov. Janet Mills vetoed a bill that would enact a statewide data center moratorium in May, many towns across the state have passed or are considering data center moratoriums on the local level.
The Hallowell Conservation Commission urged the City Council to adopt a moratorium in September, emphasizing the need for proper safeguards to protect residents and the environment before moving forward.
In a letter to the council, Conservation Commission Chair Hilary Neckles raised concerns about data centers’ significant use of electricity, water, land and local infrastructure in addition to questions about pollution, noise, emergency response, tax agreements and high electricity prices.
Neckles said Mills’ veto “left municipalities to fend for themselves” and said she still hopes to see statewide regulations in the future.
On Monday, city councilors voted unanimously to approve the second and third readings of the ordinance, making it official.
Now, city officials have six months to hear from residents, evaluate concerns and develop a proposed ordinance regulating, or even restricting, potential data center developments.

title: Kings of Leon Played Maine Before Their Biggest Hits Came Out

title: DoorDash driver mysteriously disappeared after making his last delivery, reports say
text:
BEAVER COUNTY, Pa. (Gray News) - Authorities are searching for a DoorDash driver who disappeared after making deliveries last month in Pennsylvania.
Zachariah Schuck, 32, was last seen on the evening of Oct. 22 while working in the Monaca area, according to North Sewickley police.
Investigators said Schuck completed his last known DoorDash delivery at about 6:30 p.m. His cellphone signal was lost around 8 p.m., and he has not been heard from since, WTAE reported.
Schuck was last seen between 7:30 and 8 p.m. near Route 51 in Monaca. Authorities later found his vehicle abandoned. Police have not released details about any evidence recovered from the car.
Police describe Schuck as 6 feet tall and approximately 160 pounds, with brown hair and green eyes. He was last seen wearing a blue and red flannel shirt, blue jeans and brown boots.
The circumstances of Schuck’s disappearance remain unclear. Investigators have not said whether foul play is suspected.

title: Letter: Susan Collins is not in the same league as Maine’s famed leaders
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
A week since the election, it’s clear to me that Susan Collins, the reporters and opinion editor of this paper are still looking for excuses outside of her control for her loss, rather than at the consequences of her choices, actions, and lack of political courage. Instead of giving credit to Troy Jackson for a skillful 100-day grassroots campaign that accurately communicated voter concerns or acknowledging his deep legislative experience and strong working class network, all of the focus has been on Collins.
I feel her 30-year record has never been objectively evaluated in comparison with that of other notable Maine or national senators for positive lasting legislative accomplishment or leadership ability. Her 100% voting record is meaningless unless the impact of those votes is considered. There is no Ed Muskie’s Clean Water Act, no George Mitchell as Senate Majority Leader, or Bill Cohen’s brave freshman vote to impeach President Richard Nixon.
Then of course there is Margaret Chase Smith and her Declaration of Conscience. That Collins now claims her huge defeat puts her in the same league, when her lack of political courage is why many former supporters abandoned her, speaks volumes about her idea of her job.
She took an oath to uphold and defend the Constitution and “advise and consent” not just bring home the bacon. Understanding this might have saved her or at least salvaged her legacy.
Judy Bielecki
Belgrade

title: NASA launches $1M moon base challenge for students
text:
NASA launches $1M moon base challenge for students
NASA launches $1M moon base challenge for students
NASA is inviting student teams at U.S. high schools and postsecondary schools to develop ideas for a future lunar base as part of a $1 million competition.
The agency announced the Moon Base Student Challenge on Sunday during a MAX POWER event at the Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex in Florida. Registration is open through Jan. 25, 2027, via the NASA STEM Gateway.
Related video above: New space mission set to explore Mars' moons
The multiphase competition asks teams to propose solutions in six areas: power generation and storage, construction, life-support systems, surface mobility, communications networks and astronaut safety.
"We’re looking for students ready to think creatively, work as a team, and take on real problems connected to NASA’s future on the Moon," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said. "You do not have to wait until graduation to contribute."
NASA envisions a base in the moon’s south polar region where astronauts could live, work and explore. The agency says a sustained human presence on the moon would help prepare for future crewed missions to Mars.
Students will work with environmental and mission-design parameters relevant to lunar operations. Their assignments will include trade studies, concept proposals and stakeholder briefings, giving them experience with skills used in the space industry. NASA said prior specialized engineering or technical experience is not required.
"Students bring exactly the bold ideas that we’re looking for, and I’m looking forward to their fresh perspective," said Carlos García-Galán, manager of NASA’s Moon Base Program.
NASA’s Office of STEM Engagement designed the challenge with the Moon Base Program. The Institute of Competition Sciences administers it under a NASA contract. Participants must register for the challenge through the NASA STEM Gateway. Registration will be open until Jan. 25, 2027.
Competition details, eligibility requirements and official rules are available on the Moon Base Challenge website.

title: Augusta council approves preliminary deal to process Hatch Hill trash in Hampden
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - The Augusta City Council approved a preliminary agreement with Municipal Waste Solutions to change how trash is handled at Hatch Hill, the regional landfill serving the city and seven surrounding communities.
Municipal Waste Solutions would process Augusta’s waste at a facility in Hampden.
How the proposal would work
Under the proposal, most household waste brought to Hatch Hill would be hauled to Hampden. Recyclable materials would be recovered there without residents having to separate them from their trash.
Recycling goals
City Manager Jared Mills said the plan could improve Augusta’s recycling rates and contribute to Maine’s goal of recycling 50% of the state’s municipal waste.
“What we’re doing now in Augusta, we recycle even with the bins that we have. When we had two bins that were open, we’re at like 3-5% recycling rate in Augusta,” Mills said. “This is going to boost us whether people want to recycle or not to like upwards of 30-50%.”
Landfill life and next steps
Mills said the plan could extend Hatch Hill’s life and avoid an expansion of the landfill that would cost millions of dollars.
A final contract is now being developed.

title: Atlantic menhaden catch limits reduced under Maine official's proposal
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Atlantic menhaden catch limits reduced under Maine official's proposal
The commission approved lower catch limits for 20227 and 20227 in an 11-7 vote, as Maine officials raised concerns about potential impacts on lobster bait costs
Atlantic menhaden catch limits reduced under Maine official's proposal
The commission approved lower catch limits for 20227 and 20227 in an 11-7 vote, as Maine officials raised concerns about potential impacts on lobster bait costs
The Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission (ASMFC) voted 11-7 in favor of reducing Atlantic menhaden catch limits over the next two years, approving a proposal introduced by a Maine Department of Marine Resources official.
Maine DMR official Megan Ware introduced a proposal that sets the coastwide Total Allowable Catch (TAC) at 170,000 metric tons in 2027 and 155,000 metric tons in 2028. That's a reduction of approximately 9% and 17%, respectively, compared to the 2026 limit.
During the meeting, Ware expressed concerns that reducing the TAC by too much could affect Maine's fishing industry. She highlighted that even relatively small changes to catch limits can have significant impacts on Maine's bait and lobster fisheries.
During an October meeting, the Maine Lobstermen's Association discussed concerns about menhaden bait availability. The association noted that menhaden are essential for Maine's lobster fleet as Atlantic herring landings have declined.
Following Tuesday's vote, the New England Fishermen's Stewardship Association said proposals to reduce TAC by 50% and 30% failed before the commission approved the compromised measure.
Atlantic menhaden, commonly known as pogies, are an important food source for marine predators, including striped bass. The commission uses ecosystem-based management measures to account for the role menhaden play in the food web.
The vote took place Tuesday during the commission's hybrid 84th Annual Meeting in Newport, Rhode Island. The meeting runs through Thursday, November 12, with additional Atlantic menhaden discussions scheduled for Wednesday.

title: Honoring Maine’s Veterans means addressing their lung cancer risks
Here are some of the House seats that Democrats didn't expect to win this year
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Rep. Richard Hudson of North Carolina was in charge of the National Republican Congressional Committee, the organization dedicated to supporting his party’s House campaigns.
But the seven-term congressman wasn’t able to save his own seat this year. Republicans floundered in the state after party organizations pulled support from Michael Whatley, their U.S. Senate candidate, as he failed to gain traction against Democratic nominee Roy Cooper.
Hudson lost North Carolina’s 9th district to Richard Ojeda, a former Army major who became a liberal social media phenomenon during President Donald Trump’s first term. He ran multiple races in West Virginia then moved back to North Carolina, where he had served at Fort Bragg, and successfully ran against Hudson.
“Our victory is not just impressive because of how many seats we gained — although we did gain a lot — what was incredible last night was how far we reached into deep red territory,” said Rep. Suzan DelBene, chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.
Ojeda arrived on Capitol Hill this week, one of several new members who pulled off upset victories this year. Here’s a look at some of them.
Colorado 5th district
This district is home to NORAD, Fort Carson and the Air Force Academy, as well as the evangelical group Focus on the Family.
Although Colorado Springs has been a conservative stronghold for years, the city has been slowly turning more moderate as young families move in. Its veteran population has also been unsettled by Trump’s approach to the military and the Iran war.
Jessica Killin, a Democrat and former Army captain, capitalized on this to run as a moderate against Rep. Jeff Crank, who had previously run the Colorado chapter of the conservative group Americans For Prosperity. She hammered him for falling in line behind Trump once he got into the House.
Nevada 2nd district
Former state lawmaker Teresa Benitez-Thompson made history as the first Democrat to win Nevada’s 2nd Congressional District after her Republican opponent David Flippo’s campaign was muddied by accusations of exaggerating his military record and failing to release his required financial disclosures on time.
Benitez-Thompson campaigned as a moderate with longtime northern Nevada roots, contrasting herself with Flippo, who aligned himself closely to Trump and moved from southern Nevada to join the race after longtime Republican Rep. Mark Amodei announced his retirement. Amodei refused to endorse Flippo, calling him a fraud.
For the first time ever, all of Nevada’s congressional seats will be held by Democrats.
Wisconsin 1st district
Republican Rep. Bryan Steil won all four of his previous elections in this southeast Wisconsin district by at least 9 points. Before him, former House Speaker Paul Ryan held the seat for two decades, and no Democrat had won since 1993.
All of those factors made it improbable that Democratic newcomer Mitchell Berman, running his first campaign for any office, would come out on top this year. But Berman, an emergency room nurse, tapped into voter anger and leveraged his middle-class background to beat Steil by nearly 4 points.
The outcome will ripple through Wisconsin politics because Steil was widely considered as a likely candidate for U.S. Senate down the road.
Texas 23rd district
The race opened up when Republican Rep. Tony Gonzales announced he wouldn’t run for reelection after admitting to an affair with a former staff member who later died by suicide. Primary voters chose Brandon Herrera, a gun enthusiast YouTuber with some 4 million subscribers and a history of caustic commentary, to run in his place.
Democrats put up Katy Padilla Stout, a lawyer and former teacher, but she was believed to have little chance. The district hadn’t elected a Democrat since 2012. She ended up winning by 8 points.
Texas 9th district
This district used to be considered so blue that Republicans didn’t even put up a candidate to run there in 2024. But a year later at Trump’s urging, the state legislature redrew the congressional map, making it far more conservative. Democrats and their donors figured the seat was a lost cause as Democrat Leticia Gutierrez, who had previously worked in Houston city government, went up against Republican Alex Mealer, a well-financed military veteran who was active in conservative politics.
“Everyone felt it was a done deal that this was written for Republicans,” said Gutierrez in an interview with The Associated Press. “They just weren’t going to invest their time, money, and resources into someone that had never run a congressional campaign.”
Then Gutierrez beat Mealer by a little over 15 points.
Indiana 5th district
Rep. Victoria Spartz has been a wildcard in the Republican caucus, often withholding her support for legislation until the last minutes as she seeks concessions from party leadership.
But the Ukrainian-born lawmaker seemed to be a safe reelection prospect in conservative Indiana, particularly in her affluent suburban and rural district north of Indianapolis. The seat only became more red in 2021, when the state legislature removed portions of more Democratic-leaning areas of Marion County and added conservative rural tracts. Two years ago, Trump won by 17 percentage points, and Spartz won by even more.
But this year J.D. Ford, a Democratic state senator, beat Spartz by 3.4 percentage points.
New Jersey 2nd district
There’s not many red seats left in the Northeast, but one of them has been in the southeastern corner of New Jersey. The district stretches from shore resorts to the pine barrens, and it’s been represented by Rep. Jeff Van Drew. He was first elected to Congress as a conservative Democrat in 2018 only to switch parties in 2020 after Trump’s first impeachment.
Van Drew kept winning reelection until this week, when he lost to Zack Mullock, the Democratic mayor of Cape May. Mullock focused on Van Drew’s support for the president, attacking him in a debate over the Iran war and tariffs. Van Drew argued that his connections with Trump would benefit the district.
Iowa 2nd district
When Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson decided to run for U.S. Senate, that left an open race for her House seat in the northeastern corner of Iowa. The Republican candidate was Joe Mitchell, a former state lawmaker, and Trump visited Dubuque just two days before the election to try to boost turnout.
Mitchell lost to Lindsay James, a Democratic state lawmaker and a minister.
“I am going to stay laser-focused on lowering costs for hard-working families here in my district because that’s what they have asked me to do,” James said in an interview.
Her victory was boosted by two other candidates on the ballot — one libertarian and one unaffiliated — who received more votes than James’ margin over Mitchell.
___
Associated Press writers Hannah Fingerhut, Mike Catalini, Thomas Beaumont, Jesse Bedayn, Scott Bauer and Jessica Hill contributed to this report.

title: Gov. Janet Mills joins New England governors to call for increased LIHEAP funding
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Gov. Janet Mills joins New England governors to call for increased LIHEAP funding
The governors are asking for an additional $3 billion in funding.
Gov. Janet Mills joins New England governors to call for increased LIHEAP funding
The governors are asking for an additional $3 billion in funding.
Gov. Janet Mills joined governors of New England states to call on Congress to increase funding for the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP).
In a letter to congressional appropriations leadership, the governors of all six states in New England call for an additional $3 billion, which would bring the total program funding for LIHEAP up to $7 billion. The governors say the additional funding would help vulnerable households manage rising energy costs.
"LIHEAP provides essential assistance to these households in every region of the country, helping families manage both winter heating and summer cooling costs. While energy needs vary by geography and season, the challenge is the same: ensuring that vulnerable Americans can afford the energy necessary to remain safe in their homes," the governors wrote. "These pressures are particularly acute in New England, where cold winters, older housing, and a heavy reliance on delivered heating fuel leave families especially exposed to the dramatic price increases America is currently experiencing."
“No one should be cold in their homes because Trump decided to wage an unnecessary, unwanted war with Iran,” Gov. Mills said in a statement. “That’s why I’m joining my fellow New England governors to call on Congress to release billions in federal funding for LIHEAP to provide immediate relief for vulnerable families as winter approaches.”
This comes after last month, heating oil prices in Maine reached a record $6.04 per gallon, according to the Maine Department of Energy Resources.

title: Wrongful death lawsuit filed in 2024 electrocution incident
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The family of an electrician’s helper who died from work-related injuries has filed a wrongful death lawsuit.
Brady Andrews of Brewer was 19 when he was electrocuted during his first day of work in the summer of 2024.
According to the complaint, Andrews was conducting a voltage test on a wire in a junction box above a suspended ceiling when he came into contact with an unguarded live wire.
The complaint says Bowman Constructors of Newport, the general contractor at the job site, hired Andrews’ employer, CC Electric, to assist with the project.
Berman & Simmons, the law firm representing Andrews’ family, says Bowman Constructors was negligent in failing to hire and supervise a master electrician, train and supervise workers, communicate with workers, and follow industry standards and safety regulations.
We have reached out to the company for a response but have not yet heard back.

title: US charges 3 men with plotting terror attacks, including planned assault on UK airbase
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Three men, including one already jailed in the United States, were accused by U.S. authorities Tuesday of being Iran-supported operatives who plotted nearly 20 attacks on Jewish communities in Europe and the U.S. as well as a planned assault on a British airbase used by the U.S. Air Force.
Charges against Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, were outlined in a superseding indictment unsealed in Manhattan federal court. Only al-Saadi is in custody.
U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald in New York said in a news release that al-Saadi, who was arrested in the spring, continued to coordinate with his co-defendants in the days leading up to the attempted September terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, United Kingdom, where U.S. bombers and troops had been stationed.
“These defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran that targeted Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, and the British military base, RAF Fairford, housing American service members,” McDonald said. “The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical — it is very real.”
Attorney General Todd Blanche said: “Anyone who plans a terrorist plot on a military base housing American servicemembers will be prosecuted by the United States government.”
The new indictment offers fresh insight into an episode that has been shrouded in mystery for more than a month after five men were detained after midnight on Sept. 27 on suspected explosives and terrorism offenses after three suspicious vans were spotted traveling toward the base in western England.
A sixth suspect, a British-Iranian dual national, was arrested several days later. All the men were released on bail.
British authorities linked the incident to Tehran, and though Iran denied involvement, the arrests prompted the U.S. to withdraw its bombers that had been stationed there. The bombers were redeployed to their home bases in the United States.
RAF Fairford, located 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London, has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East.
According to the indictment, al-Saadi used coded language in communications with relatives from jail to direct that money be passed along to others who could carry out attacks.
The indictment alleged that the three men conspired together to use a network of contacts in the United Kingdom to commit terrorist attacks on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, which included the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Kata’ib Hizballah.
In June, al-Saadi pleaded not guilty to charges that he plotted at least 18 attacks in Europe in retaliation for the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran. He called himself a “prisoner of war.” He has been held without bail since. His lawyers did not immediately respond to requests for comment Tuesday on the latest development.
Both Kata’ib Hizballah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps have been designated by the U.S. government as foreign terrorist organizations. U.S. prosecutors say Al-Saadi was a Kata’ib Hizballah commander.
___
Tucker reported from Washington.

title: Another country star says he was denied CMA Awards red carpet access
text:
NASHVILLE (KALB/Gray News) - Days after Sammy Kershaw made waves across the country music world, a fellow alum of the 90s and 2000s country scene announced Saturday that he, too, was snubbed by the Country Music Association after requesting red carpet access to the upcoming 2026 CMA Awards.
Rodney Atkins, known for country hits like “Honestly (Write Me a List),” “If You’re Going Through Hell (Before the Devil Even Knows)” and “Watching You,” expressed his frustration with CMA on social media, writing:
“After more than 20 years as a CMA member and countless CMA Fests I’ve played for free, Rose and I were denied red-carpet clearance just like Sammy Kershaw. So we’ve decided not to attend this year’s CMA Awards.”
Atkins also posted a video message to fans, explaining that he felt sympathetic toward Kershaw after news began to spread, only to find out later that he and his wife, fellow country artist Rose Falcon, had also been denied access to this year’s awards.
Nineties hitmaker Kershaw says he was delisted from the red carpet in a post to social media Thursday, which drew an outpouring of support from fans and fellow musicians.
The Country Music Association has not yet publicly responded to either Kershaw’s or Atkins’ comments.

title: The Latest: Hegseth says bipartisan impeachment push is about ‘policy disagreements’
text:
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth is condemning the impeachment effort against him as “a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment.” Hegseth made the comments at a news conference at the Pentagon, just a day after Rep. Thomas Massie launched an effort to impeach him over his handling of the unpopular war against Iran and other actions.
Massie, a Kentucky Republican, read the impeachment resolution from the House floor just hours after the chamber convened for the first day of sessions after the midterms.
Meanwhile, the Senate advanced bipartisan legislation on Monday to speed up permitting reviews for power data centers and other infrastructure projects. The Senate voted 73-25 to formally take up the bill, which senators and President Donald Trump have pushed as a way to meet growing demand for electricity and other energy sources that now face yearslong delays in getting to the grid.
Here’s the latest:
Thune arrives at Capitol ahead of leadership vote
Senate Majority Leader John Thune has arrived on Capitol Hill ahead of a meeting of his fellow Republicans to decide whether to delay leadership elections or select him as leader again in the next Congress.
Asked how he was feeling as he walked into his office, Thune said, “We’ll see.”
Inflation ran hotter than expected last month, underscoring affordability challenges
U.S. inflation was higher than expected last month, signaling that rising prices that powered sweeping Democratic victories in last week’s midterm elections will continue posing challenges for the White House and the Federal Reserve.
The consumer price index rose 0.4% from September to October, the Labor Department said Tuesday, down from 0.6% the previous month. The government did not report a yearly inflation rate because last year’s government shutdown meant no data was released for October 2025.
Excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core prices rose 0.3%, the same as the preceding month. Both figures were a tenth of a point higher than forecast.
A defiant Hegseth concludes news conference
Hegseth has concluded the news conference after taking six questions.
The secretary of defense was overwhelmingly defiant in his remarks from the Pentagon podium, which cast the impeachment as “sabotage” against U.S. troops. He insisted he had done nothing wrong and claimed the support of Trump and Vice President JD Vance. And when asked, he avoided questions about the political backlash against the war in last week’s midterm elections.
“I stand behind every one of these operations. I was proud to execute them, and I would do it again tomorrow,” Hegseth said.
The impeachment, he insisted, “puts a target on the backs of American warriors by signaling that Congress will undermine their missions in real time. This is not patriotism. This is sabotage.”
Trump praised Hegseth’s performance in a social media post published minutes after the press conference ended.
“Pete Hegseth gets an “A” PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!” Trump wrote.
Hegseth slams impeachment as attack on troops
Hegseth is defending himself against impeachment by describing the effort as an attack on the troops.
“On the eve of Veterans Day,” Hegseth said, “these resolutions tell every one of them that their service was a crime.”
“These are heroes, and no politician in Washington will tell them otherwise while I hold this office,” he added. “If they want to come for the warriors, they’re going to have to come through me.”
Hegseth slams impeachment effort as ‘political spectacle’
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth is condemning the impeachment effort against him as “a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment.”
Hegseth made the comments at the beginning of a morning press conference at the Pentagon. It was his first news conference from the Pentagon in six months and came just a day after Rep. Thomas Massie launched an effort to impeach him over his handling of the unpopular war against Iran and other actions.
Hegseth said Massie’s concerns are not impeachable, calling them “policy disagreements, not high crimes, not misdemeanors, not treason, not bribery, not the kinds of offenses the founders intended when they wrote the impeachment clause.”
He continued: “The proper remedy for a policy disagreement, it’s legislation, it’s debate, it’s the next presidential election.”
FBI is looking at Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese agent, Trump says
Trump said Monday that the FBI is investigating Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese government agent, but said he doesn’t think the executive who has helped to develop artificial intelligence has a reason to worry.
“I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he’ll be in good shape,” Trump said at a White House briefing.
The sudden emergence of Huang’s infidelity has rocked the political class and America’s tech sector, creating new concerns about whether China has been able to access the cutting-edge chips designed by Nvidia that are powering the development of artificial intelligence.
Trump suggested the extraordinary step of directly involving himself in a counterintelligence investigation, a sign of his friendly relationship with Huang and the possible geopolitical stakes.
Huang has acknowledged he had an affair, issuing an apology to his wife and to the company in an open letter posted on Nvidia’s website. The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence determined that the woman was gathering information for Beijing.
Thune and Schumer face questions about Senate leadership in aftermath of elections
Senators from both parties returned to Washington on Monday with questions about the future of their leadership after last week’s election decisively gave Democrats a significant new majority.
Republicans who are losing around a quarter of their conference to election losses and retirements are debating whether to immediately reelect South Dakota Sen. John Thune as leader in votes scheduled for Tuesday. Across the aisle, Democrats who could hold as many as 56 seats next year are having private discussions about whether New York Sen. Chuck Schumer is still the right person to lead them, even as he carried the party to historic wins.
Both men are expected to easily win the backing of a majority of their members in closed-door, secret-ballot elections — the Republicans this week, and Democrats likely in December. But the internal discussions on both sides could prove consequential to their parties’ effectiveness in the next Congress and how voters perceive them leading into the 2028 presidential election.
Senate advances sweeping energy legislation in first major action since midterm elections
The Senate on Monday advanced bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to power data centers and other infrastructure projects, in the first major action since last week’s election that soundly repudiated Trump and congressional Republicans.
The Senate voted 73-25 to formally take up the bill, which senators and the president have pushed to meet growing demand for electricity and other energy sources that now face yearslong delays before reaching the grid.
The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to get big energy projects started — both for clean energy and fossil fuel projects — and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over artificial intelligence data centers and rising electricity prices helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the massive, energy-hungry structures.
Hegseth is set for his first Pentagon news briefing since May as he faces possible impeachment
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is scheduled to give his first news conference from the Pentagon in six months on Tuesday, just a day after a Republican lawmaker launched an effort to impeach him over his handling of the unpopular war against Iran and other actions.
The briefing will be Hegseth’s first since May, even as the U.S. military has kept up intermittent operations against the Islamic Republic as well as fatal strikes on alleged drug-smuggling boats in Latin America.
Hegseth, who has said the news conference would focus on the impeachment threat, is gearing up for a fight, having launched a social media blitz and saying he is ready to defend his and President Donald Trump’s actions from “politically motivated people.”
Rep. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican who lost his primary to a Trump-backed opponent, filed the impeachment resolution in the House on Monday. It sets the stage for a dramatic vote on whether to remove a prominent Trump administration figure following sweeping losses for Republicans in last week’s midterm elections that many at least partly blamed on the Iran conflict and its economic impact.

title: Topgolf cutting prices at all US locations to make experience more affordable for customers
text:
DALLAS (Gray News) - Topgolf is lowering prices at all of its U.S. locations.
The sports-entertainment company announced the price reduction this week after guests shared in a survey that they would visit more often if it were more affordable.
“I heard a common theme from our guests: our experience is unmatched, from high-quality food to games and the ability to connect through friendly competition, but our prices are too high to keep them coming back,” Topgolf CEO David McKillips said in a statement.
Topgolf said it would be reducing gameplay rates by 20% nationwide, effective Monday.
According to the company, the lower rates won’t be a limited-time promotion but rather a permanent change and would not require a coupon or promotional code.
“I want our guests to know that we heard them and are now introducing our lowest prices ever,” McKillips continued. “Topgolf has always been about more play for all and by reducing the price of gameplay, we’re backing that commitment up.”
Topgolf is described as a sports entertainment complex that offers inclusive, high-tech golf games that everyone can enjoy year-round.
The upgraded golf experience was first offered in Virginia before expanding to more than 100 locations in the U.S. and internationally.
Topgolf locations can be found online, along with its pricing options.

title: Hannah Pingree says Jay shouldn’t be data center ‘testing ground’ as project restarts
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree said Tuesday that Jay should not be “the testing ground” for data centers before Maine has strong regulations in place.
Her comment to the Bangor Daily News comes one day after the owner of the former Androscoggin Mill site in Jay submitted permit applications to Maine regulators to move forward with his plan to convert the former paper mill into a data center.
“Jay deserves good jobs and investment at the mill site, but not at the cost of ratepayers, neighbors or the environment,” Pingree said in a statement.
That position previews one of the ways in which Pingree will distinguish herself from her predecessor, outgoing-Gov. Janet Mills, who vetoed a data center moratorium backed by Democrats in April because she wanted to save the Jay project.
Pingree, who served in Mills’ cabinet for more than six years until she entered the race to replace her, signaled her support for a moratorium on the campaign trail. On Tuesday, she unveiled a transition team that includes the head of Maine Conservation Voters, a Democratic-aligned group working against data center development.
Pushback against data centers has only intensified in Maine and nationally over the past year as the public grows more wary of artificial intelligence and its environmental impact. Eight more communities here added local moratoriums during last Tuesday’s midterm election, mirroring similar restrictions across the country.
Nodding to the election at a news conference in Augusta, Pingree emphasized that she “heard pretty loudly and clearly from Maine people that the development of data centers in Maine without very strong regulations in place is not something that people are interested in.”
Pingree and developer Tony McDonald of JGT2 Redevelopment said they have not yet spoken about the project. Pingree said she wants to talk with him and the Jay town manager, whom she has worked with before.
McDonald said the data center would bring jobs and property tax revenue to Jay, which lost its largest employer when the paper mill closed in 2023. The mill once employed more than 1,000 people.
But he faces pushback across the state. Maine Conservation Voters and the Natural Resources Council of Maine agreed with Pingree that safeguards for community health and the environment should come first.
McDonald said his project is different from the massive data centers in other states where residents complain of high water and electricity use. It would draw power from an existing 82-megawatt contract the mill held, and its cooling system would run in a closed loop, much like a car radiator, he said in a Tuesday interview.
The original design called for 300,000 gallons of water per day, which McDonald said was about 1% of what the paper mill used. The redesigned system uses 260,000 gallons that are reused constantly, with the first fill likely coming from the Jay Water District rather than the Androscoggin River, as some residents had worried, he said.
JGT2 filed two permit applications with the Maine Department of Environmental Protection on Monday, a development first reported by the BDN. The project had been on hold since Mills’ veto, after customers of JGT2’s partner, Sentinel Data Centers, grew worried about opposition in Maine.
McDonald said the companies never stopped working on the project, and Sentinel has since signed a new customer.
The data center will use a concept called “neo compute,” in which 100 or more smaller customers share the facility instead of one giant such as Amazon or Microsoft. McDonald said that model could ease some of the concern about huge AI data centers elsewhere.
One permit application is for an amendment to the existing permit formerly held by the paper mill that would allow the property to be used as a data center, he said. It would cover the mill and the 93 adjacent residential properties that the former mill owners purchased over the years. The second application is related to air emissions caused by two newly proposed diesel backup generators.
A public meeting is tentatively scheduled for Dec. 10 at the mill site to discuss the project’s impact on water resources, energy prices and the local economy.
Lori Valigra reports on the environment for the BDN’s Maine Focus investigative team. Email her at lvaligra@bangordailynews.com. Support for this reporting is provided by the Unity Foundation, a fund at the Maine Community Foundation and donations by BDN readers.

title: California voters reject measure to tax wealth of billionaires
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — California voters have rejected a first-in-the-nation tax on the net worth of billionaires following a contentious ballot fight that generated huge spending by some prominent tech leaders eager to stop their taxes from going up.
The measure’s failure is a win for Democratic leaders who opposed it, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, who may run for president in 2028. Critics of the tax, known as Proposition 40, said it would have prompted ultrawealthy taxpayers to leave the state.
Most Californians vote by mail, and any ballot postmarked by Election Day that arrives within a week is counted, meaning it often takes days or even weeks for close races to be settled. The Associated Press determined Monday that ‘no’ had received enough votes to win.
The “no” side raised roughly 10 times as much as the “yes” side. Google co-founder Sergey Brin alone dumped more than $100 million into a political action committee working to defeat the measure.
The measure would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of Californians whose net worth exceeds $1 billion. Most of the money would have been used to backfill federal funding cuts to healthcare, and 10% would have gone toward education and food-assistance programs. SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, which backed the tax, said it was necessary to replace an estimated $100 billion the state will lose in federal healthcare funding over five years.
Proposition 40 was the nation’s biggest test yet on an idea progressives have long championed: raising taxes on the ultra-rich by targeting the main way they make their money — through their investments as opposed to the paychecks they receive from work.
Proponents say they could put the measure back on the ballot in 2028
The measure attracted support from liberal leaders beyond the state, including Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, who rallied in cities across California in the race’s closing weeks to urge voters to pass it.
The “Yes on 40” campaign said the measure sought to protect healthcare for Californians and that they will put a tax back on the ballot in 2028 if patients are not protected.
“Buying an election is not the same as winning the debate,” the measure’s proponents said in a statement on Monday. “The billionaires may have bought themselves a temporary victory at the ballot box, but they have not bought themselves an end to this debate, and this is only round one.”
Billionaires donated millions of dollars to a political action committee, Building a Better California, working to defeat the measure. The committee, which backed other measures on the ballot designed to nullify the tax, raised more than $333 million, nearly a third of which came from Brin.
The AP Voter Poll indicates that the majority of young voters in California — those younger than 30 — voted “yes” on Proposition 40. Older voters were far less supportive, with roughly 7 in 10 voters who were 65 and older saying they voted “no” on the ballot measure.
About half of voters with a household income under $100,000 annually said they were in support of the initiative. Closer to 6 in 10 California voters with an income of $100,000 or higher said they were opposed.
Brin, along with his fellow Google co-founder Larry Page, was among the billionaires who started cutting ties with the state in anticipation of the possible tax. Another tech mogul, Mark Zuckerberg, said he would remain in the state for eight years and made a deal with Meta to help him pay the tax without losing his ownership stake in the company.
Some feared the measure could drive wealthy taxpayers out of state
Some traditional Democratic allies, including Planned Parenthood and the California Medical Association, were part of a coalition opposing it. They were concerned about how the tax revenue would be divvied up and about the potential impact on the state’s budget if there was a mass exodus of wealthy taxpayers. California’s budget relies heavily on the income tax of the state’s richest residents.
“Proposition 40 was a reckless experiment conducted on our state’s economy with little regard for the harms it would cause,” the coalition said in a statement.
Robert Swonger, an auto glass technician living near Sacramento who’s politically independent, said before voting concluded Nov. 3 that he planned to vote against it.
“Obviously, I would like billionaires not to have as much money as they do,” he said. “But I don’t believe taxing them out of existence is going to work.”
Progressive politicians, including Sanders and Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, have long supported a federal wealth tax. Newsom says a California wealth tax would disadvantage the state, but he supports a national minimum tax on anyone with a net worth above $100 million.
Days before Sanders held rallies in California cities last month, Newsom told reporters that the senator’s focus on wealth inequality was “spot-on.” But he said that “on this issue, we fundamentally disagree.”
Supporters of the California tax started running ads recently in New Hampshire, New Mexico and Virginia, states that will vote early in the Democratic presidential primary in 2028, that criticize Newsom for his opposition to the measure.

title: Maine suspends $107K in fines related to deadly Searsmont explosion
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Maine Department of Labor has cited seven emergency departments for safety violations after a fatal sawmill fire and explosion but is suspending almost all of the penalties so the towns can pay for new equipment and training to address the problems.
The May 15 explosion at Robbins Lumber in Searsmont killed three people and injured more than a dozen others. Sparks from machinery at the base of a silo ignited wood dust, triggering a massive blast.
The settlement details, published Tuesday by the Maine Department of Labor, require these fire and rescue departments to overhaul safety protocols, buy new equipment and send members to mandatory state training.
The most significant equipment purchase — a personnel tracking system that uses tags that firefighters attach to a board at an emergency scene so incident commanders can maintain a live headcount — is being funded by Knox County and donations.
Almost 300 emergency personnel from 46 fire departments responded, but the state inspected only those whose personnel suffered serious injuries or died. Mill safety conditions are regulated by the U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration.
The Maine Department of Labor fined the fire and rescue departments, which rely almost entirely on volunteers, $108,000 for citations as small as deficient record keeping to as serious as a failure to keep a live headcount of responding firefighters and staging the firefighter treatment and rest area within a possible blast zone.
All but a $1,000 fine against the Montville Fire Department was suspended. The department had been cited for the same problem — not testing that respirators fit properly — by OSHA in August 2025, according to the settlement agreement, and it was the only repeat violation.
While it’s unclear if much of the conduct that was cited could’ve prevented the serious injuries in Searsmont, the placement of the rescue and treatment area did put the EMS personnel in danger, said Kate Burkhart, the director of the Bureau of Labor Standards’ workplace safety division.
Inspectors cited Searsmont Rescue for setting up a firefighter rest area within 50 feet of the initial fire. Rescue Chief Sarah Tompkins and Lily Robbins, a volunteer EMT, were both injured in the explosion.
“When the explosion occurred, they were right there,” Burkhart said.
But Burkhart said suspending the fines will allow the mostly small cash-strapped towns to invest in safety improvements rather than paying state penalties. She said that will result in the kind of systemic change that will protect people more than any single corrective action.
“We did not waive them, we suspended them,” Burkhart said of the fines. “If any department does not meet their obligations, we can collect those penalties. It’s like a carrot and a stick wrapped in one.”
She emphasized that all the departments have worked hard over the last six months to improve safety in the wake of the catastrophic losses they experienced, including two fire trucks that burned. Tuesday’s release offers new details on how the departments involved in the explosion are adapting and learning from it.
Local leaders like Morill First Selectman Randy Place welcomed the state’s supportive approach.
“Town staff and the fire department immediately started correcting all issues that the DOL identified,” Place said. “Morrill greatly appreciated how the DOL handled our case, providing help and understanding while the town struggled with the loss of our young firefighter.”
Andrew Cross, a 27-year-old volunteer firefighter from Morrill, died at the scene. Searsmont Assistant Fire Chief Wayne Woodbury and mill co-owner Alden Robbins were severely burned and died weeks later. Eleven firefighters, two EMTs and several mill workers were injured.
State inspectors cited six departments — Appleton, Belmont, Lincolnville, Montville, Morrill and Searsmont — for not using a formal personnel tracking system during the disaster. The new system they’re implementing in response will help track firefighters and EMS personnel especially in a situation where multiple departments are on scene, said Belmont Fire Chief Ron Harford. That kind of a fire response is increasingly common as the number of volunteers at fire departments across the state has declined. Harford said his firefighters are already using the new tag-in and tag-out system at the fire station to prepare for future calls.
In Searsmont, the explosion has motivated more people to volunteer for its fire and EMS services, Selectman Chris Staples said. The town doesn’t dispute the labor department’s findings, said Selectman Pete Milinazzo.
“The town will move ahead and be better in the future than we were in the past — not that we’ve been terrible in the past,” Milinazzo said. “As a town and rescue department, every day we’re striving to do better than the day before.”
Five departments faced protective gear and mask citations for allowing their firefighters to wear heavy breathing gear without ensuring they had required medical evaluations and annual mask fit-tests, and not maintaining written plans.
Under the settlement terms, department leaders must complete safety workshops put on by the state and the Maine Fire Chiefs Association and Maine Fire Service Institute in February 2027 to keep the fines fully suspended.
Harford in Belmont said as a volunteer fire chief, every call is a learning experience. “It’s horrible how it’s all happened, but we live and learn from it,” he said.

title: Cheverus’ Skip Capone retires after decades of coaching football in Maine
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone—because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s Go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
For 50 years, Skip Capone has viewed coaching football as one of the greatest ways of building relationships and helping young people develop.
“My entire professional career has been trying to point kids in the right direction,” Capone said.
On Monday, news broke that Capone, 71, had retired as Cheverus High’s head football coach after three seasons. Capone said Tuesday that he does plan to hang up his coaching whistle, though he anticipates staying connected to the game through his involvement with the Maine chapter of the National Football Foundation and as a committee member for the James J. Fitzpatrick Trophy Award.
“I was blessed with some great coaches at the high school level and the college level and they inspired me to get into coaching,” Capone said. “It’s always been way more than Xs and Os. It’s about relationships and just trying to help kids develop.”
Capone added, “I think I’ve finally repaid my debt to the greatest game ever invented.”
A 1973 graduate of Portsmouth High in New Hampshire (Capone said he talks with his high school coach Tom Daubney on a monthly basis), Capone played football at Plymouth State College. His first assistant gig was in 1977 at Dover, New Hampshire, followed by college stops at Plymouth State and Southwest Missouri State, before returning to New England and coaching at Winnacunnet High in Hampton, New Hampshire.
“Then I had the opportunity to come to Lewiston in 1983 as the head football coach. I was there for 14 years,” as the football coach, Capone said. He led the Blue Devils to the 1987 Class A title and taught physical education at Lewiston for 35 years.
Capone said he was looking to step away from coaching for a year when he was offered a stipend position at Bates College as the offensive line coach. That began a 22-year stint with the Bobcats.
Capone returned to the high school sidelines as an assistant for Jason McLeod at Portland High and also spent a season as a part-time coach/confidant for Sam Weiss at Oceanside before taking the Cheverus positon in 2024.
This season Cheverus was 3-5 in the regular season, before losing to Biddeford in the B South quarterfinal. Capone’s three-season record at Cheverus was 9-18.
“Cheverus is a great place to coach. I coached some great kids. The parents were awesome,” Capone said. “It’s just time. I’ll be 72 in January.”
Capone said he considers himself lucky to have coached against and with “a litany” of great coaches in what he termed “a golden age of high school athletics,” from the late 1970s to the early 2000s. Capone rattled off many names across multiple sports, noting they were coaches “who dedicated their lives to helping kids and had a lot of success along the way.”
Capone’s legacy will be the hundreds, if not thousands, of connections he’s made across multiple states. It seems almost every coach in Maine knows Skip Capone.
Take Brandon Dorsett at Falmouth High for instance. Dorsett grew up in Portland, playing for the Bulldogs and Colorado State when Capone was coaching at Bates. Dorsett first met Capone when the two were player and coach with the semi-professional Maine Sabers.
“Having him as one of my coaches was great,” Dorsett said. “He just is a caring person. He cares about the kids.”
This season Dorsett and Falmouth squared off against Cheverus and Capone.
“He gave me a great big hug and we talked,” Dorsett said. “Everyone who has ever played for him just admires him.”

title: Maine logging program graduates ready to step into high-demand jobs
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Many of the 15 graduates of Maine’s 20-week Mechanized Logging Operations and Forest Trucking Program already have jobs waiting for them in a field where demand for skilled operators remains strong.
“If you like the logging industry and that’s what you want to do, you’ve got a lot of opportunity in front of you,” Duane Jordan, president of the Professional Logging Contractors of the Northeast, told the program’s 10th cohort at last week’s graduation ceremony.
$1.3B regional impact
The Northeast region’s only college training program for operators of mechanized logging and forest trucking equipment provides hands-on experience with operating commercial trucks, loading log trailers and developing the knowledge needed for forest trucking. This year’s class is the fourth to have the opportunity to earn a CDL-A permit and receive preparation for the state driving exam.
Students spent the summer and fall harvesting and hauling timber at an active job site in the woods at the Kennebec Valley Community College Alfond Campus farm in Fairfield, using sophisticated machines like those they will encounter in the logging industry.
Students also received hands-on experience operating commercial trucks, loading log trailers and gaining knowledge critical to forest trucking.
Logging and forest trucking pumped an estimated $1.3 billion into the Northeast region in 2024, with Maine contributing $534 million of that amount, according to a study released earlier this year. Maine’s figure included $283 million in total labor earnings and an estimated $23 million in state tax revenues.
The Pine Tree State numbers represented 2,744 direct logging and trucking jobs, along with an additional 1,715 indirect jobs.
The study also flagged industry challenges including the loss of markets, market uncertainty, rising costs, shrinking profits, worker shortages and a lack of succession planning.
Robust demand
Demand for logging and forest trucking operators in Maine is high and projected to remain so for the foreseeable future, said Dana Doran, executive director of the Professional Logging Contractors of the Northeast.
When mechanized logging equipment was first used by the region’s logging industry in the 1980s, loggers had to learn how to operate equipment largely on their own and made many costly mistakes, Jordan said.
The program provides an opportunity for new operators to avoid mistakes and learn directly from the instructors, all of whom are veteran operators.
Since the program was created in 2017, 110 students have graduated and 71% are working in a logging-related industry today.
Tuition-free
Funded by a $1 million grant from the U.S. Department of Labor, Employment and Training Administration, the program is administered by Kennebec Valley Community College in partnership with the PLC.
The program emphasizes safety while giving students a foundation in timber growth, tree species and markets. Tuition and fees are covered, and the program provides all personal protective equipment. Scholarships from Skowhegan Savings Bank are also available to help students with living expenses.

title: Hannah Pingree announces more than a dozen key transition leaders
text:
AUGUSTA — Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree on Tuesday unveiled the names of 22 people who will help lead her transition, vowing to cast “a wide net” as she staffs Maine’s agencies.
The 50-year-old Democrat laid out her guiding principles for choosing the heads of more than a dozen state departments and other key leaders who will have the ability to affect the lives of Mainers in ways big and small — from caring for family members to maintaining roads.
Pingree said she wants a results-oriented cabinet of individuals with integrity, accountability and a general optimism about helping Maine people.
“I also want a team that is collaborative, because the challenges facing our state are too big for one person, one party, or one region alone to solve,” she said.
The team of 22 will recruit and recommend candidates for Pingree’s 15 Cabinet positions and an appointee to the Workers’ Compensation Board.
Her transition team is mostly made up of people from outside of state government, Pingree noted. It includes leaders in labor, business and healthcare.
“Many of these folks have never worked in state government, but they know what’s needed in their communities,” Pingree said. “And I want their experience and their judgment in my administration. So again, we intend to cast a wide net, and we intend to be thorough, because Mainers deserve nothing less.”
Although Pingree worked in Gov. Janet Mills’ administration, she said any Mills-era officials who are interested in staying on must earn a position in her administration.
“No shoe-ins,” Pingree said. “Everyone’s got to compete and we will be interviewing multiple candidates for every single Cabinet position.”
The transition team is co-chaired by Maulian Bryant, a member of the Penobscot Nation and the executive director of the Wabanaki Alliance, and Roger Katz, a Republican former state lawmaker.
Katz said the team is looking for the most qualified people — regardless of their political party or who they supported in the governor’s race.
“We’ll be looking in every corner of the state,” Katz said.
Pingree hopes to have most of her Cabinet assembled before her Jan. 6 inauguration.
Here’s a look at the volunteers helping Bryant and Katz to build her team:
- Judy Camuso, who led Maine’s Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife from 2019 until May 2026. She was the first woman to serve as commissioner.
- Hannah Carter, an Aroostook County native and dean of Cooperative Extension for the University of Maine and deputy provost.
- Vicky Cohen, a recently retired Farmington teacher.
- Ken Colburn, principal of Symbiotic Strategies LLC and a retired principal and director of U.S. Programs at the Regulatory Assistance Project. He serves on the Maine Climate Council.
- Barbara Crowley, a pediatrician who also serves on the leadership team of the Children’s Oral Health Network of Maine, working to improve children’s access to oral health care.
- Maureen Drouin, executive director of Maine Conservation Voters and the Maine Conservation Alliance.
- Richard Evans, a recently retired general and colon and rectal surgeon from Dover-Foxcroft. He’s also a former Democratic state senator and U.S. Air Force veteran.
- Liza Fleming-Ives, executive director of the Genesis Community Loan Fund, a community development financial institution serving communities across Maine and northern New England.
- Elsie Flemings, executive director of Healthy Acadia since 2014.
- Marwa Hassanien, a Bangor resident, human resources director at one of Maine’s largest health systems and president of the Maine Multicultural Center’s board of directors.
- Luke Holden, a third-generation lobsterman from Cape Elizabeth and founder of Luke’s Lobster. He serves on the board of the Gulf of Maine Research Institute.
- Liam LaFountain, mayor of Biddeford since December 2025.
- Susan Nourse, retired Freeport police chief.
- Jason Parent, chief executive officer for Avec, the Community Action Agency serving Aroostook, Washington and Hancock counties.
- Grant Provost, a business agent and industry analyst for Ironworkers Local 7 in Maine and a vice president of the Maine AFL-CIO.
- Peggy Rotundo, former Democratic state senator from Lewiston and a former budget committee chairwoman.
- Claude Rwaganje, founder and executive director of ProsperityME.
- Steve Smith, former president and CEO of L.L.Bean.
- Eloise Vitelli, former Maine Senate Democratic majority leader.
- Ben Waxman, CEO and co-founder of American Roots, a Westbrook-based manufacturer of American- and union-made apparel.

title: Chinburg Properties unveils Jagger Mill complex in Sanford
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Chinburg Properties plans a ribbon cutting Tuesday to unveil the redeveloped Jagger Mill in Sanford.
The mill, at 5 Water St. in the Springvale section, dates to 1920. It was originally part of Goodall Worsted’s alpaca wool division and, in 1956, became part of Jagger Brothers, which produced yarn.
The redeveloped site is home to 86 luxury apartments. Amenities will include a clubroom, fitness room, sauna, dog-washing room and common patios. Parking and utilities are included in the rent.
“We are so appreciative of the city’s creative approach toward Jagger Mill’s redevelopment and their commitment to increasing the housing supply to add to the vibrancy of Springvale and this region,” principal Eric Chinburg said in a news release Tuesday.
Chinburg Properties is based in Portsmouth, N.H.

title: Woman runs onto high school football field during game and strangles player, police say
text:
WAYNE COUNTY, Ky. (WKYT/WYMT/Gray News) - A Kentucky woman is facing a felony charge after police say she strangled a high school football player during a game.
Kayla Barrett, 36, was charged with second-degree strangulation after Monticello Police say she assaulted a Wayne County High School football player during an Oct. 30 game against North Laurel High School.
Police say a Wayne County player was running with the ball when a tackle that ended out-of-bounds erupted into a melee between players. Barrett, of Laurel County, was standing near the sideline and chose to get involved, according to police.
“From what I understand, she ran toward the action, and somewhere in that scuffle, she grabbed one of the Wayne County athletes by the back of the neck and began choking him and shaking him,” Monticello Assistant Chief Joshua Smith said.
Police say the player who was strangled said he had trouble breathing because of the attack. He was taken to the hospital, where he was treated and released. Police believe he will be OK.
Barrett left the game after the attack, according to police.
“When it all happened, she left. She quickly left the area and drove off,” Smith said. “Our officer was able to get her identified.”
Barrett was arrested last Tuesday by the Kentucky State Police. She has since been released on bond.
“Hopefully, she’s not allowed back at a sporting event,” Smith said. “As far as the police department is concerned, our student-athletes and their protection is one of our biggest areas that we want to make sure they’re always safe.”
