title: Firefighter suffers minor injuries at house fire in Newburgh
text:
NEWBURGH, Maine (WABI) - A firefighter suffered minor injuries putting out a fire at a Newburgh home Tuesday morning after fire crews from multiple towns responded to a fire at a house on Western Avenue.
None of the occupants of the house were injured.
Multiple departments responded to the call just before 11 A.M. Tuesday.
Officials on scene said there was some minor fire damage, but the majority of the lasting impact will be from the extensive amount of heat and water used.
Hermon Fire Chief Cody Sullivan told WABI that they were in the middle of staff training at Hermon Mountain which put them right down the road.
“In this day and age staffing matters. We were up staff today due to the training, so we were able to roll in with two fully staffed trucks, a support vehicle, and an ambulance. On a normal day, that’s not what our typical response would look like. It would’ve doubled our response time, so the fire would’ve grown twice as big before we arrived. Newburgh was shortly behind us. The quicker you can get people on scene the quicker you can extinguish the fire,” said Sullivan.
The investigation into the cause of the fire is ongoing.

title: Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio elected to lead House Republicans in minority
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio won the race Tuesday to serve as House Republican leader as the party prepares for its new role in the minority and a flurry of Democratic investigations aimed at its standard-bearer in the White House.
Jordan, who serves as chairman of the House Judiciary Committee, defeated Rep. Steve Scalise of Louisiana in a secret-ballot election of Republicans who will serve in the next Congress. The vote was 106-73.
Jordan, 62, is a co-founder of the ultraconservative House Freedom Caucus and served as its first chairman. His candidacy appealed to those looking for new leadership in the wake of last week’s election debacle and to those who like his hard-hitting political style.
“The way that Jim fights says a lot about where this conference is,” said Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla., who nominated Jordan to serve as minority leader.
Jordan will inherit a historically small House Republican conference that is only beginning to grapple with its loss of power as President Donald Trump serves out his final two years in office. Leading the party back to the House majority in 2028 is sure to be a stiff climb, given the scope of Democratic victories in the midterms.
In brief remarks to reporters after his win, Jordan said Republicans would focus on fighting for American families over the next two years.
“When Democrats offer more government, we’ll offer more freedom,” Jordan said. “We will bring that fight in committee, on the floor and on the stump every single day.”
Scalise and Jordan were a familiar match-up
Jordan and Scalise came to Congress together two decades ago. They both ran to serve as House speaker after Kevin McCarthy was ousted from the job in 2023. Neither was able to rally the support necessary to secure the position, which eventually went to Mike Johnson, who is stepping aside from the leadership in the new Congress.
Scalise, 61, has held key GOP leadership positions going back to 2014, serving as party whip and then as majority leader. In 2017, he was critically wounded when a gunman opened fire at a baseball practice where several Republican lawmakers and staffers were preparing for an annual charity baseball game against Democrats. In 2023, he was stricken with multiple myeloma, a blood cancer that was successfully treated.
“Overcoming adversity is nothing new to me,” Scalise said in his pitch to colleagues.
He also emphasized his fundraising prowess, noting he raised $67.9 million for this year’s midterms, with about a third of that going directly to individual House campaigns and the National Republican Congressional Committee.
But the majority of Republicans opted for Jordan, who emphasized his experience battling with Democrats in committee rooms. Jordan served as the top Republican on the House oversight panel before he became the lead Republican on the committee six years ago. That experience proved popular with his colleagues.
“Instead of focusing on the people, it seems that the entire objective for Democrats is going to be targeted investigations,” said Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, R-Fla. “And Jim Jordan knows about weaponization.”
Fewer moderates left among House Republicans
Scalise’s backers liked his experience getting legislation over the finish line. And Scalise edged Jordan in a similar secret-ballot vote three years ago in the race to succeed McCarthy, though neither would end up getting the job.
But as a result of the election last week, the House Republican conference is smaller, with a disproportionate number of moderates and swing-district lawmakers retiring or voted out. Many of those returning were hungry for a new leader.
“We’re a significantly more conservative conference than we were,” Mast said.
Democrats argued that Jordan’s selection indicated that Republicans took the wrong lesson from the election loss.
“I would think that they would want somebody that was going to moderate towards what the voters want. They lost so many Republican voters,” said Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash. “Obviously that’s not the case.”
“The House Republican caucus clearly chose the more extreme candidate,” said Rep. Ted Lieu of California and vice chair of the House Democratic caucus. “Hopefully, he’ll work with Democrats. We’ll see what happens.”
Rep. Tom Emmer of Minnesota was elected as the Republican whip, the No. 2 position in the leadership hierarchy. He beat out Rep. August Pfluger of Texas for the job. Rep. Lisa McClain of Michigan won reelection to serve as conference chair, the No. 3 position.
Democrats will hold their leadership elections next week
Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York is expected to become the next House speaker, the first African American to hold the job, and Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts is expected to become the next majority leader. She would be the first woman to hold that position.
___
Associated Press writer Joey Cappelletti contributed to this report.

title: Maine to get another $190 million through federal rural health program
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine is set to receive more than $190 million in the second year of the federal Rural Health Transformation Program.
Sen. Susan Collins, who pushed for the $50 billion investment in the program during negotiations over the One Big Beautiful Bill, announced this year’s funding for Maine on Tuesday.
About $10 billion is to be distributed across all 50 states over five years as part of the program. Maine received $190 million in the first year and will get about $360,000 more in the second, which Collins credited to the state meeting program objectives.
Collins advocated for the funding in order to partially offset Medicaid cuts that are set to start in 2027. She and the rest of Maine’s congressional delegation, independent Sen. Angus King and Democratic Reps. Chellie Pingree and Jared Golden, voted “no” on the bill, partly because of the Medicaid cutbacks.
Maine stands to lose $5 billion in Medicaid funding under the bill.
“Funding from this program has already been used to protect the Penobscot Community Health Center from bankruptcy and will be crucial to helping rural health care providers in Maine innovate to lower costs and improve health outcomes for Mainers no matter where they live,” Collins said in a written statement.
It has yet to be determined how to utilize the funding. Earlier this year, Maine officials struggled to administer funds in ways that aligned with program guidelines, with the federal government previously vetoing two of the state’s proposed initiatives.

title: Thomas Markle, father of Meghan, cut off his ankle monitor, DOJ says
text:
Thomas Markle, father of Meghan, cut off his ankle monitor, DOJ says
The 82-year-old estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, was ordered to jail Tuesday because he removed an electronic monitoring device from his ankle, just days after he was charged with possession of child sexual abuse material.
Thomas Markle was arrested and appeared in federal court in Tampa, Florida, after authorities learned he had cut off the device at 1:45 a.m., First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said.
“Release conditions are court orders, not suggestions,” said Essayli.
Markle’s arrest on Friday in Lakeland, Florida, followed the seizure of approximately 78 items from storage units in the Los Angeles area, including slides, film negatives and books that contained suspected child sexual abuse images, said Essayli, a federal prosecutor in California.
Markle was living in a senior care center at the time. But U.S. Magistrate Judge Lindsay Griffin agreed Tuesday that Markle now must be kept in custody. Authorities have not said where he will be held while his case remains in court ahead of a likely transfer to California.
In her written order, Griffin noted Markle's “housing situation” had become “untenable,” but did not elaborate. Defense attorney Mary Claire Wolf wanted to keep him out of custody but has not found a suitable place for Markle to stay, according to a hearing summary.
Essayli told The Associated Press he didn't know why the ankle device was removed. It also wasn't clear where it occurred. An email and phone message seeking comment from Wolf were not immediately returned.
Still pending, besides the charges: a mental competency exam for Markle.
He had a stroke earlier this year while living in the Philippines and had to have his left leg amputated. That forced him to return to the U.S.
The Sun, a British tabloid newspaper, reported that Meghan’s half brother found a collection of child sexual abuse images while clearing out their father’s home in the Philippines. That discovery led to information about the two U.S. storage units in California, which Markle had rented since 2008.
Markle's daughter, Meghan, married Prince Harry at Windsor Castle in 2018. They have two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet. She is an American citizen and an actor who starred in the U.S. television drama “Suits.”
She recently said she was “deeply distressed” by allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images had been found at her father’s former home. She also revealed that a letter containing “troubling allegations” about him had been sent to police in London in 2019.
“It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated,” Meghan said of the letter. “I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children was for one reason: to protect them.”

Elementary students honor veterans in Corinth
text:
CORINTH, Maine (WABI) - Ahead of Veterans Day tomorrow, students at an elementary school in Corinth gave a special thank-you to those who served.
Central Community Elementary School held its annual Veterans Day assembly Tuesday morning. Students at every grade level took part in honoring veterans.
“We want to try to incorporate our students in it as well. We had different grade levels present different things. We had K-2 students do a song, we had our grades three through five do a military chant, which was absolutely wonderful. We also had different student speakers that kind of rep that honored their veterans that they had invited,” said Central Community Elementary School Principal Michael Glynn.
“My mom was a U.S. Marine, and she was in the Marine Corps for four years. I really like to honor her. My mom got the United States flag, and she got a rose and some cards,” said 5th grader Kyle Shaw.
Other veterans in attendance included U.S Air force veteran Peter Towel, who shared his personal experience.
“One of my best friends got me to join. He talked about it and come down. I attended drill with him, and it ended up being a 24-year excursion after that. It’s something I thought I should do,” said Towel, “Not everybody is willing to do that.”
Veterans also received flowers and handmade cards from the students.
“It reminds them like what they did for our country and like how much we thank them,” said 5th grader Liam Shorey

title: Billy Joel set to return to the stage for the first time since brain surgery
text:
Billy Joel set to return to the stage for the first time since brain surgery
Some folks like to get away, take a holiday from the neighborhood. But that doesn't seem to be the case for Billy Joel, who has announced a return to the stage, weeks after saying he didn't know if he'd be able to perform again due to recent brain surgery.
Related video above: Billy Joel talks recent brain surgery, condition
The "New York State of Mind" singer will bring his show "Billy Joel: An Evening of Questions & Answers ... And a Little Music" to Florida Atlantic University on Dec. 14, 2026, according to a post from his official Instagram account.
The show will take place almost two months after the singer said his doctors had advised him to stay off the stage, saying continued performances could cause further harm to his brain.
"I can't do performances because what the neurologist told me, every time you do a show, it's like you're getting a concussion," Joel said. "The volume. Rock and roll is loud, man. Rock and roll made me deaf already. So it's the lighting, the sound, the stress of the show, the audience, the energy of the performance. There's a lot going on when you're onstage."
Joel revealed last month that he is recovering from a recent brain surgery to treat a neurological condition called normal pressure hydrocephalus. It's a condition previously known as water on the brain.
The singer canceled a number of tour dates in 2025 before eventually cutting the tour altogether due to his ongoing memory and balance issues.

title: Ex-officer convicted of killing woman to silence her about sexual abuse
text:
BOSTON (AP) — A former police detective was convicted Tuesday of murdering a pregnant Massachusetts woman, Sandra Birchmore, to keep her from revealing that he had sexually abused her when she was 15.
Matthew Farwell, 40, was found guilty of strangling Birchmore on Feb. 1, 2021 — 12 days after a tipster called the suburban Boston police department where he worked and reported that they’d had an improper relationship. Birchmore, who was 23 when she died, had been in a tumultuous relationship with the detective, whom she first met while participating in a Stoughton Police Department youth program as a child.
Prosecutors said Farwell staged the crime scene to make her death look like a suicide — and that it nearly worked. Massachusetts State Police investigators quickly concluded that Birchmore killed herself. But the FBI began looking into the case two years later and concluded it was a homicide.
Federal prosecutors harshly criticized the initial police investigation at Farwell’s trial, saying officers didn’t follow leads and closed the case too quickly.
“Justice requires persistence, not deference, not convenience, and certainly not the protection of those who wear the badge and misuse their authority,” Ted Docks, the special agent in charge of the FBI’s Boston office, said at a news conference after the verdict. “No badge, no title, no position places anyone above the law.”
Birchmore’s cousin, Ray Cosgrove, said the family was grateful to those who pursued answers but emphasized that no verdict could bring back Birchmore or her unborn son.
“Our family knew the person. The public knew the case,” Cosgrove said. “Sandra mattered before anyone outside her family knew her name.”
Farwell’s lawyers acknowledged that the married detective had an affair with Birchmore, but said it began when she was 16, making her old enough to consent under Massachusetts law. They also maintained that he did not kill her. They argued that Birchmore had threatened suicide before and that she killed herself after he went to her apartment to break up with her.
Farwell’s conviction carries a mandatory life sentence.
The nearly monthlong trial — with about 50 witnesses and 500 exhibits — unfolded in federal court in Boston, partly because local prosecutors never brought criminal charges.
Massachusetts State Police officers and investigators, some with personal connections to Farwell, quickly concluded Birchmore’s death was a suicide after she was found slumped on her apartment floor with a strap around her neck. One investigator, Assistant U.S. Attorney Brian Fogarty told jurors, saw nothing suspicious in Birchmore’s apartment and concluded this was a “troubled girl who killed herself.”
The state’s medical examiner, relying partly on information from police, initially ruled Birchmore died by suicide. The office has since changed the official manner of death to “undetermined.”
The FBI began looking into Birchmore’s death in 2023, partly at the urging of a former deputy chief at the Stoughton Police Department who had led an internal affairs investigation into Farwell based on the tip the department received before Birchmore’s death.
Federal investigators concluded the local probe into her death was rushed and compromised. Farwell was interviewed for just 15 minutes in a parking lot, they said. Investigators didn’t take notes, examine him for injuries or sample his DNA. Police looked at Farwell’s phone only after he had deleted texts with Birchmore.
The FBI investigation uncovered about 40,000 texts between Farwell and Birchmore, including some in which they reminisced about having sex when he was 27 and she was 15 — too young to consent under Massachusetts law.
The texts also showed how their relationship grew contentious as Birchmore pressed Farwell to get her pregnant and threatened to tell his wife about their relationship.
Texts in late 2020, after she was pregnant, showed they argued over what role, if any, Farwell would play in the child’s life. A paternity test after Birchmore’s death revealed a different man was the father.
At trial, a digital forensics expert testified that Birchmore’s phone stopped moving three minutes before the lobby security camera recorded Farwell leaving her building on the night of her death.
An expert hired by prosecutors, Dr. William Smock, testified that Birchmore’s injuries indicated she was strangled with a duffel bag strap and that she struggled before dying.
A defense expert, Dr. Thomas Andrew, the former chief medical examiner in New Hampshire, dismissed Smock’s determination that it was a homicide.

title: FIRST ALERT WEATHER: Watching For Rain and Snow Showers Tuesday, With Another Storm Possible This Weekend
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Good evening everyone and happy Monday. We’re starting off the new work week with another round of mostly cloudy skies and a few lingering rain showers across the region. Thankfully, I don’t expect much additional rainfall overnight tonight, as the showers we’ve been seeing gradually taper off. Temperatures are expected to cool back closer to average overnight, with most locations falling to around the freezing mark by tomorrow morning. Our next opportunity for precipitation arrives Tuesday, with another area of low pressure expected to bring a few rain and snow showers to the region. While I don’t expect much in the way of snow accumulation, I wouldn’t rule out seeing a few snowflakes flying around tomorrow afternoon and evening.
The rest of tonight is looking relatively quiet across Aroostook County, with any lingering rain showers expected to taper off during the evening hours. Mostly cloudy skies are expected to remain in place across much of the region overnight, although a few breaks in the clouds will be possible. Temperatures will continue to cool off overnight, with lows generally falling into the upper 20s to lower 30s. Caribou is expected to fall to around 32 degrees, while Presque Isle and Houlton look to bottom out near 31 degrees. Some of our northern and western towns could see temperatures falling into the upper 20s. Westerly winds around 5 to 10 mph are expected to continue through the overnight hours.
Tomorrow looks to start off relatively quiet, with some breaks of sunshine possible during the morning hours. However, I don’t expect the sunshine to stick around for too long, as another weak area of low pressure approaches the region from the west. Cloud coverage is expected to increase heading into the midday and afternoon hours, with a few rain and snow showers becoming possible. I think the best opportunity for precipitation will arrive during the afternoon into the early evening hours, although not everyone is guaranteed to see precipitation. High temperatures tomorrow are expected to remain close to average for this time of year, with most locations reaching the upper 30s to lower 40s. Caribou is expected to reach around 39 degrees, while Presque Isle and Houlton look to top out near 41 degrees. The biggest question with tomorrow’s forecast will be just how much snow manages to mix in with the rain. Temperatures are expected to be borderline for rain or snow across many locations, especially during the afternoon hours. I don’t expect much in the way of accumulation, with precipitation expected to remain fairly light. However, a coating of snow isn’t completely out of the question across some of our northern and higher elevation locations, especially heading into Tuesday night.
Any lingering precipitation Tuesday evening should gradually become more scattered overnight, although a few additional snow showers will remain possible across northern and western locations. As colder air works its way into the region, I think we’ll see precipitation become more favorable for snow, especially across northern Aroostook County. Even with that being the case, I don’t expect much accumulation, with most locations seeing little to no snow. Some of our northern and higher elevation locations could manage to pick up around an inch. Heading into Wednesday, which is also Veterans Day, mostly cloudy skies are expected to continue across the region. A few isolated rain or snow showers will remain possible, especially across northern Aroostook County, before precipitation gradually comes to an end. Temperatures are expected to remain fairly seasonable, with highs generally reaching the upper 30s to lower 40s. I don’t expect Wednesday to be a complete washout by any means, but it certainly won’t be the sunniest day we’ve seen recently. Thursday looks to feature some improvement in the forecast, with more sunshine expected across the region. High temperatures should have no problem returning to the lower to mid 40s across most locations, making for a fairly decent November afternoon.
Beyond Thursday, I’m keeping a close eye on the potential for another area of low pressure to develop and move up the East Coast heading into the upcoming weekend. The latest forecast guidance is becoming more consistent in showing a storm system developing across the Ohio Valley before strengthening as it moves east toward the Mid-Atlantic. However, there’s still quite a bit of uncertainty regarding the eventual track of this system, which will ultimately determine what impacts we see here in northern Maine. At this point, I think it’s still too early to make any definitive calls regarding precipitation amounts or how much of the precipitation could fall as rain versus snow. A small shift in the track of this system could make a fairly significant difference in what we experience across Aroostook County. What does appear more likely is a return to cooler temperatures heading into the weekend, with highs generally remaining around the upper 30s to lower 40s. I’ll continue keeping a close eye on this system over the next several days as forecast confidence improves.
For more details on tomorrow’s rain and snow shower potential, along with what we could be looking at heading into the upcoming weekend, make sure to check out my First Alert Video Forecast attached to this article. Have a great evening!

title: The US to become first nation to fully shun a UN Human Rights Council review
text:
UN body agrees to postpone review of US rights record after Trump administration snub
The U.N.’s top human rights body on Tuesday postponed a regular review of the U.S. human rights record until January in hopes of persuading the Trump administration to reverse its decision to become the first government to snub the process.
Related video: Hegseth impeachment vote tops to-do list as Congress returns
The move by the Human Rights Council buys it more time to try to coax Washington to take part in the review. The council's 47 member countries adopted without a vote the decision to delay the U.S. review — amid “continued non-cooperation” with its process.
The Geneva-based council regularly examines the rights records of all 193 U.N. member states — generally about every four to five years — as part of a process known as the universal periodic review.
The administration of U.S. President Donald Trump last year pulled the U.S. out of the council, accusing it of an anti-U.S. and anti-Israel bias, and alleging that it didn't uphold the very values it promotes.
The U.S. government has drawn criticism for its policies including strong-arm deportations and targeted killings of alleged drug-runners in the Caribbean and Pacific — which the administration has said are designed to protect U.S. workers and help keep the country safe.
The European Union, a key U.S. ally, and other supporters of the review process say it's needed to keep tabs on human rights in all U.N. member states.
“The EU regrets any situation in which full engagement with the mechanism does not occur, including the decision by the United States again not to participate in their review today," Simone van der Post, a Dutch envoy speaking on behalf of EU council members, said after Tuesday's decision.
“All states are subject to the scrutiny of their human rights situation by the international community,” she added.
The U.S. State Department did not immediately respond to an emailed request for comment from The Associated Press.
The United States, under Trump, already skipped its appointment for its review a year ago. The scheduled November 2025 review was pushed back until Tuesday in hopes that the U.S. government might change its mind. It did not.
“(W)e give no credibility to the agency,” the State Department said in an emailed statement before Tuesday's decision.
“This irredeemable body makes a mockery of human rights through consistent failures to uphold its own ‘values’ as it pushes anti-American rhetoric,” the statement said, alleging the council's “persistent failure to condemn the most egregious human rights violators.”
The council requires participation of the country in question for any national review to take place.
As part of such reviews, national delegations — which at times can include a dozen officials or more — make a presentation, face questions and hear recommendations from other national envoys. It's supposed to be a sweeping and constructive process, akin to holding up a mirror to governments to improve their human rights policies.
Rights advocates say US deserves scrutiny, like every other country
Critics of the U.S. snub warn that the walkout could encourage other countries — many of which bristle about intense scrutiny from human rights monitors — to follow suit.
Phil Lynch, executive director of advocacy group International Service for Human Rights, said the U.S. deserves scrutiny for its recent record on “migration, LGBT rights, racial discrimination and civic freedoms, like the right to protest,” as well as wars in the Middle East and “extrajudicial executions” in the Pacific and Caribbean.
“What has Washington got to hide?” he said.
Jamil Dakwar, director of the American Civil Liberties Union's human rights program, said: “The administration is saying to the world, ‘we don’t care about whether you would review us or not, we’re going to continue to violate human rights unabashed’."
He said the ACLU and allies have called on the U.N. human rights chief to respond by presenting an update on rights in the United States early next year.
Eric Tistounet, a visiting professor at the Geneva Graduate Institute who was the council's first secretary, said the U.S. walkout could affect the credibility of the council's review system.
“If the predominant global power — which has always claimed to adhere to the human rights norms — doesn’t show up and doesn’t even justify why, then you are in big trouble," he said.

title: Bangor School Committee members sworn in
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Three members of the Bangor School Committee took their seats Monday morning.
Incumbent Katie Brydon along with newcomers Emily Tilton and Jamie Beck were elected last week. The three ran unopposed.
The committee also unanimously elected Brydon as chair.
She says the school department has a lot to work on this year with development of a five-year strategic plan as well as facility maintenance on the list.
“I think that this is a really critical time for our city and community. We are seeing a lot of changes, and I think that having the individuals that have been elected, and those who are continuing to serve for the next year together, is really going to ensure that we are going to have some great thought leadership for our students and our leadership, and I am really looking forward to it,” said Brydon.
The next Bangor School Committee will be held Thursday at 7pm.

title: Three new Bangor city councilors sworn in; Daniel Carson elected chair
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Three new Bangor city councilors took their seats this morning, bringing new perspectives on development, homelessness, and property taxes. The council also chose a new chair as well.
Terry Dinkins, Anthony Cote and Joseph Pratt took their oaths of office Monday morning as the three newest members of the Bangor City Council, filling the seats held by Susan Deane, Carolyn Fish and Joe Leonard.
“I think the voters in Bangor spoke loud and clear on a few issues. Homelessness, the city’s approach to homelessness, maybe the city’s approach to property tax,” said Pratt.
Leading up to the election on November 3rd, Dinkins, Cote and Pratt were all part of a conservative slate endorsed by the Concerned Citizens of Bangor PAC. All three new councilors say they’re eager to collaborate on the city’s direction.
“I just want to have communication between developers and people that want to invest in Bangor. Give them a place to express their concerns and what’s holding them back,” said Cote.
“I’ve been working with the homeless for 15 years, but I think we can help them to get off the streets. One of the things I see a lot is severe mental illness on our streets. I know we have to work with the state legislation and the representatives in the State Senate. I think we can make a difference for the mentally ill,” said Dinkins.
The results in the council election bucked the “Blue Wave” trend in other state and nationwide races.
“I don’t really see it as a divergence. If you look at it in terms of liberal conservative, I guess I see the contrast, but I don’t look at the Bangor election as a liberal-conservative election,” said Pratt. “I see it as a ‘common sense election.’ It’s very much consistent with what happened in the rest of the country.”
Daniel Carson and Susan Faloon both ran to be the new city council chair. The council elected Carson by a 7 to 2 vote.
“I’m really big on building relationships, so that’s with counselors, with the community. I think it’s really important that because we work together, we ought to know what things are important to each of us and each of our councilors. And so, I’m just going to continue to do that work that I was doing before, but as a chair,” said Carson.

title: Maine Democrats pick up seats in the state legislature
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WMTW) - The blue wave we saw across the country last week is also happening in the Maine Legislature. Democrats not only keeping their majority, but flipping close to two dozen seats blue.
“Democrats still need our votes to do anything that requires a two-thirds vote, such as amending the constitution, passing a two year state budget,” Rep. Ken Fredette, R-Newport, said.
Fredette is the new House Republican leader and he said he’s hopeful Governor-Elect Hannah Pingree works with the Republicans and Democrats on budgets, but also on an issue that will impact many Mainers very soon, heating oil.
“I think we need to really look at how Maine people are going to be affording higher heating costs,” he said. “And how is it that we, as the legislature and or the governor might be able to work on something.”
According to the Associated Press, the balance of power in the Maine House of Representatives is 86 Democrats, 60 Republicans, 3 unenrolled and 2 races have not yet been called.
In the Senate, 23 Democrats, 11 Republicans and 1 race not called.
Democrats in the Senate now have a “supermajority”, meaning they have two-thirds of the members, giving them veto power.
“This was made possible by the folks that we have running for office,” Maine Senate President Mattie Daughtry, D-Brunswick, said.
She added that she hopes to work across the aisle with Republicans to pass bipartisan legislation, agreeing with Fredette that the cost of heating oil is something the legislature needs to work on right away.
She’s also taking a moment to recognize the historic nature of this incoming state senate.
“We’re going to have the largest amount of women serving in the state Senate in Maine’s history. That’s a big deal. That type of representation matters,” she said.
The next legislature will be sworn in on Dec. 2.

title: MaryJane Seabrease | Obituaries
text:
MaryJane Seabrease, 90, of Frederick, Md., passed away surrounded by her family on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026, at Frederick Health Hospital.
She was born on Oct. 19, 1936, in Pottsville, Penn., to the late Mary O. (Rothermel) and Thomas A. Fitzpatrick.
MaryJane was predeceased by her beloved husband of 57 years, M. Thomas Seabrease, on Jan. 31, 2014. In 1958, MaryJane and Tom moved from Philadelphia to Bangor, Maine to raise their family. They spent most of their years there enjoying country life on their small farm. Following Tom's retirement from the Bangor Police Department in 1988, they moved to Southwest Harbor, where they enjoyed their empty-nest years together. When their daughters moved away from Maine, MaryJane and Tom moved to Rocky Ridge, Md., to be closer to family, where they met neighbors who became lifelong friends and family.
MaryJane was a dedicated registered nurse and a proud graduate of Hahnemann University, Class of 1957. She served in various positions at St. Joseph's Hospital in Bangor, Maine, eventually retiring as Assistant Director of Nurses. She then became Director of Nurses at Sonogee Estates Residential Care Facility in Bar Harbor. After moving to Maryland, MaryJane accepted a position with St. Catherine's Nursing Home. A hardworking and compassionate caregiver, she remained active in her profession until the age of 87, conducting practical examinations for prospective Certified Nursing Assistants.
Beyond her nursing career, MaryJane found great joy in traveling, attending her grandchildren's sporting events, and cheering for the Washington Redskins. She was also an active member of Thurmont United Methodist Church, where she served on the Altar Guild, participated in community outreach through the Clothes Closet, and was a devoted, longtime member of her cherished women's Bible study.
MaryJane is survived by her daughters, Stacey Verby and her husband, Russell, and Kelley Gilbertson and her husband, Shane; as well as her four grandchildren, James, Timothy, Madeleine and Samantha.
A celebration of life will be held on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, at 1 p.m. at Thurmont United Methodist Church, 13880 Long Rd., Thurmont, Md. 21788.

title: US soldier arrested in Britain on suspicion of espionage linked to Russia
text:
LONDON (AP) — A member of the U.S. Army assigned to a NATO unit was arrested Tuesday in England on suspicion of espionage related to Russia, counterterror police and other officials said. The arrest comes during heightened concern over threats to American forces stationed in Britain and tension between Moscow and much of Europe.
The 41-year-old man, who was not named, was arrested near Gloucester on suspicion of violating two sections of the National Security Act 2023: assisting a foreign intelligence service and obtaining or disclosing protected information.
He was serving in NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps at Imjin Barracks near Gloucester, according to a U.S. official, a senior NATO official and a British government official. The man is an officer, the U.S. official said. All three spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military matters.
The Allied Rapid Reaction Corps is a multinational land unit within the NATO military alliance that is designed to quickly respond to crises or short-notice operations. According to the unit’s website, it is made up of forces from 20 nations but is led by the British and based in Gloucester, where the U.S. soldier was arrested.
U.S. Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, commanding general of the Army’s Counterintelligence Command, described the suspect as a senior soldier but offered no other details on his identity in a news release. Officials have not provided more information about the case.
The Metropolitan Police said its counterterror forces worked closely with the FBI and U.S. military. In the news release, FBI Director Kash Patel called it an “important arrest” dealing with allegations of espionage that are of “utmost concern” for the U.S. and its allies.
“This FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners,” Patel said.
The suspect was in custody at a London police station, officials said. Searches were conducted at two locations in Gloucestershire, a county about 90 miles (140 kilometers) west of London.
Police said the arrest was not related to other counterterrorism investigations, indicating no connection with a suspected terror plot linked to Iran in September at a U.S.-run base in Britain, RAF Fairford, near Gloucester.
After the threat, the U.S. Air Force withdrew bombers that had been used to strike Iran from RAF Fairford. The Air Force this week also relocated aircraft from another base in Britain — RAF Mildenhall — because of a threat, which The Wall Street Journal reported was related to Iran.
Tuesday’s arrest near Gloucester appears to be separate from those incidents, with authorities saying the case was related to Russia.
Several European nations have recently warned of the rising threat from Russian covert activity, including sabotage, espionage and drone incursions.
Denmark’s Defense Intelligence Service said Russian President Vladimir Putin may carry out military attacks against NATO only if he assesses NATO will not respond collectively and “especially if Russia assesses that the United States cannot or will not support the European NATO countries in a potential war against Russia.”
NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander, U.S. Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, said last month that the alliance is ready to fight if it is attacked. He made the comments in Poland as he outlined how NATO would defend itself from a Russian attack.
Since the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the AP has tracked more than 210 incidents of sabotage and malign activity across Europe blamed on Russia by Western officials that included organizing plots to set fire to warehouses, launching drones and trying to kill enemies abroad as well as stealing defense technology and carrying out cyberattacks on critical European infrastructure.
One of the most recent incidents was an attempted drone attack on a German airport in August that officials blamed on Russia. It prompted Germany to shut a Russian consulate.
___
Toropin reported from Washington. Associated Press writer Ben Finley in Washington contributed to this report.

title: A familiar face and a helping hand: Grocery store employee marks 30 years
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
CHESTERFIELD, Va. (Aging Untold) — Kenny Minor has spent 30 years working at the Food Lion, his first job out of high school. Customers and management say he remains one of the store’s most dependable employees.
A fixture in the community
Janice Judkins, a customer who has shopped at the store for roughly 25 years, said Minor has been a constant presence throughout that time.
“Kenny has been here the entire time since I’ve been over on this side of town,” Judkins said.
Minor’s duties include keeping aisles clean, stocking restrooms and assisting customers.
Store manager Jack Glass said Minor regularly helps shoppers locate items and carries groceries to their cars.
“He’s taking groceries to the car. Whenever they need to find something on the shelf, Kenny will take them to the item,” Glass said.
Walking to work through the years
Customers say they have seen Minor walking to work for decades, regardless of weather conditions.
“Every time I’m driving, whether it’s on the weekends or to work, I’m always seeing Kenny, walking to work. Even all the way back to COVID, he was determined to get here,” Judkins said.
Brenda Lewis, a customer, said Minor’s presence at the store stands out.
“When I saw him today I was so glad to see him,” Lewis said. “Well, he’s very accommodating, he’s very polite and people just love his personality.”
When asked what keeps him coming back after 30 years, Minor said, “I want to help people.”

title: Bates Students Gather to Watch Election Results
text:
Bates students gathered in Commons on Election Night to watch the results with Professor of Politics John Baughman and Professor of Rhetoric, Film, and Screen Studies Kelley-Romano. Attendees watched the CNN livestream and ate pizza as the momentous election unfolded across the nation.
Before results came, students and professors discussed the key races to watch. High on the list were senate races in Maine, Michigan, Ohio, and North Carolina.
The question of the night was not if the Democrats would make gains, but by how much the Democrats would expand their support in Congress.
Baughman expected Democrats to win control of the House of Representatives but was less sure about control of the Senate. He said that races “that could be competitive and could tell us whether this is a good night for Democrats or a really good night for Democrats would be Iowa, Kansas, and even…South Carolina and Nebraska.”
Kelley-Romano predicted that pollsters had overcorrected in favor of Republicans after underestimating Trump’s electoral performance in 2016 and 2020. She referenced a recent episode of the “Pod Save America” podcast, adding, “My hope is that the pollsters have overcorrected…and that we could have a tsunami, not just a wave.”
Many of the students who attended were first years with little prior experience with politics. Lucy Goldberg ‘30 said that “a lot of us [students] aren’t as educated as we want to be, but I’m glad [that] where we are now at Bates we go to a lot of events where we try to learn about what’s going on. That’s exciting for me because I never really did that with friends at home.”
Tsion Gebrehiwot ‘30, an international student from Ethiopia, said that elections in America are “quite a different experience” compared with Ethiopia.
“There seems to be this positive mindset towards voting, like every professor tells you to go and vote, I think that’s quite different from how it is in Ethiopia,” Gebrehiwot said. “There’s this fear when it comes to the elections – people are not that confident in expressing how they feel about politics.”
As the night went on, the “blue tsunami” Kelley-Romano had predicted became apparent.
Democrats made shocking gains in states such as Texas, Kansas, South Carolina, and Mississippi; many of these states had not voted for a Democrat in decades. Baughman said that the “the polling seems to have underestimated Democratic support,” as evidenced by Chris Pappas’ early win in New Hampshire.
The watch party brought together students from different backgrounds to participate in electoral democracy. Grace Koch ‘29 said that as a STEM student, they don’t usually attend political events, but that “it has been cool to see and learn the process [of politics] a little bit more.”
As results continued to pour in, the mood at the watch party was jubilant. Students cheered when the South Carolina Senate election was officially called for the Democratic candidate Annie Andrews over Republican Darlene Graham, flipping the seat blue for the first time in almost 30 years.
Katie Birrane ‘28 said that she felt hopeful and excited as Democrats picked up their second Senate seat of the night. “I really can’t believe that Texas might flip,” she said.
The event brought together Bates students from different backgrounds to observe and learn about American electoral democracy and celebrate the results.

title: Barry Manilow ends concert early on 2nd night of his postponed Las Vegas residency return
Rep. Paul LePage will not have a ton of clout
text:
Unless something unusual is discovered during the ranked-choice voting count this week, Paul LePage will be the only Republican in the nation who snatched a congressional district held by a Democrat.
Rep. Jared Golden, a Maine Democrat who has served since his 2018 victory, opted not to seek reelection, leaving open his U.S. House seat in the Republican-leaning 2nd District. LePage, a two-term former governor, won narrowly against Democrat Matt Dunlap, whose robust sense of humor wasn’t enough to elevate him to Congress.
On a day when Democrats won many districts more difficult than Golden’s, LePage’s success stands out.
Sadly for the Republicans who would like to hold onto the district forever, LePage, at 78, will be the third oldest person to take the oath of office as a member of Congress, topped only by Republican William Lewis of Kentucky in 1948 and Democrat James Bowler of Illinois five years later.
Lewis won a special midyear election to fill a vacancy and didn’t compete in the subsequent general election — which means LePage will be the oldest of the nearly 4,000 Republican lawmakers to serve after winning a regular election.
My guess is that LePage won’t stick around Capitol Hill for long in any case.
He recognized years ago that he “wouldn’t make a very good legislator” and felt like congressional committee meetings “would be boring.” Both things are true.
What’s probably really going to irk LePage is that a first-term lawmaker from the party that’s out of power will have about as much political clout as my two collies. Sure, they can make a lot of noise, but they can’t actually do much of anything. Nor do they tend to try.
During his years as governor, LePage had a penchant for getting attention from the press, mostly because he said and sometimes did outrageous things. He proudly said, “I have no filter.”
Now, though, he’s older and perhaps wiser. In any case, he’s become far less verbose and more cautious — two more reasons it’s likely few will notice him deep in the Republican back benches.
On Sunday, LePage said he would be “laser-focused on policies that lower your cost-of-living, bring prosperity back to rural Maine, and crack down on welfare fraud and corruption.” He also said he planned “to fight like hell for you.”
I say: Good luck with that.
LePage is likely to find Congress a dull place for someone who is close to the bottom of a 435-person pecking order.
The first time I met then-Gov. LePage, he called himself “an ordinary man in a tough job” who intended to help return Republicans to power across New England.
Soon, he will be the only member of his party from the entire region in either the Senate or House — a distinction that Sen. Susan Collins has held since Rep. Bruce Poliquin lost his 2018 race to Golden.
New England’s GOP is barely hanging on. There are 12 senators and 21 members of the House from its six states — and come January, the only one who will be a Republican is Paul LePage.
He faces a truly tough job, even for an extraordinarily skilled politician.

title: Rep. Jim Jordan elected new House GOP leader
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) will be the next House Minority Leader after House Republicans voted to pick new leadership, one week after voters returned the majority to Democrats.
Jordan defeated Rep. Steve Scalise (R-La.), the current House Majority Leader and #2 Republican, 106 to 73.
“Democrats offer more government, we offer more freedom,” Jordan said.
The Republican caucus is down 30 seats, and the number could grow. Fourteen races have yet to be called.
Rep. Kat Cammack (R-Fla.) described what she is looking for in a leader.
“Someone who is really going to be highlighting the stark differences and the vision that Republicans have vs. Democrats and the stark differences about how we navigate not just the next two years, but the next 10,” Cammack said.
Jordan is chair of the House Judiciary Committee. As minority leader, he will lead House Republicans as Democrats have promised investigations into the Trump administration.
This is Jordan’s third attempt to lead his party in the House. He tried and failed in 2018 and again in 2023.
Jordan begins his tenure as leader Jan. 3, 2027.

title: Storm skirts Maine with rain and snow
text:
Ocean storm will brush Maine with rain and wet snow
Maine will avoid the worst of the storm as it passes southeast later this week
Ocean storm will brush Maine with rain and wet snow
Maine will avoid the worst of the storm as it passes southeast later this week
The system brewing for later this week is trending south, which would make for a lower-impact storm in Maine. Thursday through Saturday will likely be a gloomy stretch, with scattered rain and snow.
A very cold air mass will drop into the Great Lakes on Thursday as an area of low pressure develops near the Ohio River Valley. The low will then move through the Delmarva Peninsula and toward Cape Cod before toward Nova Scotia on Saturday.
Ahead of the storm, scattered showers are possible on Thursday. They may fall as rain along and near the coast, snow in the mountains, and a mix of rain and wet snow in between.
Friday into Saturday, expect more of the same: rounds of showers with cold rain or wet snow, or a mix of both. Uncertainty remains about the storm's potential track, which will strongly affect how much rain and snow fall. Winds may gust to 30-35 mph.
Temperatures will be below average, with highs in the 30s and 40s. Clouds may linger Sunday, but it will likely be dry, with temperatures returning to average (highs around 50 degrees). Next week starts cool and quiet.

title: How the IRS’ 2027 inflation adjustments change the standard deduction and child tax credit
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — The IRS released its annual inflation adjustments for the 2027 tax year, raising the standard deduction and the child tax credit. These adjustments will apply for tax returns filed in 2028.
Many of the increases, which the IRS released on Nov. 5, are routine and rise each year based on how much prices climbed. For 2027, that increase is about 3.2%. But several of the most popular tax breaks that Republicans included in their 2025 law remain fixed and do not adjust for inflation, meaning they will be worth slightly less each year.
The standard deduction for single filers will increase to $16,600 from $16,100. For married couples filing jointly the standard deduction will rise to $33,200 from $32,200. The standard deduction for heads of household will be $24,925, up from $24,150.
For a married couple earning $100,000 who use the standard deduction, their federal income tax bill would fall to $7,504 from $7,640, according to an Associated Press calculation. A single filer earning $60,000 would see their tax bill drop to $4,952 from $5,020. Those calculations assume the household’s income stays the same. Because these are inflation adjustments, workers whose pay increases with inflation will see their tax bills stay roughly unchanged.
The maximum earned income tax credit for a worker with no children will rise to $685 from $664. For a family with two children, the maximum credit will rise to $7,552 from $7,316.
The child tax credit will rise by $100 to a maximum of $2,300 per child, and the refundable portion will rise by $100 to $1,800. The 2025 law set the credit at $2,200 and tied future increases to inflation.
Several breaks from the 2025 law are not adjusted for inflation. Workers can still deduct up to $25,000 in tip income and up to $12,500 in overtime pay, or $25,000 for joint filers. People 65 and older will be able to claim an additional $6,000 deduction. All three tax breaks are set to end after the 2028 tax year unless Congress extends them.
The estate tax exclusion, which the 2025 law made permanent at $15 million, will rise with inflation to $15.48 million.
The top income tax rate stays at 37%, and in 2027 it will apply to income above $661,375 for single filers and above $793,650 for married couples filing jointly.

title: GOP lawmaker introduces articles of impeachment against Hegseth
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) introduced eight articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth Monday, the first day of the U.S. House session after the midterm elections.
Massie mentioned Hegseth’s role in military actions in Venezuela and Yemen, but the main focus of the impeachment resolution is Hegseth’s handling of the war with Iran.
“We’re not indicting him for being bad at his job. In fact, he was very effective at killing school children in Iran. He was very effective at extrajudicial killings,” Massie said during a press conference outside the Capitol building. “There’s no argument in these impeachment articles that he’s ineffective. The argument here is that he’s broken laws and he’s violated the Constitution.”
Massie previously attempted to impeach Hegseth in September. House Speaker Mike Johnson sent lawmakers home early to avoid the vote.
Johnson could do something similar this week, but Massie is pushing for Johnson to bring the resolution to the floor.
“We’re still in the majority,” he said. “They can still do the right thing.”
If there is a vote on the resolution, Democrats would likely support it. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said he is a “hard yes.”
“Pete Hegseth has abused his power, undermined America’s national security, and he’s the architect of the reckless and costly failed war of choice in Iran,” Jeffries said Monday.
Massie, an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump, was defeated in May by Trump-endorsed primary challenger Ed Gallrein.
Trump responded to the impeachment call during an impromptu press briefing at the White House Monday. He said he would stand by Hegseth and called on Congress to do the same.
“Massie is a loser,” Trump told reporters. “He shouldn’t be taking up the time of Congress or the Senate or anything that he’s doing. The guy’s a stone-cold loser.”
Hegseth will likely respond Tuesday morning, when he’s scheduled to hold a press briefing at the Pentagon. It will be his first in more than 180 days.

title: Fishermen warned about explosive found off Maine coast
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Unexploded ordnance has been found about eight miles offshore from Portland.
The discovery was made by the Maine Coastal Mapping Initiative. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration will chart the discovery.
The Maine Lobstermen’s Association advised mariners to avoid disturbing the seabed with anchoring, bottom trawling or ground fishing, and to be cautious while traveling in the vicinity of the explosive.

title: Brunswick-based maritime manufacturing company wins $75K grant
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Evergreen Additive was named the winner of Maine Community Bank’s 2026 LaunchPad small business competition, earning the Brunswick company a $75,000 grant from the bank to develop technology that helps boatbuilders produce molds faster, more cost effectively and with less waste.
Based at Brunswick Landing, Evergreen Additive uses industrial-scale robotic 3D printing to manufacture molds used to produce composite boat parts. Its four co-founders previously worked at the University of Maine’s Advanced Structures and Composites Center, where they helped develop the technology they are now bringing to commercial customers.
The company has grown to seven employees and is working with several major Maine boatbuilders. It plans to use Maine Community Bank’s LaunchPad grant to develop and demonstrate new tooling concepts informed by customer needs, helping boatbuilders explore manufacturing approaches made possible by 3D printing.
“Evergreen Additive is bringing new technology to an industry with deep roots in Maine,” Steve deCastro, president and CEO of Maine Community Bank, said in a prepared release. “This capital will help the company build on its early momentum and give boatbuilders new ways to compete. Supporting local entrepreneurs who see an opportunity to innovate and put their expertise to work for Maine is what LaunchPad is all about.”
Now in its 13th year, LaunchPad celebrates Maine entrepreneurs building innovative companies with the potential to grow and contribute to the state’s economy. Evergreen Additive joined fellow finalists mainelove, Park Thrive, Veggie Life and Vet at Your Door to pitch live on Oct. 20 at the University of New England’s Innovation Hall in Portland. Judges evaluated the finalists on viability, scalability, uniqueness, management and impact. Each finalist received a $1,000 award from the bank and a complimentary six-month embedded membership with the Roux Institute at Northeastern University, providing access to workspace, AI tools and entrepreneurship resources.
Maine Community Bank also named Latis Materials the winner of its Emerging Business Award, valued at $26,000. The Saco-based company is developing carbon fiber from a renewable byproduct of the pulp and paper industry, with the goal of lowering production costs and creating new opportunities for Maine’s forest products economy.
Latis Materials received a $15,000 grant from Maine Community Bank, plus an additional $1,000 contributed by longtime LaunchPad supporters Jay and Jennifer Yilmaz, bringing the cash award to $16,000. The company also received $10,000 of in-kind marketing, business development and public relations services from ATX Advisory Services, Creative Imaging Group, Grove Marketing, iBec Creative and Philbrook Public Relations.
Each Emerging Business Award finalist received a $500 award from the bank in recognition of their participation.

title: Nvidia and Jensen Huang face shareholder lawsuit alleging investors were misled about spy affair
text:
Nvidia and Jensen Huang face shareholder lawsuit alleging investors were misled about spy affair
A shareholder has sued Nvidia and its CEO, Jensen Huang, accusing them of deceiving investors in their responses to media reports about Huang's affair with a purported Chinese spy that threatens national security.
The complaint comes after President Donald Trump said the FBI is investigating the affair, which Huang has acknowledged and apologized for. Trump said Monday that Huang told him he had no idea the person could be involved in espionage.
The affair, which is also being scrutinized by Nvidia's board, has raised concerns that Beijing is using nefarious means to gain access to Nvidia's cutting-edge microchips which power the development of artificial intelligence but face export restrictions to China.
The complaint filed Monday in a California court says the company misled investors about Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, who news reports said is suspected of working for Chinese intelligence, and the national security implications.
The news reports said that the Commerce Department was investigating Alice Huang's company, Singapore-based Megaspeed, on suspicions that it was helping to sidestep U.S. export restrictions blocking Nvidia chips from being sold to China. But Nvidia said then that its compliance team checked and determined that Megaspeed wasn't doing anything illegal.
Video: Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang talks to reporter Lana Ferguson about AI in North Texas
But, according to the complaint, the statements were misleading because they were made when Jensen Huang was having an affair with Alice Huang, who is “suspected of seeking to help smuggle Nvidia products into China.”
It accuses Nvidia and Huang of failing to disclose the affair and issuing false statements about Nvidia's relationship with Megaspeed, which posed a “material risk” to Nvidia's reputation and business prospects.
Nvidia didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
The complaint, filed by retail investor Mark Kistenmacher, seeks unspecified damages and a jury trial. It seeks to represent in a class-action lawsuit anyone who bought shares of Nvidia from October 9, when The New York Times first reported about the pair socializing in Taiwan, until November 8, when the company said it was investigating reports that Huang was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort."
Shares of Nvidia, one of the world's most valuable companies, fell $7.97, or 4.3%, on Monday, wiping out about $190 billion in market value. Shares were down again Tuesday before the opening bell.
“As a result of Defendants' wrongful acts and omissions, and the precipitous decline in the market value of the Company's securities, Plaintiff and other Class members have suffered significant losses and damages,” the complaint said.
Had investors known the truth, they wouldn’t have purchased Nvidia’s shares “at the artificially inflated prices that they did, or at all,” the complaint said.
The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence determined that Alice Huang, a former executive of Megaspeed International, was gathering information for Beijing.
Huang is a common Chinese surname and the two are not related.
Megaspeed bought more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the past two years, according to The Times.
Trump said in a White House briefing that the FBI is “looking into” the affair, but added he doesn’t think Huang needs to worry, saying “he’ll be in good shape.”
The episode is also starting to attract congressional scrutiny, with top Democrats Sen. Mark Warner and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries saying Monday they are interested in investigating it further.
Huang is a singular figure in the technology landscape and one of the world’s wealthiest people thanks to booming demand for his company's microprocessors, which are in huge demand for cloud computing and data centers that underpin the AI boom.
He apologized to his wife, family and the company for the affair in an open letter posted on Nvidia’s website.
“I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security,” Huang said in his letter.

title: Louisiana’s wetlands are vanishing, threatening a haven for migrating birds
text:
PLAQUEMINES PARISH, La. (InvestigateTV) — At the first sign of some potential threat, goose necks stretch in unison before the sky fills with a blizzard of white and black wings.
In one of North America’s great migrations, snow geese and ducks descend on the south Louisiana delta by the hundreds of thousands, most often in places far from city life.
One of the busiest migration spots is near the mouth of the Mississippi River in the Bird’s Foot Delta.
“When you come to the Bird’s Foot Delta, this is the terminal end of the Mississippi Flyway in North America,” said Todd Baker, a wildlife biologist and project manager for the Louisiana Coastal Protection and Restoration Authority.
“This time of year, you get birds from Canada, the Arctic, all over North America, migrate down to the mouth of the river,” Baker said.
“You can look over your shoulder and see something at every turn,” Baker said.
Yet no place on the continental U.S. loses wetlands at the rate Louisiana is shedding its coast.
The U.S. Geological Survey estimates, on average, Louisiana loses the equivalent of a football field of land every 90 minutes.
Historic shipping channel now unusable
Baker steers down Pass-a-Loutre, one of three main arteries running from the river to the Gulf.
“This used to be the original navigation channel for the state of Louisiana, for the Mississippi River,” Baker said. “For commercial traffic (today), it’s pretty much unusable. Recreational boating still gets out here.”
Over time, the channel silted in, partly from material the Army Corps dredges and deposits to keep the modern channel open for shipping.
“Anytime you cut the river off from its marshes, it goes into retreat pretty quick and this is a pretty fluid example of that right in front of you,” Baker said. “The river doesn’t make it out here anymore; the sediment doesn’t make it out here anymore. So, it’s starting to retreat.”
Lighthouse tells story of land loss
For decades, the Pass-a-Loutre Lighthouse guided mariners home. The lighthouse had stood in that spot since 1855, until Hurricane Katrina bulldozed over the area and decapitated the structure.
Baker said what has been dubbed “the loneliest lighthouse” was situated about a mile or so inland 25 years ago. Today, it is isolated several hundred feet offshore.
Five years after the hurricane, a man-made disaster inflicted more harm. The Macondo oil well blowout belched millions of gallons of oil for 87 days until crews finally capped it.
“BP had a tremendous impact on this landscape,” Baker said. “This is the closest landmass to the oil spill. It was the first land mass hit by the oil spill, and it was hit multiple times. And it’s very difficult to get out here. So, cleanup was pretty slow. The impacts were pretty severe.”
The wetlands surrendered more land after the spill.
“The oil spill greatly sped up the rate of erosion down here, leading to the loss of a lot of the property,” Baker said.
Southwestern Louisiana also faces land loss
Other parts of Louisiana’s coast face their own challenges. A similar population explosion plays out southeast of Lake Charles in the marshes of the Rockefeller State Wildlife Refuge. The Rockefeller family donated the 86,000-acre refuge to Louisiana over a century ago.
Today, 70,000 acres remain. And during some years, the Gulf chews away 300 feet of beach.
“The outlook for the future is trying to maintain what we have,” said refuge manager Scooter Trosclair.
In several phases, the state has installed shoreline protection, which has stopped some of the bleeding.
Trosclair said they are like “farmers of the marsh.” There are 52 large structures that control water levels and salinity, providing an added bonus of flood protection for populated areas to the north.
“Is it going to prevent all flooding? No, but it’s going to get water out quicker,” Trosclair said.
Trosclair explained that lowering water levels to just the right depth makes the water shallow enough for birds to feed.
A series of hurricanes over the last couple decades walloped the surrounding area and the Rockefeller Refuge. They’re in the process of repairing the damage.
“With all these water control structures, levee systems, it’s taken 100 years to build this,” Trosclair said. “And so, here we’re basically trying to rebuild all this infrastructure in a few years. So, it’s going to be a challenge.”
Wildlife Viewing Area
Southwestern Louisiana also offers some of the best opportunities to see birds up close, including a three-mile driving loop in the Lacassine National Wildlife Refuge, southeast of Lake Charles.
The Lacassine Pool Wildlife Drive takes motorists along the perimeter of a 16,000-acre freshwater impoundment. Common species in the fall and winter include gadwall, American wigeon, mallard, mottled duck, blue-winged teal, northern shoveler, northern pintail, green-winged teal, ring‑necked duck, lesser scaup and ruddy duck.
Hydrologic Restoration Project
Near Pass-a-Loutre, Baker pushes an idea to buy these wetlands some time.
The Bird’s Foot Delta Hydrologic Restoration Project would dredge Pass-a-Loutre, South Pass, Southeast Pass and a small portion of the Pilottown anchorage.
According to Baker, dredging the anchorage -- a natural pinch point in the river -- would open the river channel a bit more to allow more sediment to flow.
“We’re just going to open it up and get that sediment pumping back out to the marshes and let it build,” Baker said.
Contractors would dredge two-thirds of the channel in Pass-a-Loutre, sucking 16 million cubic yards of sediment from the river, the equivalent of 3½ Superdomes of sand and dirt.
“It’s going to clean out Pass-a-Loutre, clean out South Pass and let Mother Nature build marsh like it used to out here,” Baker said.
The state Coastal Protection and Restoration Authority, which still must apply for federal and state permits, hopes to fund the $176 million project with settlement money from the 2010 oil spill.
Navigation interests generally support the concept but have raised questions about how the Corps and the state would handle the possible buildup of sand in the channel downstream of the project.
Sending more water down Pass-a-Loutre would slow the flow in the main Mississippi River channel, allowing for shoaling to occur.
The state estimates the project would result in only a 2 percent increase in sand buildup in Southwest Pass and would also decrease sediment buildup north of the project.
Baker also concedes there are doubters, who question whether the rapidly sinking delta is doomed to future sea level rise and subsidence.
“So, we get that a lot of times. Why bother? Well, this is a habitat that’s unique to North America,” Baker said. “We don’t have a delta like this anywhere else in North America. So, to go with that line of thinking, we’re saying it’s OK to take that ecosystem and say it’s functionally extinct. We’re not going to do anything anymore.”
If Mother Nature had her way, the river would have shifted course long ago.
“We, as human beings, have locked this system into where it’s at,” Baker said. “So, it’s not a natural system anymore.”
Rather than abandon the delta, he argued, “it’s important to preserve that habitat where we have it.”

title: Chronic pain doesn’t have to be a choice between suffering and strong medication
text:
(Aging Untold) — If you live with chronic pain, it can feel like you only have two choices: tough it out or take strong medication.
There are other ways to manage chronic pain that may help you sleep better, move better and get your life back. It starts with finding out why the pain is there.
Start with the source of the pain
The first thing to do is find the root cause or the source of the pain. That will determine how to treat it, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
She said the pain could come from a damaged muscle, damaged tissue, nerves or a nervous system that’s overly sensitive.
“Your treatment is going to depend on why you have the pain,” Rogers said.
She said the cause also leads to other options, such as movement and stretching.
Don’t overlook sleep
Rogers said sleep is something people often overlook.
“I know that pain a lot of times interferes with sleep. But if you get really good sleep, then it can actually help your pain, if you can get to that point,” Rogers said.
Experts share what worked for them
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said she had chronic back pain around age 50 and kept returning to a chiropractor for adjustments.
She said he eventually told her she could keep coming back or stop doing some of the things that might be causing the pain. His tips included no longer wearing high heels, using an ergonomic cushion at work and no longer running.
“I think about what you shouldn’t do,” O’Rourke said. “I was so grateful that he told me what not to do to help my pain get better.”
O’Rourke also said she went to a physiatrist, whom she described as a sports medicine doctor, for a hip issue. She said walking up and down stairs made it worse, and she was taught to sleep on her side with a pillow between her legs.
“And I don’t have pain anymore,” O’Rourke said.
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said she injured her lower back in her 20s and was told surgery was an option, but she declined. Another doctor told her to push her car seat up, she said.
Cradduck said other options for pain relief include acupuncture, dry needling, chiropractic care, cognitive behavior therapy and massage therapy.
She also described a transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation unit, a machine used for muscle pain and to loosen muscles.
Rogers said several aesthetics places also have machines that do something similar.
“It increases blood flow, it helps mobility,” Rogers said. “People can move their arms and all that. And it helps a lot with the pain.”
As always, contact your health care provider for medical advice.
Inflammation, deconditioning and movement
Inflammation can make pain worse, Rogers said.
“Just look for the source of the inflammation that you have, because that’s what’s making it worse,” she said.
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said deconditioning can also play a role.
“Sometimes it’s just deconditioning, like we haven’t been working out like we should, and then we become weaker, then it is kind of a cascade of things,” Ambrose said.
Movement is important, Rogers said, because a lot of times people become stiff when they are not moving.
“When you’re moving, you have blood flow and everything is made a lot easier,” she said.
Physical therapy can help work the muscles around an injury to provide support while healing, O’Rourke said.
Medication and asking questions
Cradduck said people should not be so afraid of medications that they avoid it when needed.
She said she has seen 95-year-olds who have had hip replacements decline prescribed medication because they feared addiction.
How much pain is too much
The goal is not always to be 100% pain-free, Cradduck said.
“How much pain can I have and still live a normal life and not have it interfere with my life?” Cradduck said. “It’s when pain interferes with your daily living that you have to really be concerned.”
“I think sometimes we just accept pain as aging when that’s not the case,” Ambrose said.
Key takeaways
- Treat the source. Focus on treating the source of chronic pain, not just masking symptoms with medication.
- Know the cause. Pain can come from a damaged muscle, damaged tissue, nerves or an overly sensitive nervous system, and treatment depends on which it is.
- Keep moving. Many times pain results from deconditioning due to lack of movement. Movement increases blood flow.
- Work with specialists. A specialist such as a sports medicine doctor could help you regain function and treat the root cause of your pain.

title: Bob Boone, legendary MLB catcher and Gold Glove winner, dies at 78, son says
text:
(Gray News) — Legendary MLB catcher Bob Boone has died, according to his son. He was 78.
“My dad- He was my mentor, my coach, my rock. He taught me how to be a pro and more importantly, how to be a man. He was one of the highest integrity people I’ve ever known and I’m going to miss him dearly. Baseball lost a great one yesterday. R.I.P dad, I love you,” Boone’s son, former MLB player Bret Boone, wrote on X.
According to Sports Illustrated, Bob Boone won four Gold Glove Awards in seven seasons as the California Angels’ catcher in the 1980s. He won the award in 1982, 1986, 1987 and 1988.
Bob Boone was originally from San Diego and played college baseball at Stanford University.
His MLB debut was with the Phillies in 1972. He helped the team win its first-ever World Series in 1980, according to Sports Illustrated.
Bob Boone spent his first 10 seasons with the Phillies before playing seven seasons with the California Angels, followed by two seasons with the Kansas City Royals. He also went on to manage the Royals from 1995-97 and the Cincinnati Reds from 2001-03, according to ESPN.
According to MLB, Bob Boone played an integral part in “one of baseball’s most historic families.”
“Along with his father Ray, and his sons Bret and Aaron, the Boones became the first family to field three generations of Major League players, all of them All-Stars,” MLB wrote on X.
A cause of death was not yet given.
