title: Drivers keep hitting Waymos and taking off, police records show
text:
PHOENIX(InvestigateTV) — Waymo’s own roadside assistance crews have been telling police about a surprising pattern: drivers who crash into the company’s robotaxis frequently take off.
“It’s quite shocking how many people just take off,” a Waymo roadside assistance specialist told a Phoenix police officer.
An investigative analysis of more than four years of police records backs that up.
Nearly half of the Waymo crashes reported to police in metro Phoenix were hit-and-runs. Accounting for miles driven, Waymos were involved in police-reported hit-and-runs at 2.4 times the rate of drivers in Maricopa County.
Waymo reviewed the methodology and said its researchers “appreciated the rigor and thought” behind it. But the company argues it is impossible to determine whether its vehicles are actually involved in more hit-and-runs, or whether Waymo simply reports the incidents to police more consistently than the general public.
‘They just leave’
Body camera footage from March 2024 shows Chandler Officer Seth Chavez responding to a crash near Ray and Price roads where someone hit the back of a driverless Waymo and drove away. Chavez told the roadside specialist waiting at the scene that he’d never handled a call quite like it.
“People rear-end these things all the time,” the specialist responded. “Most of the time, they just leave.”
Months later, in October 2024, a truck damaged a Waymo near Buckeye Road and 2nd Street in Phoenix and drove off. Another Waymo roadside specialist let the responding Phoenix officer in on the same secret.
“I don’t know how many of these reports you do, but I’m surprised at how many hit-and-runs we honestly get, and where it’s a good amount of damage,” the Waymo specialist said. “Like, do you not realize there’s cameras on these?”
43 of 88 crashes
Arizona’s Family Investigates spent 10 months collecting police crash reports and body camera footage from the five cities in Waymo’s Valley service area: Phoenix, Scottsdale, Chandler, Mesa and Tempe.
There were 88 police-reported crashes involving Waymo vehicles from Sept. 1, 2020, through Dec. 31, 2024. Of those collisions, 43, or 49%, were classified as hit-and-runs in which the Waymo stayed and the other driver left. In most cases, the damage was minor.
To compare the rate of those crashes with human drivers, Arizona’s Family worked with a traffic safety researcher to calculate hit-and-run rates per million miles driven for Waymo and for the general public in Maricopa County.
Waymo: ‘The standard today is not perfection’
Camille Dredge, Waymo’s senior director for ride-hail operations, spoke with Arizona’s Family in 2025.
“The standard today is not perfection,” Dredge said. “Collisions will and can occur. We are absolutely prepared to respond to them.”
Waymo declined a request for a new interview about the findings, providing written responses instead.
In a statement, Waymo said the safety of riders and communities is its “absolute priority.” The company said that across more than 90 million fully autonomous miles in Phoenix, its vehicles cut crashes involving serious injuries or worse by 90% compared with human drivers.
Waymo said hit-and-runs are uncommon relative to the more than 4 million autonomous miles its vehicles drive each week across more than 15 U.S. cities. The company did not say whether it tracks hit-and-runs internally or how many it has recorded.
Dredge did not offer a theory for the hit-and-runs. In a few cases, the reason seems apparent. In a 2020 Mesa crash, among the earliest in the records, officers suspected the driver who hit a Waymo was impaired.
“You’re real loopy,” an officer told him on body camera video. “Your speech is slurred.”
Most police reports, however, offer no clue about why drivers leave.
Experts point to confusion, sudden braking
Missy Cummings, a George Mason University professor, and Phil Koopman, a professor emeritus at Carnegie Mellon University, are two leading researchers on autonomous vehicles.
“We researchers and the government need to do more to try to figure out what is going on with this and how to mitigate it,” Cummings said.
They offered two possible explanations for why drivers leave. The first is that drivers are confused about how to exchange information with an autonomous vehicle.
“I’ve noticed that police have trouble interacting with these vehicles. Emergency responders have trouble interacting with these vehicles. They’re not sure what to do,” Koopman said. “Ordinary drivers don’t go through how-to-talk-to-a-robotaxi training.”
“If there’s no one there to trade insurance cards with, then what do you do?” Cummings said.
A 2022 Chandler police report illustrates the problem. After a minor crash in a 7-Eleven parking lot near Warner and Dobson roads, the at-fault driver walked up to the Waymo with her “driver’s license and vehicle registration in hand,” according to the report. But the vehicle was driverless, and with no one to give her information to, the woman left.
Waymo said it invests heavily in educating drivers on how to exchange insurance information. Once drivers submit their information through one of its digital options, the company said, they don’t need to wait at the scene.
The second theory Cummings and Koopman offered is that Waymos may be prone to a type of crash that gives human drivers an incentive to flee.
“I’ve done an analysis on the publicly available data, and Waymos get hit from behind two times more than your average human driver does,” Cummings said.
She pointed to what researchers call phantom braking, when an autonomous vehicle stops suddenly for something that isn’t there.
“Everyone hears about hallucinations with generative AI. These are real hallucinations,” Cummings said. “The cars see something that isn’t there. And the car’s response is to do an emergency braking because, to them, it appears that something is there.”
“If they’re not sure, the safe thing, tactically, is to stop,” Koopman said. “But what you have to take into account is that following drivers, if there’s no reason to brake, they’re not expecting it.”
Waymo disputes that sudden braking is a significant factor. The company said rear-end crashes are the most common type of crash for both human and autonomous drivers. It said that over 270 million autonomous miles, Waymos were involved in 41% fewer rear-end crashes causing airbag deployment than human drivers in its cities.
A peer-reviewed analysis by Waymo found its vehicles were fully stopped in 72% of rear-end crashes that deployed airbags and 20% of those causing injuries. The company said the analysis found its vehicles were not hard braking in any of the airbag crashes or in 75% of the injury crashes.
‘It should be on the robotaxi companies’
Some drivers do wait for Waymo’s roadside team and exchange information. Arizona law requires drivers who hit an unattended vehicle to locate the owner or leave their contact information.
Both Cummings and Koopman said Waymo should make the information exchange easier.
“If robotaxi companies are putting vehicles on public roads that interact with other people, it should be on the robotaxi companies to figure out how to make that interaction happen,” Koopman said.
Waymo said drivers do not need to wait for a company representative to arrive at the scene.
People involved in a crash with a Waymo can:
- scan the QR code on the driver’s side door
- contact Waymo through its app
- fill out a form at Waymo.com/notify
- call 844-263-9885
- email insurance@waymo.com
- speak with a roadside assistance representative, if one is at the scene

title: 3 charged following deadly shooting at youth football championship game
text:
MADISON, Mo. (KMOV/Gray News) - Three people have been charged in connection with a shooting at a Missouri youth football championship game that killed one and injured three others earlier this month.
Carl Tucker, 18, faces one count of first-degree murder and three counts of aggravated battery with a firearm following the shooting. He faces an additional count of first-degree murder as an alternative theory charge.
Jeffery Mosby, 42, faces charges of aggravated discharge of a firearm, reckless discharge of a firearm, aggravated unlawful use of weapons and possession of a controlled substance.
Brianna Simms, 31, also faces a charge of obstruction of justice after police said she provided false information to investigators.
The shooting occurred during a youth football championship game at Madison Senior High School on Nov. 1.
A fight then broke out on the field, and adults ran onto the field to break it up. According to law enforcement, a second altercation then arose at the entrance before gunfire erupted.
Four people were shot, including Steve Smith, 64, a grandfather who died from his injuries.
“Mr. Smith was at a youth football game — a place where families should be able to gather, enjoy watching their children and grandchildren and share in the excitement of the game,” Madison County State’s Attorney Tom Haine said. “Instead, his family is now mourning his death. It is difficult to comprehend how an event like this could end in such tragedy.”
The other shooting victims were a 36-year-old man who was shot in the face, a 33-year-old man who suffered a gunshot wound to the hip and a 22-year-old woman shot in the thigh.
Additional people were also injured in the ensuing crowd surge.
“This was a 9-and-under and a 12-and-under football game, and these kids heard gunshots ringing out,” Haine said. “If anyone knows anything about this case, we encourage you, for the sake of these children and for the sake of justice in our community, to bring it to our attention.”
The investigation into the shooting remains ongoing.
Authorities have additionally noted a person of interest in the case, but that person has not been immediately charged with a criminal offense.

title: Baker who's legally blind pursues dream of running his own bakery. He faces unique challenges
text:
Baker who's legally blind pursues dream of running his own bakery. He faces unique challenges
Lino uses his phone and memory to follow recipes as he takes on the challenge of running his own bakery.
Baker who's legally blind pursues dream of running his own bakery. He faces unique challenges
Lino uses his phone and memory to follow recipes as he takes on the challenge of running his own bakery.
For Lino, reading a recipe takes more than a quick glance.
The Albuquerque, New Mexico, baker is legally blind and says he cannot read recipes — even with glasses. Instead, he takes pictures of them on his phone and zooms in. He relies on his memory, often learning a recipe after seeing it a few times.
Now, Lino is pursuing a longtime goal of owning a bakery. When the place where he worked closed, he decided to take it over and reopen Bumblebee Bakery & Coffee.
"I always wanted a bakery," Lino said.
He added that changing jobs and adjusting to another kitchen would be difficult, so he decided to take over the space and try running it himself.
Lino said technology helps him work, but baking while legally blind remains challenging.
"It’s tough. It’s not easy to be legally blind and being a baker," he said.
Opening the bakery brought challenges outside the kitchen, too. Katelyn Turnbow said the process of completing paperwork and waiting for approvals took longer than expected.
Lino said his vision is worsening as he gets older, but for now, he hopes to continue baking for a little while longer.
"It’s hard. It’s not easy, but I’m here, you know," he said.

title: States like Maine need the Electoral College
text:
I’m writing in response to the letter of Nov. 5 regarding the abolition of the Electoral College.
A constitutional amendment is required to get rid of the Electoral College. Three-fourths (38) of the states would have to ratify the amendment. What’s in it for them? With the Electoral College, smaller states, such as Maine, have a more equal voice in the election of our nation’s president. Without it, larger states such as California and Texas would overshadow smaller states and, effectively, would dictate who would be our president.
Why would small states ratify an amendment that would effectively silence their votes? That’s why the Founding Fathers set up the Electoral College.
Mary Caliandro
Long Island

title: Got this voicemail? It could be a scam targeting your Venmo account

Got this voicemail? It could be a scam targeting your Venmo account
Venmo users are being warned about a vishing scam where fraudsters use automated phone calls to try to steal sensitive information and gain access to accounts.
Got this voicemail? It could be a scam targeting your Venmo account
Venmo users are being warned about a vishing scam where fraudsters use automated phone calls to try to steal sensitive information and gain access to accounts.
Scammers are targeting Venmo users with a voice phishing scheme, using fake automated calls to try to steal sensitive information.
An automated voicemail obtained by the Hearst Television National Consumer Unit states: "This call is because of an attempt to change the password on your Venmo account. If this was not you, please press one."
Venmo confirmed that the message is part of a vishing scam, short for voice phishing. In these scams, fraudsters try to trick people into handing over passwords or other sensitive information.
Venmo says it will never ask customers to share passwords, verification codes or financial information by email, text message or phone.
If you receive a call like this, don't engage with it. Do not press any numbers or provide information, and block the number.
What happens if a scammer gets into your Venmo account?
Venmo's User Agreement says that if someone steals or fraudulently obtains a customer's password and uses it to send money from the account, that is considered an unauthorized transaction.
The agreement says Venmo will cover the full amount of unauthorized activity if the customer follows its procedures, including reporting the incident promptly.
Customers who wait more than 60 days to report an unauthorized transaction could lose that protection.
The National Consumer Unit asked Venmo to confirm whether a customer would be reimbursed if a scammer used this specific vishing scam to take over an account and transfer money without authorization.
Venmo did not directly answer the question, saying individual cases are reviewed separately. The company instead encouraged customers who believe they have been targeted by a potential scam to contact customer service directly.
Consumers who encounter the scam should report it to Venmo, even if they did not lose money. They can also report it to the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

title: Texas man accused of cruise ship murder had argued with woman in their cabin, FBI says
text:
Texas man accused of cruise ship murder had argued with woman in their cabin, FBI says
A cruise ship passenger accused of killing a woman shortly after the vessel departed from Texas told FBI agents he beat and choked her in their cabin after an argument caused him to “snap,” according to court documents.
Jason Watford, 48, of Tyler, Texas, was set to make an initial federal court appearance on a murder charge Tuesday in Galveston. He was being held at a county jail. It was not immediately clear if he had a lawyer who could respond to the allegations.
A man who said he is Watford’s son declined to comment Tuesday when reached at a phone listing in public records for relatives.
Related video: A dog is rescued by a boat tour crew after being swept miles out to sea all alone in a kayak
The alleged killing happened aboard the MSC Seascape, a towering white vessel that has 2,270 cabins and can host nearly 5,900 guests on five- and seven-night trips to the Caribbean, according to the company’s website.
The woman, who was not immediately identified, was killed Sunday after the vessel left Galveston, according to an FBI affidavit filed in federal court. A ship investigator contacted authorities to report that the woman was found dead in her room with multiple facial injuries.
A housekeeper who knocked to deliver towels saw the woman lying motionless on the floor and what looked like blood on Watford's hands and pants when he opened the door, the affidavit said.
In an interview with FBI agents after the ship returned to Galveston on Monday morning, Watford said he and the woman had boarded the vessel together Sunday and began arguing while having dinner at one of the ship's restaurants, according to the affidavit. The argument continued in their room, it said.
Watford told agents he struck the woman several times and “applied pressure” to her neck “for approximately four to five minutes” until he became exhausted, the affidavit said. He said she lay motionless for about 10 minutes until the housekeeper arrived.
Surveillance video showed that Watford entered the room at 7:46 p.m. and the victim went in about 25 minutes later, authorities said. At 9:15 p.m., he was seen on the video leaving the room wearing a different shirt and pants, according to the complaint, and sat on the hallway floor looking at his phone.
MSC Cruises said authorities told the ship to return to Galveston after the crew reported the passenger's death, and that the vessel resumed its voyage Monday. The company said it was cooperating with authorities and providing support to those impacted.
___
Associated Press writer Claudia Lauer in Philadelphia contributed.

title: These Aroostook students are tackling ‘Les Mis’
text:
Aroostook school theater director Doug Clapp thought his group would perform ‘Phantom of the Opera’ this fall, but a delayed renovation and student pleas changed everything.
Instead, Clapp’s Fort Kent Community High School group is rehearsing “Les Miserables,” the famed musical depicting a time of rebellion in France.
Several Maine groups have tackled the 46-year-old show. The Schoolhouse Arts Center in Standish and Some Theater Company in Bangor are among those with upcoming productions. The Fort Kent program joins the ranks and will bring it to The County next week.
Designed to coincide with the grand opening of a new auditorium at the University of Maine at Fort Kent, “Phantom” took a turn when Clapp learned construction wouldn’t quite be finished in time.
“‘Phantom’ basically comes down to three major actors, and some of my other kids said, ‘Can’t you pick something with a bigger cast?’” Clapp said Friday. “I knew we had some great voices, but it’s just amazing. They can hit those notes, they can sing these songs, and most of them are sophomores.”
Based on Victor Hugo’s 1862 novel of the same name, “Les Miserables” tells the story of recently paroled thief Jean Valjean, the detective who pursues him, and a doomed factory worker named Fantine and her child, set against the backdrop of a student-led uprising.
The musical debuted in Paris 46 years ago, and five years later its English translation opened in London.
Opening night is slated at 6 p.m. on Thursday, Nov. 19, at the high school cafetorium, with other shows at 6 p.m. on Friday and Saturday, Nov. 20 and 21, and at 2 p.m. on Sunday, Nov. 21.
Cast members include Troy Celik as protagonist Jean Valjean, William Gullick as revolutionary leader Enjorlas, Olorin Braun Epp as Detective Javert, Cameron Jandreau and Madison Ecker Boucher as the unscrupulous Monsieur and Madame Thenardier and Shanelle Rossignol in a double role as Fantine, an abused factory worker, and her daughter Cosette.
Other key actors are Kaden Mathieu as Marius, Samantha Chasse as Eponine, Bryce Littrell as Gavroche and Madison Granatowski as young Cosette.
Several cast members talked about the show following a Friday theater preview at The Common Gallery that was part of Presque Isle’s First Friday Art Walk.
Celik found two things particularly challenging about playing Valjean: the range needed for the songs and understanding a character who is his opposite.
“Valjean has an absolutely insane range for a performer [which] is over two octaves,” he said. “And he’s a hardened criminal. He’s been in prison for 19 years. I haven’t even lived 19 years.”
Celik worked hard on imagining the character and even tried to enact facial details, he said.
She didn’t know the storyline at first, but Rossignol researched the character of Fantine and watched different versions of the story and musical. Being in the production has been exciting, she said.
What will stay with her most is Fantine’s story, she said.
“She really went through a lot. She was abused and people were just horrible to her,” Rossignol said. “Her story is really strong and I think it should be told more.”
Mathieu described his character Marius as “a classic example of an overconfident, rich schoolboy.”
As happens in many musicals, Marius meets a girl and falls in love at first sight.
“And he is also in this really complex relationship with revolutionary students, and that conflicts with his love,” Mathieu said.
Jandreau found smarmy innkeeper Thenardier fun to play.
“He lures you in, basically, and robs you without your knowing,” he said. “He seems like a fun guy, but you leave with less stuff than you came with.”
For Braun Epp, the fact that there are no spoken lines at all in the show was intense, but bringing Javert to life proved fascinating. The detective, determined to uphold the law, has made it his life’s quest to hunt down Valjean and make him pay for his crimes, he said.
“My favorite part is definitely exploring where his mercy lies and where I can find those moments, because he does break at the end,” Braun Epp said. “Exploring that was the most interesting part.”
Rounding out the production is an ensemble cast which includes Abigail Thibeault, Brianna Nadeau, Brie Robichaud, Devin Dumais, Etta Jandreau, Halle Jandreau, Hannah Pelletier, Haven Thurston, Isabelle Nichols, Izzy Forino, Jeremy O’Clair, Lacey Jackson, Lance St. Germain, Mikayla Ayers, Nila Bonenfant, Peter Smith, Piper Caron, Rylee Hafford, Sadie Law and Zoey Dumont.
Tickets are $14 for adults and $8 for students and can be purchased at Fort Kent Community High School or Fort Kent Elementary School.

title: Millinocket Marathon Takes Place Saturday December 5th With A 10 AM Start Time, Now In Its 11th Year
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Countdown Is On For Maine’s Most Fun, One-Of-A-Kind Winter ‘Marathon’
They're prepping the lines and counting down the days till one of Maine's most fun, one-of-a-kind winter marathons kicks off.
It's a marathon that's not just a huge local hit, but is internationally known for its awesomeness, too. (Check this video out and tell me that's not cool!)
The Millinocket Marathon will take place this year on Saturday, December 5th with a start time of 10 AM. Typically, folks start to show up the day before (Friday) for opening festivities and bib pickup.
Read More: Look Up, Maine! November's Night Sky Is Going to Be Incredible
The race started 11 years ago as a fun way to inject some excitement and some revenue into the sleepy little former mill town.
It went from a flash mob of just a few dozen people to an event that brings thousands of people into the Katahdin area each year.
Funded entirely by donations and run entirely by a small army of volunteers, this race brings folks of all walks of life, ability levels, and ages (the youngest last year was 8, the oldest 85) together for what participants have called one of their favorite "races" of all time.
Lynn Marie Casey is from Millinocket and has run the half marathon once before. She says the event is something you have to be a part of to understand.
"The Millinocket Marathon has grown so much in the last 11 years; I love how people from all around have come and participated and have grown to love our quaint little town. One would have to come and experience it; having it in December in northern Maine is definitely not what a mid-summer race would feel like."
"There have been years when it was -20°; the racers and walkers still come, some in athletic wear and some in Paul Bunyan attire and also carrying a chainsaw....The best thing is how our town comes together to welcome all the racers and their loved ones to the area and the camaraderie we all share at each mile marker during the race on the Golden Road, from tasting Oysters, Fireball Shots, BBQ's, baked goods, etc. It's like no other race."
Casey says that for those interested in preparing ahead of time for the race, she would suggest getting your body ready for running in the cold.
"...train well, get out there in the early mornings and get at least a good five to ten miles on a day, pack for temps from 0° to 30° wind, snow and rain."
The race is an official United States Track & Field qualifier for the NYC, Boston, and Chicago Marathons, with one 13.1-mile loop for the half marathon and two 13.1-mile loops for the full marathon.
According to organizers, the terrain encompasses everything from gravel to paved to logging roads.
"The first mile exiting town on Poplar Road is a paved climb. The next six miles are run on the Golden Road, which is a gravel, privately owned logging road. The race secures permission to run on the Golden Road via multiple permit applications, both of which require additional insurance."
"The final six miles are on pavement starting on the Millinocket Lake Road and working back into town. Runners MUST keep to the LEFT side of the road, facing oncoming traffic."
The race course is often lined with "pop-up" watering stations (never guaranteed, but many show up, year after year, to help runners along the way)
Denise Deshane has been participating in one of those stations called "Top of the Hill Bar & Grill" for the past couple of years.
They hand out everything from water, Gatorade, and even shots of Fireball, to goodies and treats for runners to grab along their way.
"I think seeing the smiles and hearing the appreciation from the runners and walkers for us being there to support them in every bit of weather that has been thrown at us all."
It's not the course, necessarily, that's the draw for this race, although the views are incredible.
What people always come back to is the amazing sense of camaraderie they feel when running it, and the atmosphere in town during the event.
Aside from the actual running of the marathon, there are so many other things to do, too.
There's a running list of places to stay, events, and special celebrations at the Millinocket Marathon & Half Marathon Runners Facebook Page.
Festivities usually begin a night or two before the race, as people travel into the area.
You can expect concerts and breakfasts, spaghetti suppers and artisan fairs, Christmas portraits and fundraisers. There's a ton of activity in the area that spans the weekend.
Last year, former Boston World Series-winning Red Sox pitcher (from 2003 to 2005), Bronson Arroyo, brought his band to town and kicked things off with a show at one of the local spots in town.
If you are planning to visit the area that weekend, don't forget to check out the antler wings while you're there.
Read More: How Moose Wings Transformed Millinocket's Eyesore Into Art
To find out more information on the Millinocket Marathon, you can check out their Facebook Page or the Crow Athletics website for a schedule and links to register for the race.

title: Hannah Pingree announces more than a dozen key transition leaders
text:
AUGUSTA — Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree on Tuesday unveiled the names of 22 people who will help lead her transition, vowing to cast “a wide net” as she staffs Maine’s agencies.
The 50-year-old Democrat laid out her guiding principles for choosing the heads of more than a dozen state departments and other key leaders who will have the ability to affect the lives of Mainers in ways big and small — from caring for family members to maintaining roads.
Pingree said she wants a results-oriented cabinet of individuals with integrity, accountability and a general optimism about helping Maine people.
“I also want a team that is collaborative, because the challenges facing our state are too big for one person, one party, or one region alone to solve,” she said.
The team of 22 will recruit and recommend candidates for Pingree’s 15 Cabinet positions and an appointee to the Workers’ Compensation Board.
Her transition team is mostly made up of people from outside of state government, Pingree noted. It includes leaders in labor, business and healthcare.
“Many of these folks have never worked in state government, but they know what’s needed in their communities,” Pingree said. “And I want their experience and their judgment in my administration. So again, we intend to cast a wide net, and we intend to be thorough, because Mainers deserve nothing less.”
Although Pingree worked in Gov. Janet Mills’ administration, she said any Mills-era officials who are interested in staying on must earn a position in her administration.
“No shoe-ins,” Pingree said. “Everyone’s got to compete and we will be interviewing multiple candidates for every single Cabinet position.”
The transition team is co-chaired by Maulian Bryant, a member of the Penobscot Nation and the executive director of the Wabanaki Alliance, and Roger Katz, a Republican former state lawmaker.
Katz said the team is looking for the most qualified people — regardless of their political party or who they supported in the governor’s race.
“We’ll be looking in every corner of the state,” Katz said.
Pingree hopes to have most of her Cabinet assembled before her Jan. 6 inauguration.
Here’s a look at the volunteers helping Bryant and Katz to build her team:
- Judy Camuso, who led Maine’s Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife from 2019 until May 2026. She was the first woman to serve as commissioner.
- Hannah Carter, an Aroostook County native and dean of Cooperative Extension for the University of Maine and deputy provost.
- Vicky Cohen, a recently retired Farmington teacher.
- Ken Colburn, principal of Symbiotic Strategies LLC and a retired principal and director of U.S. Programs at the Regulatory Assistance Project. He serves on the Maine Climate Council.
- Barbara Crowley, a pediatrician who also serves on the leadership team of the Children’s Oral Health Network of Maine, working to improve children’s access to oral health care.
- Maureen Drouin, executive director of Maine Conservation Voters and the Maine Conservation Alliance.
- Richard Evans, a recently retired general and colon and rectal surgeon from Dover-Foxcroft. He’s also a former Democratic state senator and U.S. Air Force veteran.
- Liza Fleming-Ives, executive director of the Genesis Community Loan Fund, a community development financial institution serving communities across Maine and northern New England.
- Elsie Flemings, executive director of Healthy Acadia since 2014.
- Marwa Hassanien, a Bangor resident, human resources director at one of Maine’s largest health systems and president of the Maine Multicultural Center’s board of directors.
- Luke Holden, a third-generation lobsterman from Cape Elizabeth and founder of Luke’s Lobster. He serves on the board of the Gulf of Maine Research Institute.
- Liam LaFountain, mayor of Biddeford since December 2025.
- Susan Nourse, retired Freeport police chief.
- Jason Parent, chief executive officer for Avec, the Community Action Agency serving Aroostook, Washington and Hancock counties.
- Grant Provost, a business agent and industry analyst for Ironworkers Local 7 in Maine and a vice president of the Maine AFL-CIO.
- Peggy Rotundo, former Democratic state senator from Lewiston and a former budget committee chairwoman.
- Claude Rwaganje, founder and executive director of ProsperityME.
- Steve Smith, former president and CEO of L.L.Bean.
- Eloise Vitelli, former Maine Senate Democratic majority leader.
- Ben Waxman, CEO and co-founder of American Roots, a Westbrook-based manufacturer of American- and union-made apparel.

title: MaineHealth Franklin Hospital to celebrate Veterans Day and honor local Veterans
What to know about the latest iron deficiency guidelines
text:
What to know about the latest iron deficiency guidelines
More people are low in iron than in any other micronutrient, according to the American Society of Hematology. But many live with fatigue, weakness, brain fog and other symptoms for months or years before a deficiency is caught.
Previous video coverage above
Nearly one-third of adults in the United States may be iron deficient, according to a 2024 study. And routine screening among children and pregnant women — who are at high risk — may miss more than 70% of cases.
Some people online are self-diagnosing, citing dark under-eye circles and pale skin as evidence that they are low in iron. Social media influencers call the look “ferritin face,” named after a protein that stores the element in the body.
Iron deficiency is common, prevalent and underrecognized, said Dr. Ariela Marshall, associate professor of medicine at the University of Minnesota. New diagnostic recommendations, which ASH released in September, aim to ensure more patients secure early treatment.
The difference between iron deficiency and anemia
Anemia is a condition that occurs when there are not enough red blood cells to carry oxygen to the body’s organs and tissues. Patients with anemia may feel tired, dizzy or short of breath, and they may have heart palpitations, cold hands and feet, pale skin, brittle nails or hair loss.
Anemia is often caused by a lack of iron, which supports brain and muscle function and is used to make hemoglobin, the molecule that transports oxygen in the blood. Stored in the protein ferritin, iron is recruited to make the hemoglobin in new red blood cells. When ferritin is low, it means there isn’t enough iron available to make red blood cells, which can lead to anemia.
But iron deficiency can cause the same sorts of symptoms without affecting hemoglobin or red blood counts. Having low iron can also cause restless leg syndrome and pica — cravings for nonfood items such as ice or clay. (Doctors are not sure why; it may be a sign that the body is seeking out iron from the environment.)
It is “a common misperception” that iron deficiency without anemia can’t cause symptoms, “and one that we definitely need to correct,” Marshall said.
Standard blood tests that count how many red blood cells a person has won’t catch iron deficiency that has not progressed into anemia.
“The symptoms of iron deficiency can be very subtle, or they can be attributed to many different things,” said Dr. Jacquelyn Powers, section chief of hematology at Texas Children’s Hospital and lead author of the 2026 guidelines. “Providers are not always thinking, ‘Oh, I need to check iron labs.’”
What the new iron testing guidelines say
The amount of iron in a person’s blood cannot provide an accurate diagnosis of deficiency because it will vary depending on what they have eaten and how recently. Ferritin tests are the gold standard for assessing iron levels, Powers said. But until now, there has not been a single agreed-upon results threshold to determine who has iron deficiency.
The World Health Organization recommends using a ferritin concentration below 15 ng/mL for diagnosing school-age children and adults with iron deficiency. But researchers have questioned that math, expressing concern that such a low threshold misses many people whose iron stores are higher than that but still insufficient.
Some blood-testing laboratories use even lower cutoffs, meaning some patients’ lab tests may come back as “normal” even if their ferritin levels are very low.
The new ASH guidelines establish 20 ng/mL or less as the appropriate cutoff for children, 30 ng/mL for most adults, and 50 ng/mL or less for those with heavy menstrual bleeding or other risk factors such as a vegan diet or long-term antacid use for reflux. For adults with inflammatory issues, the new limit is 100 ng/mL, and the group suggests an additional test, called transferrin saturation.
“One of the goals of the guidelines was to highlight why testing for iron deficiency — regardless of whether the patient is anemic or not — is important because there are interventions that you can do to prevent later complications and address more subtle symptoms,” Powers said.
Who should be tested for iron deficiency?
People with iron deficiency may have “a whole range of symptoms, from tiredness and fatigue to brain fog or cloudy thinking to feeling like you want to chew on things like ice,” Marshall said. “Somebody can have all of those. They can have one of them. They can have none of them.”
Social media posts claim that the signs of iron deficiency, including a pale complexion, hair loss and dry skin, are identifiable as ferritin face. But Powers and Marshall were skeptical that it is possible to diagnose low iron via selfie.
Though some people with restrictive diets may have trouble getting enough iron each day, Marshall said that isn’t usually the cause of deficiency in the U.S. More common causes are blood loss and digestive conditions.
Women are more likely than men to have iron deficiency because of the loss of blood that comes with menstruation. Women who experience heavy periods are particularly susceptible.
Children and pregnant people are also at higher risk for iron deficiency because they use a lot of iron for growth and development. Rates of iron deficiency among pregnant people increase every trimester, Powers said.
People with chronic gastrointestinal conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome and celiac disease may not be able to absorb enough of the iron they get from their diet. Deficiency may also come about from gastrointestinal blood loss, which can be an early sign of colon cancer.
Endurance athletes require more iron than most people, so they are also more likely to be deficient. One of the signs of deficiency is not being able to exercise as hard as you used to.
If a person eats well, gets good sleep and is “doing everything else that you associate with optimal health, but they’re still really tired, then I think it’s very reasonable to check their ferritin,” Powers said. “It’s an easy test, and there’s an easy intervention.”
Taking oral iron supplements can alleviate symptoms in weeks or months. If that course of action helps, it means low iron was contributing to your health problems. But it’s important to work with your doctor to figure out why your iron levels were low to begin with, Marshall said.

title: How a routine robotic surgery turned into a nightmare
text:
ATLANTA, Ga. (InvestigateTV) - An Atlanta mother checked into the hospital for a hysterectomy, expecting to be home from that same day. Instead, she didn’t leave for nearly three months.
Star Button had persistent pain and excessive bleeding for years. The chronic issues interrupted every part of her life, including work.
Doctors confirmed the issues stemmed from fibroids, or noncancerous tumors. To get rid of them, Button opted for a robotic hysterectomy at Southern Regional Medical Center. The procedure surgically removes the uterus.
What a robotic hysterectomy is
A robotic hysterectomy is considered the least invasive and quickest for recovery because doctors use the device to make very small incisions in the abdomen. Once inside, the robot’s tiny arms are controlled by the surgeon who is standing feet away.
“I wasn’t actually going to the hospital initially thinking I was going to be a resident in its ICU following this procedure,” Button said.
Photos documented Button’s journey of days in a coma and nearly three months awake in the ICU battling blood loss and infections.
Button is now suing both Southern Regional Medical Center and the physician, Dr. Beverly Love, for negligence. The lawsuit alleges the hospital failed to maintain its equipment and the doctor “failed to exercise degree of care and skill.” The lawsuit also claims Dr. Love wrongfully removed her right ovary.
An expert hired by Button’s attorneys to review the case wrote the incident required doctors to “recognize and treat active bleeding” but they “failed to adhere to standard of care.”
Although Dr. Love has since passed, lawyers for his estate deny all wrongdoing, blaming Button’s own medical history for complications.
Surgeon describes technical challenges and conversion mid-procedure
In cellphone video recorded after the procedure, Dr. Love told Button’s husband about issues during surgery.
“Well, what happened was we had some technical challenges and I couldn’t manipulate the uterus the way I wanted to so I couldn’t really get to the blood vessels the way I wanted to so I said uh…we just converted to just going straight taking it out through the vagina and we stopped the robot," Dr. Love said.
Button said the robot used was the Da Vinci, a robotic surgical system that has been used in millions of various surgical procedures globally. However, Da Vinci and its manufacturer, Intuitive Surgical, are not mentioned or named as a defendant in the lawsuit.
From 2016 to 2025, Atlanta News First Investigates uncovered at least 434 “adverse events” — like death, injury, or malfunctions — reported to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) related to any Da Vinci device used in any surgery. At least 49 of those reports specifically involved devices used in hysterectomies. The Da Vinci device has been used in millions of various surgical procedures globally.
Manufacturer emphasizes safety record, notes limits of FDA database
“Patient safety is our highest priority,” an Intuitive Surgical company spokesperson said. “More than 20 million procedures have been performed globally using Da Vinci systems. The safety and effectiveness of our systems are supported by more than 48,000 peer‑reviewed publications, which, in aggregate, demonstrate positive clinical outcomes for patients."
The FDA maintains a database that tracks adverse events involving medical devices. “As the FDA itself recognizes, reports in the database have significant limitations and are not intended to evaluate device-related adverse event rates or establish causality between use and a potential injury,” the spokesperson said.
Dr. Love practiced for more than 40 years. Although he was in good standing with the Georgia Composite Medical Board, the agency said there was no medical malpractice insurance on file for him.
Malpractice insurance protects both doctors and patients who want to seek financial damages, but Georgia does not require doctors to carry it. Only seven states currently mandate it: Colorado, Connecticut, Kansas, Massachusetts, New Jersey, Rhode Island and Wisconsin.
“I need insurance to drive my car,” Button said. “But with the hospital, in that sense, when it crashed and burned, they started pointing fingers.”
OBGYN: robot can be safer, but surgeons must be ready without it
Dr. Timothy Cowthorn said his local hospital required him to carry medical malpractice insurance to operate at its facility. Cowthorn is not connected to Button’s case, but the OBGYN just completed his 1,000th robotic hysterectomy.
Asked whether the robot adds risk, Dr. Cowthorn said that even if it malfunctioned, he would still have to complete the surgery, so he must be prepared to operate without it.
With his experience at a local hospital and his private practice at Greystone, Dr. Cowthorn said the device transformed healthcare.
“These cutting instruments, which on the robotic arms are wristed so they can turn like your wrist of your own hand,” he said. “Going to the platform or going to the console where we manipulate those instruments is literally like being inside a patient. To me, it’s safer.
“Not only is it more precise, but I have less complications and less infections. Over the years, this has been one of the greatest technologies for women.”
What Button wants now: damages and policy change
Button’s complications didn’t stop when she left the hospital.
She said the medical bills eventually forced her out of her home; the long recovery cost her job; and her marriage did not survive the ordeal. Button described the ordeal as devastating, and said the severe PTSD, health issues, and ongoing sepsis have made it an uphill battle to rebuild her life.
Button is hoping her lawsuit does more than recover damages. She wants it to change how hospitals protect patients and how Georgia protects them from doctors without insurance. She started a fundraiser to help with legal costs.
Southern Regional Medical Center declined to answer questions about insurance requirements and what happened in this case. “Our focus remains on providing high-quality, compassionate care and serving the patients and communities who rely on us every day,” it said. “Due to pending litigation, we are not able to comment on this matter.”
Attorneys for Dr. Love’s estate did not respond to requests for comment.

See which parts of Maine flipped hardest in last week’s historic election
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
A Democrat’s 50-vote win in a western Maine Senate district was the largest improvement on 2024 by any legislative winner in a competitive race this year.
Elizabeth Bosworth, a Democrat from historically conservative Fryeburg, beat former Rep. John Andrews, R-Paris, in a district Republican Rick Bennett won by 29 points two years ago before leaving it to run for governor as an independent.
A Bangor Daily News analysis shows how far down the ballot Tuesday’s wave reached. We compared each candidate’s 2026 margin with their party’s margin in the same district in 2024, covering 154 candidates in races where the opponent spent at least $5,000 and drew outside spending.
Democrats expanded their majorities in both chambers, including the first Democratic supermajority in the Maine Senate since 1985. Of the 42 Democrats who won competitive races, 39 ran ahead of their party’s 2024 margin, typically by about 8 points. Only six of 22 winning Republicans did the same.
Sanford produced the next-largest gains among Democrats who flipped seats last week. Democrat John Henkelman turned a House seat Republicans won by 15 points in 2024 into a 10-point win. Ayn Hanselmann, also of Sanford, grew a 2-point Democratic edge to 25 in another House district.
Two Auburn Democrats flipped Republican seats with double-digit gains. Dana Staples ousted Rep. Quentin Chapman, R-Auburn, and Pamela Hart won the seat Rep. Laurel Libby, R-Auburn, carried in 2024. Chris Lewey of Fryeburg erased a 15-point Republican margin against former Rep. Caleb Ness, R-Fryeburg.
Bosworth acknowledged last week that her margin was thin, saying it would weigh on her work in Augusta.
“People are probably ready for a little bit of a change, but I also know that it’s not just strictly Democrats out there, and that we really need to show up for our entire community,” she said. “I mean, I didn’t win by much.”
Some Democrats who lost still cut deep into Republican margins. Dean LePage of Limerick lost a York County House race by 6 points after his party lost it by 35 in 2024. Mark Vigliotta of Lebanon came within 5 points of Sen. Matthew Harrington, R-Waterboro, who won by 21 last time.
Republicans had few bright spots. Susan Bernard of Fort Fairfield, making an unorthodox move back to the House after a term in the Senate, grew her party’s edge in an Aroostook County House seat from 8 points to 15, with two small towns still out. Former Lewiston City Councilor Lee Clement of Lewiston flipped his party’s only seat by a few dozen votes.

text:
SHERIDAN, Maine (WABI) - A fire destroyed a home in Sheridan and sent a man to the hospital Monday afternoon, authorities said.

title: 6-year-old drowns after falling into manure pit at Pennsylvania farm, coroner says
text:
6-year-old drowns after falling into manure pit at Pennsylvania farm, coroner says
A 6-year-old boy drowned after he fell into a manure pit on a southeastern Pennsylvania farm, according to local officials.
Dispatchers said crews responded to a farm near the intersection of Meadville and Churchtown roads in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, at 4:04 p.m. on Nov. 8.
Officials later said the victim, Leon Blank, 6, died after he was believed to have fallen into a manure pit on the property.
Lancaster County Coroner Dr. Stephen Diamantoni told Hearst sister station WGAL that no one saw the child fall. A fence surrounded the manure pit, but Diamantoni said the child may have climbed it before falling in.
"The death of a child that way is an absolute tragedy," Diamantoni said.
The coroner ruled the child's death an accident.
Manure pit dangers
Manure pits are structures used to store and decompose animal waste, according to Penn State Extension. The pits can pose risks, including gas exposure, falls, drowning and trauma from equipment.
Diamantoni said the pits are especially dangerous for children, who may be overcome by gas or drown after falling in.

title: Paul McCartney achieves billionaire status, becomes world’s third-richest musician
text:
Paul McCartney achieves billionaire status, becomes world’s third-richest musician
Paul McCartney reached the realm of billionaire status Monday after Forbes valued his net worth at a colossal $1.4 billion – making him the world’s third-richest musician.
Related video above: Memories of the Beatles' first — and only — Pittsburgh concert
McCartney’s wealth ranks behind his friend Taylor Swift ($2 billion), with whom he performed The Beatles’ first U.S. number 1 “I Want To Hold Your Hand” during the pop performer’s star-studded wedding to Travis Kelce at Madison Square Garden in July.
Jay-Z topped Forbes’ revered chart at $2.8 billion.
Forbes credits McCartney’s ascension to the number three spot to a lifetime of prolific songwriting, a series of savvy business moves and an impressive art collection.
But the 84-year-old rocker’s beginnings were humble, growing up in a working class household in Liverpool, northwest England.
Despite The Beatles’ phenomenal success, the Fab Four saw little of the cash their hard work generated at the height of Beatlemania – Forbes reported that their initial record deal provided them with less than a penny per album sold.
“No matter how successful we made the company, we didn’t get a raise,” McCartney wrote in a 2017 Forbes essay.
Seeking a solution, McCartney established a publishing company of his own in 1969 – MPL Communications. This marked the first time the musician managed his intellectual property, providing him with a far greater cut of the royalties.
MPL has been extremely lucrative to McCartney, as he has also used the company to purchase the copyrights to thousands of tracks including the back catalog of rock ’n’ roll pioneer Buddy Holly – who McCartney has cited as a major influence on The Beatles.
The publisher also owns the rights to an array of Christmas favorites, including “It’s Beginning To Look A Lot Like Christmas” and “Baby, It’s Cold Outside,” as well as musicals such as “Grease” and “Annie.”
Streaming those Christmas classics, or even performing in a high school production of those musicals, enhances the Brit’s wealth.
McCartney, who is a father of five and grandfather of eight, fought several legal battles to ensure he and his fellow Beatles and their estates were entitled to optimal royalties. The outfit’s Apple Corps holding company now earns more than $50 million annually from streams, vinyl sales and merchandise.
The Liverpool lad’s share of The Beatles’ song writing copyrights also makes him at least $10 million per year, Forbes has estimated.
Forbes also noted that real estate across the United Kingdom and the Hamptons, and an art collection boasting works by Picasso and Magritte, upped McCartney’s net worth.

title: James Gunn’s DCU: What Should Be Kept, And What Should Go?
text:
James Gunn’s DCU: What Parts Should Be Kept, And Which Should Go?
James Gunn and Peter Safran are out at DC Studios. Jeremy Latcham is the new president and chief creative officer.
What happens now?
In the short term, probably nothing. DC still has Gunn’s Man of Tomorrow due in theaters next summer. If things don’t fall any further behind schedule, The Batman Part II follows in early 2028.
In the long term, things get murkier. When Gunn and Safran first joined DC Studios as co-CEOs, they announced an ambitious plan for ten interconnected movies and TV shows, most of which never saw the light of day. Later they announced more projects that weren’t even part of their original slate. The fate of all those films and shows remains cloudy.
DC fans are nothing if not opinionated, and as DC fans here at ScreenCrush we have a few of our own to share. If the company asked for our feedback on the DC Universe so far, and what aspects of it should stay and which should go, here’s what we would say....
KEEP: The Superman Franchise Going
Gunn and Safran’s DCU got off to a great start with Superman, a colorful, upbeat, and hopeful superhero movie that understood the Man of Steel down to his inspirational core. Gunn did a superb job filling out Superman’s cast. David Corenswet wasn’t just a beefy hunk in a blue suit; he radiated that innate goodness that’s essential to the character’s timeless appeal. Superman also featured arguably the best cinematic Lex Luthor to date (Nicholas Hoult) and the best Jimmy Olsen too (Sklyer Gisondo).
Gunn’s already got Man of Tomorrow coming next summer. If it does well, DC should let him keep making Superman movies as long as he wants.
READ MORE: Who Is Jeremy Latcham, the New Head of DC Studios?
CHANGE: The Focus on Obscure DC Characters
Actually did Gunn and Safran’s DCU get off to a great start? Technically, their first project wasn’t Superman, it was the HBO Max series Creature Commandos, an animated show about a group of monsters who work as a black ops team for the Suicide Squad’s leader, Amanda Waller. The team is so obscure a lot of active DC fans had never read one of their comics.
Creature Commandos wasn’t an isolated example, either. Gunn and Safran also made Clayface, a dark horror film about a relatively unknown Batman villain, and just a few months ago there were reports that they were also developing a film focused on two more DC baddies, Deathstroke and Bane. Meanwhile they left all sorts of better-known heroes and villains on the sidelines.
During Gunn’s time at Marvel he showed the value of great storytelling wedded to lesser-known superheroes. The Guardians of the Galaxy were at best a C-level property before Gunn got his hands on them. But Marvel had already established a pretty sturdy foundation with films like Iron Man, Captain America, and Thor before they got to Guardians. Starting a new DC Universe with the Creature Commandos is like making a Clayface movie before you introduce Batman! Who would do something like that??
KEEP: Aaron Pierre's John Stewart
I wasn’t the biggest fan of Lanterns, but I loved Aaron Pierre and his gruff, take-no-s— performance as John Stewart. He will supposedly return as the character in Gunn’s Man of Tomorrow and I look forward to seeing him there. I don’t know if I need another season of Lanterns if it’s going to continue to deemphasize the characters’ powers and depict the entire Lantern Corps as a bunch of unfeeling killers. But a Lanterns season focused on John Stewart as he tries to do right with his Power Ring sounds good to me.
CHANGE: Just Make The Batman the DCU Batman
I know that The Batman predated Gunn and Safran’s tenure at DC Studios, and their plan was always to develop their own Batman movie (titled The Brave and the Bold) and cast a new actor as their Dark Knight.
Beyond the obvious fact that Gunn and Safran didn’t have a hand in developing and designing Robert Pattinson’s Batman, I have never understood why they couldn’t just grandfather The Batman into their DCU the same way they grandfathered Gunn’s The Suicide Squad and Peacemaker into it. I actually think Corenswet’s upbeat Superman and Pattinson’s moody Caped Crusader would make for a perfect onscreen contrast, and you’ve already got The Batman Part II coming in 2028 anyway. Throw a Corenswet cameo in after the credits and see what happens. If the Batmobile ain’t broke, don’t fix it.
KEEP: The People v Gorilla Grodd
While I do think DC could stand to emphasize more of its flagship characters, I do hope they follow through with the recently announced The People v Gorilla Grodd series for HBO Max, which they described as an “eight-part “true” crime docuseries” about “the Daily Planet’s Jimmy Olsen ... investigating whether Gorilla Grodd was wrongly convicted in one of Metropolis’ most famous murder trials.”
As I already said, I really enjoyed Gisondo’s Jimmy Olsen, and would love to see him in his own show — let alone a show that’s a legal thriller about an intrepid reporter helping a talking gorilla. It also sounds like the kind of premise that only a risk-taking, DC Comics-loving nerd like James Gunn would greenlight. The odds of the new regime taking a chance on something as weird as TPvGG in the future seems very low, so I hope this one manages to make it onto streaming.
CHANGE: There Should Only Be One DC Universe
When Gunn and Safran took the job at DC, they announced their own slate of ten interconnected movies and shows that would also be set in one shared universe. DC projects started before their tenure — like The Batman or Todd Phillips’ Joker sequel — were branded as “Elseworlds” projects, a term DC uses for alternate reality stories set in different corners of their comic-book multiverse.
Respectfully, I think I speak for a lot of comic-book fans when I say that the multiverse feels a little played out right now. And I am certain I speak for a lot of casual moviegoers who do not want lectures from goobers like me why Robert Pattinson and David Corenswet can’t meet, or why Joaquin Phoenix‘s Joker has nothing to do Robert Pattinson’s Batman.
If Hollywood is going to persist in building large cinematic universe, then they should aim to make them as streamlined and as easy to understand as possible. Gunn and Safran’s notion that they could have two Batmans at the same time, or a new sequel to Keanu Reeves’ Constantine that’s totally separate from Superman or Supergirl or the Justice League, seems like a recipe for audience confusion and disinterest.

title: Cause of death revealed for 5-year-old Saylor Hayes 2 months after parents charged
text:
GEORGETOWN COUNTY, SC (WMBF/Gray News) - The investigation into the death of Saylor Hayes has concluded.
The Georgetown County Coroner’s Office determined the 5-year-old’s cause of death and announced it had concluded its investigation.
Saylor was reported missing in August while vacationing with her family in the Pawleys Island area. Her body was later found in the waters near where she was last seen.
Following an investigation, coroner Chase Ridgeway determined Saylor’s cause of death to be asphyxia due to drowning, with child neglect identified as a contributory factor.
The manner of death has been classified as undetermined. This classification reflects the inability to conclusively determine whether Saylor’s death was accidental or the result of a homicidal act, according to the coroner’s office.
According to the arrest warrants, Saylor, described as being severely nonverbal and autistic with a history of wandering and a known affinity for water, was left unsupervised near a body of water before she went missing.
Saylor’s parents, John Hayes III and Geordyn Hayes, were arrested after investigators alleged they misled deputies during the search for their daughter.
Washington County Sheriff Blake Andis said Saylor had been enrolled in the agency’s Project Lifesaver program since June 2024.
Project Lifesaver helps authorities find people who are at risk of wandering because of cognitive conditions or other special needs. People in the program wear a small transmitter that emits a radio frequency, helping authorities track missing people.
A helicopter equipped with the technology was even deployed to help locate her. However, Weaver said they couldn’t get a ping from Saylor.
Andis said it was discovered that Saylor did not have her transmitter when she went missing after wandering from her family’s rental home. Instead, investigators found the tracker in a vehicle on the property.
According to the warrants, John Hayes and Geordyn Hayes encouraged deputies to use Project Lifesaver, despite knowing Saylor did not have her transmitter.
The two also allegedly tried to divert the search efforts away from the nearby water.
“It is important to understand that Project Lifesaver is a voluntary program,” Andis said. “A parent, guardian or caregiver is responsible for ensuring the transmitter remains properly secured to the client. The transmitter is attached using a specialized band designed for continuous wear. It cannot simply be unclasped or removed by the client; the band must be physically cut in order to remove the transmitter.”
Andis reiterated that Project Lifesaver works and he believes that if Saylor had been wearing her transmitter, deputies could have found her much sooner.
John and Geordyn Hayes were arrested in Tennessee and charged with unlawfully placing a child at risk, or willfully abandoning a child, according to the Georgetown County Sheriff’s Office.

title: Chronic pain doesn’t have to be a choice between suffering and strong medication
text:
(Aging Untold) — If you live with chronic pain, it can feel like you only have two choices: tough it out or take strong medication.
There are other ways to manage chronic pain that may help you sleep better, move better and get your life back. It starts with finding out why the pain is there.
Start with the source of the pain
The first thing to do is find the root cause or the source of the pain. That will determine how to treat it, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
She said the pain could come from a damaged muscle, damaged tissue, nerves or a nervous system that’s overly sensitive.
“Your treatment is going to depend on why you have the pain,” Rogers said.
She said the cause also leads to other options, such as movement and stretching.
Don’t overlook sleep
Rogers said sleep is something people often overlook.
“I know that pain a lot of times interferes with sleep. But if you get really good sleep, then it can actually help your pain, if you can get to that point,” Rogers said.
Experts share what worked for them
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said she had chronic back pain around age 50 and kept returning to a chiropractor for adjustments.
She said he eventually told her she could keep coming back or stop doing some of the things that might be causing the pain. His tips included no longer wearing high heels, using an ergonomic cushion at work and no longer running.
“I think about what you shouldn’t do,” O’Rourke said. “I was so grateful that he told me what not to do to help my pain get better.”
O’Rourke also said she went to a physiatrist, whom she described as a sports medicine doctor, for a hip issue. She said walking up and down stairs made it worse, and she was taught to sleep on her side with a pillow between her legs.
“And I don’t have pain anymore,” O’Rourke said.
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said she injured her lower back in her 20s and was told surgery was an option, but she declined. Another doctor told her to push her car seat up, she said.
Cradduck said other options for pain relief include acupuncture, dry needling, chiropractic care, cognitive behavior therapy and massage therapy.
She also described a transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation unit, a machine used for muscle pain and to loosen muscles.
Rogers said several aesthetics places also have machines that do something similar.
“It increases blood flow, it helps mobility,” Rogers said. “People can move their arms and all that. And it helps a lot with the pain.”
As always, contact your health care provider for medical advice.
Inflammation, deconditioning and movement
Inflammation can make pain worse, Rogers said.
“Just look for the source of the inflammation that you have, because that’s what’s making it worse,” she said.
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said deconditioning can also play a role.
“Sometimes it’s just deconditioning, like we haven’t been working out like we should, and then we become weaker, then it is kind of a cascade of things,” Ambrose said.
Movement is important, Rogers said, because a lot of times people become stiff when they are not moving.
“When you’re moving, you have blood flow and everything is made a lot easier,” she said.
Physical therapy can help work the muscles around an injury to provide support while healing, O’Rourke said.
Medication and asking questions
Cradduck said people should not be so afraid of medications that they avoid it when needed.
She said she has seen 95-year-olds who have had hip replacements decline prescribed medication because they feared addiction.
How much pain is too much
The goal is not always to be 100% pain-free, Cradduck said.
“How much pain can I have and still live a normal life and not have it interfere with my life?” Cradduck said. “It’s when pain interferes with your daily living that you have to really be concerned.”
“I think sometimes we just accept pain as aging when that’s not the case,” Ambrose said.
Key takeaways
- Treat the source. Focus on treating the source of chronic pain, not just masking symptoms with medication.
- Know the cause. Pain can come from a damaged muscle, damaged tissue, nerves or an overly sensitive nervous system, and treatment depends on which it is.
- Keep moving. Many times pain results from deconditioning due to lack of movement. Movement increases blood flow.
- Work with specialists. A specialist such as a sports medicine doctor could help you regain function and treat the root cause of your pain.

title: US soldier arrested in Britain on suspicion of espionage linked to Russia
text:
US soldier arrested in Britain on suspicion of espionage linked to Russia
A U.S. Army soldier was arrested Tuesday in England on suspicion of espionage related to Russia, counterterror police said.
The 41-year-old, who was not named, was arrested near Gloucester on suspicion of violating two sections of the National Security Act 2023 for assisting a foreign intelligence service and obtaining or disclosing protected information.
The Metropolitan Police said its counterterror forces worked closely with the FBI and U.S. military.
FBI Director Kash Patel called it an “important arrest" dealing with allegations of espionage that are of “utmost concern” for the U.S. and its allies.
“This FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners," Patel said.

title: US Air Force relocates aircraft from a base in England because of a threat, US official says
text:
LONDON (AP) — The U.S. Air Force has relocated aircraft from a base in eastern England because of a threat, U.S. officials told The Associated Press.
The Military Air Tracking Alliance, a team of about 30 open-source analysts that routinely analyzes military and government flight activity, said that it spotted 13 U.S. aircraft stationed at RAF Mildenhall departing for bases in Scotland, Spain and Germany.
The Wall Street Journal, which first reported the evacuation, said that the threat related to Iran. The report cited “people familiar with the matter.”
The relocation of the aircraft came less than two months after the U.S. Air Force withdrew its bombers from another U.S.-run base in Britain, RAF Fairford, as police investigated a suspected terror plot linked to Iran. Bombers flying out of RAF Fairford had been used to strike Iran during the Middle East conflict.
Some of the aircraft that were relocated were permanently based at RAF Mildenhall, while others were there on rotation and included a combination of Osprey aircraft and midair refueling tankers, the Military Air Tracking Alliance said.
The base also raised its alert level to FPCON Charlie — the second highest level — the organization said. That applies when an incident occurs or intelligence is received indicating that some form of terrorist action targeting personnel or facilities is likely.
The decision to move the aircraft was proactive rather than reactive, a U.S. official said, adding that the U.S. military is agile to potential threats. Some of the planes that left were in transit while others were permanently stationed at RAF Mildenhall and they may return, the official said. The official didn’t elaborate on the nature and source of the threat.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that the United States is “constantly repositioning forces around the world for a variety of reasons,” and referred questions to the Pentagon, which didn’t provide immediate confirmation.
An official from the U.S. Air Force in Europe told the AP that the U.S. is “taking coordinated and appropriate actions” to ensure the safety and security of U.S. and U.K. personnel and their families. The official said that aircraft are rotated between bases for various reasons, including training and “real world requirements.”
The official said that the U.S. military constantly assesses a variety of factors that determine what security measures are implemented. The official wouldn’t provide further information on movement of assets or specific force protection for reasons of operational security.
Both officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak publicly about sensitive military matters.
The U.K. prime minister’s office said that British air bases are safe and their security is a top priority. The office said that the U.K. is in constant communication with the U.S., sharing intelligence and assessing threats together.
RAF Mildenhall, a U.K. base operated by the U.S. Air Force, hosts the 100th refueling wing, the only permanent refueling wing in the European region. It operates the KC-135 Stratotanker, a four-engine jet aircraft with a wingspan of 131 feet (40 meters) that can carry up to 83,000 pounds (nearly 38,000 kilograms) of cargo.
Five men were detained on Sept. 27 after three suspicious vans were spotted traveling toward RAF Fairford. The U.K.-owned base has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East, including the Iran war.
Other arrests followed and two men have been charged under the National Security Act.
The U.K. Defense Ministry said in a statement that it doesn’t comment on the activity of other nations and said aircraft and other assets move regularly according to operational requirements.
___
Konstantin Toropin reported from Washington.

title: Average price of gas falls below $4 a gallon across the US
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(CNN) - The average price of gas is now below $4 a gallon.
According to AAA, the national average is $3.98.
Although the number doesn’t mean anything specific economically, $4 acts as a psychological threshold for gas prices. Falling below that makes the price seem much cheaper.
Prices are trending down primarily due to falling demand caused by the end of summer driving and the return to standard time.
Long term, gas prices still face serious headwinds. Fighting in Russia and the Middle East has damaged refineries there.
Many in the United States will have to go offline in the near future for maintenance.
They’ve been deferring maintenance this year to keep supplies steady.
