title: Meet the York resident documenting aging burial plots before it’s too late
text:
YORK — Nate Losier poked at the ground with an old orange snow stake. It crunched against the leaves as he kicked autumn debris from his path during a trek through Cape Neddick on Nov. 1.
The stake hit dirt and sticks and pebbles as Losier searched for signs of treasure buried at his feet. Then, he struck something that didn’t give — the thing he’d come to find.
“So this is the base, the concrete base with the key that it sits in,” Losier explained, bending down to swipe away more leaves. “And then, that’s the rest of it.”
Suddenly, Losier, 52, and his friend Andy Webster, 56, towered above Samuel Todd’s headstone. It had been toppled sometime in its roughly 200-year existence. Other members of the Todd family lie beneath crumbling memorials close by: Samuel’s wife Mercy, their three young children under tiny footstones and several others.
A little over three years ago, Losier started a project he calls History Search Party in a quest to find 220 old family burial plots in and around York. He takes photos, posts them on a Facebook page dedicated to York history and shares their stories. Then, a friend adds them to FindAGrave, a website where users across the country can locate buried ancestors.
Losier only has a couple dozen more plots to find. Toddville — the aptly named family plot where Samuel was buried in 1807 — was his 196th. Before long, he’ll be looking for his next project.
PRESERVING HISTORY
Losier hasn’t always been so enthusiastic about history. But when the eighth-generation York resident’s grandparents died, he realized his connections to the past were fading, so he wanted to try and document what was still around before it’s too late.
“I really wish I had interest in (history sooner), and I could ask them more questions and hear stories,” Losier said, remembering his grandparents. “There’s a lot of stuff that’s changing in the town.”
Change has been a contentious topic recently in York, one of Maine’s most historic towns. A few miles down the road from the Toddville plot, a 1760 home that doubles as a bagel shop is due to be demolished or relocated. A stone’s throw away, a 70-year-old honey locust tree is at the center of a preservation debate, while a store in town that Losier’s family has owned for a few generations is due to be demolished next year.
So when Losier and Webster stumble upon an untold story, they know it’s a matter of time before it’s gone.
At the Toddville plot, one side of the iron fence surrounding the cemetery has bent beneath the weight of a fallen tree, its roots dangling a couple feet from where the Todd children are buried.
“I see this, and I so badly want to fix it,” Losier said. But he knows it’s a difficult job.
According to state law, if a homeowner in Maine buys property with a plot located on it, they can choose to maintain it — but aren’t required to. Descendants who wish to visit plots must be allowed access, though, and some of them may also choose to do some upkeep.
But more often than not, the sites Losier finds aren’t properly cared for. Like Toddville, several are deep in the woods and hard to access with the necessary resources to fix them. In some cases, the descendants of those buried there are long gone from the area. Others simply don’t know about their family plots.
Caring for aging headstones requires finesse and unique resources, and state law only mandates that municipalities care for certain cemeteries — usually, only sites where veterans from the Revolution onward are buried. Smaller family plots normally don’t have a designated caretaker.
“It’s not long before that’s just gone, that it’s just buried by leaves and soil,” Losier said, pointing to Samuel Todd’s grave.
Losier says his searches are about more than just headstones. He’s found pennies from the 1800s and apothecary bottles and gold. He’s even uncovered personal family ties.
“Nate did some digging and found that we’re actually distantly related,” Webster laughed.
Losier documents old wells and rubble from bygone homes using directions and maps from the late 1800s to the early 1900s. Not much is the same.
“‘Take a left at the big oak,’” Losier recalls reading during a search for an elusive plot in nearby Ogunquit. “Right. That’s not there anymore.”
Liz Boardman, who owns a home close to the Toddville plot, said she’s spent years exploring acres of land behind her home and still makes daily discoveries. Despite her searching, she’s still trying to find signs of an old Toddville barn and an outhouse. For her, Webster and Losier, the fun is just as much about the hunt as it is the discovery.
“There’s a cemetery that we’ve been trying to find for a couple years now, and we go back every once in a while and we still can’t find it. But now, we have an idea of where it might be,” Webster said. Their next visit to the area could be a milestone in the project.
CONTINUING THE SEARCH
Losier says he’d been holding out on exploring the Cape Neddick area of York. It’s a daunting way to finish the search.
One of the maps he’s been referencing for the area is from 1872 and is broken up into 15 sections. He’s hitting them one by one, exploring every corner until the search is exhausted.
“This area has so much stuff,” Losier said. “I know we’re going to be spending so much time in this area, and now that I’m trying to finish up the cemeteries, I think it’s time to come out here.”
Losier wanders frequently on his walks. He sees a piece of carved granite in the distance, or the chiseled key of a headstone, and peels off to investigate. He says he’ll be revisiting the area for quite some time.
Losier has thought about how he might expand his search or learn more about how to preserve the sites for future generations. He’s even tried to get the York Parks and Recreation Department to hire him as a steward for family plots but hasn’t had any luck.
The graveyard hunter has plans to keep the History Search Party going after he finds his 220th plot, but he doesn’t have his heart set on his next quest. He frequently gets feedback on his online posts from descendants, thanking him for finding their relatives and requesting that he find others.
He might resurrect another online group he tried to start in the spring: “Tombstone Tourist,” where he documented similar cemetery history in Kittery and Wells.
“We’ve also been looking for gold,” Losier said, pondering his next adventure.

title: Voter participation is nowhere near enough
text:
American registered voters reportedly managed to come up to about 50% of eligible voters casting a ballot during this midterm election cycle. Fifty percent didn’t even bother to vote.
That means there were no winners in this election except for the politicians. The losers are the American people, the free and the brave, of whom a significant number are just too busy or can’t be bothered to vote to begin with.
Democrat, Republican, independent or unenrolled, it doesn’t matter. The politicians know it and they play us hard. It’s the same old song and dance. And, sadly, it’ll take another 9/11 or worse to bring us together and even then, it seems, only fleetingly.
Paul Bonenfant
South China

title: Bob Boone, World Series champion and part of 3-generation baseball family, dies at 78
text:
Bob Boone, World Series champion and part of 3-generation baseball family, dies at 78
Bob Boone, the catcher on the Philadelphia Phillies' first World Series championship team in 1980 who won seven Gold Gloves and was part of baseball's first three-generation family, has died. He was 78.
Boone's son, Bret, announced his father's death Tuesday on social media. The Phillies said in a statement Boone died Monday. No cause of death was announced.
“He was a man of great integrity. He was a great dad, husband, and patriarch. It was a privilege to call him my father. Baseball lost a great one today,” Bret Boone wrote.
Boone spent his first 10 seasons with the Phillies, played seven with the California Angels and two with the Kansas City Royals. He also managed the Royals and Cincinnati Reds.
“Bob was an incredible player, teammate and family man. He embodied everything we believe exemplary athletes should represent, both on and off the field,” the Phillies said in a statement. “We were proud to have him as part of the Phillies family during one of the most historic runs in team history. His impact on our organization, his teammates, and everyone who had the privilege of knowing him will never be forgotten.”
Boone's father, Ray, played 13 seasons in the majors and was a two-time All-Star with the Detroit Tigers. Bob Boone's two sons both enjoyed long baseball careers. Aaron Boone played 13 seasons in the majors and played for the Reds when Bob managed the team. Aaron now manages the New York Yankees. Bret Boone was a three-time All-Star over a 14-year career spent largely with the Seattle Mariners. A third son played in the minor leagues. Bret's son, Jake Boone, works in the New York Mets' front office after playing at Princeton and briefly in the minors.
“His legacy is profound, and we can see the values he embodied carried forward by his son, Aaron, in his leadership of the Yankees,” the Yankees wrote in a statement.
Bob Boone was a sixth-round draft pick as a third baseman out of Stanford in 1969. He was converted to catcher in the minor leagues and caught 1,095 games with Philadelphia, second on the Phillies’ all-time list to Red Dooin (1,124). Boone caught 2,225 games overall in 19 big league seasons.
“We played in the minors together where he gave up third base so I could play it, only to become one of the best catchers in baseball history,” Phillies Hall of Famer Mike Schmidt said. “Bob was a great father and husband. Our lives and careers were intertwined, we pursued our Christian faith together, worked out together, and became world champions together.”
He was the first Phillies catcher to win a Gold Glove (1978, 1979) and led the Phillies with a .412 batting average in their 1980 World Series win over the Kansas City Royals.
“Bob Boone was a quiet leader, both on and off the field,” said Larry Bowa, the shortstop on the 1980 team. “I had the privilege of playing alongside him for nearly my entire career, and without question, he was the backbone of our team.”
A native of San Diego, Boone made NL All-Star teams in 1976, 1978 and 1979. He set the record for career games caught by a catcher with 1,919 in Kansas City. He was 41 years old when he won his final Gold Glove with the Royals in 1989.
Ivan Rodriguez (2,427) and Carlton Fisk (2,226) have since passed Boone on the career games caught list.
“I grew up watching Bob with the great Phillies teams of the 70’s. His play and mastery of catching inspired me to want to play the position,” Hall of Fame catcher Mike Piazza posted on social media.
Boone caught the final out of the 1980 Game 6 clincher when Tug McGraw struck out Willie Wilson to win the World Series. Boone was involved in a more famous play earlier in that inning when he ran after Frank White's foul pop near the home dugout in Veterans Stadium. The ball bounced off Boone's mitt and straight into Pete Rose's glove for an out — a catch played on countless highlight reels through the decades in Philadelphia.
Boone was added to the Phillies' Wall of Fame in 2005.
Boone won four more Gold Gloves, made another All-Star team and twice led the Angels to the playoffs. He went 10 for 22 (.455) with a homer and two RBIs against Boston in the 1986 American League Championship Series.
“Our franchise leader in games caught, Boone’s leadership, exceptional defense and knowledge of the game made him an invaluable presence behind the plate and helped the Angels win two division titles,” the Angels said in a statement.
Boone went 371-444 overall as a manager, spending three seasons with the Royals and three with the Reds. He joined the Washington Nationals' front office in 2005.
Washington won the World Series in 2019, the first championship in franchise history. Boone resigned in 2021 rather than comply with the organization’s COVID-19 vaccine mandate.

title: Investigators recover voice recorder from jet crash in Florida that killed 9
text:
(AP) - Investigators said Monday they have recovered the cockpit voice recorder from a business jet that plummeted from the sky amid severe weather in Florida last week, killing all nine people on board.
The recorder was found at the site where the Bahamas-bound Learjet slammed into the ground and erupted in a fireball Nov. 1, the National Transportation Safety Board said in a statement posted to social media.
If data from the device can be recovered, it could provide crucial details about what the pilots said to each other as they encountered turbulence, ice formed on the wings and they lost control of the aircraft.
It was not immediately known if the recorder had been damaged or if it was working in the first place. The NTSB said the device was being evaluated at a lab in Washington.
From photos the agency posted online, showing the recorder’s orange-painted metal shell, it appeared to be in decent shape, aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti told The Associated Press.
“It’s very plausible that any info on the recorder survived,” Guzzetti said. “If they can recover it, and it’s from the accident flight, that will be a huge help to investigators.”
He noted that when the NTSB recovered the cockpit voice recorder from a medical transport plane that crashed in Philadelphia in January 2025, killing seven people, it turned out the device likely had not been functioning for several years.
Witnesses captured dramatic video as the business jet plunged nose-first into the ground, and air traffic control transmissions recorded the disturbing moments as the pilots realized their fate. But the cockpit voice recorder could shed light on other aspects of the crash, including why the Learjet appeared to steer around a large storm cell only to head directly into a rapidly developing smaller one.
Investigators have said pieces of a key part of the tail called the elevator, which controls the plane’s pitch, were found more than a mile away from the main crater, confirming the plane started to break apart before impact.
The co-pilot told air traffic controllers that the plane was being thrown up and down more than 700 feet (213 meters), and she asked them for a better route through the area.
Generally, it takes 12 to 18 months for the NTSB to complete a crash investigation, but complicated cases can take longer. The NTSB’s roughly 400 workers are pursuing more than 1,200 active investigations.
Investigators will review maintenance records and any history of problems with the plane. They will also interview officials at Upper Jets, the company that operated the flight, as well as air traffic controllers and people who work at the airport in Austin, Texas, from where the plane departed.

title: Trial for Charlie Kirk accused killer set for summer 2028
text:
Utah judge sets summer 2028 trial for the man accused of killing Charlie Kirk
The man accused of assassinating conservative activist Charlie Kirk will stand trial in the summer of 2028, a Utah judge ruled Monday.
Related previous coverage in the player above: Surveillance video shows Tyler Robinson’s movements on Utah Valley University before Charlie Kirk shooting, prosecutors say
Attorneys for defendant Tyler Robinson, 23, proposed a trial starting in 2029. But District Judge Tony Graf faced pressure from Kirk's family and supporters, including President Donald Trump, to speed up court proceedings that already have lasted more than a year.
Robinson has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder in the killing of Kirk, 31, as the activist spoke to several thousand people at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10, 2025. Robinson could face the death penalty if convicted.
Graf allocated 105 days for the trial, beginning with jury selection on June 21, 2028. He said the dates balance Robinson’s right to prepare his defense with the rights of Kirk's widow, Erika Kirk, to a speedy resolution.
Erika Kirk's attorney disagreed with the schedule but said there is no choice but to accept it.
“A trial in the summer of 2028, three years after Charlie’s assassination, does not feel very speedy to the Kirk family,” attorney Jeffrey Neiman told the judge. He had argued the trial should start next October.
In a statement after Monday's hearing, the Kirk family characterized Graf’s decision as a “delay” and said, “every additional day without justice prolongs our family’s pain.”
Robinson’s defense team declined to comment after the hearing.
The defendant turned himself in a day after the shooting. His lawyers have not offered alternative theories for Kirk’s death.
Prosecutors had said they could be ready for trial by October 2027. Rather than hold the proceedings during the Thanksgiving and Christmas holidays, they proposed a January 2028 start date.
Kirk helped galvanize young voters around Trump during the 2024 election. Trump weighed in on the trial in a social media post last month, saying Robinson should be tried “within a month.” The Republican president criticized Graf, a former prosecutor appointed judge last year, for “taking forever to ask questions that people already know the answer to.”
Utah County prosecutors allege Robinson targeted Kirk for his political beliefs. They say a bullet found in the rifle used to kill Kirk was engraved with the words “Hey Facist! CATCH!” and that Robinson wrote in a text message about Kirk: “I had enough of his hatred. Some hate can’t be negotiated out.”
Robinson’s attorneys said in court documents that they must sift through tens of thousands of files turned over by prosecutors. They plan to conduct extensive investigations into Robinson’s life in search of mitigating factors that could influence his sentence if convicted.
Defense attorneys have said they will conduct surveys to see if it's possible to seat an impartial jury in Utah County. Depending on the results, they may ask to hold the trial elsewhere. The judge said he will hear arguments about the venue next December.
___
Associated Press journalist Matthew Brown contributed from Billings, Montana.

title: A record number of veterans are attending UMaine on the GI Bill
text:
Andrew Gregory used to go to the University of Maine’s Veterans Center in Memorial Union as a quiet place to get work done. Now, he can hardly focus.
“There’s so many people, there’s always conversations you’re getting pulled into, or your ears perk up,” said Gregory, 29, a senior at the university originally from Pittsburgh. “It’s been phenomenal. On some of our busier days, we have 20 people in there at any given time.”
The active duty Marine helicopter crew chief is one of a record number of students — 530, to be exact — enrolled at the flagship public university this fall who are paying for their education thanks to benefits from the GI Bill.
That number has climbed every fall for six years, increasing by more than 50% in that time, according to data from the university, which prides itself on the support it provides for veteran students and their families.
Students attending college on the GI Bill, first passed in 1944 to allow former service members to seek higher education, get the full cost of tuition and any mandatory fees covered, plus an allowance for housing and a stipend for books.
The university also waives all tuition and fees for spouses or dependents of veterans, which 192 current students are taking advantage of.
Gregory, who is studying wildlife ecology at UMaine while preparing to be an officer in the Marine Corps, said the benefits have long been an important recruitment tool for the military, and one that influenced his decision to join the Marines.
Education was also a major factor in Malachi Lakey’s decision to enlist in the Navy.
Lakey, 34, from Lancaster, Pennsylvania, served for five years as an aerial photographer and is now in the reserves. Years ago, he got an undergraduate degree in English, and later enlisted knowing he’d like to return to school one day.
“The GI Bill is miraculous,” Lakey said. “It’s amazing that it works as well as it does.”
Gregory and Lakey are both involved in leadership of the UMaine Veterans Association, and help organize social events like potlucks for the growing community.
Lakey said he didn’t set out to find a community of fellow veterans in college, but he’s grateful it happened anyway.
“I find myself really, really appreciating the fact that there are so many veterans on campus that you can connect with,” he said. “It keeps you going, because they may not be in the exact same circumstances, but they’re in a similar place.”
Like Gregory, he’s in his final year of a wildlife ecology degree. While he chases a second undergraduate diploma, he is now debating between pursing a career in wildlife law enforcement as a game warden or going into ecology research and getting a graduate degree.
They both chose UMaine because they were looking for a strong wildlife program based on the East Coast.
Unlike Lakey, who has completed his time in the Navy and is now a reservist, much of Gregory’s service is ahead of him.
He’s part of the Marine Enlisted Commissioning Education Program, which allows him to go to college while serving as an active duty Marine. He previously attended officer candidate school, and now gets four years to focus on his education. While in school, he’s a part of UMaine’s ROTC unit, where he trains cadets, and he is technically assigned to Maine Maritime Academy.
He said attending college at a later point in life has been beneficial.
“I was more deliberate with my time, the classes I took, and the degree I’m getting,” he said.
After he gets his bachelor’s, Gregory will go directly to Quantico, Virginia, for basic officer school, then he’ll spend the next decade as an officer in the Marines. He’s hoping to earn a graduate degree during that time by conducting wildlife research with the game wardens on the base where he’s stationed.
After his military career is over, he wants to work in wildlife enforcement.

title: It’s never too late to become a Junior Ranger in Maine
text:
Doug Woodsum of Oakland is a retired teacher, a Maine master naturalist and a volunteer conservationist.
On Election Day 2026, twenty-four first graders from Damariscotta elected to hike 1.2 miles up Mount Battie in Camden.
At the summit, they shook hands with a park ranger as they received their Junior Ranger certificates and patches. For weeks, two teachers had helped the aspiring rangers complete eight of the 22 activities in the Camden Hills State Park Junior Ranger Activity Book.
Junior Ranger programs in state and national parks educate children, require outdoor activity, invite reflection on nature and nurture creativity. At Camden Hills, children ages 4 to 7 years old must complete at least eight of the activities. Those 8 and older must complete at least 12.
The vision statement at Great Salt Bay School in Damariscotta describes “collaboration among staff, students, families and local partners” in a “culture of curiosity and kindness.” That vision brought together two classes, two teachers, four parent chaperones, a master naturalist, a wilderness first responder and a state park ranger. We enjoyed over three hours on a balmy leaf-littered day that peaked at the summit’s Memorial Tower or “castle,” as some students called it.
On the hike, students learned about safety, trail etiquette and tree identification. They stopped, looked and listened, gathering sensory information to help with various activities in the Junior Ranger booklet.
Junior Ranger programs emphasize the ancestral homelands of indigenous people, natural history and more recent history such as the World War I Memorial Tower. The first graders connected the dots, completed a maze, did a word search and colored by numbers. But, to complete eight activities, they also drew pictures, journaled, wrote poetry and pondered what a ranger does when dangerous, careless or illegal situations arise.
I am both a Junior Ranger and a one-time state park ranger here in Maine. Knowing the value and potential benefits of Junior Ranger programs, I collect materials from state and national parks, and I am proud of my multiple Junior Ranger credentials. Though designed for youngsters, adults learn too when they complete the requirements. Plus, it is just plain fun and refreshing mental and physical exercise.
In the Belgrade Lakes region of Maine, there are no state or national parks. But who needs a park? 7 Lakes Alliance in Belgrade maintains 20 miles of trails, several of them up mountains. The vast watershed stewarded by 7 Lakes Alliance is larger than most state parks. Finally, their interpretive programs number in the dozens.
One volunteer, yours truly, thought, “Why not create our own Junior Ranger program?” Before long, a team of conservation professionals were working on their own activity book, and a Junior Ranger program was born.
The staff at Camden Hills shared an electronic template of their activity book with us. We borrowed, modified and created new activities that fit the lakes and trails around us. A donor funded the initial expenses, and, later, a grant provided for printing the activity booklets. This collaboration echoes the vision statement of the Great Salt Bay School.
When I did the preliminary hike with the Wilderness First Responder, we met a couple hiking with their 6-year-old daughter. My partner asked, “How hard would you say this hike is?” The girl hesitated and her mom replied, “Rice Krispies Treats help.”
So, after the steepest .7-mile stretch of our field trip, we had a Rice Krispies Treat snack break. The last .5-mile stretch was a breeze after that. As we finished the saran-wrapped snacks, we discussed one final teachable moment: Leave no trace; carry in and carry out.
It’s never too late to become a Junior Ranger. No matter your age or the time of year, nature waits. All Maine state parks that offer camping and 7 Lakes Alliance await too for you and your young friends and family.
Junior Rangers like to have fun, observe animals and plants, conserve state park lands and tell others about the wonderful state park experience. Ditto 7 Lakes Alliance. And the icing on the cake? School buses pay no fee to enter Camden Hills State Park.

title: These side hustle apps are offering users a way to earn extra money
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (InvestigateTV) - Apps that let people rent out things they already own are offering users a way to earn extra cash without taking on an in-person part-time job.
Instead of signing up to drive for a rideshare service or deliver groceries, some people are turning to rental platforms that allow them to make money on their own schedule by listing items they already have at home.
Reese Grau has been renting out her closet on the Pickle app for the last five years.
“Basically, if I rent it out four times, I make my money back,” Grau said. “So, it’s kind of like girl math…return on my investment.”
Pickle allows users to list items from their real-life closet on the app, from accessories and shoes to clothing. Grau said larger rentals, such as higher-end dresses, can bring in more money.
“I get some bigger rentals — like a nicer dress — I can make more,” she said. “There’s been weeks where I’ve made $200 a week.”
Over the last year, Grau said she rented out 85 items and earned about $1,300.
For families looking to put outgrown baby gear to use, BabyQuip offers another option by connecting travelers and parents with providers who rent out items such as strollers, cribs, toys and fans.
Kierstyn Stewart, a BabyQuip provider based out of Franklin, Tennessee, said she joined after her children started outgrowing their equipment.
Stewart said she has been renting out baby gear for a little more than two years and has completed around 150 rentals. Business can spike during peak travel seasons, she said, including spring break and major holidays.
“There are different parts of the year where you’re going to be busier: spring break, Thanksgiving, Christmas,” Stewart said. “You’re going to find that you’re just busier those times of the year, and throughout the year, it’s sprinkled in.”
BabyQuip said providers keep 78% of their rental and delivery fees and 100% of tips.
Other platforms offer similar opportunities with different kinds of property. Swimply allows homeowners to rent out pools, hot tubs and even sports courts — such as pickleball — as well as backyards for events. Another app, Neighbor, allows users to rent out space such as driveways.
Both women said the side income is helpful, but the work is also something they enjoy.
“I’ve been kind of trying to get some side hustles going, and this has been great for me,” Grau said. “I’ve gotten a lot of my friends on it too.”
Pickle, the clothing rental app, said in 2025 some of their top lenders made around $5,000 a month.
By 2034, the global peer-to-peer rental apps market size is expected to be worth around $49.3 billion.

title: Obituary: Dorothy Ann Tweer
text:
PORTLAND – Dorothy Ann Tweer, 82, of Portland, passed away peacefully at her home on Nov. 5, 2026.
Born in Augusta, on March 2, 1944, Dottie spent much of her adult life in Worcester, Massachusetts, working in human resources across industries ranging from injection molding to private prisons. After retiring she returned to Maine, settling in Portland in 2012.
Fiercely independent and sharp as a tack to the end, Dottie possessed a wicked sense of humor, a fondness for terrible puns, and a healthy dose of Irish stubbornness. A proud dual American and Irish citizen, she loved growing flowers, scratch tickets, and a properly set table, preferably showcasing her famous deviled eggs. Her beloved red Volkswagen Beetle, affectionately known as Red Dot, was nearly as iconic as she was. She spoiled her grandchildren without shame or contrition.
Dottie’s politics were every bit as unapologetic as her humor. A passionate, outspoken progressive, she followed every election with intense dedication and never hesitated to speak her mind. As if determined to have the last word, she held on just long enough to see one final blue wave.
She leaves behind her son, Sean Dundon, and his wife, Cordelia; her daughter Deirdre Dundon, and her partner, Paul; her cherished grandchildren, Eamonn (and his fiancée Canela) and Lucie; her adoring great-granddaughter, Layla; her former daughter-in-law Victoria (and her husband Marc); her niece Kathy Rushworth (and her husband Jim); her nephew Jason Wolfson; and her beloved cat, Bella. She also leaves behind a wide circle of extended family, lifelong friends, and caring neighbors who became like family over the years.
A celebration of Dottie’s life will be held in the spring. In the meantime, her family encourages well-wishers to plant something beautiful, buy a scratch ticket, tell an irreverent joke, and, above all, keep voting and organizing for a causes you support and wish to champion.
Please visit. http://www.jonesrichbarnes.com to view Dottie’s tribute page and to sign her online guestbook.

title: LIV Golf files bankruptcy plan and sets sight on January liquidation
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(AP) - LIV Golf filed a Chapter 11 bankruptcy plan with a New Jersey court Tuesday, along with a proposed schedule for a final hearing on its disclosure statement on Jan. 7 that would begin liquidation.
LIV Golf filed for bankruptcy on Sept. 8 after the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia, which had bankrolled the breakaway league from the start, said a change in strategy meant it would no longer pay for LIV after the 2026 season.
The bankruptcy plan is for an orderly wind down of LIV. The restructuring agreement with BC Partners Credit, which had pledged $300 million, failed to garner enough support for a LIV 2.0 version that would have kept the league going in 2027.
“Debtors have determined that no viable restructuring transaction remains available due to lack of player participation and BC Partners’ termination of the Restructuring Support Agreement,” LIV said in a summary of the bankruptcy plan.
It said PIF invested approximately $5 billion in equity capital and that LIV Golf continually operated at a loss and was years away from profitability. The filing also revealed LIF laid off 289 employees and furloughed 22 others roughly a week before filing for bankruptcy.
This was about a month after it finished paying $15.6 million in retention bonuses to seven executives LIV said was essential to finishing the 2026 season and making plans for restructuring.
A hearing is scheduled for Nov. 24 to conditionally approve the disclosure statement, which requires adequate information for those to whom LIV owes money and begins the wind-down phase of LIV operations.
The six weeks in between the Jan. 7 hearing to approve the statement are to determine voting rights and take any objections from those who have claims. A wind-down trust would oversee payments to creditors, resolve legal claims and handle other financial matters.
The judge last week approved Jon Rahm’s separation from LIV, which cost the two-time major champion a reported $100 million he was owed from when he joined the Saudi-funded league at the end of 2023. Rahm won last week in Abu Dhabi for his first regular European tour title since 2022.
The other LIV players, who have been banned by the PGA Tour, now must figure out where to play. Some have European tour membership or can try to get sponsor exemptions to tournaments, though not the strongest events on the schedule.
The PGA Tour has not indicated a path back for players and likely won’t until the bankruptcy proceedings are over.

text:
Dead candidate leads California election two months after falling, dying while door-knocking
A political candidate in California is leading a Board of Supervisors race two months after he died, according to the Calaveras County results.
Bruce Giudici has received 56.99% support with 1,982 votes in the Board of Supervisors District 5 race. Clyde Clapp has received 43.01% support with 1,496 votes.
As of the last report from the county, there were 322 ballots still unprocessed and 340 more "left to cure," which means that signatures either didn't match what was on file or were missing.
Giudici's campaign said he fell while door-knocking on a steep driveway on Aug. 30, and a homeowner called 911. He died the next day.
The Giudici campaign urged voters to still vote for him after his death.
"It was a very complicated decision to decide to keep going and an emotional one and we felt very strongly that Bruce had wanted to do this, and that was his mission and our goal was to finish his mission," said Carrie Biggs-Adams, a volunteer with the campaign.
"Bruce was a man who cared deeply about Calaveras County and believed District 5 deserved honest, ethical, accountable leadership," Giudici's campaign said after his death.
If Giudici wins the seat, the governor would need to appoint someone to fill the vacancy "until the election or qualification of a successor," according to California law.
The campaign expresses gratitude to voters who supported Giudici.
"We just really appreciate the people who trusted us that a good person would come forward and be a better alternative as their district five supervisor," Biggs-Adams said. "And we appreciate their support and their trust and now will help make sure somebody good is selected."

title: It’s never too late to become a Junior Ranger in Maine
text:
Doug Woodsum of Oakland is a retired teacher, a Maine master naturalist and a volunteer conservationist.
On Election Day 2026, twenty-four first graders from Damariscotta elected to hike 1.2 miles up Mount Battie in Camden.
At the summit, they shook hands with a park ranger as they received their Junior Ranger certificates and patches. For weeks, two teachers had helped the aspiring rangers complete eight of the 22 activities in the Camden Hills State Park Junior Ranger Activity Book.
Junior Ranger programs in state and national parks educate children, require outdoor activity, invite reflection on nature and nurture creativity. At Camden Hills, children ages 4 to 7 years old must complete at least eight of the activities. Those 8 and older must complete at least 12.
The vision statement at Great Salt Bay School in Damariscotta describes “collaboration among staff, students, families and local partners” in a “culture of curiosity and kindness.” That vision brought together two classes, two teachers, four parent chaperones, a master naturalist, a wilderness first responder and a state park ranger. We enjoyed over three hours on a balmy leaf-littered day that peaked at the summit’s Memorial Tower or “castle,” as some students called it.
On the hike, students learned about safety, trail etiquette and tree identification. They stopped, looked and listened, gathering sensory information to help with various activities in the Junior Ranger booklet.
Junior Ranger programs emphasize the ancestral homelands of indigenous people, natural history and more recent history such as the World War I Memorial Tower. The first graders connected the dots, completed a maze, did a word search and colored by numbers. But, to complete eight activities, they also drew pictures, journaled, wrote poetry and pondered what a ranger does when dangerous, careless or illegal situations arise.
I am both a Junior Ranger and a one-time state park ranger here in Maine. Knowing the value and potential benefits of Junior Ranger programs, I collect materials from state and national parks, and I am proud of my multiple Junior Ranger credentials. Though designed for youngsters, adults learn too when they complete the requirements. Plus, it is just plain fun and refreshing mental and physical exercise.
In the Belgrade Lakes region of Maine, there are no state or national parks. But who needs a park? 7 Lakes Alliance in Belgrade maintains 20 miles of trails, several of them up mountains. The vast watershed stewarded by 7 Lakes Alliance is larger than most state parks. Finally, their interpretive programs number in the dozens.
One volunteer, yours truly, thought, “Why not create our own Junior Ranger program?” Before long, a team of conservation professionals were working on their own activity book, and a Junior Ranger program was born.
The staff at Camden Hills shared an electronic template of their activity book with us. We borrowed, modified and created new activities that fit the lakes and trails around us. A donor funded the initial expenses, and, later, a grant provided for printing the activity booklets. This collaboration echoes the vision statement of the Great Salt Bay School.
When I did the preliminary hike with the Wilderness First Responder, we met a couple hiking with their 6-year-old daughter. My partner asked, “How hard would you say this hike is?” The girl hesitated and her mom replied, “Rice Krispies Treats help.”
So, after the steepest .7-mile stretch of our field trip, we had a Rice Krispies Treat snack break. The last .5-mile stretch was a breeze after that. As we finished the saran-wrapped snacks, we discussed one final teachable moment: Leave no trace; carry in and carry out.
It’s never too late to become a Junior Ranger. No matter your age or the time of year, nature waits. All Maine state parks that offer camping and 7 Lakes Alliance await too for you and your young friends and family.
Junior Rangers like to have fun, observe animals and plants, conserve state park lands and tell others about the wonderful state park experience. Ditto 7 Lakes Alliance. And the icing on the cake? School buses pay no fee to enter Camden Hills State Park.

title: Dan LeGage hired as new Portland High boys basketball coach
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
Dan LeGage was on the first Portland High boys basketball team coached by Joe Russo.
Thirty-six seasons later, LeGage will be Russo’s replacement as the Bulldogs’ head coach.
“I graduated from Portland High in 1991. My senior season was Joe’s first year at Portland High,” LeGage said.
On Monday, the school announced that LeGage will replace Russo, who retired in October.
LeGage, 53, had been Russo’s varsity assistant the past four seasons. Prior to that he was a successful head coach at Deering and Westbrook. LeGage was considered Russo’s likely heir apparent by many, but the position was posted and interviews were held last week.
“I feel blessed to have the opportunity to try to continue that tradition that Joe’s established over the past 36 years,” LeGage said. “We both care about this deeply and it matters. You’re making sure players who come through this program know, yes, success is important, but what’s equally important is to learn all those skills that help you later in life: perseverance, teamwork, communication.”
As a young coach, LeGage was on Russo’s staff as an assistant. LeGage said Russo encouraged him to go to a different school and become a head coach. It turned out the opportunity was across town at Deering High.
LeGage led Deering to its only two boys basketball championships in 2006 and 2012. In 11 seasons as Deering’s head coach from 2002-2013, LeGage had an overall record of 145-70. LeGage was also the head coach at Westbrook High for four seasons, taking the Blue Blazes to the 2018 Class A South final, where they lost to Greely.
LeGage, who teaches science at Portland High, returned to the Bulldogs’ bench as Russo’s assistant for the 2022-23 season when LeGage’s son Lucas was a freshman. This past season, Portland and Russo won their sixth state championship in 36 years when Portland beat Camden Hills, 70-60, in the 2026 Class A title game. Lucas LeGage scored 19 points on 7 of 11 shooting in his final high school game.
Dan LeGage was a two-time all-conference and All-Maine Team selection at the University of Maine-Farmington, where he scored 1,368 points and held the school record for made 3-pointers when he graduated in 1995. He was inducted into UMF’s Hall of Fame in 2012.
LeGage and the Bulldogs will start their 2026-27 title defense at Deering on Dec. 4. The first official practice is Monday. Portland was a senior-led squad last year but does return top talents Maddox Meas and Ephraim Luseko.
“My expectation is that we’re going to play with a purpose and a spirit and a togetherness, and to be a team that everyone in the city can be proud of,” LeGage said.

title: Gorham farm required to reimburse customers after selling invasive trees
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
GORHAM — The state is requiring a farm to refund customers who destroy invasive trees they purchased there from from May through September.
Gary Fish, a Maine state horticulturist at the Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry, said the agency discovered King’s Farm Market in Gorham had sold crimson k ing Norway and flame Amur maple trees from May to September after receiving an inquiry about a project involving 11 of the trees in Rangeley. Both species were placed on Maine’s “do not sell” list in 2018 because they spread quickly and disrupt natural ecosystems.
The department found that King’s Farm Market had purchased 27 Norway and 24 Amur maples in April from an auction in Pennsylvania, where the trees are legal to sell. Fish said that everyone who purchased the trees should ensure they are dead by cutting the base and disposing of the root balls in the trash.
A social media post from the department instructs customers to call the market at 207-839-5844 to confirm reimbursement requirements, which include taking a picture of the disposed tree.
Barry King, owner of King’s Farm, declined to comment when a reporter visited the farm Tuesday and said he would sue if the paper reported on the issue.
Crimson king Norway maple leaves have three to five lobes and exude milky sap from their base when removed from their twig, according to the Ohio Woodland Stewards Program. Flame Amur maple leaves have three lobes, and the middle lobe is typically much longer than the side lobes, according to the Western New York Land Conservancy.
Fish said there have been few instances of these maple species being sold in Maine since they were banned. It is more common for small hobbyists to be found selling wreaths with bittersweet or multiflora rose berries, he said, which are also banned.
More information about Maine regulations on holiday-related plant sales and the “do not sell” list can be found on the department’s website.

title: Senate Republicans vote to keep Thune as leader after steep election losses
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Senate Republicans reelected South Dakota Sen. John Thune as their leader Tuesday after a tense day of private discussions about steep losses in the midterm elections that cost them their majority.
Thune was always expected to prevail, as he is popular with his GOP colleagues and was running unopposed in the secret-ballot election. But Senate Republicans vented their frustrations in three separate meetings Tuesday after an election wipeout that cost them at least seven Senate seats.
Some Republicans had tried to delay the leadership decision, but the conference voted 31-15 to proceed with a vote after Thune made his case to his colleagues, laying out his vision for the minority and also promising that they will try and do as much as they can in their final two months in the majority.
“We’re going to make the most of the time we’ve got,” Thune said after he was elected by acclamation, without a roll call vote.
As for next year, Thune said that told his colleagues that they will “come out swinging, and realize we’ve got a lot of work to be done to get back in the majority.”
The day’s meetings were a combination of venting and thoughtful conversation, with some senators who won and lost elections this year sharing their thoughts and others questioning if they should be quickly endorsing their leadership slate after a significant defeat.
West Virginia Sen. Jim Justice said that there was a “legitimate argument that, good gracious, if we lost as badly as we lost, why would we continue on with the same leadership?”
At the same time, the current GOP leadership “didn’t cause this problem to happen,” Justice said. “They do a good job.”
Republicans’ angst and indecision come as frustrated Republicans are just beginning to reckon with what the election results mean for their future — and for their relationship with President Donald Trump, as voters resoundingly rejected their two years of single-party rule in Congress and the White House. Two additional Senate races remain uncalled in Alaska and Mississippi that could further deplete their numbers.
“If you don’t think after losing seven Senate seats minimum that we need to change course, I don’t know what planet you’re on,” said Missouri Sen. Josh Hawley, who voted to delay the elections. He said he wasn’t aware of anyone else running for leader, but “maybe there would be” if they waited.
No alternative to Thune emerged
Thune, who replaced Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky as leader in early 2025, pushed back on the idea of a delay, questioning what it would achieve. Several senators backed him up, including his South Dakota colleague Mike Rounds, who countered the calls for postponement with the successful motion to vote immediately.
Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia, who was reelected to her leadership position as GOP policy chair, said that Thune wasn’t the reason they suffered losses. “I don’t think it was the fault of our leadership, quite frankly,” she said.
Sen. Roger Wicker, R-Miss., said he had confidence in the newly re-elected slate. The discussion was mainly “about policy,” he said.
Republicans in the meeting were also pushing Thune to stay in session around the clock in the coming weeks to push through war spending and other party priorities before they lose power in January. Republicans are trying to wrap up the year’s work — funding the government, confirming Trump’s nominees and seeing if there are some issues where they can work with Democrats, including an energy permitting bill that moved forward on a bipartisan vote Monday evening.
Before the vote on Thune, the conference adopted a resolution to maximize the time they have left and to “confirm every judicial nominee and every executive nominee that the conference approves of.”
“We need a plan to get the Republican agenda done,” said Florida Sen. Rick Scott.
Wisconsin Sen. Ron Johnson circulated a letter before the meeting asking for the delay. He said the conference needs to do some “real soul-searching” but also conceded that there was no one else on the ballot.
“That’s part of our problem, who would want the job?” he said on Monday, turning to a reporter and joking, “Do you want it?”
Oklahoma Sen. Jim Lankford said that there was “widespread support” among Republican senators for Thune, who has made it a point to hear out different viewpoints before he makes major decisions and has maintained close relationships with the rank and file — a different approach from his predecessor, McConnell.
Lankford said he supported having the elections on Tuesday because many of the new GOP senators were already in town for freshman orientation.
“It’s a pretty complicated role to be able to manage,” Lankford said of Thune’s leadership post. “No one wants that job.”
Thune has navigated Trump in his first two years as leader
Thune has spent much of the last two years navigating Trump, who has often been at odds with the Senate.
While backing Trump on most policies, Thune has refused to change Senate rules and scrap the filibuster to pass voting legislation that would require proof of citizenship for all voters — a position that frustrated Trump and enraged some in the president’s political base.
Still, Trump hosted Thune and his family at the White House in October. He said Monday that the GOP leader is “a very fine man.” The election is “up to the Senate,” Trump said.
Thune has emphasized his collaborative approach to his colleagues and pointed out what they did get done in the last two years — including Trump’s sweeping tax and spending cuts legislation and an attempt at reining in the chaotic annual spending process.
“We’re not going to be running this place next year, the Democrats are,” Thune said afterward. “But you can be assured that we will be very, very active in asserting conservative priorities.”

title: Republicans leave closed-door meeting without a decision on whether to reelect John Thune as leader
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Senate Republicans were meeting for a second time Tuesday as they decide whether to delay elections for Republican leadership. South Dakota Sen. John Thune is seeking to keep his post as Republican leader just a week after steep losses in the midterm elections that cost them their majority.
Thune is expected to eventually win, given that he remains popular with his GOP colleagues and is so far running unopposed in the secret ballot election. But senators left the closed-door meeting after two hours of discussions Tuesday morning with no resolution on a way forward after an election wipeout that cost them at least seven Senate seats.
As they reconvened Tuesday afternoon, Republican senators were divided on whether a delay of anywhere from a week to a month would be productive. Votes were expected on whether to postpone.
“We want to be thoughtful and do the right thing,” said West Virginia Sen. Jim Justice as the meeting broke up. He said no obvious alternative had emerged, but “there is a legitimate argument that, good gracious, if we lost as badly as we lost, why would we continue on with the same leadership?”
At the same time, the current GOP leadership “didn’t cause this problem to happen,” Justice said. “They do a good job.”
The angst comes as frustrated Republicans are just beginning to reckon with what the election results mean for their future. Two additional Senate races remain uncalled in Alaska and Mississippi that could further deplete their numbers.
Several senators had already called on the Republican leadership to delay the elections, which include contests for other party leaders as well and are held in the small Old Senate Chamber.
Missouri Sen. Josh Hawley said he isn’t aware of anyone else running for leader, but “maybe there would be” if they waited.
“I just think that we’ve got a lot of things that we’ve got to think through, and I think that to just rush into this and just ratify all of the same leadership, what message does that send?” Hawley told reporters after walking out.
“If you don’t think after losing seven Senate seats minimum that we need to change course, I don’t know what planet you’re on,” he said.
Thune, who replaced Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky as leader in early 2025, said before the meeting that they would have a “very fulsome, robust conversation about where we go from here and then we’ll see what the consensus of the conference is.”
No alternative to Thune has emerged
Thune has not yet made his case for leadership, senators emerging from the meeting said, and has instead been listening to his colleagues’ concerns. Hawley said the discussion was a “frank” and “honest” open- microphone meeting and some senators discussed their own races this year — some who won, and some who lost.
Republicans in the meeting were also pushing Thune to stay in session around the clock in the coming weeks to push through war spending and other party priorities before they lose power.
“We need a plan to get the Republican agenda done,” said Florida Sen. Rick Scott.
Before the meeting, Wisconsin Sen. Ron Johnson had circulated a letter asking for the delay. He said the conference needs to do some “real soul-searching” but conceded that there’s no one else on the ballot.
“That’s part of our problem, who would want the job?” he said, turning to a reporter and joking, “Do you want it?”
Oklahoma Sen. Jim Lankford said that there is “widespread support” among Republican senators for Thune, who has made it a point to hear out different viewpoints before he makes major decisions and has maintained close relationships with the rank and file — a different approach from his predecessor, McConnell.
Lankford said he supported having the elections on Tuesday because many of the new GOP senators are already in town for freshman orientation.
“It’s a pretty complicated role to be able to manage,” Lankford said of Thune’s leadership post. “No one wants that job.”
Walking into the meeting, South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds said most senators are ready to move forward. It is time to have “leadership in place,” he said.
Thune has navigated Trump in his first two years as leader
Thune has spent much of the last two years navigating President Donald Trump, who has often been at odds with the Senate.
While backing up Trump on most policy, Thune has refused to change Senate rules and scrap the filibuster to pass voting legislation that would require proof of citizenship for all voters — a position that frustrated Trump and enraged some in the president’s political base.
But Trump hosted Thune and his family at the White House in October. He said Monday that the GOP leader is “a very fine man.” The election is “up to the Senate,” Trump said.
The soul-searching comes as lawmakers are trying to wrap up the year’s work — funding the government and seeing if there are some issues where they can work together, including an energy permitting bill that moved forward on a bipartisan vote Monday evening.
When he gets the chance to speak at the meeting, Thune is expected to emphasize his collaborative approach to his colleagues and point out what they did get done in the last year — including the tax and spending cuts legislation and an attempt at reining in the chaotic annual spending process.
In a Senate floor speech Monday, his first extended remarks since the election, Thune said the midterm election was a “tough night” and previewed his pitch to his colleagues who may be looking for answers on how they will navigate the minority.
Republicans will be willing to work with Democrats, Thune said, but “the American people are not looking for socialist government and leftist fantasies.”
Despite gains, Democrats are having similar conversations
Across the aisle, Democrats who could hold as many as 56 seats next year are having private discussions about whether New York Sen. Chuck Schumer is still the right person to lead them.
Schumer has found critics on the left and the right of his caucus as candidates from both sides declined to say in the campaign whether they would support him as leader. Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen and Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin have both considered challenging Schumer, but neither has announced a run.
Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, Schumer’s New York colleague and the head of the Democratic Senate campaign arm, predicted that he will win enough support. Schumer not only won the Senate back but he “cares deeply, and he understands politics well,” she said.

title: Billings Road In Hermon Closed After Crash Near Bryant Rd, Drivers Asked To Find Another Route
text:
Billings Road In Hermon Shut Down Monday Evening After A Motor vehicle Crash; Drivers Advised To Seek Alternate Route
There's a heavy presence of first responders in Hermon this evening, with members of the Penobscot County Sheriff's Office and EMTs both in one section of town.
Read More: Mexico Man Charged With Aggravated Assault In Rumford Slashing
We're getting reports of a motor vehicle accident that took place around 9 PM, in the area of Billings Road tonight. Not much is known at the moment about the vehicles or individuals involved yet.
What we do know is that part of Billings Road near Bryant Rd. has been shut down and is expected to remain closed for several hours, as first responders and authorities work to tend to those involved, clear away debris, and reconstruct the scene.
You will not be able to turn onto Billings Road from Union Street if you're heading in that direction. You will need to go to Levant and loop around the back way.
Drivers are advised to find an alternate route and to avoid the area, if possible.
We've also been told by authorities that while the cause of this particular accident is unknown at the time, speed has been a factor in many crashes across Penobscot County recently. They ask motorists to slow down and pay attention to their surroundings while behind the wheel.

title: Woman flown to hospital after Van Buren apartment fire
text:
VAN BUREN, Maine (WABI) - A person was flown to a hospital in Portland with serious injuries after a fire at an apartment in Van Buren.
The fire occurred at a 16-unit apartment building on Roosevelt Ave. Sunday afternoon.
Firefighters responded to an apartment and found Cynthia Loux, 73, inside her apartment.
Fire officials said she sustained burns to 40% of her body. She is also being treated for smoke inhalation.
Investigators with the Fire Marshal’s Office said the fire started on the kitchen stove and was ruled accidental.
Authorities also said the sprinklers prevented the fire from spreading to neighboring apartments.

title: Snow is flying and ski season is about to begin in Maine
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Snow is flying and ski season is about to begin in Maine
Some snow has already fallen in the higher elevations in Maine and ski areas have been making snow. Some areas could also pick up some snow this weekend. That means it is time for ski season to begin in Maine.
Opening day at Sugarloaf Mountain in Carrabassett Valley is Friday, Nov. 20. On November 9, the mountain shared a picture saying snow had reached all the way to the base.
Sunday River has been targeting an opening date of Nov. 15 with the Locke Mountain Triple lift spinning first and the Jordan 8 lift right on its heels. As of Tuesday morning, the resort in Newry had not made an official announcement. On Monday afternoon, the resort said an opening day announcement is "right on the doorstep."
On Monday, the resort posted video of snow on Sunday and said all eight peaks got a little taste of winter and the trails received their first natural snowfall of the season.
On Tuesday morning, Saddleback in Rangeley said they were less than a month away from first tracks. Saddleback has been targeting Dec. 4 for an opening day.
Pleasant Mountain in Bridgton started testing its snow guns on Oct. 26, but as of Tuesday had not announced an opening date.
On Sunday, Titcomb Mountain in Farmington said mountain bike trails would be closing soon and the mountain would be getting ready to open for winter operations, but no specific date was provided.
On Monday, officials at the Camden Snow Bowl in Camden said they fired up their snowmaking system and started testing the snow guns. They were waiting for colder weather before they could consider a possible opening date.
As of Tuesday morning, places like Black Mountain of Maine in Rumford, Lost Valley in Auburn, Hermon Mountain in Hermon, and Spruce Mountain in Jay had not made any announcements about the upcoming season.

title: Missing 11-month-old found, survived 24 hours after father buried him alive in a dog crate, sheriff says
text:
LEXINGTON COUNTY, S.C. (WIS/Gray News) — Authorities in South Carolina said an 11-month-old baby miraculously survived after they believe his father buried him alive in a dog crate.
Koah Sharpe was found alive Tuesday afternoon just over 24 hours after he was last seen with his father, 25-year-old Michael Comer.
Lexington County Sheriff Jay Koon said Koah was found buried in a dog crate wrapped in a towel.
“By the grace of God, [it] probably provided enough air for him to survive an estimated 24 hours under that dirt,” Koon said.
The sheriff said Comer’s mother was caring for the child when Comer arrived at the home on Monday. She then left Koah in Comer’s care while another caregiver was on the way.
“By the time the caregiver got there, Michael was gone and Koah was gone with him,” Koon said.
Other members of Koah’s family filed a missing persons report Monday afternoon. Koon said authorities went to the nearby home of Comer’s father, where they found both doors open and Koah’s belongings, but no sign of either Comer or Koah.
Authorities also believe Comer was in multiple locations across Lexington County on Monday, but they said that he does not have access to a vehicle. That is why an Amber Alert was never issued.
“To be able to issue an Amber Alert, you have to have a known description of a car and a license plate to put that out,” Koon explained Tuesday.
The sheriff said it’s believed Comer asked for rides to get from place to place. Video footage also pointed to Comer being in the Batesburg-Leesville area, but with no baby.
Authorities arrested Comer Monday night on a burglary charge after finding him in a shed in Batesburg. Koah, however, was not with him.
The search for the 11-month-old extended into Tuesday, with local, state and federal agencies joining the search.
Koon said it wasn’t until authorities looked near Comer’s father’s house that they found pine straw and “freshly disturbed dirt.” Once they started digging, they heard Koah crying.
“So, as you imagine, the race was on,” Koon said. “Everybody’s getting down there trying to get him out.”
Koon said it’s believed that Koah was buried for around 24 hours.
“It [the dog crate] was buried, and it was wrapped with a towel. So probably created an air pocket, if you can imagine,” Koon said.
The sheriff said Koah is being treated at a hospital. Comer, meanwhile, remains in custody as of Tuesday afternoon.
Comer’s arrest comes just over a month after he was placed on probation following a guilty plea for aggravated breach of peace, according to public court and state records.
Court records also show Comer had previous arrests earlier this year for domestic violence, as well as a weapons-related charge.

title: Wildfire in White Mountain National Forest more than 50% contained
text:
The Wild River Fire just over the Maine border in New Hampshire now encompasses 821 acres and is 53% contained, the U.S. Forest Service said on Tuesday.
The Forest Service first responded to the fire in an area of the White Mountain National Forest about 7 miles southeast of Gorham, New Hampshire, on Nov. 1. It’s on the northwest side of the Wild River, just west of Mount Hastings in Maine’s Oxford County.
Early last week, the Forest Service estimated that the fire had grown from a few hundred acres to nearly 1,000 acres. At that point, it was just 11% contained.
As firefighters shifted to the offensive late last week, they narrowed their estimate of the Wild River Fire to about 856 acres. Over the weekend, they pegged it at about 821 acres, where it still stood Tuesday.
While the fire’s footprint has been slow to shrink, firefighters’ containment of the blaze has grown exponentially over the weekend and into early this week.
The Forest Service estimated the fire was roughly 20% contained by Friday, 29% by Sunday and, on Tuesday, they said the Wild River Fire was approximately 53% contained.
The portion of the perimeter contained in the first full week of fighting was largely limited to the banks of the Wild River and a stretch of the blaze’s northeast border, which is roughly a half-mile from the state line.
However, Tuesday’s update showed progress in other areas, including along a brook on the west side of the fire, and segments of the fire’s jagged northern edge.
The size of the response — which peaked at 140 assigned personnel on Friday — dwindled over the weekend and was down to 88 assigned personnel as of Tuesday.
“As fire behavior has moderated, and the potential for the fire to spread continues to be reduced, incident managers have begun adjusting resources to better align with operational needs,” the Forest Service said in its update Monday.
As they did last week, officials detailed the large-scale response at a public meeting in Shelburne, New Hampshire, on Tuesday night.
Ben Wagner, an operations section chief assigned to the wildfire, said they have divided the fire into three sectors: One encompasses nearly the entire south side of the blaze, along the Wild River, while the northeast and northwest edges make up the other two. A division of firefighters is assigned to each of the three sectors.
Wagner said much of the area that has yet to be contained is in mountainous terrain, which can be especially hazardous for firefighters to navigate.
“If you can imagine hiking 2,500 vertical feet carrying chainsaws and leaf blowers and everything you need, and then breaking your leg on that mountain,” Wagner said, “the arduous work would then be to take that person and hike them down the mountain and cross over a river — and trying to do that within daylight.”
No firefighters have been injured during the response, due in large part to only attacking the fire where and when it’s safe to do so, officials said Tuesday.
But some conditions have gone the Forest Service’s way. For instance, Wagner explained that the spread of the fire, which has been thriving off felled hardwood, has naturally slowed or halted in areas with conifer fuels. Water sources, like brooks and creeks, have also served as natural means of controlling the spread.
And the icing on the cake has come in the form of sorely needed precipitation.
“The rain, the snow, the increase in moisture that’s permeating down into the ground, has really helped us a great deal in holding this fire where it’s at,” Wagner said.
He later added: “For as difficult a ground it is to work, we do have some things that are working in our favor.”

title: Bangor installs traffic cameras designed to keep cars moving
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - If you’ve ever sat alone at a red light wondering whether the signal knows you’re there, Bangor officials say new traffic detection cameras are designed to help.
The city has installed Miovision cameras at intersections across Bangor to detect waiting vehicles and help signals serve those traffic movements. City Electrician Chris Hawkins said the new equipment replaces aging infrastructure that required constant repairs.
“It’s solved a lot of the issues that we’ve had with the older systems,” Hawkins said.
A clearer view of traffic
Hawkins said the new cameras are better positioned to avoid direct sunlight than outward-facing cameras. That can give them a clearer view of vehicles approaching or waiting at an intersection.
The system also includes an artificial intelligence engine called Mateo, which collects traffic data to help local engineers track traffic patterns.
Not Flock cameras, city says
After the city posted about the installation on Facebook, officials addressed questions about the cameras.
“It is absolutely not a Flock camera,” Hawkins said. “It’s purposefully using a 400P resolution so facial ID is not possible, license plate readers are not possible, it’s not intended for it in any way.”
Hawkins said 42 cameras are active across most of Bangor. The installation took more than three years, and about a dozen more cameras are expected to be installed within the next year.

title: Woman killed, three people hurt in crash in Hermon
text:
Woman killed, three people hurt in crash in Hermon, Maine
A woman is dead and three other people are seriously hurt after a crash in Hermon on Monday night.
The Penobscot County Sheriff's Office says the crash happened at about 8:45 p.m. on Billings Road, near Bryant Road, and involved a single vehicle. There are no corners in the road in that area.
When deputies arrived, they found a passenger, a 37-year-old woman, dead. Three other people in the vehicle, including the driver, were taken to Northern Light Eastern Maine Medical Center in Bangor with what police said were serious injuries.
As of Tuesday morning, police were not releasing the names of any of the people involved. The cause of the crash was still under investigation.

title: Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio elected to lead House Republicans in minority
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio won the race Tuesday to serve as House Republican leader as the party prepares for its new role in the minority and a flurry of Democratic investigations aimed at its standard-bearer in the White House.
Jordan, who serves as chairman of the House Judiciary Committee, defeated Rep. Steve Scalise of Louisiana in a secret-ballot election of Republicans who will serve in the next Congress. The vote was 106-73.
Jordan, 62, is a co-founder of the ultraconservative House Freedom Caucus and served as its first chairman. His candidacy appealed to those looking for new leadership in the wake of last week’s election debacle and to those who like his hard-hitting political style.
“The way that Jim fights says a lot about where this conference is,” said Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla., who nominated Jordan to serve as minority leader.
Jordan will inherit a historically small House Republican conference that is only beginning to grapple with its loss of power as President Donald Trump serves out his final two years in office. Leading the party back to the House majority in 2028 is sure to be a stiff climb, given the scope of Democratic victories in the midterms.
In brief remarks to reporters after his win, Jordan said Republicans would focus on fighting for American families over the next two years.
“When Democrats offer more government, we’ll offer more freedom,” Jordan said. “We will bring that fight in committee, on the floor and on the stump every single day.”
Scalise and Jordan were a familiar match-up
Jordan and Scalise came to Congress together two decades ago. They both ran to serve as House speaker after Kevin McCarthy was ousted from the job in 2023. Neither was able to rally the support necessary to secure the position, which eventually went to Mike Johnson, who is stepping aside from the leadership in the new Congress.
Scalise, 61, has held key GOP leadership positions going back to 2014, serving as party whip and then as majority leader. In 2017, he was critically wounded when a gunman opened fire at a baseball practice where several Republican lawmakers and staffers were preparing for an annual charity baseball game against Democrats. In 2023, he was stricken with multiple myeloma, a blood cancer that was successfully treated.
“Overcoming adversity is nothing new to me,” Scalise said in his pitch to colleagues.
He also emphasized his fundraising prowess, noting he raised $67.9 million for this year’s midterms, with about a third of that going directly to individual House campaigns and the National Republican Congressional Committee.
But the majority of Republicans opted for Jordan, who emphasized his experience battling with Democrats in committee rooms. Jordan served as the top Republican on the House oversight panel before he became the lead Republican on the committee six years ago. That experience proved popular with his colleagues.
“Instead of focusing on the people, it seems that the entire objective for Democrats is going to be targeted investigations,” said Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, R-Fla. “And Jim Jordan knows about weaponization.”
Fewer moderates left among House Republicans
Scalise’s backers liked his experience getting legislation over the finish line. And Scalise edged Jordan in a similar secret-ballot vote three years ago in the race to succeed McCarthy, though neither would end up getting the job.
But as a result of the election last week, the House Republican conference is smaller, with a disproportionate number of moderates and swing-district lawmakers retiring or voted out. Many of those returning were hungry for a new leader.
“We’re a significantly more conservative conference than we were,” Mast said.
Democrats argued that Jordan’s selection indicated that Republicans took the wrong lesson from the election loss.
“I would think that they would want somebody that was going to moderate towards what the voters want. They lost so many Republican voters,” said Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash. “Obviously that’s not the case.”
“The House Republican caucus clearly chose the more extreme candidate,” said Rep. Ted Lieu of California and vice chair of the House Democratic caucus. “Hopefully, he’ll work with Democrats. We’ll see what happens.”
Rep. Tom Emmer of Minnesota was elected as the Republican whip, the No. 2 position in the leadership hierarchy. He beat out Rep. August Pfluger of Texas for the job. Rep. Lisa McClain of Michigan won reelection to serve as conference chair, the No. 3 position.
Democrats will hold their leadership elections next week
Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York is expected to become the next House speaker, the first African American to hold the job, and Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts is expected to become the next majority leader. She would be the first woman to hold that position.
___
Associated Press writer Joey Cappelletti contributed to this report.
