title: Voter participation is nowhere near enough
text:
American registered voters reportedly managed to come up to about 50% of eligible voters casting a ballot during this midterm election cycle. Fifty percent didn’t even bother to vote.
That means there were no winners in this election except for the politicians. The losers are the American people, the free and the brave, of whom a significant number are just too busy or can’t be bothered to vote to begin with.
Democrat, Republican, independent or unenrolled, it doesn’t matter. The politicians know it and they play us hard. It’s the same old song and dance. And, sadly, it’ll take another 9/11 or worse to bring us together and even then, it seems, only fleetingly.
Paul Bonenfant
South China

title: Are these deer hunting gadgets really worth the money?
text:
Outdoors
The BDN outdoors section brings readers into the woods, waters and wild places of Maine. It features stories on hunting, fishing, wildlife, conservation and recreation, told by people who live these experiences. This section emphasizes hands-on knowledge, field reports, issues, trends and the traditions that define life outside in Maine. Read more Outdoors stories here. 
Just before rifle deer season opened, a friend of mine was in dire need of a new pair of hunting boots. So, on a Sunday before a Patriots game, we took a ride to our favorite hunting, fishing and everything-outdoors store.
I didn’t really need anything, but while my friend was busy trying on different styles and makes of boots, I went for a stroll to bide the time. Like many deer hunters, I enjoy my gadgets and toys. Who knows? I just might spot something new, innovative or different that I simply have to try. To my surprise, I did.
The first thing I came across was a hunter’s umbrella. I have owned and used one of these gadgets before and loved it, but it got ripped or otherwise destroyed. I can’t remember which. Since a replacement had yet to appear for my birthday or under the Christmas tree despite several hints, and since it’s a sure bet the weather will turn foul at some point before rifle or muzzleloader season comes to an end, I bit the bullet and bought one.
Hunting in a light rain, drizzle or falling snow is one of my favorite things. Truth be known, I have killed as many deer in wet, foul weather as I have under blue skies. But I am not crazy about getting wet. In my experience, rain gear and water-resistant outer garments keep you dry for only so long. An umbrella, however, sheds precipitation away, just as it is designed to do.
The one I bought comes with a post that screws into a tree. An adjustable strap goes around the tree to hold the umbrella upright, so it makes no difference whether I’m hunting from a stand or sitting on the ground. The instructions say it can even be used as a ground blind shield, although I’ve never used one that way.
It weighs just 1.5 pounds, comes in a nylon carrying bag and is light, compact and easy to carry in a pack. When open, it provides 54 inches of coverage, plenty of protection from the elements.
Rattling and using grunts and other calls have never been a big part of my deer hunting strategy. Maybe they should have been. Perhaps more big bucks would be hanging on our walls. But I do own some artificial rattling antlers, a couple of grunt calls and deer cans. Even though I seldom take them into the woods, I do like giving them a try from time to time when the timing is right.
That’s why I stopped at a display loaded with various rattling systems and calls during my trek around the store. One in particular caught my attention.
It’s called the Pack Rack and is made by Knight & Hale, a name I was familiar with. Apparently, it has been on the market for a while, but I had never heard of it. That goes to show how little I know about these gadgets. What caught my attention was its unusual appearance.
It’s made of some kind of high-density plastic and consists of two parts. Each part has a hollow hand grip. The two pieces fit together to form a light, compact unit that can easily be carried in a backpack or fanny pack, which I liked.
When separated, banging the two parts together with a back-and-forth twisting action is supposed to imitate two bucks rattling. The rattling tone or intensity can supposedly be varied by cupping your hands over the hollow grips or keeping your palms flat against them.
I was curious, so I tried it in the store. Doing so drew some attention from people walking by, so I figured it might work. For $20 plus tax, I figured, what the heck? The worst that can happen is I’ll feel like an idiot, which happens more times than I like to admit in the deer woods.
I was on my way back to meet my friend when I stopped at a table marked with a sign advertising discounts of 50% to 60% on discontinued items. Signs like that always draw my attention, so I figured it wouldn’t hurt to make my friend wait a few more minutes.
Sifting through the various items on display, I found a grunt call. It’s made by Flextone, a name known for its game calls. Called the Buck Crusher, it’s constructed of some kind of plastic molded to resemble part of an antler, which I thought was neat and unusual.
Unlike many grunt tubes that hang around the neck, this call comes with a wrist strap that keeps it conveniently handy but out of the way. It has three different calls: doe, wheeze and buck.
It was still wrapped in its original plastic clamshell, so I couldn’t give it a try, as much as I wanted to. But I liked the way it looked and the wrist strap attachment, so I put it in my cart.
I have no idea why this particular call was being discontinued and marked down. Maybe it didn’t sell well, or perhaps the manufacturer no longer offers it. But at $12, down from around $30, I figured I couldn’t go wrong.
We’re still in the middle of deer season, and muzzleloader season is still to come. I don’t know if the deer gadgets I recently purchased will be worth the money, but we’ll see. Do you have yours?

title: Florida cowboys rescue farm animals left stranded by flooding: 'It's gut-wrenching'
text:
Florida cowboys rescue farm animals left stranded by flooding: 'It's gut-wrenching'
Flooding in DeSoto County, Florida, has left dozens of animals stranded in high water since last week, prompting a group of cowboys to step in and rescue them.
"Seeing all those cattle standing up there on that little bit of a hill with their heads poked out of the water, nearly drowning, it's gut-wrenching," Brady Adams of the Arcadia Cowboys said.
The Arcadia Cowboys have been cutting through fences and riding through flooded areas, searching for hours to save animals from the flood.
"It's sad that some don't make it, but with as much water here, I can understand, you know, it doesn't come quick," Pete Brewer, one of the Arcadia Cowboys, said.
So far, the group has rescued 23 cows, goats and donkeys.
"We'll take it and put it on dry ground until the owner comes and picks it up. So, we'll just take it to our house and put it on dry ground so the owners can come get it," Brewer said.
Neighbors have also joined the effort, venturing into the floodwaters to help save animals.
"We were out and about, actually, in the nighttime on a boat, actually going through the pastures and try to actually get the animals out," resident Jason Reid said.
Despite their efforts, the cowboys said they have found at least eight cows that drowned.
"Seeing those animals dead like that, you know, especially horses and cows, just no good," Adams said.
The search continues, with the Arcadia Cowboys still looking for a donkey and a goat. Floodwaters are beginning to recede, and the area, which was underwater last week with water reaching nearly waist-deep, now looks much different.

title: Daycare provider sentenced to up to 50 years in prison in toddler’s death
text:
EMMETSBURG, Iowa (KTIV/Gray News) - An Iowa judge has sentenced a daycare provider to prison after nearly a four-year infant death investigation.
On Monday, 31-year-old Hannah Priest was sentenced to up to 50 years in prison for one count of child endangerment resulting in the death of Sebastian Jespersen, a 23-month-old who died in 2023.
Priest was the child’s daycare provider at the time.
In September 2023, Priest initially pleaded not guilty, then changed her plea to guilty in October 2026.
On Jan. 19, 2023, Priest reportedly found the infant unresponsive on his sleeping cot.
EMTs responded to the daycare and the child was taken to a hospital in Des Moines.
A few days later, on January 24, 2023, the child died at the hospital.
An autopsy by the Iowa State Medical Examiner determined that the infant had died from brain trauma consistent with inflicted injuries.
After an investigation carried out by the Iowa Department of Criminal Investigation, Priest was arrested on Sept. 1, 2023.
During a May 2023 interview, court documents showed Priest admitted to being frustrated with the infant around naptime because he hadn’t gone to the bathroom yet that day.
She also admitted to putting the infant in the cot by the shoulders and may not have known her own strength while doing so.
During the interview, Priest reportedly admitted to setting him into the cot out of frustration.
Court documents stated that over the course of three interviews between Priest and investigators, she maintained that the infant was acting normally before she put him down for a nap that afternoon.
She had also denied that the infant suffered any accidental head injuries that day. Also denying that any other kids at the daycare struck the 23-month-old child.
Authorities said Priest would be eligible for parole.

title: AI scanners at rental car lots are ‘definitely not perfect,’ watchdog says
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Several rental car companies are now using AI scanning systems to check vehicles for damage, and a consumer watchdog says renters should document the car themselves to avoid a surprise bill.
The scanners look like a car wash at pick-up or drop-off. Cameras take photos and videos from different angles, looking for damage.
Teresa Murray, consumer watchdog director with the U.S. Public Interest Research Group, said the technology comes with both benefits and drawbacks.
Murray said artificial intelligence can make mistakes that matter in a rental car setting.
“We know that artificial intelligence can hallucinate. We know AI can fabricate data, misinterpret data, and in the case of damage in a rental car, it could mean that a splotch of dirt gets mistaken for a dent. You know, some kind of shadow could look like some pretty significant damage. So, it’s definitely not perfect,” Murray said.
Murray’s advice is the same whether a company uses AI or an employee looks the vehicle over: take a few minutes to inspect the car closely before leaving the lot.
“People should take pictures of every single thing and they should take walk around video. If you need to crouch down on the ground to get up under it, you know, the wheels and all that kind of stuff. The hubcaps, the interior, the trunk, you know, the glass, I mean everything. Do it. And I mean, if you’re going to rent a car, you need to allow 5 to 10 minutes to do this, depending on whether it’s with a live worker or without,” Murray said.
If a company uses an AI scanner, Murray recommends doing the same inspection before and after the trip. Having your own photos gives you a way to challenge a charge if a damage bill arrives later.

title: NTSB recovers cockpit voice recorder from Learjet 60 crash in Florida
text:
NTSB recovers cockpit voice recorder from Learjet 60 crash in Florida
Investigators announced Monday they had recovered the cockpit voice recorder from the Learjet crash in Greenacres, Florida, on Nov. 1, which killed all nine people on board.
The National Transportation Safety Board released photos late Monday afternoon showing the orange case containing the so-called black box. The NTSB hopes the device will shed light on what caused the crash.
"It's more information, and more information is always good in an investigation," said John Gagliano, a former Navy pilot and licensed aviation lawyer.
Gagliano explained that the black box contains a cockpit voice recorder, which captures all conversations in the cockpit.
"We get some insight into what was going on in the cockpit. We already have some because the co-pilot was transmitting out to air traffic control," Gagliano said.
Recordings of those transmissions were released shortly after the crash.
In those transmissions, the co-pilot, Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras, can be heard giving updates as the plane began to malfunction.
"We are descending from 22,000 feet," Filgueiras said in one transmission. "And we are banking."
Gagliano said there were conversations had in the cockpit that were not transmitted.
It's those conversations that might shed light on what caused the crash.
"They might have been talking to each other about things that they were seeing, things that they were doing, a checklist they were considering."
The NTSB has taken the cockpit voice recorder to its Vehicle Recorders Laboratory in Washington, D.C., where they will analyze the data.
Gagliano noted that whether the recordings are intact remains uncertain, as the box could have been damaged in the crash. However, he emphasized that these devices are designed to survive impacts like this.
At this point, there is no timeline for when the NTSB may determine the cause of the crash.
Officials confirmed that excavation work on Military Trail, the road where the impact site is located, has been completed. However, Military Trail remains closed between 10th Avenue North and Cresthaven Boulevard.
Meanwhile, Palm Beach County officials announced today that residents of the mobile home park near the crash site in Greenacres can now return home. They also said that people living in the Greenacres Community Center who cannot return home due to damage have been provided temporary housing.

title: Better late than never for a true celebration of America
text:
How dispiriting it was that July 4 came and went this year with so few positive and inspiring celebrations of America’s 250th birthday. With a crook and a narcissist in the White House, we got wrestling matches, car races and the destruction and defacement of the people’s property all across our nation’s capital. With so many of our nation’s hard-fought values being trampled by the White House and Republican Congress, state and local communities struggled to rouse pride in our country.
Little did we know that the most meaningful celebration of our nation’s founding would take place late in this anniversary year — on Nov. 3.
We reaffirmed, resoundingly, the core of our democracy, with citizens turning out in record numbers to exercise their right to vote. Not only did our democracy hold, the power of the people prevailed over mountains of money. And we elected dozens of excellent candidates who care about our country and our communities, and whose diversity on so many fronts reflects the strength of America.
Happy 250th, America. Thank you for reminding us what’s truly worth celebrating about our democracy.
Kathy Mills
Yarmouth

title: Rep. Jim Jordan picked to be GOP's new House leader
text:
Rep. Jim Jordan to succeed Rep. Mike Johnson as House GOP's minority leader
Rep. Jim Jordan has been selected by the Republican caucus to replace Rep. Mike Johnson as the party's House leader.
Jordan will be the House minority leader at the start of the next congressional session in January. According to CNN, Jordan defeated Rep. Steve Scalise in the caucus vote, 106-73.
Shortly after the party's overwhelming midterm defeat, Johnson announced that he would not seek reelection to the party's leadership.
Jordan, 62, is a co-founder of the ultraconservative House Freedom Caucus and served as its first chairman. His candidacy appealed to those looking for new leadership in the wake of last week’s election debacle and to those who like his hard-hitting political style.
Jordan, as minority leader, will inherit a historically small House Republican conference that is only beginning to grapple with its loss of power as President Donald Trump serves out his final two years in office. Leading the party back to the House majority in 2028 is sure to be a stiff climb, given the scope of Democratic victories in the midterms.
Jordan warned of the coming Democratic efforts on oversight, with numerous investigations of the Trump administration expected.
“Our job cannot be merely to spotlight how radical this new Democratic Party is — offense, not defense, wins elections,” Jordan said, a nod to his pugnacious reputation in committee hearings.
President Donald Trump said he was staying out of the race.
Rep. Tom Emmer of Minnesota was elected as the Republican whip, the No. 2 position in the leadership hierarchy. He beat out Rep. August Pfluger of Texas for the job.
Three candidates were seeking to serve as conference chair: Reps. Lisa McClain of Michigan, Erin Houchin of Indiana and Greg Steube of Florida.
Democrats will hold their leadership elections next week.
Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York is expected to become the next House speaker, the first African-American to hold the job, and Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts is expected to become the next majority leader. She would be the first woman to hold that position.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Aging Untold: Chronic pain doesn’t have to be a choice between suffering and strong medication
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we explore life-changing health and savings strategies.
We explore opioid-free options to manage chronic pain.
Then we offer practical tips to cut your monthly prescription costs.
Plus, learn how a free genetic test can reveal hidden cancer risks before symptoms start.
If you have chronic pain, you might have more options than toughing it out or taking strong medication.
Finding out what will work for you starts with finding the root cause of the pain, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, says.
“Your treatment is going to depend on why you have the pain,” Rogers said.
She said the cause also leads to other options, such as movement and stretching.
The Aging Untold experts are sharing tips and what has worked for them.
If your prescription costs are high, there are options to explore that could bring them down.
One place to start is with the doctor or pharmacist.
They might have free prescription drug programs, samples or cards that can reduce medication costs.
Are you on Medicare? Aging expert Amy O’Rourke recommends reviewing Medicare Part D coverage every year to see if the premium can be lowered.
A nurse practitioner and mother of four in Nebraska with little family history of cancer says a free genetic research study likely saved her life after she learned she carries a BRCA2 gene mutation.
Erin Thoman’s sister participated in the Genetic Insights Project at Nebraska Medicine and learned she had the BRCA2 gene mutation. When Thoman and her mother were tested through the same study, they both learned they also carry the mutation.
Thoman has met with a breast surgeon at Nebraska Medicine and a double mastectomy is expected to drop her breast cancer risk from around 60% to less than 10%.
Dr. Doug Stoller, a cardiologist involved in the study, said the goal is early detection. Researchers want to enroll up to 100,000 people in Nebraska and 3 million nationwide.
For 30 years, Kenny Minor has greeted customers at his Food Lion.
Minor has worked at the store since high school, walking to work in all kinds of weather, and customers look forward to seeing him.
Along with cleaning the aisles, store manager Jack Glass said Minor regularly helps shoppers locate items and carries groceries to their cars.
What drives Minor to go above and beyond? Read the full article here.

title: These side hustle apps are offering users a way to earn extra money
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (InvestigateTV) - Apps that let people rent out things they already own are offering users a way to earn extra cash without taking on an in-person part-time job.
Instead of signing up to drive for a rideshare service or deliver groceries, some people are turning to rental platforms that allow them to make money on their own schedule by listing items they already have at home.
Reese Grau has been renting out her closet on the Pickle app for the last five years.
“Basically, if I rent it out four times, I make my money back,” Grau said. “So, it’s kind of like girl math…return on my investment.”
Pickle allows users to list items from their real-life closet on the app, from accessories and shoes to clothing. Grau said larger rentals, such as higher-end dresses, can bring in more money.
“I get some bigger rentals — like a nicer dress — I can make more,” she said. “There’s been weeks where I’ve made $200 a week.”
Over the last year, Grau said she rented out 85 items and earned about $1,300.
For families looking to put outgrown baby gear to use, BabyQuip offers another option by connecting travelers and parents with providers who rent out items such as strollers, cribs, toys and fans.
Kierstyn Stewart, a BabyQuip provider based out of Franklin, Tennessee, said she joined after her children started outgrowing their equipment.
Stewart said she has been renting out baby gear for a little more than two years and has completed around 150 rentals. Business can spike during peak travel seasons, she said, including spring break and major holidays.
“There are different parts of the year where you’re going to be busier: spring break, Thanksgiving, Christmas,” Stewart said. “You’re going to find that you’re just busier those times of the year, and throughout the year, it’s sprinkled in.”
BabyQuip said providers keep 78% of their rental and delivery fees and 100% of tips.
Other platforms offer similar opportunities with different kinds of property. Swimply allows homeowners to rent out pools, hot tubs and even sports courts — such as pickleball — as well as backyards for events. Another app, Neighbor, allows users to rent out space such as driveways.
Both women said the side income is helpful, but the work is also something they enjoy.
“I’ve been kind of trying to get some side hustles going, and this has been great for me,” Grau said. “I’ve gotten a lot of my friends on it too.”
Pickle, the clothing rental app, said in 2025 some of their top lenders made around $5,000 a month.
By 2034, the global peer-to-peer rental apps market size is expected to be worth around $49.3 billion.

title: Obituary: Robert H. Easter
text:
WINTHROP – Robert H. Easter, 68, of Stanley Road died on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026, at his home with his loving siblings by his side, following a long illness.
Bob was born in Keene, NH on Dec. 10, 1957, the son of the late Reginald H. and Geraldine M. (Sylvia) Easter.
For most of his life, Bob worked as a contractor building anything from homes, to garages to whatever you needed, a career that spanned more than 40 years. After retiring from building, he worked at the Winthrop American Legion where he would do any of their maintenance, cooked for many of the events and was a big part of the annual 4th of July Celebration. He was a member of the Son’s of the American Legion and was a Past Commander, adjutant and finance officer of the Son’s of the American Legion.
In his spare time, Bob loved gardening and would often have the most amazing vegetable and flower gardens. He enjoyed feeding the birds or any animal that appeared on his doorstep hungry. When his illness no longer allowed him to do the things he loved, he took up crafting and would do anything just to keep busy. He loved to cook, read mystery novels and could often be found mowing the back field.
Bob was predeceased by his loving wife Rhonda in 2023; an infant daughter; and a great niece, Jaidyn Bigelow.
He is survived by two sons, Robert and Stephanie Easter of Mount Vernon and Daniel Easter and his companion Brittany Holland of Oakland, a daughter, Sarah Easter and her companion Joey Wade of Wiscasset; seven grandchildren, Jeffrey, Connor, Noah, Kayla, Chrissy, Alex and Lukas; two great grandchildren, Genesis and Aura; a brother, Ronald and his wife Lorene Easter of NY, a sister, Donna and her husband Aubrey MacLeod of Canada; several nieces and nephews.
At the request of the family, all services will be private. Arrangements and guidance are under the direction of Roberts Funeral Home and Cremation Care, 62 Bowdoin Street, Winthrop, Maine.
Condolences, memories and photos may be shared with the family by visiting the Roberts Funeral Home website http://www.KHRFuneralHomes.com

contributions in
Roberts memory to:
Son’s of the American Legion Post #40
117 Bowdoin St.
Winthrop, ME 04364

title: White Sox’s Will Venable beats out Red Sox’s Chad Tracy for AL Manager of the Year
text:
Will Venable won the AL Manager of the Year award after the Chicago White Sox made the playoffs this year following three 100-loss seasons in a row.
The White Sox became the first team in major league history to reach the playoffs after consecutive 100-loss seasons. Only the third of those came under Venable after he took over in 2025. Chicago went 84-78 this year.
Pat Murphy from first-time World Series champion Milwaukee was among the NL finalists along with Philadelphia’s Don Mattingly and Atlanta’s Walt Weiss. Murphy was seeking later Tuesday night to become the first manager in either league to win the award three years in a row. The Brewers had an MLB-high 103 wins during the regular season.
Venable got 15 of 30 first-place votes and 111 points in balloting by the Baseball Writers’ Association of America that was conducted before the postseason and announced Tuesday night. The other AL finalists were two-time winner Kevin Cash of the AL champion Tampa Bay Rays, who got 12 first-place votes and 98 points, and Chad Tracy, who took over the Boston Red Sox in April and led them to the playoffs.
Venable, a former big league outfielder, got his first managerial job when the White Sox were coming off 121 losses in 2024 and 101 the previous season. They went 60-102 in Venable’s debut and followed that this season by making the playoffs for the first time since 2021.
After sweeping Houston in two games on the road in the AL Wild Card Series, they had a 2-0 series lead before losing a five-game AL Division Series to Cleveland.
Before he was hired by the White Sox, Venable was on manager Bruce Bochy’s staff in Texas and was part of the Rangers’ only World Series title in 2023.
Venable is first White Sox manager to win the award since Ozzie Guillen in 2005.
Tracy went 77-58 after taking over when the Red Sox fired Alex Cora on April 25. Boston struggled early in Tracy’s tenure before a 27-3 stretch from July 3-Aug. 8 vaulted it into playoff contention. That stretch included a franchise-recording tying 15-game winning streak.
Boston removed the interim tag and gave Tracy a three-year contract on Sept. 22.
Venable earned 15 first-place votes and finished with 111 total. Cash was second with 12 first-place votes. Tracy earned three first-place votes and finished third.

title: Massachusetts ex-police officer found guilty of killing woman he had relationship with as a minor
text:
Former Massachusetts police officer found guilty of killing woman he had sexual relationship with as a minor
Former Stoughton, Massachusetts, police officer Matthew Farwell was found guilty of killing Sandra Birchmore and her unborn child by a federal jury on Tuesday.
Video above: Matthew Farwell found guilty in death of Sandra Birchmore: Legal analysis
Farwell was accused of killing Birchmore in 2021 and staging her death as a suicide to conceal a sexual relationship that began when she was a minor.
After about 15 hours of deliberating, the jury on Tuesday found him guilty on charges of killing a witness or victim and protection of unborn children. Quiet sobbing and cries could be heard in the courtroom as the verdict was read.
"Evil. Demonic. Predator ... that would be the word I'd use. Predator," Birchmore's cousin, Barbara Wright, said of Farwell outside the Moakley Federal Court House after the verdict.
"It is the outcome Sandra, her unborn child, and her family have deserved for more than five years," Stoughton police acting Chief James O’Connor said in a statement. "What happened to Sandra is a profound betrayal of the trust every police officer is sworn to uphold."
The verdict came after the jury of eight men and four women told the judge Monday afternoon that they were "in a deadlock that looks like it will not change any time soon." They resumed deliberations Tuesday morning.
Farwell will be sentenced on Feb. 3.
Video: Former Mass. AG explains what could happen next
Prosecutors argued that Farwell killed Birchmore, who was pregnant, because he suspected she had revealed their sexual relationship, which began when she was underage.
"We want to make sure that the public understand what happens to a child when they are groomed, and it is even more disgusting that the people she should have been able to turn to are the people that abused her," family spokesperson Melissa Berry said.
Video below: Vigil held outside courthouse
Friends and family of Birchmore attended the trial throughout its duration.
Farwell is accused of killing the pregnant Birchmore on Feb. 1, 2021, three days before she was found by police in her Canton apartment.
Birchmore's death was originally ruled a suicide, but federal prosecutors took over the case in 2024 and charged Farwell with murder. Her death certificate was updated this year to change the manner of death from "suicide" to "undetermined."
Key testimony from Week 4
- Dr. Max Noureddine, a DNA forensic expert for the defense, testified about how evidence can be contaminated at crime scenes and how multiple DNA samples can be present at the same location.
- Dr. Heather Garvin, a board-certified forensic anthropologist, focused on the structures of the neck, specifically the hyoid bone, a small U-shaped bone in the front of the neck. Garvin testified that peer-reviewed studies show the hyoid bone can break during hangings. However, she said studies do not show a conclusive link between hangings and fractures in the hyoid bone.
- Daniel Loper testified on Wednesday about his review of data taken from devices owned by Sandra Birchmore and Matthew Farwell. Those devices included iPhones, Apple Watches, and laptops.
- Dr. Thomas Andrew, a forensic pathologist, was also called to testify on Wednesday afternoon. He opined that Birchmore's apartment did not display signs of a struggle and said the injury to her hyoid bone likely occurred when her blood pressure was low or after her death.
Key testimony from Week 3
- Dr. Maria Capo-Martinez, a medical examiner, said she performed Birchmore's autopsy on Feb. 5, 2021, the day after her body was discovered in her Canton apartment. She initially ruled the cause of death as asphyxia by hanging and the manner of death as suicide. However, she told the jury that State Police did not provide her with any reason to believe the death was suspicious.
- Prosecution witness William Farwell, the fraternal twin brother of Matthew Farwell, testified under an immunity agreement with the federal government about his relationship with Sandra Birchmore. William Farwell said he began a sexual relationship with Birchmore in 2018, the year she turned 21, and stated that they had sex while he was on duty as a Stoughton police officer. He testified that Matthew Farwell told him about wiping his phone and destroying data that could connect him to Birchmore  Hearst Owned
- Dr. William Smock testified about hair tangled on the strap found around Birchmore’s neck, saying it was "one of the biggest red flags of a homicidal event." He also claimed that evidence, including an imprint on her chest and a broken bone, indicated the crime scene was staged. Don Drake
- Digital forensics expert Jessica Hyde walked jurors through her analysis of Sandra Birchmore's iPhone. She testified the phone's last recorded button press and last recorded steps were at 9:40 p.m. on Feb. 1, just minutes before surveillance video shows a man identified as Matthew Farwell leaving Birchmore's apartment building at 9:43 p.m.
Key testimony from Week 2
- FBI Special Agent Heidi Kelsch testified over three days about evidence found on Birchmore’s cellphone and Apple Watch, including graphic sexual fantasy text chains between the two in the months and weeks leading up to her death. Of the 40,000 text messages exchanged between Birchmore and Farwell, Kelsch said Birchmore initiated 60% of the conversations, a figure that eventually grew to 70%. Farwell often blocked Birchmore on his cellphone. Don Drake
- Former Stoughton police dispatcher James Fitton testified about a call that came into the department a week and a half before Sandra Birchmore died. He said the female caller alluded to a relationship between her friend and Detective Matthew Farwell.
- Dr. Priyanka Venkataraman, who was Birchmore’s OB/GYN, testified about some of her medical records. Birchmore had been prescribed the antidepressant Zoloft, and during cross-examination, the doctor agreed that the drug can cause suicidal thoughts or actions.
- Jason Pickard testified in federal court about his relationship with Birchmore, whom he met in 2019 while working as a recruiter for the U.S. Army.  He told the jury that he only learned last year that he was the father of her unborn child. Don Drake
- Jurors heard additional testimony from a forensic scientist at the state crime lab. She said Farwell's DNA was found on the strap prosecutors allege was used to kill Birchmore. She also testified that DNA testing revealed both Farwell's and Pickard's DNA on Birchmore's underwear.
- Three women also told the jury about affairs they had with Farwell. Prosecutors fought to include their testimony, while the defense argued that surveillance video showing him wearing a mask the night Birchmore died was intended to help conceal the affair from his wife. However, the women testified that Farwell did not wear masks or disguises during their encounters.
- Friend and former classmate Lindsey Crean testified that Birchmore had babysat for Farwell's children. She also said that Birchmore was “very, very happy” about her pregnancy but that Farwell had grown angry after Birchmore said he did not have to be on the birth certificate, did not have to attend the birth and only asked that he stop by on holidays.
- Diala Alkhalil, a licensed mental health counselor, testified that Birchmore's last session was the day before her death. She said Birchmore, like many other clients, was on Zoloft. Alkhalil also testified that Birchmore was ecstatic about her pregnancy.
Key testimony from Week 1
- The first witness called in the case was Det. Heather Cheever, of the Stoughton Police Department. She knew Birchmore, who was in the department's Explorers program as a minor. Cheever testified that she had heard Birchmore was pregnant before her death, which was originally described as a suicide. She also testified that she recognized Farwell in surveillance video leaving Birchmore's apartment building wearing a mask, but noted he had told her that he never believed in COVID-19.
- Cheryl Carlson, an assistant principal who hired Birchmore to work as an instructional assistant in Sharon Public Schools, said that Birchmore's death "didn't make sense" because she was excited about her pregnancy. Jurors heard from Erin Porter and Carlos Verissimo, who work at Canton Woods, about the layout of the building where Birchmore lived and the video recovered from the property.
- Canton School Resource Officer Ensley Cotard testified that he was asked to conduct the well-being check in Birchmore's apartment. Photos of Birchmore's body were introduced into evidence during his testimony.
- Massachusetts State Police homicide investigator Trooper Matt Dunne testified that after seeing the footage of Farwell entering and leaving Birchmore's apartment building on Feb. 1, 2021, investigators decided they needed to speak with Farwell immediately. That interview took place in a Stoughton school parking lot on a weekend, and it was not recorded. He called that a "tactical decision." According to Dunne, Farwell told investigators he went to Birchmore's apartment to end their relationship. Hearst Owned
- Lesley Davis, one of Birchmore's friends, testified that Birchmore appeared excited about becoming a mother, saying Birchmore asked her to be the godmother and seemed to be in one of the happiest periods of her life.
- Stoughton police Sgt. Robert Kuhn testified that it was odd to see Farwell wearing a mask in surveillance footage because Farwell "despised" masks during the COVID-19 pandemic. Kuhn also testified that Farwell's drinking was excessive in late 2020 and early 2021.
- Stoughton police Chief Donna McNamara testified Thursday that she knew Birchmore through the department's youth mentor program and that the department opened an internal affairs investigation after Birchmore's death, according to her testimony. McNamara identified Farwell as the subject of that investigation and said referrals were made to the POST Commission and the district attorney's office.
- FBI master digital forensic examiner Christopher Beckstrom testified that he found a list of baby names on Birchmore's phone and FBI Special Agent Heidi Kelsch also testified to the recovery of 40,000 communications between Farwell and Birchmore dating back to 2019. She said that some indicated the two first had sex when Birchmore was 15 years old.
- FBI Special Agent Heidi Kelsch read messages from 2020 to the jury, including one where Birchmore and Farwell discussed a sexual encounter in 2013, when she was 15 years old and he was 27. Farwell looked down as the messages were read aloud.
"I had butterflies so bad the day you took my virginity," Birchmore wrote in the message read.
Case background: How we got here
Farwell, 40, is a U.S. Army veteran who served as an explosives expert from 2004 to 2008. He became a police officer in Stoughton in 2012.
Birchmore first applied to join the Stoughton Police Explorers Academy in 2010. According to prosecutors, her mother wanted Birchmore to join the program to help her interact with role models.
She met Farwell in 2012, while she was 15. Prosecutors said they became friends on Facebook, Farwell tutored her at the library, and their relationship developed a sexual component. According to documents filed in the case, prosecutors believe the two first had intercourse when Birchmore was 15 and Farwell was 27.
Additionally, prosecutors said evidence including text messages and journals reflect discussions of choking, role-playing and examples of Farwell demanding control over elements of Birchmore's life.
Their extramarital relationship allegedly continued for years, and prosecutors alleged in an indictment that Farwell met Birchmore for sex while on duty. During the years from 2013 to 2020, Farwell's twin brother, William Farwell, and former Stoughton police Deputy Chief Robert Devine are also accused of having inappropriate contact with Birchmore.
Prosecutors said Birchmore presented Farwell with an ultimatum in October 2020. She demanded that he try to conceive a child with her in exchange for her silence about their relationship and his conduct.
On Dec. 28, 2020, Birchmore sent to Farwell a picture of a poster reading "Congrats we are goin to be parents" with an ultrasound image, court records show. According to the prosecution, Birchmore told friends that Farwell became violent with her after that.
On Jan. 20, 2021, prosecutors wrote in an indictment that a friend of Birchmore's disclosed their relationship to the Stoughton Police Department. A few days later, prosecutors said that Farwell requested a spare key to Birchmore's apartment.
Birchmore was found dead on Feb. 4, 2021. It was originally ruled a suicide, and the defense said she'd run a search for "What color is the suicide ribbon?" But federal prosecutors said Birchmore had been working on plans for her future child, including obtaining newborn photos and clothing.
Prosecutors said video showed Farwell entering Birchmore's apartment at 9:14 p.m. on the night she died, and leaving the building at 9:43 p.m., three minutes after Birchmore's phone recorded its final movement. Birchmore was found by police three days later with a duffle bag strap around her neck and attached to a closet doorknob.
An Internal Affairs report in August 2022 delivered findings of severe misconduct against Farwell, his brother and Devine. All three resigned.
Birchmore's family filed a wrongful death lawsuit in December 2022 and retained a pathologist, Dr. Michael Baden, who issued a report on June 18, 2024, which concluded her death was a homicide staged to look like a suicide.
Farwell was arrested by the FBI on Aug. 28, 2024. The initial charge was killing a witness or victim. Prosecutors said warrants allowed them to obtain his DNA, which was linked to samples from the ligature and Birchmore's clothing, but not the unborn child.
A federal grand jury returned a superseding indictment on Oct. 28, 2025, adding a count pertaining to the death of the unborn child. In December 2025, the Department of Justice announced it would not seek the death penalty in this case.
Earlier this year, Birchmore's death certificate was updated by the Massachusetts Office of the Chief Medical Examiner. The manner of death was changed from "suicide" to "undetermined."

title: Jayson Tatum gets better of Jaylen Brown as Celtics beat 76ers
text:
PHILADELPHIA — Jayson Tatum scored 21 points and outplayed former Boston teammate Jaylen Brown, and Paul George hit six 3-pointers and scored 36 points in his return to Philadelphia, leading the Celtics past the 76ers 123-101 on Tuesday night.
Brown ran into early foul trouble and scored only 13 points in his first game against Boston since the 2024 NBA Finals MVP was traded over the summer to the Sixers. His head-to-head showdown with Tatum was one of the more anticipated early-season matchups with both players refusing to say much about their frosty relationship.
Tatum tried to dap up Brown before the opening tip with a tap on the shoulder and thump on the chest that his former teammate ignored. Tatum shook hands and exchanged a big hug with LeBron James.
Brown picked up two quick fouls in the first quarter and was whistled for his fourth early in the second half.
George, traded for Brown after two seasons with the 76ers, enjoyed the homecoming. He appeared to give the finger in a bowling motion near the visitor’s bench after he sank his fourth 3 of the game for a 100-82 lead that pushed the Celtics to their ninth win in 10 games.
The Sixers survived a scare late in the second half when Joel Embiid landed awkwardly and hit the court on a missed layup attempt. The oft-injured big man curled up on the court while VJ Edgecombe dunked over him.
Embiid gingerly ran down the court and hunched over as the halftime horn sounded with the Celtics up 62-51.
Embiid’s health has been a career-long issue for him, and the Sixers have declined to play him in back-to-back games. A two-time NBA scoring champion, Embiid has slumped with his shot this season, with no game worse than last Friday in Cleveland when missed all nine shots from the floor and scored only two points.
He had missed 27 of 30 (and 20 consecutive) 3-pointers entering the game. Embiid missed two 3-point attempts in the first half but opened the second with his first 3 since the second game of the season.
Tyrese Maxey led the Sixers with 24 points.
Up next
Boston completes a back-to-back at Toronto.
The Sixers host the Raptors on Thursday.

title: Operation Fuzzy Socks brings warm clothing to Maine cancer patients
text:
Melissa Marshall never expected to be drowning in boxes in her Rangeley home, but now, four weeks into an annual donation drive she started, it’s the best feeling in the world.
Every October since 2020, Marshall has run a drive from her Facebook page to gather warm socks for breast cancer patients at the Harold Alfond Center for Cancer Care in Augusta.
Her motivation is personal. In 2017, her sister, Tiffany Andrews, died at 47 after a two-year battle with breast cancer. Marshall remembers how cold her sister got through her 16 rounds of chemotherapy.
To warm herself up, Andrews bought thick fuzzy socks to wear while undergoing her treatment.
“She said, ‘Yep, I’m going to wear fuzzy socks now every time I come for chemo because I’m cold,'” Marshall remembered.
Three years later, Marshall and some co-workers brainstormed how best to give back to their community for the holidays. Her manager, Kelly Martin, recommended donating to cancer patients, while her co-worker Nadine Jones suggested the name, Operation Fuzzy Socks.
With Maine battling the COVID pandemic at the time, the Alfond Center for Cancer Care was the only one taking donations, so Marshall brought her first donation there and has maintained that connection ever since.
The drive is held in October to coincide with Breast Cancer Awareness Month.
Since then, Marshall has led the effort to gather friends, family and strangers alike to donate goods online. Donors mainly use an Amazon page that she set up, preloaded with options for socks and other comforts for patients in Augusta.
She remembers how her sister’s lips would chap during her chemo, so she added lip balm to the list this year.
“I try to keep it not too expensive,” she said. “Maybe something’s 20 bucks. Maybe something is seven to nine. No donation is too small.”
Others have donated cash, or purchased socks at the store and mailed them directly to Marshall. What matters most to her is supporting those going through treatment.
“Every year, they start crying when they see me walk in,” she said. “It’s what Tiff would want.”
Tiffany was the biggest New York Yankees fan, Marshall recalled. She called a spade a spade, loved cribbage and chocolate. She was frugal.
“(She) had the first penny she ever made, unlike me,” she joked.
This is the fifth year that Marshall is doing Operation Fuzzy Socks. She took one year off in 2022 after her father died. She said the amount she received from her community this year is the most it’s ever been.
“The generosity this year has been huge,” she said. “It hasn’t just been an Amazon delivery of two or three socks. It’s been boxes of just everything on the list.”
Denise Krula, who lives in Rangeley part time, has contributed socks, hats and lip balm to Marshall’s cause for the past two years. Cancer has affected her life and she has friends who have been through chemo. She’s seen firsthand how cold patients get, so the donation of warm clothes is important to her.
The fact that she can see her donation going straight to the people it helps draws Krula back.
“I like donating to her because I know she’s bringing it right to the hospital,” Krula said. “I know they’re getting 100% of the donation, which makes my heart happy.”
In the boxes piled in Marshall’s living room are vacuum-sealed socks, prayer books, beanies and journals. At the end of October, Marshall gathers all the materials and prepares to deliver them herself. This week, she’ll drive them to Augusta.
Deb Bowman, the associate vice president of oncology services at MaineHealth’s Harold Alfond Center, said the donations give patients a necessary boost in morale.
“The patients are literally overwhelmed with gratitude,” she said. “They are always shocked when something’s handed to them.”
When the donations come into the hospital, Bowman and her co-workers bag up the items for patients to accept. She said that even though many of the donations that the hospital receives are anonymous to those undergoing treatment, it is just as impactful to them.
“There’s something about knowing somebody’s out there and has got your back, but you’re never going to meet them face to face,” Bowman said. “That’s pretty special, too.”
Even a small donation means the world to some patients.
“There’s some people who come in with so little,” she said. “Even the socks are a big deal.”
This year’s drive has ended, but Marshall said she will always accept donations for the following year. With five years of organizing under her belt, she doesn’t plan to stop any time soon.
“I will do it forever,” she said.

title: Prince Harry's wife Meghan makes first public appearance since father's arrest
text:
Prince Harry's wife Meghan makes first public appearance since father's arrest
Prince Harry urged tech companies to be more transparent about issues involving children as he and his wife, the former Meghan Markle, made their first public appearance on Tuesday since her father’s arrest on suspicion of possessing images of child abuse.
Harry spoke at the European Parliament in Brussels during the opening of a memorial to children who have died as the result of harm suffered on social media. The Lost Screen Memorial features replicas of oversized smartphones with the photo of a deceased child on each home screen.
Meghan, also known as the Duchess of Sussex, was originally scheduled to speak alongside Harry but withdrew because she was not “strong enough emotionally,” a person familiar with her reasoning said. She still accompanied her husband to the event.
Video: Thomas Markle, father of Meghan, arrested on charges related to child sexual abuse materials
The allegations against Thomas Markle Sr. surfaced last month. He appeared in a Florida courtroom on Friday charged with possessing child sexual abuse material. The 82-year-old has previously strongly denied the allegations, labelling them as “sick lies.”
Harry appeared emotional during his speech as he urged social media companies to avoid showing children content they would not show their own children. He also called on the companies to be more transparent and helpful to parents, particularly those seeking access to their children’s devices and social media accounts to understand what happened to them online.
“For many parents, even though their child killed themselves, they’ve had to wait years – in some instances, eight years – to get access to their child’s phone,” Harry said. “Because of the company’s privacy policies, the parents were blocked from finding out how their child died. That cannot be right.”

title: ‘Most rewarding’: 97-year-old who left school to take care of her family receives honorary diploma
text:
BAY ST. LOUIS, Miss. (WLOX/Gray News) — A Mississippi woman received her long-awaited high school diploma this week.
Etta Mae Williams, 97, received an honorary diploma from the Bay-Waveland School District on Monday.
Williams put on her cap and gown and accepted the diploma as a member of the Class of 2026.
“Good things come to those who wait, and I patiently waited,” Williams said. “I’ve been waiting for this for a long time. But I got it.”
Williams left school when she was young to help support her family. Years later, she tried to go back to school, but COVID-19 derailed those plans.
“I finally got this piece of paper I always wanted,” Williams said. “I worked the whole way through it. Thank the Lord I got it.”
Her great-niece, Britney Williams, has admired that determination.
“She had to drop out of school to help out. She had to work. She had to help provide for the family when her father passed,” Britney Williams said. “And so, just to keep striving. Just to keep going on. To fulfill her education means a lot.”
Etta Mae Williams’ dream came true after a community member asked Superintendent Sandra Reed if the district could help make it happen.
Reed said the decision was easy, especially after she learned all eight of Etta Mae Williams’ children graduated from Bay High School.
“I can honestly say that this was the most rewarding diploma that I’ve ever handed out,” Reed said. “Just the joy, the love, the grace were just overflowing from her. And it was just my honor.”
Mississippi Rep. Jeffrey Hulum III also presented Etta Mae Williams with a proclamation honoring her hard work.
“You’re never too old to learn,” Etta Mae Williams said. “I tried, I tried, I tried, and I succeeded. Thank you.”

title: Obituary: Gregory Fortin Sr
text:
VASSALBORO – Gregory Fortin, Sr., 79, passed away peacefully on Nov. 5, 2026, with his loving family at his side. He was born in Waterville, on March 28, 1947, to the late Bernard H. and Phyllis I. (Dyer) Fortin.
Greg was married to Rose-Marie Fortin of Vassalboro for 59 years. Together they raised three sons and enjoyed traveling, fishing, gardening, and especially spending time with their grandchildren.
Greg attended Lawrence High School and earned an Associate’s Degree from the University of Maine, Orono. He served his country honorably in the Army National Guard and the Air National Guard. He was a self-employed plumber and worked at Bath Iron Works as a pipefitter for 25 years.
Gregory was a life-time resident of Vassalboro and served on the Vassalboro Volunteer Fire Department for a number of years, was the Plumbing Inspector for Vassalboro for several years, and served as Scoutmaster Troop 410 for about eight years, seeing all three of his sons earn their Eagle Scout rank. Greg enjoyed fishing Moosehead Lake, hunting, bowling, tying streamer flies, spending countless hours on his zero-turn mower, and putting up with the shenanigans of his three sons and grandchildren. He also was also an avid reader and cribbage player.
Gregory was predeceased by his parents, Bernard and Phyllis (Dyer) Fortin, grandparents, and numerous aunts and uncles.
Gregory E. Fortin, Sr. is survived by his loving wife of 59 years, Rose-Marie (Lemieux) Fortin; his three sons, Gregory E. Fortin, Jr. and his wife Jennifer (Cole) of Vassalboro, Robert C. Fortin and his wife Michelle (Gavin) of Surry, and Bernard P. Fortin and his wife Jennifer (McGreevy) of Vassalboro.
He also leaves behind his beloved grandchildren, Emma, Morgan, Cole, and Brandon Fortin, and Zackery and Jacob Lewis; and Breanna McGreevy; and his great-grandchild, Ashton McGreevy. He is also survived by a special cousin, Timothy and Corrine Dyer of Yucca Valley, Calif.
A Catholic Mass will be celebrated at Notre Dame Catholic Church, 116 Silver St, Waterville, on Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, at 9 a.m. A graveside service for family and friends will follow directly at the North Vassalboro Village Cemetery on Cemetery Street in Vassalboro with a Reception to follow at the Notre Dame Reception Hall.
The family would like to thank Dr. Polkinghorn, the wonderful nurses at the Harold Alfond Center for Cancer Care and the doctors and nursing staff at Maine General for their wonderful care.

title: Rep. Paul LePage will not have a ton of clout
text:
Unless something unusual is discovered during the ranked-choice voting count this week, Paul LePage will be the only Republican in the nation who snatched a congressional district held by a Democrat.
Rep. Jared Golden, a Maine Democrat who has served since his 2018 victory, opted not to seek reelection, leaving open his U.S. House seat in the Republican-leaning 2nd District. LePage, a two-term former governor, won narrowly against Democrat Matt Dunlap, whose robust sense of humor wasn’t enough to elevate him to Congress.
On a day when Democrats won many districts more difficult than Golden’s, LePage’s success stands out.
Sadly for the Republicans who would like to hold onto the district forever, LePage, at 78, will be the third oldest person to take the oath of office as a member of Congress, topped only by Republican William Lewis of Kentucky in 1948 and Democrat James Bowler of Illinois five years later.
Lewis won a special midyear election to fill a vacancy and didn’t compete in the subsequent general election — which means LePage will be the oldest of the nearly 4,000 Republican lawmakers to serve after winning a regular election.
My guess is that LePage won’t stick around Capitol Hill for long in any case.
He recognized years ago that he “wouldn’t make a very good legislator” and felt like congressional committee meetings “would be boring.” Both things are true.
What’s probably really going to irk LePage is that a first-term lawmaker from the party that’s out of power will have about as much political clout as my two collies. Sure, they can make a lot of noise, but they can’t actually do much of anything. Nor do they tend to try.
During his years as governor, LePage had a penchant for getting attention from the press, mostly because he said and sometimes did outrageous things. He proudly said, “I have no filter.”
Now, though, he’s older and perhaps wiser. In any case, he’s become far less verbose and more cautious — two more reasons it’s likely few will notice him deep in the Republican back benches.
On Sunday, LePage said he would be “laser-focused on policies that lower your cost-of-living, bring prosperity back to rural Maine, and crack down on welfare fraud and corruption.” He also said he planned “to fight like hell for you.”
I say: Good luck with that.
LePage is likely to find Congress a dull place for someone who is close to the bottom of a 435-person pecking order.
The first time I met then-Gov. LePage, he called himself “an ordinary man in a tough job” who intended to help return Republicans to power across New England.
Soon, he will be the only member of his party from the entire region in either the Senate or House — a distinction that Sen. Susan Collins has held since Rep. Bruce Poliquin lost his 2018 race to Golden.
New England’s GOP is barely hanging on. There are 12 senators and 21 members of the House from its six states — and come January, the only one who will be a Republican is Paul LePage.
He faces a truly tough job, even for an extraordinarily skilled politician.

title: ‘Marriage is a gift’: Officer shot 6 times in line of duty celebrates the wedding he almost missed
text:
BUFFALO, N.Y. (WKBW) - Months after a New York police officer was shot six times in the line of duty, he celebrated a moment that once seemed far from certain: marrying his fiancée.
Buffalo Police Officer Marc Hurst, a nine-year veteran officer, was shot six times May 26 while responding to a domestic violence call – once in each calf, once in the upper thigh, once in the upper arm and twice in his bulletproof vest. He remembers realizing that despite being shot multiple times, he was still breathing and able to think.
“I was still thinking, so I couldn’t have been that bad, as good as you can be for being shot multiple times. I just remember, and I believe it’s just from the Lord, this overwhelming peace,” Marc said.
As he focused on getting out of the house where the shooting took place, another thought crossed his mind: his upcoming wedding to his then-fiancée, Haley Hurst.
“I remember being down on the ground and focusing on getting out of the house that we were in but also being like, ‘You know what? She’s gonna be really ticked off if I miss this wedding,’” Marc said.
Marc was rushed to the hospital, and one of his friends in the police department called Haley with the terrifying news.
“I was like, ‘You need to tell me what’s going on,’” Haley recalled. “And he said that Marc had been shot. I was obviously freaking out, like, ‘He’s been shot everywhere.’”
Marc suffered serious injuries but survived. After six days in the hospital, he wowed his fellow officers as he walked out on his own two feet. Last month, he received the City of Buffalo’s Medal of Honor.
Through it all, Haley has been by his side.
“It’s been humbling and emotional,” she said. “Even when I would go back and forth from the hospital to get him more clothes and everything that week, like thinking about, ‘Oh my God, we still get married in a couple of months, and we almost didn’t.’”
The couple got married Friday.
Marc said surviving the shooting has changed the way he looks at moments that might otherwise seem ordinary from watching his nieces walk down the aisle to seeing family and friends gathered together.
“When you go through something traumatic like this, you appreciate even the littlest things a little bit more,” he said. “I’m just so thankful that we are celebrating our marriage… and my family and my fiancée is not mourning the loss of me.”
But for Marc, the wedding was about much more than celebrating. It was also a reminder of what he nearly lost.
“To see Haley coming down the aisle, I can’t even put it into words right now, compared to what could have been. I’m just so grateful,” he said. “Marriage is a gift. Haley’s a gift… and I’m just so, so blessed.”
Police identified the man accused of shooting Marc as 33-year-old Minhaz Siddiqui. He was charged with multiple felonies, including first-degree attempted murder.

title: Van Buren braces for upcoming 12-hour power outage
text:
VAN BUREN, Maine (WAGM) - If you live in Van Buren, you’ll lose power on Thursday. Van Buren residents will experience an extended power outage lasting up to 12 hours.
On Thursday the Van Buren Light and Power District will be replacing a malfunctioning substation transformer. So, officials have a few tips on how people can get through the extended outage.
Darren Woods, Director of the Aroostook Emergency Management Agency says, “It is a rough time of year to do it, but it is necessary. So, what homeowners need to be thinking about is what they can do at home to prepare. Some of the big things that we see that people forget is they’ll open and close their fridge a little too much. Things like putting freezer packs in your freezer and letting things freeze up. So, when the power does go out those packs can maintain the temperature within that unit. Keeping that unit closed as much as you can. That’s your freezer and your refrigerator and also thinking about things like well water. So, if you’re on a well that requires a pump and power for that well you have to think about the water you’re gonna need for drinking as well as for hygiene ahead of time.”
Since the temperature outside is getting colder, Woods also has some tips to keep residents warm during the outage. “You want to make you’ve got your home up to temperature. It might be a good idea to turn a couple of degrees higher than maybe you normally would have it. Just to let that cool down a little bit as you go through the outage. It’ll sustain you just a little bit longer. I’m positive Van Buren Light and Power will get that back on just as quickly as they can. So, we’re hoping that it’s gonna be less than a 12 hour, but people should really be prepared just in case.”
For those with generators, there are also some things to keep in mind.
“Making sure you do not run them inside. Keep your generator away from doors and windows and make sure you have good, working smoke and carbon monoxide detectors inside your home,” said Woods.
To help residents keep warm during the outage, the town of Van Buren will be opening a warming shelter at the town’s Community Center at 130 Champlain Street. Officials encourage residents needing a place to go during the extended outage should stop in and warm up.

title: House Republicans quash effort to impeach Defense Secretary Hegseth
text:
WASHINGTON — The House on Tuesday turned aside a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, halting an effort to remove the Pentagon chief for his conduct in office and his handling of the war in Iran.
The vote came as Republicans grapple with the fallout from sweeping midterm losses that some in the party have blamed on the war in Iran and the resulting surge in gas prices. But after President Donald Trump signaled strong support for Hegseth, GOP lawmakers largely stood by the secretary on Tuesday. They rejected the impeachment effort led by Kentucky Republican Thomas Massie and backed by Democrats.
The vote may only delay an impeachment push against Hegseth, with Democrats set to take control of the House and Senate in January.
The House is set to vote Tuesday on whether to advance an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has accused lawmakers of undermining American troops in war zones by targeting him over mere “policy disagreements.”
The procedural vote will either block the impeachment resolution or set up a final vote Wednesday. With Democratic leadership backing the effort brought by GOP Rep. Thomas Massie, the outcome will likely hinge on whether Republican lawmakers break ranks after their sweeping losses in the midterm elections.
Hegseth dug in for a congressional fight in his first news conference in months on Tuesday, portraying Massie as a rogue lawmaker and arguing that he had committed none of the high crimes required in the Constitution for his removal. He framed the effort as an indictment against the nation’s service members and their successes while undermining American forces “in real time.”
“This is not patriotism,” Hegseth said. “This is sabotage.”
Massie’s resolution includes eight counts of impeachment. It largely focuses on the war in Iran but also includes references to Hegseth’s role in carrying out military actions in Yemen and Venezuela.
Massie, a Kentucky Republican leaving Congress in January after losing his primary to a Trump-backed opponent, says Hegseth has “knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders.”
Hegseth holds rare press conference
Tuesday morning, Hegseth gave a defiant and politicized defense of his stewardship of the U.S. military in his first news conference at the Pentagon in six months. He chose to hit back at the rising bipartisan anger over battlefield strategy while offering few details about intermittent operations against Iran or fatal strikes on alleged drug-smuggling boats in Latin America.
President Donald Trump praised Hegseth’s performance at the briefing in a social media post, while Vice President JD Vance said in his own post that the impeachment effort is “a ridiculous show that stands in for actual policymaking.”
Hegseth said the impeachment resolution “tells our enemies — Iran, the cartels, every adversary watching — the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership for successfully executing lawful military operations.”
This isn’t the first impeachment attempt in recent years
Hegseth cast Massie’s resolution in historic terms, arguing that no defense secretary has been impeached in the nation’s 250-year history “for carrying out lawful military operations.”
But more recently, a Cabinet official in President Joe Biden’s administration, Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas, was impeached by House Republicans over his handling of the U.S.-Mexico border. But the Senate dismissed all impeachment charges, shutting down his trial before arguments even began.
Mayorkas, who did not appear to testify before the impeachment proceedings, put the border crisis squarely on Congress for failing to update immigration laws during a time of global migration. Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer had said then, in April 2024, that House Republicans’ charges failed to meet “the high standard of high crimes and misdemeanors” and could set a dangerous precedent.
Republican Rep. Nick LaLota, who voted to impeach Mayorkas, said he didn’t believe Hegseth had committed any impeachable offense.
“Impeachment has been watered down,” LaLota said.
Before Mayorkas, no sitting Cabinet secretary had ever been impeached. It was nearly 150 years ago that the House voted to impeach President Ulysses S. Grant’s war secretary, William Belknap, over a kickback scheme in government contracts. He resigned before the vote.
Trump offers support for Hegseth
Trump has backed Hegseth in the wake of Massie’s impeachment resolution, pointing to the U.S. military raid to capture then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January as well as operations against Iran that he asserts have “obliterated” its navy and air force.
“Pete Hegseth gets an “A” PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!” Trump wrote Tuesday on Truth Social.
Iran, however, has been able to keep striking U.S. military bases in the Middle East and has disrupted shipping in the Strait of Hormuz during the more than 8-month-old conflict, driving up global oil prices.

title: Gunman wishes woman ‘a blessed day’ after church parking lot robbery, police say
text:
SPARTANBURG, S.C. (WHNS/Gray News) - Police in South Carolina say a woman told them a man wished her a “blessed day” after robbing her at gunpoint in a church parking lot.
The woman was attending a dance recital at a Spartanburg church Thursday when she walked to her car in the parking lot, according to a Spartanburg Police incident report. She said she noticed a silver Chevy Malibu with dark-tinted windows backed into a space two spots away from her car. Its lights were on.
The woman told police she approached the Malibu to see who was inside but changed her mind and turned around to walk back into the church. That’s when she heard a door open and turned around to see a suspect wearing a gray hoodie running toward her, according to the report.
The suspect had a gun and said, “Give me your money, or I will kill you,” and “I already killed two people; there are no cameras here,” the report said.
The woman told the suspect her purse was inside and offered to leave her car keys while she retrieved it, according to the report. She then returned and handed the suspect money.
The suspect returned her keys and told her, “Have a blessed day,” before getting back into his car and driving away, the report said.
Police said the woman memorized the car’s license plate, which helped officers identify the suspect as 26-year-old Demarieia Quartez Collins. Collins was taken to the Spartanburg County jail and charged with armed robbery, officials said.
The Rev. Heather Humphries of St. James United Methodist Church made the following statement after the incident:
“Our hearts are deeply troubled by the armed robbery that occurred in the parking lot of St. James United Methodist Church on Thursday. An act of violence in a place dedicated to worship, fellowship, and service is especially unsettling for our congregation and our community. Our immediate concern is for the victim of this frightening incident. We lift her and her loved ones in prayer, asking God to surround them with peace, comfort and healing. The safety and well-being of everyone who enters our church property remains our highest priority. We take this incident seriously and are committed to working with law enforcement by, among other actions, providing access to recordings made by our security cameras. We also are already reviewing our own security measures and taking appropriate steps to help ensure that St. James remains a safe and welcoming place for all. We ask for your continued prayers for all who have been affected, including the young man arrested in connection with this incident. Even in moments of fear and uncertainty, we remain steadfast in our faith and our calling to be a community of love, hope, and peace.”

title: Topgolf cutting prices at all US locations to make experience more affordable for customers
text:
DALLAS (Gray News) - Topgolf is lowering prices at all of its U.S. locations.
The sports-entertainment company announced the price reduction this week after guests shared in a survey that they would visit more often if it were more affordable.
“I heard a common theme from our guests: our experience is unmatched, from high-quality food to games and the ability to connect through friendly competition, but our prices are too high to keep them coming back,” Topgolf CEO David McKillips said in a statement.
Topgolf said it would be reducing gameplay rates by 20% nationwide, effective Monday.
According to the company, the lower rates won’t be a limited-time promotion but rather a permanent change and would not require a coupon or promotional code.
“I want our guests to know that we heard them and are now introducing our lowest prices ever,” McKillips continued. “Topgolf has always been about more play for all and by reducing the price of gameplay, we’re backing that commitment up.”
Topgolf is described as a sports entertainment complex that offers inclusive, high-tech golf games that everyone can enjoy year-round.
The upgraded golf experience was first offered in Virginia before expanding to more than 100 locations in the U.S. and internationally.
Topgolf locations can be found online, along with its pricing options.

title: A note to ‘46’: Donald Trump’s private message to Joe Biden emerges in new White House memoir
text:
President Donald Trump, who for years disputed his loss in the 2020 election and publicly decried the result having been stolen from him by Democratic forces, privately lauded incoming President Joe Biden as someone he believed “will be true to yourself and the American people.”
That sentiment, along with others, was part of the letter Trump left for Biden upon leaving office in January 2021. Biden showed the note to some members of his staff after his inauguration in 2021 but didn’t let anyone read it, describing it later that day as “very generous” but otherwise saying he considered it to be private.
Inclusion of the letter in Biden’s “Promise Me, America,” his White House memoir slated for release Nov. 17, was first reported Tuesday by The New York Times. The Associated Press has reviewed a photocopy of the two-page letter, handwritten in Trump’s trademark black Sharpie on White House stationery and addressed “To ‘46,’” denoting Biden’s place as the 46th U.S. president.
“Many presidents have come and gone who simply governed as Republicans or Democrats,” Trump wrote. “Largely, they did not change history, they were just swept along in its relentless tide. This will not happen to you because I know how much you love the American people.”
At the time of transition, Biden was said to have been surprised by how gracious he thought the letter was, given the animosity between the political rivals. Trump had opted out of other presidential traditions, like attending Biden’s inauguration, or hosting the incoming president and first lady for tea at the White House.
Trump has said he thought it was up to Biden to share the letter, calling it “a nice note” during a September 2023 interview with NBC’s “Meet the Press,” adding, “I took a lot of time in thinking about it.”
Elsewhere in the memoir, the first excerpt of which was published Monday by the Atlantic, Biden wrote of the deep damage Trump has inflicted, with an administration determined to “tear down institutions and inflame hatreds.”
Lamenting Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency and his aggressive reversal of many of his policies, Biden wrote of Trump’s “dismissive and destructive nature,” describing his predecessor and successor as someone “who seemed unable to tolerate the idea that someone else’s accomplishments might be worth building on rather than tearing down.”
But Biden’s harshest characterization so far was focused on Trump’s role in the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol, as Congress met to certify the 2020 election, which Biden had won. Writing that Trump “led an insurrection,” Biden said Trump’s ”goal was to remain in power after the American people had voted him out of office.”
“What Trump did on January 6, 2021, should never be forgotten,” Biden wrote. “It should follow him to his grave.”
Asked for comment on both the letter and Biden’s memoir, White House communications director Steven Cheung called the former president “a disgrace” who “should have heeded the President’s wise words, but instead he tried to destroy this country and weaponize the justice system against his political enemies.”

title: Hallowell police chief now supports renewing Quarry Tap Room liquor license
text:
HALLOWELL, Maine (WABI) -Hallowell Police Chief Zachary Kindelan now says he supports renewing the Quarry Tap Room’s liquor license.
Initial letter cited public safety concerns
The chief’s initial letter to the city council raised public safety concerns, including more than a dozen arrests and OUI incidents related to the bar.
Meeting with owners and officials
The new recommendation comes after the Quarry’s owners and management met Monday with the chief, fire officials and state liquor enforcement agents.
“The meeting went extremely well and productive, and we look forward to continuing our work and relationship with them. The issues in the letter have largely been addressed,” said Steven Lachance, co-owner of the Quarry Tap Room.
In a letter to the council, Kindelan said his initial recommendation was based on the information available to him at the time.
Public hearing
A public hearing on the renewal is scheduled for Monday night at City Hall.
