title: Ex-officer convicted of killing Sandra Birchmore to keep Massachusetts woman quiet about sex abuse
text:
BOSTON (AP) — A former police detective was convicted Tuesday of murdering a pregnant Massachusetts woman, Sandra Birchmore, to keep her from revealing that he had sexually abused her when she was 15.
Matthew Farwell, 40, was found guilty of strangling Birchmore on Feb. 1, 2021 — 12 days after a tipster called the suburban Boston police department where he worked and reported that they’d had an improper relationship. Birchmore, who was 23 when she died, had been in a tumultuous relationship with the detective, whom she first met while participating in a Stoughton Police Department youth program as a child.
Prosecutors said Farwell staged the crime scene to make her death look like a suicide — and that it nearly worked. Massachusetts State Police investigators quickly concluded that Birchmore killed herself. But the FBI began looking into the case two years later and concluded it was a homicide.
Federal prosecutors harshly criticized the initial police investigation at Farwell’s trial, saying officers didn’t follow leads and closed the case too quickly.
Farwell’s lawyers acknowledged that the married detective had an affair with Birchmore, but said it began when she was 16, making her old enough to consent under Massachusetts law. They also maintained that he did not kill her. They argued that Birchmore had threatened suicide before and that she killed herself after he went to her apartment to break up with her.
Farwell’s conviction carries a mandatory life sentence.
The nearly monthlong trial — with about 50 witnesses and 500 exhibits — unfolded in federal court in Boston, partly because local prosecutors never brought criminal charges.
Massachusetts State Police officers and investigators, some with personal connections to Farwell, quickly concluded Birchmore’s death was a suicide after she was found slumped on her apartment floor with a strap around her neck. One investigator, Assistant U.S. Attorney Brian Fogarty told jurors, saw nothing suspicious in Birchmore’s apartment and concluded this was a “troubled girl who killed herself.”
The state’s medical examiner, relying partly on information from police, initially ruled Birchmore died by suicide. The office has since changed the official manner of death to “undetermined.”
The FBI began looking into Birchmore’s death in 2023, partly at the urging of a former deputy chief at the Stoughton Police Department who had led an internal affairs investigation into Farwell based on the tip the department received before Birchmore’s death.
Federal investigators concluded the local probe into her death was rushed and compromised. Farwell was interviewed for just 15 minutes in a parking lot, they said. Investigators didn’t take notes, examine him for injuries or sample his DNA. Police looked at Farwell’s phone only after he had deleted texts with Birchmore.
The FBI investigation uncovered about 40,000 texts between Farwell and Birchmore, including some in which they reminisced about having sex when he was 27 and she was 15 — too young to consent under Massachusetts law.
The texts also showed how their relationship grew contentious as Birchmore pressed Farwell to get her pregnant and threatened to tell his wife about their relationship.
Texts in late 2020, after she was pregnant, showed they argued over what role, if any, Farwell would play in the child’s life. A paternity test after Birchmore’s death revealed a different man was the father.
At trial, a digital forensics expert testified that Birchmore’s phone stopped moving three minutes before the lobby security camera recorded Farwell leaving her building on the night of her death.
An expert hired by prosecutors, Dr. William Smock, testified that Birchmore’s injuries indicated she was strangled with a duffel bag strap and that she struggled before dying.
A defense expert, Dr. Thomas Andrew, the former chief medical examiner in New Hampshire, dismissed Smock’s determination that it was a homicide.

title: Housekeeper finds woman dead in cruise ship cabin, man standing at door with bloody hands, FBI says
text:
(AP) - A cruise ship passenger accused of killing his wife after the vessel set off from Texas told authorities that he struck her in their cabin and strangled her after an argument caused him to “snap,” according to an FBI affidavit made public Tuesday.
Jason Watford, 48, appeared in federal court on a murder charge in Galveston, where the MSC Seascape had departed over the weekend but returned to port after security aboard the ship discovered a body in his room.
The victim was identified as Susan Watford, the suspect’s wife, FBI spokesman Connor Hagan said. He added that a child was found unharmed when law enforcement responded. Court records show that Jason Watford had previously pleaded guilty to a charge of assaulting his wife in 2024.
Javier Martinez, a public defender assigned to represent Jason Watford, did not respond to a phone message Tuesday. A man who said he is Watford’s son declined to comment when reached by phone.
Couple had boarded the ship together, authorities say
The MSC Seascape is a towering white vessel that has 2,270 cabins and can host nearly 5,900 guests on five- and seven-night trips to the Caribbean, according to the company’s website.
In an interview with FBI agents Monday, Watford said he and Susan boarded the vessel together Sunday and started to argue while having dinner at one of the ship’s restaurants, according to the affidavit. The argument continued in their room, it said. Watford told agents he struck the woman several times and “applied pressure” to her neck, the affidavit said.
“Subject stated that Victim 1 and he continued to engage in an escalating verbal dispute that caused him to ‘snap,’” the agent wrote in the affidavit, referring to the couple.
Jason Watford opened their room’s door for a ship housekeeper with blood on his hands and clothes, according to court records. The housekeeper spotted a woman on the floor with facial injuries, and an investigator on the cruise ship contacted authorities.
Surveillance video showed that Watford entered the room at 7:46 p.m. and Susan went in about 25 minutes later, authorities said. At 9:15 p.m., he was seen on the video leaving the room wearing a different shirt and pants from when he answered the door for the housekeeper, according to the complaint, and sat on the hallway floor looking at his phone.
Husband was taken into custody after ship returned
Watford was taken into custody the next morning after the vessel returned to Galveston, where a passenger on the ship posted a video of Watford being escorted off the ship in handcuffs.
Court records show Watford, of Tyler, Texas, was arrested in September 2024 after Susan Watford told an officer that her husband grabbed her wrist during an argument over money in Smith County, about 100 miles (161 kilometers) east of Dallas.
The officer wrote that Susan Watford had recorded audio of the incident in which her husband could be heard becoming aggravated as she yelled at him to back away, court records show. She ran and used a stun gun, according to court records.
Jason Watford pleaded guilty to assault causing bodily injury to a family member and was placed on community supervision for 15 months, court records show.
The cruise resumed its voyage Monday. MSC Cruises said in a statement that it was cooperating with authorities and providing support to those impacted.
Watford’s next court appearance in Galveston was set for Monday.
Homicide investigations on cruise ships are uncommon. Earlier this year, a teenager was charged with murder and aggravated sexual abuse in the death of his 18-year-old stepsister on a Carnival Cruise ship out of Florida.
___
Associated Press writer Claudia Lauer in Philadelphia contributed.

title: Hegseth defends record amid impeachment effort
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth defended his military record Tuesday amid a potential impeachment in Congress, arguing the effort was over mere “policy disagreements” and high crimes and misdemeanors.
Hegseth held his first Pentagon news conference in six months, a day after Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky reintroduced eight articles of impeachment. Hegseth called the effort “a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment.”
Massie’s resolution cites U.S. military action in Yemen and Venezuela, but the case centers on the war with Iran, which Massie says the Trump administration waged without congressional approval.
“There’s no argument in these impeachment articles that he’s ineffective,” Massie said. “The argument here is that he’s broken laws and he’s violated the Constitution.”
Hegseth said the military operations at issue were lawful.
“I stand behind every one of these operations,” he said. “I was proud to execute them, and I would do it again tomorrow.”
President Donald Trump said Monday he stands by Hegseth. On Tuesday, he further backed Hegseth on social media, giving the secretary’s press conference an “A plus, plus, plus.”
Several House Democrats have said they’ll support impeachment, including Rep. Steny Hoyer of Maryland. Massie says he’s confident other House Republicans will join him, but it remains unclear how many will vote with him.
Rep. Darrell Issa (R-Calif.) said he expects the effort to fail if it reaches the Republican-controlled Senate.
“Look, this is a reaction by a member who was defeated in the primary,” Issa said. “It’s popular with Democrats. It’s going to die in the Senate.”
The House could first vote on whether to set the resolution aside or send it to committee. If neither happens, lawmakers could vote on whether to impeach Hegseth later this week.

title: A record number of veterans are attending UMaine on the GI Bill
text:
Andrew Gregory used to go to the University of Maine’s Veterans Center in Memorial Union as a quiet place to get work done. Now, he can hardly focus.
“There’s so many people, there’s always conversations you’re getting pulled into, or your ears perk up,” said Gregory, 29, a senior at the university originally from Pittsburgh. “It’s been phenomenal. On some of our busier days, we have 20 people in there at any given time.”
The active duty Marine helicopter crew chief is one of a record number of students — 530, to be exact — enrolled at the flagship public university this fall who are paying for their education thanks to benefits from the GI Bill.
That number has climbed every fall for six years, increasing by more than 50% in that time, according to data from the university, which prides itself on the support it provides for veteran students and their families.
Students attending college on the GI Bill, first passed in 1944 to allow former service members to seek higher education, get the full cost of tuition and any mandatory fees covered, plus an allowance for housing and a stipend for books.
The university also waives all tuition and fees for spouses or dependents of veterans, which 192 current students are taking advantage of.
Gregory, who is studying wildlife ecology at UMaine while preparing to be an officer in the Marine Corps, said the benefits have long been an important recruitment tool for the military, and one that influenced his decision to join the Marines.
Education was also a major factor in Malachi Lakey’s decision to enlist in the Navy.
Lakey, 34, from Lancaster, Pennsylvania, served for five years as an aerial photographer and is now in the reserves. Years ago, he got an undergraduate degree in English, and later enlisted knowing he’d like to return to school one day.
“The GI Bill is miraculous,” Lakey said. “It’s amazing that it works as well as it does.”
Gregory and Lakey are both involved in leadership of the UMaine Veterans Association, and help organize social events like potlucks for the growing community.
Lakey said he didn’t set out to find a community of fellow veterans in college, but he’s grateful it happened anyway.
“I find myself really, really appreciating the fact that there are so many veterans on campus that you can connect with,” he said. “It keeps you going, because they may not be in the exact same circumstances, but they’re in a similar place.”
Like Gregory, he’s in his final year of a wildlife ecology degree. While he chases a second undergraduate diploma, he is now debating between pursing a career in wildlife law enforcement as a game warden or going into ecology research and getting a graduate degree.
They both chose UMaine because they were looking for a strong wildlife program based on the East Coast.
Unlike Lakey, who has completed his time in the Navy and is now a reservist, much of Gregory’s service is ahead of him.
He’s part of the Marine Enlisted Commissioning Education Program, which allows him to go to college while serving as an active duty Marine. He previously attended officer candidate school, and now gets four years to focus on his education. While in school, he’s a part of UMaine’s ROTC unit, where he trains cadets, and he is technically assigned to Maine Maritime Academy.
He said attending college at a later point in life has been beneficial.
“I was more deliberate with my time, the classes I took, and the degree I’m getting,” he said.
After he gets his bachelor’s, Gregory will go directly to Quantico, Virginia, for basic officer school, then he’ll spend the next decade as an officer in the Marines. He’s hoping to earn a graduate degree during that time by conducting wildlife research with the game wardens on the base where he’s stationed.
After his military career is over, he wants to work in wildlife enforcement.

title: Kennedy family members ask a judge to block Trump's Arlington memorial arch
text:
Nine family members of the Kennedy political dynasty asked a judge Tuesday to block President Donald Trump’s plan to build a towering memorial arch, saying the 250-foot (76-meter) structure would cast a shadow over their relatives’ gravesites at Arlington National Cemetery.
The shadow would “fundamentally alter the experience of visiting the gravesites,” the relatives argued. They filed a motion to intervene in two existing lawsuits seeking to block construction of the arch.
U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan last week prohibited the Trump administration from breaking ground on the structure for 14 days.
The nine Kennedy family members who filed suit are children and grandchildren of Robert F. Kennedy and Edward M. Kennedy, brothers of the slain U.S. president John F. Kennedy, both of whom served in the U.S. Senate. They are buried close to the eternal flame that marks JFK’s gravesite, a trio of memorials that are a major draw for the millions of people who visit the Arlington cemetery each year.
Building the arch would be a “permanent denigration” of the gravesites, and the Kennedy offspring “would never again be able to appreciate both sites as they always have before, and as the Kennedy family always intended,” lawyers for the relatives wrote. They are represented by veteran Washington lawyer Norm Eisen and Democracy Defenders Fund.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Trump’s health and human services secretary who has a fractured relationship with many of his relatives, did not join the lawsuit.
The arch is one of several projects around Washington that the Republican president has undertaken as he alters the capital to his tastes — from renovating one of its storied public golf courses to threatening to demolish the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. Those projects could soon face intense scrutiny after Democrats gained control of Congress in the midterm elections this week.
The White House last week unveiled a glitzy new website to showcase the arch, which is slated to rise in a mass of gold ornamentation and stately gray granite between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

title: 'This was a chance to get ahead:' Sen. Collins campaign manager reflects on election loss
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
'This was a chance to get ahead:' Sen. Collins campaign manager reflects on election loss
Sen. Susan Collins and Senator-Elect Troy Jackson are in Washington this week, but for very different reasons. Collins, resuming work after Election Day, and Jackson, attending orientation after unseating the 30-year senator last Tuesday.
Collins' longtime chief of staff and campaign manager, Steve Abbott, along with the rest of the team, are winding down after their efforts to get the longtime senator elected for a sixth term.
In a sit-down interview with Maine's Total Coverage, Abbott says Maine passed up the opportunity to have a senator with high power serve again. He adds six more years of Collins' service would have been good for the state.
"This was a chance to get ahead," Abbott said. "It's just, you know, sad that we walked away from that."
It's been a week since Jackson unseated Sen. Collins. The senator lost Bangor, Augusta, Lewiston and Auburn, which are all areas she won back during her re-election in 2020.
Maine was one of many states that flipped seats in the midterm elections.
"She knew full well what she was getting herself into," Abbott said. "She knew that midterm of a of a Trump presidency was going to be brutally tough for Republicans, but she just thought it was too important for Maine to give that up."
Although Abbott said he has no regrets about this campaign, he says they were up against unpopular federal policies like tariffs and ICE operations. He says the main component that hurt the campaign was the rising cost of gas and heating oil. Despite the senator's efforts, Abbott said the prices weren't budging.
"Global forces much bigger than that were in control," Abbott said. "That was a real challenge for us.
Collins will leave Washington with three decades of service. Abbott said he hasn't talked to Collins about whether or not she will aim for federal office again in the future, such as another Senate seat or presidential run, and he adds no paperwork has been filed.
"I do not see that as a likely scenario," Abbott said.

title: US Air Force evacuates tankers from base in England due to Iran threat, WSJ reports
text:
US Air Force evacuates aircraft from a base in England because of a threat, US official says
The U.S. Air Force has relocated aircraft from a base in eastern England because of a threat, a U.S. official told The Associated Press.
The Military Air Tracking Alliance, a team of about 30 open-source analysts that routinely analyzes military and government flight activity, said that it spotted 13 U.S. aircraft stationed at RAF Mildenhall departing for bases in Scotland, Spain and Germany.
The Wall Street Journal, which first reported the evacuation, said that the threat related to Iran. The report cited "people familiar with the matter."
The relocation of the aircraft came less than two months after the U.S. Air Force withdrew its bombers from another U.S.-run base in Britain, RAF Fairford, as police investigated a suspected terror plot linked to Iran. Bombers flying out of RAF Fairford had been used to strike Iran during the Middle East conflict.
Related video: President Trump comments after 5 people detained in RAF Fairford air base incident in the UK (Sept. 2026)
Some of the aircraft that were relocated were permanently based at RAF Mildenhall, while others were there on rotation and included a combination of Osprey aircraft and midair refueling tankers, the Military Air Tracking Alliance said.
The base also raised its alert level to FPCON Charlie — the second highest level — the organization said. That applies when an incident occurs or intelligence is received indicating that some form of terrorist action targeting personnel or facilities is likely. There was no immediate confirmation from the Pentagon.
The decision to move the aircraft was proactive rather than reactive, a U.S. official said, adding that the U.S. military is agile to potential threats. Some of the planes that left were in transit while others were permanently stationed at RAF Mildenhall and they may return, the official said. The official didn't elaborate on the nature and source of the threat.
An official from the U.S. Air Force in Europe told the AP that the U.S. is “taking coordinated and appropriate actions" to ensure the safety and security of U.S. and U.K. personnel and their families. The official said that aircraft are rotated between bases for various reasons, including training and “real world requirements.”
The official said that the U.S. military constantly assesses a variety of factors that determine what security measures are implemented. The official wouldn't provide further information on movement of assets or specific force protection for reasons of operational security.
Both officials spoke on condition of anonymity, because they weren't authorized to speak publicly about sensitive military matters.
The U.K. prime minister's office said that British air bases are safe and their security is a top priority. The office said that the U.K. is in constant communication with the U.S., sharing intelligence and assessing threats together.
RAF Mildenhall, a U.K. base operated by the U.S. Air Force, hosts the 100th refueling wing, the only permanent refueling wing in the European region. It operates the KC-135 Stratotanker, a four-engine jet aircraft with a wingspan of 131 feet (40 meters) that can carry up to 83,000 pounds (nearly 38,000 kilograms) of cargo.
Five men were detained on Sept. 27 after three suspicious vans were spotted traveling toward RAF Fairford. The U.K.-owned base has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East, including the Iran war.
Other arrests followed and two men have been charged under the National Security Act.
The U.K. Defense Ministry said in a statement that it doesn’t comment on the activity of other nations and said aircraft and other assets move regularly according to operational requirements.
___
Konstantin Toropin reported from Washington.

title: Hegseth slams his potential impeachment as a ‘political spectacle’ that undermines US troops
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The House on Tuesday turned aside a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, halting an effort to remove the Pentagon chief for his conduct in office and his handling of the war in Iran.
The vote came as Republicans grapple with the fallout from sweeping midterm losses that some in the party have blamed on the war in Iran and the resulting surge in gas prices. But after President Donald Trump signaled strong support for Hegseth, GOP lawmakers largely stood by the secretary Tuesday, blocking the effort in a near party-line vote.
The effort was led by Kentucky Republican Rep. Thomas Massie and backed by Democrats. The vote Tuesday may only delay an impeachment push against Hegseth, with Democrats set to take control of the House and Senate in January.
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become the next speaker when Democrats take charge in January, stood firmly behind the push, saying Hegseth has “abused his power” and “undermined America’s national security.”
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer endorsed Hegseth’s impeachment as well.
Hegseth rebuked the effort Tuesday in his first news conference in months, portraying Massie as a rogue lawmaker and arguing he had committed none of the high crimes required in the Constitution for his removal. He framed the effort as an indictment against the nation’s service members and their successes and said it was undermining American forces “in real time.”
“This is not patriotism,” Hegseth said. “This is sabotage.”
Massie’s resolution included eight counts of impeachment. It largely focused on the war in Iran but also included references to Hegseth’s role in carrying out military actions in Yemen and Venezuela.
Massie, a Kentucky Republican leaving Congress in January after losing his primary to a Trump-backed opponent, says Hegseth has “knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders.”
Hegseth holds rare press conference
Trump praised Hegseth’s performance at the briefing in a social media post, while Vice President JD Vance said in his own post that the impeachment effort is “a ridiculous show that stands in for actual policymaking.”
Trump celebrated the House vote later Tuesday, saying on social media that it was the exoneration of “a Great American Patriot.”
Impeachment effort falls short
Massie filed the resolution in the House on Monday as lawmakers returned to Washington. Tuesday’s vote was a procedural attempt to stop the impeachment push outright by sending the matter back to committee. The motion succeeded 211-204, with a number of Democrats missing the vote.
Massie’s resolution had eight counts of impeachment that focused on U.S. military actions or changes on Hegseth’s watch. They include reported reductions in staff and resources at a Pentagon office focused on mitigating civilian harm, which preceded a U.S. missile striking an Iranian primary school during the war, killing up to 168 people.
“The law requires our military to withdraw from hostilities within 60 days if Congress does not authorize the activity,” Massie wrote on social media Tuesday. The Iran war “has been underway for 256 days. Congress has not authorized it. Hegseth is breaking the law.”
Another article of impeachment focused on Hegseth’s attempt to punish Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly, a retired Navy pilot, for participating in a video that called on troops to resist unlawful orders. Massie also called out U.S. military strikes on alleged drug-smuggling boats in Latin America and the failure to rescue survivors, which Massie argued will encourage adversaries to treat American forces the same way.
What constitutes “high crimes and misdemeanors” is not spelled out in the Constitution, leaving it to lawmakers to decide what are impeachable acts.
House Speaker Mike Johnson called it a “political gambit for attention” and predicted Republicans would defeat it “one way or the other.”
Some Republicans were critical of Hegseth in the run-up to the vote, but said they didn’t believe he had committed impeachable offenses. Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon, a Republican who is retiring after this year, said he didn’t agree with the “merit” of the impeachment although he is “critical of the secretary.”
“I have a lot of other things I thought were failures by the secretary,” Bacon said. “We control the agenda. We should be doing hearings.”
This isn’t the first impeachment attempt in recent years
Hegseth cast Massie’s resolution in historic terms, arguing that no defense secretary has been impeached in the nation’s 250-year history “for carrying out lawful military operations.”
But more recently, a Cabinet official in President Joe Biden’s administration, Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas, was impeached by House Republicans over his handling of the U.S.-Mexico border. The Senate dismissed all impeachment charges, shutting down his trial before arguments even began.
Trump offers support for Hegseth
Trump backed Hegseth in the wake of Massie’s impeachment resolution, pointing to the U.S. military raid to capture then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January as well as operations against Iran that he asserts have “obliterated” its navy and air force.
___
Associated Press writer Steve Peoples in New York and Lisa Mascaro in Washington contributed to this report.

title: Trump '100%' backs bill to make data centers pay more, potentially lowering electricity costs
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Trump '100%' backs bill to make data centers pay more, potentially lowering electricity costs
President Trump says the White House is "100% behind" a bipartisan bill that could reduce electricity bills by requiring data centers to pay more for energy infrastructure.
Trump '100%' backs bill to make data centers pay more, potentially lowering electricity costs
President Trump says the White House is "100% behind" a bipartisan bill that could reduce electricity bills by requiring data centers to pay more for energy infrastructure.
President Donald Trump said Monday he is fully behind bipartisan legislation that could lower Americans' electricity bills by requiring large data centers to shoulder more of the costs of expanding the nation's electrical grid.
"We are behind it 100%," Trump told reporters when asked about the legislation.
Congress is considering the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act as electricity demand grows rapidly across the country, driven in part by the explosion of artificial intelligence and data centers.
The legislation would speed up federal approval of energy infrastructure projects while requiring large data centers to contribute more toward the costs of expanding the electrical grid.
An analysis by Grid Strategies estimates that, under the legislation, data centers would pay an additional $35 billion toward transmission infrastructure over the next decade, compared with what they would otherwise pay under current policies.
A separate analysis from Rhodium Group estimates the bill could save the average American household between $50 and $78 a year on electricity by 2040, compared with what households would otherwise pay without the legislation.
Both analyses examined an earlier version of the bill, before lawmakers released amendments Saturday. The savings are projections, not guaranteed reductions from today's electricity bills.
"This bill has specific provisions related to data centers where they pay more. In fact, they pay more than their fair share. Intentionally to enable them to pay for more of the grid and then other rate payers, you and me. And homes and businesses. We would all pay relatively less," said Rob Gramlich, president of Grid Strategies.
How the legislation would work
Energy experts say the country faces an infrastructure bottleneck as electricity demand grows. Building the power plants and transmission lines needed to keep up can take years, with federal permitting among the obstacles.
The legislation aims to speed up that process by setting stricter deadlines for environmental reviews and making it easier to approve new transmission lines.
It would also give states additional options to require data centers to pay more than the cost of serving them and use the additional revenue to reduce electricity costs for other customers.
States including Virginia, Ohio and Florida have already approved special electricity rate structures designed to make large power users shoulder more of the infrastructure costs associated with serving them.
Why the bill faces opposition
The legislation would also make it easier to approve fossil fuel projects, drawing opposition from environmental groups. Critics warn it could weaken federal safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge new projects.
The bill was negotiated by four senators: Republicans Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah, and Democrats Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island.
The four lawmakers released amendments Saturday aimed at addressing some of those concerns, including strengthening consultation with Native American tribes and giving states more opportunities to weigh in on proposed projects.
Major industry groups representing renewable energy developers and oil and gas companies support the legislation.
The bill also includes a provision that Whitehouse says would prevent the Trump administration from continuing to pay offshore wind developers to abandon their projects. The administration has spent nearly $4 billion on such settlements, according to the Associated Press.
Despite endorsing the legislation, Trump continued criticizing wind energy Monday, telling reporters that "wind turbines are a major loser."
Will Congress pass it?
The bill's future remains uncertain despite bipartisan support and the president's endorsement.
Some Democrats helped write the legislation and want it passed now, while others, including House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, are pushing for changes. Jeffries' office said last week that the legislation "falls short" in several areas.
The debate comes just days after Democrats won control of Congress, giving them more leverage to negotiate energy legislation when the new Congress takes office in January.
The Senate scheduled a procedural vote for Monday evening on whether to advance a legislative vehicle for the permitting proposal. The vote requires 60 senators to move forward and would not constitute final passage of the legislation.

title: Republicans leave closed-door meeting without a decision on whether to reelect John Thune as leader
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Senate Republicans were meeting for a second time Tuesday as they decide whether to delay elections for Republican leadership. South Dakota Sen. John Thune is seeking to keep his post as Republican leader just a week after steep losses in the midterm elections that cost them their majority.
Thune is expected to eventually win, given that he remains popular with his GOP colleagues and is so far running unopposed in the secret ballot election. But senators left the closed-door meeting after two hours of discussions Tuesday morning with no resolution on a way forward after an election wipeout that cost them at least seven Senate seats.
As they reconvened Tuesday afternoon, Republican senators were divided on whether a delay of anywhere from a week to a month would be productive. Votes were expected on whether to postpone.
“We want to be thoughtful and do the right thing,” said West Virginia Sen. Jim Justice as the meeting broke up. He said no obvious alternative had emerged, but “there is a legitimate argument that, good gracious, if we lost as badly as we lost, why would we continue on with the same leadership?”
At the same time, the current GOP leadership “didn’t cause this problem to happen,” Justice said. “They do a good job.”
The angst comes as frustrated Republicans are just beginning to reckon with what the election results mean for their future. Two additional Senate races remain uncalled in Alaska and Mississippi that could further deplete their numbers.
Several senators had already called on the Republican leadership to delay the elections, which include contests for other party leaders as well and are held in the small Old Senate Chamber.
Missouri Sen. Josh Hawley said he isn’t aware of anyone else running for leader, but “maybe there would be” if they waited.
“I just think that we’ve got a lot of things that we’ve got to think through, and I think that to just rush into this and just ratify all of the same leadership, what message does that send?” Hawley told reporters after walking out.
“If you don’t think after losing seven Senate seats minimum that we need to change course, I don’t know what planet you’re on,” he said.
Thune, who replaced Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky as leader in early 2025, said before the meeting that they would have a “very fulsome, robust conversation about where we go from here and then we’ll see what the consensus of the conference is.”
No alternative to Thune has emerged
Thune has not yet made his case for leadership, senators emerging from the meeting said, and has instead been listening to his colleagues’ concerns. Hawley said the discussion was a “frank” and “honest” open- microphone meeting and some senators discussed their own races this year — some who won, and some who lost.
Republicans in the meeting were also pushing Thune to stay in session around the clock in the coming weeks to push through war spending and other party priorities before they lose power.
“We need a plan to get the Republican agenda done,” said Florida Sen. Rick Scott.
Before the meeting, Wisconsin Sen. Ron Johnson had circulated a letter asking for the delay. He said the conference needs to do some “real soul-searching” but conceded that there’s no one else on the ballot.
“That’s part of our problem, who would want the job?” he said, turning to a reporter and joking, “Do you want it?”
Oklahoma Sen. Jim Lankford said that there is “widespread support” among Republican senators for Thune, who has made it a point to hear out different viewpoints before he makes major decisions and has maintained close relationships with the rank and file — a different approach from his predecessor, McConnell.
Lankford said he supported having the elections on Tuesday because many of the new GOP senators are already in town for freshman orientation.
“It’s a pretty complicated role to be able to manage,” Lankford said of Thune’s leadership post. “No one wants that job.”
Walking into the meeting, South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds said most senators are ready to move forward. It is time to have “leadership in place,” he said.
Thune has navigated Trump in his first two years as leader
Thune has spent much of the last two years navigating President Donald Trump, who has often been at odds with the Senate.
While backing up Trump on most policy, Thune has refused to change Senate rules and scrap the filibuster to pass voting legislation that would require proof of citizenship for all voters — a position that frustrated Trump and enraged some in the president’s political base.
But Trump hosted Thune and his family at the White House in October. He said Monday that the GOP leader is “a very fine man.” The election is “up to the Senate,” Trump said.
The soul-searching comes as lawmakers are trying to wrap up the year’s work — funding the government and seeing if there are some issues where they can work together, including an energy permitting bill that moved forward on a bipartisan vote Monday evening.
When he gets the chance to speak at the meeting, Thune is expected to emphasize his collaborative approach to his colleagues and point out what they did get done in the last year — including the tax and spending cuts legislation and an attempt at reining in the chaotic annual spending process.
In a Senate floor speech Monday, his first extended remarks since the election, Thune said the midterm election was a “tough night” and previewed his pitch to his colleagues who may be looking for answers on how they will navigate the minority.
Republicans will be willing to work with Democrats, Thune said, but “the American people are not looking for socialist government and leftist fantasies.”
Despite gains, Democrats are having similar conversations
Across the aisle, Democrats who could hold as many as 56 seats next year are having private discussions about whether New York Sen. Chuck Schumer is still the right person to lead them.
Schumer has found critics on the left and the right of his caucus as candidates from both sides declined to say in the campaign whether they would support him as leader. Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen and Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin have both considered challenging Schumer, but neither has announced a run.
Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, Schumer’s New York colleague and the head of the Democratic Senate campaign arm, predicted that he will win enough support. Schumer not only won the Senate back but he “cares deeply, and he understands politics well,” she said.
___
Associated Press reporter Seung Min Kim contributed to this report.

title: Family remembers Bangor woman known as ‘Ma’ after fatal house fire
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Loved ones of 80-year-old Kathleen Mackie are remembering her generosity and working to keep her legacy alive after a fire at her Bangor home on Oct. 14.
The Medical Examiner’s Office has not yet officially identified Mackie, but her loved ones say she died in the fire at the home on the corner of Cedar and Second streets. Known to many as Kathy, she was called “Ma” by people she helped care for and raise.
“She was truly an angel walking among the rest of us,” a loved one said. “The world knew her as Kathy, but to those of us she helped care for and helped raise she will forever be called ‘Ma.’”
Remembering ‘Ma’
Family members say Mackie opened her home and heart to people who needed support.
“She was one of the most caring souls I’ve ever met,” said her daughter, Jessica Martin. “Never met a person that she wasn’t willing to take in, especially if they didn’t have family.”
Rachelle, who became part of the family and built a sisterhood with Jessica, recalled being welcomed into Mackie’s home.
“She brought me back to her house, and Ma said that I could stay,” Rachelle said.
Benefit supper planned
The family is hosting a benefit supper and silent auction on Friday, Nov. 13, from 6 to 8 p.m. at the Hilton Garden Inn in Bangor. Rachelle says all proceeds will go to family members directly affected by the fire. Two couples were living with Mackie at the time of the fire, she said.
The family is also awaiting Mackie’s remains and says a backlog at the Medical Examiner’s Office has delayed funeral planning.
As loved ones mourn, they hope to carry Mackie’s love for the community forward.
“Nothing is promised, so just if I had one word of advice for everyone out there, live your life like it’s going to be your last, live it to the fullest extent that you can,” Krishauna Boucher said.
Support the family: A GoFundMe and additional information are available through the family’s fundraiser.

title: CD-2 ranked-choice tabulation continues, triggers pause in Ellsworth City Council recount
text:
STATEWIDE/ELLLSWORTH -- The ranked-choice voting tabulation for the Congressional District Two race continued Tuesday in Augusta.
It got Monday morning underway. Staff there worked all day Tuesday. We're told they have gotten through all the write-in ballots.
Secretary of State Shenna Bellows has predicted that they will know official results by the end of the week.
Meanwhile, the city of Ellsworth is rescheduling its recount of results for a close city council race.
The city said in a post on its website that since the state is currently conducting a ranked-choice tabulation of the CD-2 race, the state has taken custody of the state election ballots.
The city says they'd need to review those ballots as part of their own recount. They say the candidate who requested the recount has asked the city to wait until the CD-2 ranked-choice tabulation is complete and state ballots have been returned to Ellsworth before they proceed with the city council recount.
A date for the recount has not been established. Multiple people were vying for two open seats on the council.

title: InvestigateTV+: Vanishing wetlands threaten haven for migrating birds
text:
(InvestigateTV) — InvestigateTV+ takes you to the mouth of the Mississippi River for an in-depth look at the multi-million-dollar fight to save a disappearing coastline.
Plus, a surgical nightmare that left one Georgia mother fighting for her life, and the questions her case raises about medical accountability.
Then, the inspiring story of an artist creating miniature wonders that bring big joy.
A threatened migration
In the winter months, birds journey down the Mississippi Flyway, a migratory superhighway for more than 300 species. Annual surveys estimate 3 million snow geese choose Louisiana and Texas for their wintertime retreats.
Yet no place on the continental U.S. loses wetlands at the rate Louisiana is shedding its coast.
Robotic surgery leads to lawsuit
An Atlanta mother checked into the hospital for a hysterectomy, expecting to be home from that same day. Instead, she didn’t leave for nearly three months.
Star Button had persistent pain and excessive bleeding for years. The chronic issues interrupted every part of her life, including work.
Doctors confirmed the issues stemmed from fibroids, or noncancerous tumors. To get rid of them, Button opted for a robotic hysterectomy at Southern Regional Medical Center.
Side hustle apps
Apps that let people rent out things they already own are offering users a way to earn extra cash without taking on an in-person part-time job.
Instead of signing up to drive for a rideshare service or deliver groceries, some people are turning to rental platforms that allow them to make money on their own schedule by listing items they already have at home.
Hand-painted seashells
An ordained minister, Gil Ames has not let anything get in the way of his passion for painting. He volunteered with the Red Cross at 52 national disasters, including ground zero in New York.
He also spent 25 years as a long-haul truck driver. He pivoted to something more portable to paint on during that time.
